title: What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why? | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Offences including manslaughter have been excluded from changes to sentencing rules amid an overcrowding crisis
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Offences including manslaughter have been excluded from changes to sentencing rules amid an overcrowding crisis
Content: HMP Wandsworth in London. The government has said adult male prisons are at 98% capacity.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHMP Wandsworth in London. The government has said adult male prisons are at 98% capacity.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationExplainerWhat is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?Offences including manslaughter have been excluded from changes to sentencing rules amid an overcrowding crisisJamie GriersonSun 30 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrooming gang perpetrators and killers, including thoseresponsible for PC Andrew Harper’s death, will be blocked from early prison release under changes announced by Andy Burnham after a backlash over the scope of the scheme.Here is a primer on how the crisis unfolded and what the upshot of Burnham’s decision could be.What is happening to prison sentences?From 1 October 2026, a change to sentencing rules means some adults serving a standard prison sentence in England and Wales will be released earlier than the date originally planned,the Institute for Government explains.Prisoners convicted of less serious offences, who currently spend 40% or 50% of their sentence in prison, will leave prison after a third of their sentence. A second group, currently released after two-thirds of their sentence, will leave after half.Leaving prison does not end the sentence. The person serves the rest of their sentence in the community on licence, under conditions set by probation, and can be returned to prison if those conditions are breached.Murderers or people handed life or extended sentences have never been included in any proposals for reducing sentences and will stay locked up until they go before the Parole Board.Why is this happening?The Labour government says it inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse, with fewer than 100 spaces left in the summer of 2024. No 10 says a lack of investment in the prison estate, with just 500 net places added over a decade, has led to a situation where adult male prisons are now at 98% capacity. It says the steps are necessary while itbuilds capacity.Has this been controversial?Very. The controversy stemmed from who was set to be released. Initially, all adults serving a standard determinate sentence were to be released early, including those sentenced for serious violent and sexual offences. In early August, the government said the scheme would not apply to sentences for rape and serious child sex offences.There had been longstanding concern about those parts of the proposals, but the backlash intensified in late July and early August when it emerged that the killers of a police officer, PC Andrew Harper, who were sentenced for manslaughter, would be eligible for early release under the proposal.The issue presented the first real headache for Burnham, who was appointed as prime minister on 20 July.What has been proposed as a solution?On Sunday, two days before parliament’s return from recess,No 10 announcedthat sentences for unlawful killing would be blocked from the early release scheme. This means Harper’s killers, among many others, will not be eligible for early release.Historical grooming offences, any form of manslaughter, causing death by dangerous driving and causing or allowing the death of a child will also be barred from the changes to the prison sentences.What else has been proposed?Burnham also announced that he wouldend imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentencesduring this parliament, due to end in 2029. The IPP was introduced in 2005 and gave offenders a minimum jail tariff but no maximum. It was used much more widely than intended and many prisoners have languished in prison well beyond their minimum tariff, in some cases for less serious offences.No 10 said the move was to address an “injustice” but it is also likely to free up space in the creaking prison system. However, Downing Street has said it will take time.What will happen to those released early?Burnham said that to protect victims, the government would be introducing the “toughest ever” supervision measures for offenders, including tagging and, for the first time, putting restriction zones in place to stop offenders getting near their victims.What will be the impact on the prison overcrowding crisis?Prison reform campaigners are sceptical. Mike Trace, the chief executive of the Forward Trust, a social justice charity that supports people in recovery from addiction or leaving crime behind, said: “Today’s announcement delays rather than deals with the problem of prison overcrowding. By sticking with a policy of early rather than earned release, the PM will likely face many more instances like with the killers of PC Andrew Harper case where prisoners are being released when it is not safe to do so.“The only way to reduce prison numbers safely is to create a justice system that is genuinely rehabilitative. We urge the government to start doing the kind of things – like expanding access to rehabilitation services and creating an earned, early release scheme for prisoners committed to recovery – that shift us out of crisis management and build a system that protects, saves and improves lives.”Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “The prime minister has indicated that further changes will be made to the implementation of the Sentencing Act. Further direction should come on Tuesday, but we are concerned that the details announced so far will make it even harder to tackle the prison capacity crisis in the short term.“Prisons up and down the country have been under tremendous pressure in recent weeks and, with the start date of October fast approaching, it is crucial that they receive the clarity they need to ensure people leave custody with appropriate support.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceSentencingAndy BurnhamLabourexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Vigil review – this police thriller is twisty, explosive … and so boring | Television | The Guardian
description: Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie are back trying to stop a third world war in the Arctic. There’s plenty of action – but it’s hard to root for heroes whose biggest personality traits are ‘being nice’ and ‘wears good glasses’
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie are back trying to stop a third world war in the Arctic. There’s plenty of action – but it’s hard to root for heroes whose biggest personality traits are ‘being nice’ and ‘wears good glasses’
Content: Rose Leslie and Suranne Jones in Vigil.Photograph: BBC/World Productions/Mark MainzView image in fullscreenRose Leslie and Suranne Jones in Vigil.Photograph: BBC/World Productions/Mark MainzTV reviewTelevisionReviewVigil review – this police thriller is twisty, explosive … and so boringSuranne Jones and Rose Leslie are back trying to stop a third world war in the Arctic. There’s plenty of action – but it’s hard to root for heroes whose biggest personality traits are ‘being nice’ and ‘wears good glasses’Rachel AroestiSun 30 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 18.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike many a police procedural, Vigil always begins with a cold open. This time round, however, it’s absolutely freezing. We are, as per, thrown headlong into a niche and tangentially Scottish military world where a murder has occurred.The first seriestook place on board a nuclear submarine (the show is, confusingly, still named after the vessel), whilethe secondsplit the action between an army airfield in Scotland and the fictional Middle Eastern nation of Wudyan.For its third outing, we find ourselves in the (real) Arctic region of Svalbard. The area is supposedly demilitarised, but four British special forces agents are working undercover at a research centre, and tonight their mission is to extract a Chinese scientist who has made a discovery that could either save or destroy the world. En route, they’re ambushed by Russians who want whatever world-saving-or-destroying stuff she’s got. The scientist escapes – but one of the Brits later turns up dead in a Russian enclave.The action moves from (slightly less) snowcapped (than they used to be) mountains to the snuggly Glasgow bedroom of Vigil’s police protagonists: DCI Amy Silva (Suranne Jones) and her colleague and girlfriend DI Kirsten Longacre (Rose Leslie), who has spent the past year looking after the pair’s baby son, Fergal. As far as I can gather, Silva and Longacre are relatively run-of-the-mill detectives, yet Vigil relies on them being assigned to cases that could feasibly trigger a third world war on at least an annual basis. You know when people say returning to work after maternity leave feels like a nice break from relentless childcare? I don’t think that applies when your first day back involves flying nearly to the north pole to investigate a murder while ensuring the UK avoids an international incident with Russia. But at least Longacre gets some peace and quiet on the plane.Silva, to her slight chagrin, is ordered to stay on home turf. Little does she know that’s where the explosive drama is. It’s climate conference season and a Scottish scientist has flown back from Svalbard with suspicious haste for the occasion. Moments after Silva doorsteps him at his university, he is blown up by a bomb in his lab. As she enters, another man runs out – a climate activist with a rather convoluted grudge.In the Arctic, meanwhile, the violence is more psychological. In order to keep the peace, Svalbard’s Norwegian police chief must treat Russian and UK representatives with strict equality. That means the Russians are permitted to appoint their own detective, Col Zamorin, to the investigation. But is he friend or foe? And who will find the Chinese scientist and her mysterious grail first?View image in fullscreenFriend or foe? … Tornike Gogrichiani as Col Zamorin in Vigil.Photograph: Mark Mainz/BBC/World ProductionsVigil is, obviously, not your standard murder mystery – each series is set on the precipice of an alarmingly realistic geopolitical crisis. The second series revolved around the sale of British arms to the Middle East; this time themes include Russian expansionism, our age of trollish diplomacy and how the interests of the global energy industry trump concerns about the climate crisis (PS: we’re doomed). Playing out over this chaotic backdrop of current affairs is a stream of individual deceptions: pretty much every character is harbouring a major secret. Like a global Line of Duty, this is essentially a programme about not being able to trust a soul in the police, the intelligence services or the military. Far from being a guarantee against criminality, rank is probably a confirmation of it.Wanton complexity isn’t always a bad thing in a thriller, especially in the age of second screening-related simplicity. The problem is that Vigil’s twist-rate is too high for any revelation to effectively land. The levels of conspiracy are flummoxing and seemingly never-ending: just as one layer of lies has been peeled off, we’re confronted by another. The capacity to be surprised is stripped away in the process.If you can’t invest in the case, you need to be able to invest in the leads. Unfortunately, this is Vigil’s weakest link. Silva is essentially a blank slate: the closest thing she has to a personality trait is putting on and swiftly taking off a massive pair of reading glasses. Leslie assumes a very broad Glaswegian accent to play Longacre, whose defining characteristic is that she’s … quite nice? Not to suggest Silva isn’t also quite nice – she is! The pair’s working relationship is not impeded by their romantic one, either. They are both too sensible and professional for their (mild) domestic friction to tip over into popcorn-crunching drama.Instead, what we’re left with is a mystery designed to wrongfoot the viewer to a tedious degree, which plays out over a backdrop of urgent real-world jeopardy. Unfortunately, those two things end up cancelling each other out. Vigil makes it hard to keep caring, even when it’s the planet’s future that is at stake.Vigil is on BBC One and iPlayer in the UK and SBS and SBS on Demand in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing | Far right (US) | The Guardian
description: ‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: ‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APFar right (US)‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for ReformHelena HortonSun 30 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump administration, the far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos may be wondering what lies ahead for him in his native country.The “alt-right” agitator, 41, made his name in the US by promoting Donald Trump and associating with his allies before the 2016 election.But now the Trump administration has unceremoniously dumped the former Breitbart News editorback in the UKafter he allegedly overstayed his visa. He has also made plenty of disparaging comments about the president, including that he is “firmly off the Trump train”.Those in the rightwing ecosystem in the UK say Yiannopoulos is now too extreme to find a prominent berth back home.The commentator started his career at the Daily Telegraph, where he wrote a controversial blog until 2011, when he started his own website, the Kernel. In 2014 he started working for the former Trump adviser Steve Bannon at Breitbart News, before moving to the US and promoting far-right causes.He left Breitbart after a controversy over a video in which he appeared tocondone sexual relationswith boys as young as 13. He later said “sloppy editing” and his “British sarcasm, provocation and gallows humour” had created the wrong impression and denied endorsing paedophilia.Since he left the UK,GB Newshas become the ascendant broadcast outlet of the right, but he is unlikely to find a place there. A source at the channel said: “We wouldn’t touch him with a barge pole, not in a million years. GBN had a few odd people to start with and we’ve got rid of them.”Yiannopoulos after his arrest by federal immigration agents in New Orleans.Photograph: Department of Homeland Security/ReutersOf the provocative positions that brought him notoriety in the US, the GB News source said: “He won’t make much money out of it here, he appeals entirely to an American audience. It’s a bigger country and you have a bigger pool of fruit loops.”There is a growing subsection of rightwing provocateurs in the UK who have been deemed too controversial for the main channels but have established niche brands of their own. The journalist Dan Woottonwas suspended from GB Newsafter a guest on his show made sexually inappropriate comments about a female journalist, andafter leavinghe now has his own channel.The former TalkTV host Mike Graham has also set up his own independent show. He wassackedafter the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on one of his social media accounts. Graham said the racist comment had been the result of his account being hacked.It is understood thatReform UKwill not accept him into its ranks. His former colleague at Breitbart, Raheem Kassam, is close to the party’s leader, Nigel Farage, and is in the UK for Reform’s national conference.Kassam, who is British but now lives in the US, claimed he was kept updated on the deportation of Yiannopoulos, who he accused of making “lurid and false accusations” against him.He added: “I got word last month that he was about to be deported. On Thursday night, I got a call. As overly dramatic as it may seem. ‘We got him. In Louisiana.’”The Maga influencer Laura Loomer has claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to immigration enforcement over his expired visa.View image in fullscreenLaura Loomer (front, centre) celebrates with Yiannopoulos at a congressional primary election night event in West Palm Beach, Florida, in August 2020.Photograph: Allen Eyestone/APOne political party that may accept Yiannopoulos isRestore Britain, which is led by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP who had a falling-out with Farage.Restore has accepted a number of characters viewed as too extreme for Reform, including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson.Yiannopoulos has praised Lowe, calling him “fantastic” and urging those on the UK hard-right to join Restore. He said “the rising generation of young British activists” all “support Restore” and has taunted Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, online, telling him “you’re gonna lose all your votes to Rupert”. The Guardian contacted Lowe to ask whether he would accept Yiannopoulos as a party member or adviser but did not receive a response.Kassam said: “He’s certain to resurface in Britain shortly. Perhaps as an adviser to Rupert Lowe, or perhaps as a contestant on some third-tier reality TV show.”Yiannopoulos used to have more political influence; he was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.He was deported to the UK on Friday, according to US authorities. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.In 2022, Yiannopoulosworked onKanye West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working one of the rapper’s companies.Last year, Yiannopoulossaidhe was “never going back home” because the UK needed a “mass deportation programme”.Yiannopoulos was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFar right (US)US immigrationFar rightGB NewsReform UKRestore BritainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He says he feels pride about being English, but I don’t’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A retired software engineer and a planetary scientist disagreed about putting up flags and nationalising private companies, but were they worlds apart on legalising drugs?
Author: Erica Buist
Headline: A retired software engineer and a planetary scientist disagreed about putting up flags and nationalising private companies, but were they worlds apart on legalising drugs?
Content: Finley (left) and Gavin. All photographs: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFinley (left) and Gavin. All photographs: Sarah Lee/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘He says he feels pride about being English, but I don’t’A retired software engineer and a planetary scientist disagreed about putting up flags and nationalising private companies, but were they worlds apart on legalising drugs?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howErica BuistSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinley, 23, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationPlanetary scientistVoting recordLabour before the last election, where he voted Green, and will stick to Green “if Andy Burnham goes ahead with North Sea oil drilling”Amuse boucheDuring university, he worked on a project with Nasa on Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons. He loved it so much he got a tattoo of Europa on his right shoulderGavin, 54, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationRetired software engineerVoting recordTory “out of habit and upbringing” until Brexit; ever since then, Lib Dem and sometimes GreenAmuse boucheHe and his wife went on holiday to Australia in 2003 and met the actor Rob Lowe at their hotel, but had never seen him in anything so didn’t recognise him. When they later asked for a photo, his “jokey condition” was that they watch The West Wing when they got homeFor startersGavinWe got on very well. I wouldn’t normally go to a vegan restaurant, but my daughter is vegan and I’ve told her she should go there.FinleyIt was extremely enjoyable – my nerves melted away quickly. The food was fantastic, and Gavin and I got along better than I expected.GavinI started with roti with three sauces. Then I had chickpea curry with greens, and a beer. It was all very nice.FinleyI started with amazing deep-fried dumplings. Then I had plant-based fish with coconut, lentils and braised tomatoes, and some pineapple and kimchi pholourie, which were almost like pakoras. Fantastic.View image in fullscreenThe big beefGavinI don’t think the state should try to compete with the open market; the open market is always going to be cheaper, as they will always try to reduce costs.Dining across the divide: ‘At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you seem quite privileged”’Read moreFinleyIf you give power to the state to control, for example, utility companies, the service will be provided for the constituents’ benefit, not the shareholders’ benefit.GavinWe did talk about Thames Water. I think in the case of utilities, state-run companies actually could do a better job than the free market – but they will also be somewhat hamstrung by unions.FinleyWe talked about how privatisation essentially ruined a lot of utility companies, because there was no motivation for the shareholders to provide a good service. They just want profits, which is why the CEOs at water companies have been reporting record-high wages as the service worsens.View image in fullscreenSharing plateGavinI would be in favour of legalising drugs. The tax could provide another revenue stream for the government – plus, it takes away the incentive for crime. I think people should be allowed to do whatever they want as long as they don’t hurt anyone else.FinleyI think if we decriminalise drugs and treat addiction like a healthcare problem, the symptoms suffered by wider society will also be treated – as we’ve seen in Portugal. Instead of spending millions on drug policing, spend it on rehabilitation and healthcare programmes that will target the issue in a more humane manner.View image in fullscreenFor aftersGavinI don’t find flags hung from lamp-posts intimidating – a lot of flags give a positive message, such as the Ukraine flag when the war started, LGBTQ flags – but context matters. During the World Cup, when I saw St George’s flags, I’m annoyed that I had to stop and think: “Wait, what does that mean?” because the England flag has been purloined by the far right.FinleyWhen you’re putting flags in a public place where communities are diverse, it has the connotation of division. Gavin says he feels some pride about being English, but I don’t. There seems to be something about Englishness that’s violent and divisive. I don’t really want to see the English flag wherever I go – even during the World Cup, knowing domestic abuse rates go up when England lose.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysGavinFinley gave me hope. I think part of the problem with politics is it pushes people into pigeonholes: left wing or right wing. And actually, if you have a proper conversation, you realise everyone wants broadly the same thing.FinleyI think people from older generations need to be more optimistic. If we lean in to cynicism, nothing will get done. But Gavin was also really climate positive, and that was so refreshing to hear. I think this type of conversation should be had more often, and food is a fantastic way to facilitate that.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeGavin and Finley ate atJam Delishin London.Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Love Cheats review – one romance scam is so hideous that a woman takes it to parliament  | Culture | The Guardian
description: From a man with triple lives to fake family deaths, the lies told by seemingly devoted partners in this series are shocking. But this is more than true crime entertainment – it is an enraged warning for other victims
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: From a man with triple lives to fake family deaths, the lies told by seemingly devoted partners in this series are shocking. But this is more than true crime entertainment – it is an enraged warning for other victims
Content: Stark, shocking … DJ Liv Nervo and sister Mim in season two of Love Cheats.Photograph: FotoFotoFoto/Angel EyeView image in fullscreenStark, shocking … DJ Liv Nervo and sister Mim in season two of Love Cheats.Photograph: FotoFotoFoto/Angel EyeTV reviewCultureReviewLove Cheats review – one romance scam is so hideous that a woman takes it to parliamentFrom a man with triple lives to fake family deaths, the lies told by seemingly devoted partners in this series are shocking. But this is more than true crime entertainment – it is an enraged warning for other victimsHannah J DaviesSun 30 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmodel turned DJ, Liv Nervo had forged an enviable career travelling the world with her sister and musical collaborator, Mim. Old cliches about being a strong, independent woman and not needing a man aside, it’s clear that Liv already had a fantastic life before she met her former partner, Matthew. A successful businessman, their paths first crossed when she played a private party on Richard Branson’s Necker Island. “I thought I had found the best guy in the world,” she says. “But it was all a lie.”So begins the second series of Love Cheats, a stark and shocking true-crime show about people who think they’ve found the love of their life but are instead being pulled into audacious romance scams. Series one featured a fraudster impersonating a member of the nobility while leaving their victims to foot the bill for their lavish life, and another faking terminal cancer. Series two keeps the bar for grim deception high, beginning with Liv’s whirlwind romance with Matthew, who was desperate to have a family with her. Mim was equally taken in by her sister’s devoted new partner, who had made his fortune selling honey but wasn’t a fusty corporate type. “[Liv] used to date men with a briefcase,” she clarifies. “I wouldneverdate a man with a briefcase!”What’s intriguing about Liv’s case is that Matthewwasactually wealthy, and his stories of business success and a billionaire mother back in New Zealand were true. Everything else, though, was fiction. Once Liv was pregnant, he became angry and withdrawn, and even skipped a gender-reveal party in Liv’s native Australia. So concerned was her mother, Flaviana, that she hired a private investigator to trail him. It’s hardly a spoiler to say that what was found – and how Liv used the information to inform her own investigation – was not very good.Somehow – despite being heavily pregnant and finding out some of the worst news she could have imagined about the baby’s father – she had the wherewithal to record Matthew on her phone as she confronted him, and the audio is wild. He wasn’t leading a double life, Liv explains, “it was a triple life … I felt totally violated – mind, body and soul”. She feels she was deceived into having a child without knowing all of the facts, leading to questions around informed consent.Easily the series’ most notable case, it’s probably not a coincidence that the producers chose to put Liv’s story at the start. As well as pursuing legal action against Matthew, she has since become an outspoken voice against reproductive coercion, working alongside the Good Law Project. There’s footage of Labour MP Natalie Fleet raising the issue in parliament, mentioning Liv by name. It is interesting and enraging, but it is also bigger than Love Cheats the series, and it feels as if we only scratch the surface when it comes to Liv’s activism.Elsewhere, there’s Fiona Mulkerrins-Dixon from Exeter, who was taken in by the lies told by former partner Ben Millin. (Among them: a dead father who was actually alive, a dead sister who had never existed, and a heart condition that could kill him at any moment). Millin was in fact perpetrating what DC Claire Morgan of Avon and Somerset police describes as “a massive web of lies and deceit” that saw him extract huge amounts of money from different women. It’s less high-profile than Liv’s case, but no less terrifying – not least when Fiona thinks that an incommunicado Ben must be in a ditch somewhere, only to find out that he is in prison.Love Cheats rarely elevates the true crime genre. As is in vogue in 2026, there’s some shaky use of AI here, too – uncanny valley face renderings and homes that look as if they’re made of Lego. It does, however, give a voice to people who are desperate to tell their stories – partly as catharsis, but also to warn others about how easy it is to be conned by people who aren’t so much love cheats as life cheats.In Fiona’s case, Ben was convicted of fraud, and sentenced to 34 months in prison but served just five. It was so much more than just financial crime, she says, and something that will “sit with me for ever”. Natalie, who was conned by her former partner Stewart, says: “How do you trust people? How do you let people in? How do you move on?” Michelle, swindled by the same man, had some of her debts wiped but is still repaying more than £6,000. Sure, this is primarily intended as entertainment, but if it can also stop these grifters – or others – in their tracks, then it will also have done a multitude of good.Love Cheats is available on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsCultureTV reviewChannel 4DocumentaryFactual TVTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’
Content: HMP Wormwood Scrubs in London. Offenders guilty of manslaughter, rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will not be eligible for early release.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHMP Wormwood Scrubs in London. Offenders guilty of manslaughter, rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will not be eligible for early release.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationPrisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release schemeCritics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 14.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention byAndy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were each jailed for 13 years over the killing of PC Harper, had been eligible for early release under the Sentencing Act until Burnham’s intervention.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PASpeaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?Read moreHarper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force,said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, butgovernment figuressuggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a reviewled by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for18% of those in prison.“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accusedLabourof avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationAndy BurnhamLabourUK criminal justiceCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Relatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the dead
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Relatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the dead
Content: A Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianNepal-Tibet flood disasterDevastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homesRelatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the deadHannah Ellis-Petersenin DevighatSun 30 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys ofNepaland Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.Satellite image of Nepal showing location of DevighatDNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.Residents try to salvage belongings from their damaged homesIn an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.View image in fullscreenPeople searching for their belongings in their mud-damaged home in Devighat.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianEven in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnelRead moreThose who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.View image in fullscreenPeople in Devighat salvage what possessions they can from their damaged homes.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.View image in fullscreenMany returned to Devighat to pack up their belongings before leaving, never to return.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianIn the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsiaFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: US says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forces
Content: The islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). The strikes were the first known American attacks since July.Photograph: Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). The strikes were the first known American attacks since July.Photograph: Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranUS strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in JordanUS says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forcesAgenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island,” a US official said on Sunday. “Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and ​would be met with a “response ‌and punishment” from ‌Tehran, Iranian state media reported.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreIn response, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.A spokesperson said the US would pay for the attack economically and militarily, according to the semi-official news agency Fars.Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US attack was ‌a drone strike.On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying that all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.The exchange of strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.The US said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway.Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening ​to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.The US andIsraelattacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now ⁠crossed its six-month mark.Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared“economic warfare” against Tehran.US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on ​Lebanon have killed thousands ​and displaced millions. Eighteen US service ​members have been killed in the conflict.The war has ​led to the ‌blockade of the ​strait of ​Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranIsraelStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: At least eight dead and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Authorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted for
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Authorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted for
Content: Survivors arrive onshore after being rescued from the capsized boat off Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSurvivors arrive onshore after being rescued from the capsized boat off Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.Photograph: ReutersCyprusAt least eight dead and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern CyprusAuthorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted forHelena Smithin Athens,Angelique Chrisafisand agenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least eight people have died and 18 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said.The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for.“Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish ​Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy ‌at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister.The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from footage of rescued passengers.Photograph: Reuters TV/ReutersThe port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people ⁠and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey.Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence.“We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian.Location mapHours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.”Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.Video footage from the scene showed people wearing life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel. When the ship capsized, passengers clung to its overturned hull.The Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation reported the boat was new and that when it began taking in water four miles from the coast, the captain had told the passengers to put on lifejackets.View image in fullscreenA rescue helicopter winches up a passenger.Photograph: Reuters TV/ReutersErhürman told CNN’s Turkish channel he was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life.He said: “The ship capsized. It has sunk in an area where the water is 514 metres deep. So far, we have reached 244 people.”Speaking from the crisis centre set ⁠up in the area, he said: “There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... We are extremely saddened. Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort.”A source close to Erhüman said the ferry was a popular means of travel between the mainland and the island for Turks working in northern Cyprus.“It’s much cheaper than the plane and only fakes a few hours. A lot of Turkish citizens use it to travel and see their families back home,” said one official requesting anonymity. “You could say that a lot of the passengers were poor. It’s all just so very sad.”Four coastguard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, local officials said.With Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsCyprusTurkeyWater transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayor | James Cleverly | The Guardian
description: Conservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Conservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’
Content: James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to stand for mayor of London.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenJames Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to stand for mayor of London.Photograph: James Manning/PAJames CleverlyCleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayorConservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJames Cleverly has pledged to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting that his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister.The former home and foreign secretary denied he had resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership.However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture war issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader.“I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor ofLondon, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio.“That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.”If he wins his party’s nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the last Tory candidate, Susan Hall. Shedrew criticismfor claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to getLondonback.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote.Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift and said he thought it unlikely the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said.Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to Cleverly’s2024 speechduring the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” Dilnot said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”View image in fullscreenSadiq Khan (centre) stacks shelves in a Sainsbury’s in London with Andy Burnham, the prime minister, and Pat McFadden, work and pensions secretary.Photograph: WPA/GettyProf Tony Travers, of the London School of Economics, said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” Travers said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe entrance of a Conservative big-hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan, who was first elected in 2016, will run for a fourth term, a question he has thus far avoided.AYouGov survey this monthfound that 56% of Londoners thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found that Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while other potential candidates in the Labour ranks include Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.“Andy Burnham just doesn’t get it,” he said. “He’s got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner.”Explore more on these topicsJames CleverlyMayoral electionsConservativesLocal governmentLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Nathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspension
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Nathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspension
Content: Nathan Cofnas said in a post on X he was grateful to Ghent’s rector ‘for allowing me to stay’.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixView image in fullscreenNathan Cofnas said in a post on X he was grateful to Ghent’s rector ‘for allowing me to stay’.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixJason ArdayJason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchNathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspensionChris OsuhSun 30 Aug 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProf Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.Cofnas, an American academic, wassuspendedfrom his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution earlier this month pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed that it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.The US ambassador toBelgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been controversial. In May, the university’s philosophy departmentalleged to the institution’s leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise”for his role researching “the future of liberalism” and that he had a “far-right agenda”.In July Cofnas accused Arday, a University of Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging also that there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August.View image in fullscreenJason Arday was found dead on 14 August. He was accused of plagiarism by Cofnas.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianWhite, aDonald Trump supporter, donor and fundraiser, had called Cofnas’s suspension “truly unacceptable”, calling earlier this month for De Sutter to rescind it immediately.On Friday, White wrote on his personal X account: “I just saved Belgium from a complete global media meltdown and well deserved spanking by @elonmusk and everyone by resolving the UGHENT Cofnas matter – quite quickly.”The previous night, Cofnas thanked White and the US state department for “defending American values” on X, adding: “It was beyond my imagination that such a person would take an interest in the fate of a postdoc. The Ambassador responded with great support which helped to bring about a just outcome.”Cofnas has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, and was reportedly among bloggersrecommended to the Palantir founder Peter Thielby a “race science” researcher.Cofnas has also hit out at Trump and Maga in his writing, while claiming the US president’s executive orders against diversity, equity and inclusion in the US were a “cause for celebration”.In a piece in April last year he said the Republican party had “degenerated into a low-IQ cult of personality”.Hitting out at Trump’s tariffs, he said the effect “will be to halt the American economic juggernaut, discredit the anti-woke movement, pave the way for a leftwing populist … [and] stop the right’s momentum in other countries”.In October, he wrote: “The right simply does not have the human capital to retake the institutions and run them effectively. The vast majority of intelligent, psychologically stable, and public-spirited Americans remain left and woke. The Trump administration’s war on universities, science, and data has only reinforced smart people’s identity as leftists.”Asked by the Guardian if he stood by previous criticisms of Trump and Maga, Cofnas said: “I voted for Trump three times and I am still a registered Republican. I strongly criticised some Maga policies, particularly tariffs. There are other Maga policies that I support, such as interventions on behalf of free speech.”Ghent University said it did “not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding this matter … ongoing preliminary disciplinary inquiries must be allowed to proceed calmly, independently and with full respect for the rights of all those involved”.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayBelgiumUniversitiesEuropeHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign
Content: Ontario premier Doug Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign near Grimsby, Ontario, after Trump’s order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersView image in fullscreenOntario premier Doug Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign near Grimsby, Ontario, after Trump’s order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersDonald TrumpCanada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalatesMeanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America signEdward HelmoreSun 30 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald TrumpandCanadacontinued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.0:54Ontario premier unveils Lake Ontario sign in response to Trump’s ‘Lake America’ order – videoWith talks to resolve the tradedispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.View image in fullscreenLake Ontario renamed as Lake America on US-facing Google Maps.Photograph: Google MapsLake Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or ​how the rest of the ‌world refers to the ‌lake”, Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names”.Google had done similarly in Trump’sexecutive orderfor the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Google Map users in the US fornow seethat body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery forwhich he has shown a penchant.He posted one such video of anarmy of Canada geesewith Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himselfkicking over a Lake Ontario signand replacing it with Lake America while he danced in hisdistinctive wayto a soundtrack of the Village People hitYMCA, which he hasincorporatedinto his public appearances for years.Across the US’s northern border, Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, replied with a two-stories-high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.He appeared on Sunday on the ABC News program This Week and remarked that Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming order was like “something out of Saturday Night Live,’” the famous NBC sketch comedy show.“No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford said. “It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.Trump on Sunday afternoon published a social media post declaring “Canada to be the worst”.“I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” Trump also wrote, referring to the ongoing US-Canada trade war.Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpCanadaAmericasUS politicsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Man killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tribute | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Robert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Robert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’
Content: Robert Guanco: ‘His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him,’ the church said.Photograph: gofundmeView image in fullscreenRobert Guanco: ‘His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him,’ the church said.Photograph: gofundmeWest SussexMan killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tributeRobert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’Harry CockburnSun 30 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 41-year-old manwho died after a large wooden sign fell at a Christian festival on Fridayhas been named as Robert Guanco, a pastor at a church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.A tribute from his church on Sunday described him as a respected pastor who was a “loving husband” and “a devoted and caring father”.Six other people were injured when the overhead sign fell at the Big Church festival (BCF) near Steyning in West Sussex, including four who were taken to hospital.Festivalgoers said they rushed to lift the heavy sign, which read “Everything’s Unmissable”, after it was blown over in the wind.Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne named Guanco, describing him as “our beloved brother, friend and pastor”, in a GoFundMe to help his family, who it said faced “unimaginable loss” following his death.It said: “Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love and his service to God will never be forgotten.”It added: “He was also a good friend, mentor and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers and encouragement, he touched many lives.“His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”View image in fullscreenOrganisers of the Big Church festival said they were ‘heartbroken’ by Guanco’s death.Photograph: BigchurchfestivalOrganisers of the BCF, billed as the UK’s biggest Christian festival, said they were “heartbroken” by Guanco’s death and cancelled the rest of the event.“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026, in which Pastor Robert Guanco tragically lost his life and others were injured,” they said in a statement.“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Particularly with the family, friends and church of Pastor Guanco as they process the immense grief of his loss.”They added: “We are working with the police, the Health and Safety Executive and others as they establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.”The festival opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday. The event, which includes worship, music and various performances, first took place in 2009.The archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” by the incident. “I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve,” she said. “I pray for those receiving treatment and the healthcare workers looking after them.“And I pray too for the other festivalgoers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.”Many people at the festival were first alerted to the tragedy when God TV announced that “due to unforeseen circumstances” the festival live stream had been paused.Sussex police’s Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said: “Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the man who died and all others who have been affected by this tragic incident.”He urged anyone among the “thousands of people” at the festival on Friday who had information or video footage to come forward.Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Previous advice stressed risks of sleeping in but about 90 minutes extra could prevent high blood pressure
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Previous advice stressed risks of sleeping in but about 90 minutes extra could prevent high blood pressure
Content: Weekend catch-up sleep is associated with a 6% reduction in the odds of hypertension.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWeekend catch-up sleep is associated with a 6% reduction in the odds of hypertension.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesSleep‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts sayPrevious advice stressed risks of sleeping in but about 90 minutes extra could prevent high blood pressureAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichSun 30 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor years, experts have stressed the risks of lie-ins, warning that catching up on missed sleep at the weekend can disrupt the body’s internal clock and trigger adverse health effects.Now analysis has produced a heartening caveat to that advice: if you do not overdo it, weekend lie-ins may be good for you, with an ideal benchmark of 1hr 27min extra in bed to protect against high blood pressure.Most experts still agree that setting a routine bedtime and wake-up time is key to maintaining good health. But a new study shows a modest amount of catch-up sleep – one to two hours extra – after a long week is associated with a lower prevalence of high blood pressure.Irregular sleep pattern raises risk of stroke and heart attack, study findsRead moreGlobally, more than 1.3 billion people have hypertension. They face a much higher risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and early death.While other ways to avoid high blood pressure remain crucial – such as staying active, maintaining a healthy weight and eating well – the study suggests people should no longer feel guilty about getting up late at the weekend, experts said.The research was presented in Munich at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology, the world’s largest heart conference.The study author, Dr Nawon Lee of Korea University in Seoul, said: “Not getting enough sleep puts extra stress on the body. It keeps the heart and blood vessels working harder and can increase blood pressure.“Getting some extra sleep on the weekend may give the body a chance to recover and reduce some of that stress.“People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend. If they have not been able to get enough sleep during the week, some extra sleep on the weekend may simply be the body’s way of recovering from that sleep loss.”The research looked at 40,000 adults in South Korea over a period of seven years. Weekend catch-up sleep was defined as the difference between weekend and weekday sleep duration.13 surprising reasons you’re always dog tired – and what to do about itRead moreOverall, weekend catch-up sleep was associated with a 6% reduction in the odds of hypertension.A slightly greater benefit was seen in people who were considered to be physically inactive. They were 6.9% less likely to have hypertension if they had a weekend lie-in.Analysis identified the 1hr 27min benchmark as the ideal amount of catch-up sleep, Lee said.
