Someone getting this amount of extra sleep would be 9% less likely to have high blood pressure.Not getting enough sleep is known to prevent blood pressure from falling at night, which raises the risk of developing high blood pressure.Experts have previously stressed the importance of having a regular bedtime and wake-up time and dismissed the idea that you can catch up on missed sleep at the weekend.However, while the new research showed that getting some catch-up sleep could boost heart health, getting too much could be harmful, Lee cautioned. For instance, people sneaking in more than four hours extra sleep at the weekend were at greater risk of hypertension.“I think moderate weekend catch-up sleep may have a protective effect because, in people who are sleep-deprived during the week, the benefit of compensating for insufficient sleep may outweigh the potential harm from having an irregular sleep schedule,” said Lee.We know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why?Read more“However, when weekend catch-up sleep becomes excessive, the degree of sleep irregularity and circadian disruption may increase, which could offset that benefit.”She added: “Keeping a regular sleep schedule is still important, but getting a moderate amount of catch-up sleep may be beneficial rather than something to feel bad about.”Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation, who was not involved with the research, said: “Many of us struggle to get enough sleep during the week due to work, family and social commitments, so it’s natural if we find ourselves enjoying a lie-in at the weekend in an effort to catch up on missed sleep.“This study is not a green light for physical activity to take a back seat, but for now, perhaps we don’t need to feel guilty about getting up late at the weekend.”Explore more on these topicsSleepHealth & wellbeingHigh blood pressureHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: The sadistic online groomers targeting victims around the world – and a mother’s struggle to keep her daughter safe | Online abuse | The Guardian
description: This month a predator with ties to the online extortion group known as 764 was sentenced to decades in prison. The mother of one of his victims wants parents to know the truth about this ‘harrowing’ global trend
Author: Ariel Bogle
Headline: This month a predator with ties to the online extortion group known as 764 was sentenced to decades in prison. The mother of one of his victims wants parents to know the truth about this ‘harrowing’ global trend
Content: Illustration: Avinash Weerasekera/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Avinash Weerasekera/The GuardianOnline abuseThe sadistic online groomers targeting victims around the world – and a mother’s struggle to keep her daughter safeThis month a predator with ties to the online extortion group known as 764 was sentenced to decades in prison. The mother of one of his victims wants parents to know the truth about this ‘harrowing’ global trendSadistic online exploitation: five warning signs for parents - and how to keep young people safeAriel BogleSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTShare“My beautiful, kind, intelligent, trusting daughter had the misfortune of stumbling across a link in a Discord server that led her to your evil and cruel group.“The grooming of her started immediately, and what followed was unimaginably harrowing and traumatic. You were just one of the group members who abused her, who made her do things that no young person should ever be made to do.”These are the words that came to an Australian mother, Olivia*, as Kyle Spitze was sentenced to 77 years in prison this month in Tennessee –the longest federal sentence yetimposed on what the US government has called a “nihilistic violent extremist”.Spitze, 27,pleaded guiltyto abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material (CSAM) offences, with victims around the world – some who have still not been identified. His lawyer said he plans to appeal the sentence.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association withan online network known as “764”, known for its sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world.Olivia told the Guardian the early days after she discovered her child’s abuse by these networks were terrifying.“I had no idea what was happening or what to do, so I just focused on trying to keep my child as physically safe as possible while I tried to figure out what to do next,” she saidThe platforms where her daughter had interacted with this network were not the “dark web”. They were apps like Discord, Telegram, Instagram and Snapchat. At the time, local police did not seem able to assist because the offenders were overseas.Inside the horrifying online network where children coerce others to commit violence and self-harmRead moreYears later, she could not believe it when she heard Spitze had received such a long sentence.“Pretty soon the tears started as I was flooded with relief, but also as I reflected on how long and hard we’d fought to get to this point,” she said.Normalising explicit materialIn December 2023, the chat platform Discord sent the FBI a 29-page report with a list of accounts it said were involved in “high harm activities”.The users were, in Discord’s words, engaged in “sextortion, solicitation of minors to perform online sexual acts, self-harm coercion, swatting and conspiring to commit real world acts of violence”. Swatting is when someone calls in a fake threat to provoke an armed police response.One username was “CRIMINALOLI”, prosecutors said. This was Spitze, then in his early 20s. Earlier that year, others had also sent tips to police alleging he was “grooming minors”.Police found a video on a Telegram channel he ran that showed minor girls exposing their breasts and bodies, with his moniker sometimes “written in blood or carved on their bodies”.He demanded one girl kill animals on video. If she hesitated, according to the prosecution, he threatened to dox and swat her and her parents. She was 12 when they met online, and thought she was his girlfriend.In May, his father was sentenced to nearlysix years’ imprisonment for attempted tampering with a victim, including asking her to destroy any evidence. Michael Spitze called the victim, 15, and told her to set up an account to speak to his son in prison, which she did out of fear. Kyle Spitze then called her 51 times.In court documents, the prosecutor said 764 and similar groups “work in concert” to normalise explicit material to minors and “groom them towards future violence”, creating video records of victims: “Ultimately, these videos are placed on the network servers to gain notoriety and spread fear.”According to Discord, the company has shared insights about these “harm groups” to law enforcement since it became aware of their activity in 2021.“Discord is continuing to invest in new ways of detecting these groups, including if they attempt to return to Discord after being removed,” the company said.Grooming manualsAbout one year before authorities received tips about Spitze, in June 2022, a teenager in Australia sent an email to police in Inglewood, California.The thread was disturbing. She alleged that a man called Dong Hwan Kim had sent her explicit messages, according to the criminal complaint, urging her to show him her body on camera. She said he threatened to send photos and videos of her to her father and even to her work if she did not show him naked imagery again.The tip-off was one of several that led to a police investigation, and in April, Kim, who was 27 when he was arrested, pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child sexual exploitation material. He is yet to be sentenced. His lawyer did not respond to a request for comment.The government says in court records that Kim’s crimes also occurred as part of his association with 764, and that he and his associates ran multiple online forums in which they “enticed, persuaded, and coerced minors” into creating CSAM.Both US cases, and others currently before the courts, demonstrate the complex global nature of these crimes, with victims and perpetrators spread across borders. There have been a spate of global arrests but these groups and their propaganda continue to spread and change.Groups such as 764 are understood to be part of the Com – the term for a broad online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.This network does not have a traditional organised crime structure; it is decentralised and very fluid. “The other primary difference is that predominantly it involves young people, both as perpetrators and victims,” said AFP cybercrime commander Graeme Marshall.Sadistic online exploitation as part of these groups can be driven by “gamification”, as well as a means to build status and notoriety. It is this type of Com activity that the AFP observes most often in Australia, although the scale is unclear.The typical perpetrator, according to the AFP, is a young white male aged between 11 and their early 20s. The victim will often be a young woman in a similar age bracket.The Guardian has seen Telegram channels that claim to be new iterations of 764, as well as manuals that provide guidance about how to groom and extort young people and where to store files. Court records suggest “content” is often traded, and allegedly used as means of entry to certain closed online spaces.Marshall said the AFP has worked to increase awareness of theCom from local police, who need to know what questions to ask – and from parents and caregivers, who need to be aware of the warning signs.“I still find it hard to believe that kids as young as 13 are even involved in these criminal groups, let alone perpetrating crimes,” Marshall said. “So, it’s completely understandable that parents, educators and health professionals would have that type of reaction as well. It is a broader education and awareness piece that is needed.”Sadistic online exploitation: five warning signs for parents – and how to keep young people safeRead moreWarning signsThe conviction of Spitze and others in 764 and other extortion networks often came off the back of tips from victims, families and their friends, court records show.Before Spitze was arrested, a video spread online of him being shot in the ear during an altercation with his mother’s partner. He even gave interviews about the incident on YouTube.This was when Olivia was able to “put a face to the name”.“I couldn’t believe that he’d exposed himself so publicly, and after that more and more people started speaking out on [social media] about who he really was and what he’d been doing to young girls,” she said.Olivia believes there is increasing awareness about how serious these groups are “and how easily kids can accidentally end up in contact with a predator”.Some of thepotential warning signsshe wants parents to look out for include: increased time on devices, as well as distress and anger if separated from those devices; a child becoming extra secretive or distrusting of those closest to them; self-harm; and, random gifts or deliveries.Olivia said that in her experience, the most significant thing a parent can do to help a child in this situation is to not blame them and to help them feel safe. “It sounds simple, but unfortunately it’s something that a lot of parents struggle with,” she said.Today she would tell Spitze that although he was just one of the group members who abused her daughter, this doesn’t absolve him of responsibility for the “wilful destruction of lives that [he] gleefully participated in”.“We’re doing a lot better, but our lives are forever changed,” she said. “Life is still incredibly difficult most days.”Do you know more? Email ariel.bogle@theguardian.comIn Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. In the US, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is 1-800-273-8255. In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123.Other international suicide helplines can be found atbefrienders.org

title: Tom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in Spain
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in Spain
Content: Willem Dafoe in Late Fame and Zendaya in Dune: Part ThreeComposite: Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreenWillem Dafoe in Late Fame and Zendaya in Dune: Part ThreeComposite: Guardian Design/AlamyAutumn arts preview 2026MoviesTom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in SpainSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?All release dates are UK and subject to changeLaurence Phelan,Andrew PulverandCatherine ShoardSun 30 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareLate FameView image in fullscreenPoetic postal worker … Willem Dafoe with  Greta Lee in Late Fame.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWillem Dafoe is typically grizzled and poetic for this study of a near-retirement postal worker who, it turns out, was a beatnik rhymester of cachet – but no lasting renown – back in the day, and who has now been rediscovered by a new generation of literary hipsters. Director Kent Jones, adapting a novella by Arthur “La Ronde” Schnitzler, was the longtime head of the New York film festival; he might be in for a spot of late fame himself.AP4 SeptemberEverybody Digs Bill EvansGrant Gee’s stylishly monochrome, coolly composed musical biopic finds the great jazz pianist at something of a crisis point in 1961, grieving for his bassist, facing down some demons, painfully thin and heroin addicted – and living with his parents while he tries to kick the habit. Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf are terrific as Mr and Mrs Evans, while Anders Danielsen Lie stars as the tortured artist on the cusp of making musical history and quitting.LP11 SeptemberPractical Magic 2If you wait long enough, everything will go into development for sequel, but they don’t always happen. This one, almost randomly, has:Sandra Bullockand Nicole Kidman’s nicely judged 90s witch tale, with equal helpings of empowerment and romance, is broomsticking into cinemas. Bullock and Kidman are back, a quarter century on, with the younger generation represented by Joey King and Maisie Williams.AP11 SeptemberQueen at SeaView image in fullscreenActing masterclass … Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Queen at SeaPhotograph: © Seafaring LLCAnother late-period acting masterclass fromTom Courtenayin a shattering drama from Lance Hammer. Courtenay plays Martin, whose wife (Anna Calder-Marshall) is in the grip of dementia. He tries to keep their connection alive with sex. But can she consent? Is it rape? Her daughter by an earlier marriage, played by Juliette Binoche, certainly thinks so, setting the stage for a heartbreakingly emotional confrontation.AP18 SeptemberDe Gaulle: LibertéNational heroes don’t come much more totemic than Charles de Gaulle, wartime resistance leader turned peacetime statesman. This is the second instalment of the two part film in which Simon Abkarian plays the legendary general as the momentum to liberate Paris builds up towards the end of the second world war.AP18 SeptemberShaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy BottomEveryone’s favourite flock is back for a Halloween instalment, 11 years afterShaun the Sheep Movie(masterpiece) andFarmageddon(superb). This plasticine mashup of Frankenstein and Weird Science sees Shaun brewing up a potion to supersize pumpkins ahead of the autumn fair, while the farmer turns to a hair-restoring lotion to pluck up the courage to ask the vet on a date. Hope the two bottles don’t get muddled …Catherine Shoard18 SeptemberSense and SensibilityView image in fullscreenAusten for the Insta age … Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesThirty-one years after Emma Thompson’s swift, witty take on Austen’s classic – still much loved today – Georgia Oakley (Blue Jean) gives us a version for the Instagram age, replete withHamnet-ish strings and many shots of women in fields with closeups on bugs. Daisy Edgar-Jones is Elinor, Esmé Creed-Miles is Marianne, George MacKay is Edward Ferrars and Frank Dillane is the dastardly Willoughby.CS25 SeptemberHer Private HellWe nearly lostNicolas Winding Refna couple of years back, when the Danish enfant terrible had a heart scare. Happily, everyone’s favourite sadomasochistic softie is back with a sci-fi set in a weirdly misty futuristic metropolis haunted by a “deadly and elusive entity”. Sophie Thatcher and Charles Melton star. There will be blood.CS25 SeptemberKnife: The Attempted Murder of Salman RushdieOscar-winning film-maker Alex Gibney tackles the shocking assassination attempt on the great writer in this unsparing and remarkably graphic documentary featuring the man himself, as well as his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths.CS2 OctoberDiggerView image in fullscreenOligarch oilman … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTaking a well-earned rest from running and jumping and saving the world, Tom Cruise teams with Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman,The Revenant) to do some acting, not action. He’s still trying to save the world but here he is the paunchy and balding oligarch oilman Digger Rockwell, who deigns to intervene to avert an environmental calamity of his own making. Filmed in VistaVision and billed as “a comedy of catastrophic proportions”, it looks like Dr Strangelove with shades of Les Grossman, Cruise’s hilarious cameo as a film studio head in Tropic Thunder.LP2 OctoberThe Social ReckoningView image in fullscreenGeek chic … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyJeremy Strong pulls on the geek-chic fleeces and takes over from Jesse Eisenberg in Aaron Sorkin’s what-Zuckerberg-did-next companion piece toThe Social Network. Oscar-winningAnorastar Mikey Madison plays whistleblower Frances Haugen, who went public about all of Facebook’s algorithmic wrongdoings in 2021.LP9 OctoberThe UprisingView image in fullscreenA riot … Andrew Garfield leads a peasants’ revolt.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyTaxes are too high, the boy-king Richard II is out of touch with his subjects and serfdom needs abolishing … say Wat?! Andrew Garfield plays the hunky farmer turned sword-wielding leader of a revolt against tyranny in a medieval action film from Paul Greengrass, the director of several docudrama classics and multiple Jason Bourne movies.LP9 OctoberKlara and the SunJenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered companion robot yearning and learning to become a real family member, in a colourful adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s soulful sci-fi novel byTaika Waititi. Waititi looks to have mined the story for every bit of comedy he can, and Ortega inhabits the uncanny valley with bright-eyed good cheer. Amy Adams and Natasha Lyonne also star.LP23 OctoberAli G: Who Iz I?View image in fullscreenCourting controversy? … Sacha Baron Cohen, who returns as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?, is seen in character at this year’s Wimbledon tennis tournament.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyIt’s the return of the West Staines Massiv, Mr Shell Suit himself, Alistair Graham – otherwise known as Ali G.Sacha Baron Cohen(for it is he) has unretired the character and has shot a new film in secret … though perhaps not so secret, as he was spotted in full costume at Cotswold Wildlife Park and at Wimbledon this summer. Baron Cohen is in the director’s seat for the first time; it’ll be interesting, as much as anything else, what sort of fist he makes of it.AP23 OctoberFatherlandPolish film-makerPaweł Pawlikowskimade his early strides in the UK, with a series of brilliant literary documentaries and then a shift into features including Last Resort and My Summer of Love. Since moving back to mainland Europe, Pawlikowski has gone from strength to strength; this latest, his third black-and-white film in a row, takes us into Germany of the immediate postwar era, using a trip by novelist-in-exile Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika (Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller) back to their homeland as a way of examining both sides of the east-west divide.AP23 OctoberGentle MonsterLéa Seydoux gives an awards-tipped performance as a musician and mother whose comfortable domestic life fractures the moment that police arrive at her door to arrest her husband and confiscate his hard drives. An impressive handling of tricky material by Austrian film-maker Marie Kreutzer, inspired in part by the arrest of an actor in her previous film,Corsage, forpossession of child sexual abuse imagery.LP30 OctoberAnimolAfter So Solid Crew, Top Boy and – yes – Grange Hill, Ashley Walters steps into the director’s chair for this jailhouse drama written by The Football Factory’s Nick Love. Tut Nyuot is a new arrival who pals up with Polish kid Vladyslav Baliuk; Sekou Diaby is the fearsome inmate who runs things, and Stephen Graham is on hand as a prison care worker. Tough stuff, not unlikeWastemanfrom earlier this year. AP30 OctoberI Love BoostersView image in fullscreenMellow yellow … Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige and Keke Palmer in I Love Boosters.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyKeke Palmer, LaKeith Stanfield and Demi Moore star in this wacky, maximalist, anticapitalist agitprop and fashion-biz satire weird-a-thon from rapper and Sorry to Bother You creatorBoots Riley. It’s a madcap, colour-saturated crime caper about a gang of shoplifters raiding fashion stores to redistribute style to the masses. There are also claymation sequences, cartoony slapstick and demons.LP30 OctoberWickerOlivia Colman continues her journey into the wilder reaches of the cinematic imagination, and you can’t say she hasn’t earned it. This is one of her weirdest films yet: a kind of satirical fairytale in which she plays a fisher whose pungency is such she is doomed to remain single, so she gets the local basket-maker to make her a husband out of, yes, wicker. (Cue wicker sex, for those interested.) It’s a film that has produced divided reactions, shall we say, but will definitely kick up a stink, to coin a phrase.AP30 OctoberGodzilla Minus ZeroView image in fullscreenA monster of a film … Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyThe 2023 period-set Japanese kaiju epicGodzilla Minus Onewas almost certainly the most real, most sincere, most impressive Godzilla film made to that point – and there have been about 40 so that’s no small boast. Writer-director Takashi Yamazaki brings back the surviving characters for the follow-up – and it’s filmed for Imax, to make all the enormo-destruction extra enormo.LP6 NovemberWild Horse NineAfter the comparatively sombre and reflective Banshees of Inisherin,Martin McDonaghrevisits larkier In Bruges territory with this bickering odd-couple black comedy. In place of Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson as hitmen in Belgium, we have John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents/hitmen on Easter Island, prior to the 1973 Chilean coup.LP6 NovemberI Play RockyView image in fullscreenEvery underdog has its day … Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyWhen Rocky took on all comers at the box office and Oscars in 1976, the legend of its production fed into its rousing tale of an underdog having his day. Sylvester Stallone was a penniless nobody when he reputedly wrote the script in three days – then turned down six-figure offers for it, as he insisted on playing the lead role himself. Now Green Book’s Peter Farrelly directs a biopic telling that story, and fires up the brassy theme music to rouse audiences all over again.LP6 NovemberLa Bola NegraThis won the best director award at Cannes, jointly with Fatherland, for its sweeping, time-crossing evocation of queer identity and experience in Spain. Starting in the early 1930s, it moves from Spain’s suffocating patriarchy through the turmoil of the civil war years, and on to the 21st century, showing how persecution and trauma descend through the decades. Penélope Cruz puts in a cameo as a nightclub singer.AP6 NovemberJosephineBeth de Araújo made a splash and won the top two prizes at Sundance with this raw and intense study of the after effects of a sexual assault on the family of an eight-year-old girl who witnesses it, has nightmares about it and is called on to testify against the perpetrator. Channing Tatum gives a nuanced turn as the traumatised girl’s father.LP20 NovemberFocker-in-LawView image in fullscreenNew blood … Ariana Grande with Robert De Niro in next gen Focker-in-Law.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyAriana Grande is the new blood added to the Focker family in this next-gen fourquel to Meet the Parents. Or she will be, if avuncular grandpaRobert De Niroadmits her to his circle of trust, and if overprotective prospective father-in-law Ben Stiller doesn’t do as was done unto him all the way back in 2000, and put her off marrying his son.LP25 NovemberThe Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff BoothThe cool-under-fire character Brad Pitt played in Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood gets to perform more laid-back (anti-)heroics in a spin-off episode – but now he has been promoted from a stuntman to a studio fixer. Twice upon a time, Tarantino has written the script butDavid Fincher– whom Pitt previously worked with on Seven and Fight Club – directs.LP25 NovemberI See Buildings Fall Like LightningThis is British director Clio Barnard’s first film since Ali & Ava in 2021, put together with what we now know is her customary empathy and intelligence, in a drama about life choices and the way things work out differently for different people. Five friends get together for a birthday; some have made good, others less so, and they each face up to their uncertain futures. The title refers to the demolition of tower blocks in Birmingham: a key symbolic event.AP4 DecemberAvengers: DoomsdayCan the Avengers (Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Paul Rudd, et al) unite with the X-Men (Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Channing Tatum), the Thunderbolts (Florence Pugh, David Harbour, Sebastian Stan) and the Wakandans (Letitia Wright, Winston Duke) to save the universe fromsuperhero fatigueDoctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr)? Marvel is betting a cast this star-studded must surely obliterate any and all resistance.LP18 DecemberDune: Part ThreeView image in fullscreenReturning … Jason Momoa as Hayt in Dune: Part Three.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesThe newDunefilm finally arrives, completing the projected trilogy conceived on a colossal scale from director Denis Villeneuve, featuring Timothée Chalamet’s floppy-haired Paul Atreides. This one is adapted from Dune Messiah, Frank Herbert’s follow-up to his original doorstep-size chunk of space fantasy, in which the emperor’s holy war is lurching out of control. Zendaya, Florence Pugh and Jason Momoa all return, with the ubiquitous Robert Pattinson brought in to play chief nasty Scytale, out to overthrow Paul. If this goes well, there are – count them – four more Dune novels on the shelf … be very afraid …AP18 December

title: ‘It’s therapy by stealth’: the adult fans helping Lego build its billions in sales | Lego | The Guardian
description: A growing number of people are rediscovering their love of plastic bricks in later life and boosting the Danish company’s bottom line
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: A growing number of people are rediscovering their love of plastic bricks in later life and boosting the Danish company’s bottom line
Content: Adult Lego Fans gather at the Old London Road Cafe in Kingston. Loretta Piare holds up her completed Lego Cactus.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAdult Lego Fans gather at the Old London Road Cafe in Kingston. Loretta Piare holds up her completed Lego Cactus.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianLego‘It’s therapy by stealth’: the adult fans helping Lego build its billions in salesA growing number of people are rediscovering their love of plastic bricks in later life and boosting the Danish company’s bottom lineGeorge Francis LeeSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a cosy cafe in Kingston upon Thames on the outskirts of London, nine people gather in the early evening to drink and talk. To the casual observer it may look like a book club, but when the friends reach into their bags it’s not paperbacks they produce – but packs ofLego.Geoff Lay, who organised the gathering, worked in software development before recently starting Noble Brick, a Lego-focused events organisation.“I was one of those kids where you couldn’t go into my bedroom because the floor was covered in pieces,” he says. But after a break with the hobby, the 44-year-old rediscovered Lego 10 years ago – after being given a set recreating London’s Tower Bridge. He has been building ever since.The allure of a Lego set may conjure childhood fun, but a growing number of adult enthusiasts is one of the reasons behind a surge in sales which has helpedincrease the Danish toymaker’s revenues by 21%.View image in fullscreenGeoff Lay helps his fiancee, Lauren Marshall, centre, and fellow enthusiast Holly Nessling get to grips with their Lego Darth Vader figure.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianThanks to collaborations with the likes of the World Cup and Stranger Things, as well as mini figures of popular football players, more and more are finding themselves returning to the brand in later life.The Lego Group was founded in 1932 and has built a lucrative plastic empire, generating £4.8bn in revenue in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the 1990s, Lego has expanded its products to include brand tie-ins, video games, television shows and sets tailored towards adults – often costing hundreds of pounds.Lay is confident that a new demographic of older Lego enthusiasts is here to stay. He says: “The idea that Lego is for kids is banished.” His 40-year-old fiancee, Lauren Marshall, agrees: “You don’t have a typical Lego fan any more.”Marshall “didn’t have Lego as a child”, but got into the hobby as an adult after her partner’s fervour rubbed off on her. As she assembles the legs of a large Darth Vader, she says sets are “a lot like jigsaws”, and they are “completing something like a puzzle”.View image in fullscreenAdult Lego Fans gather at the Old London Road Cafe in Kingston. Tim Hirst working on his DeLorean Car Lego.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianSomeone who was raised on a less structured style of Lego play is 28-year-old Loretta Piare. “Growing up, I loved Lego. We always had huge boxes of it,” she says, as she constructs a cactus from the company’s botanical series. “We could never afford one of the fancy sets. My mum would get the big boxes of mixed colours.”double quotation markWhy can’t we play with Lego? Some people might say it’s for kids but there are so many of usJordan Wiltshire, GertLUGShe stopped playing with Lego in her teens – “I used to love building houses and making it up” – but the cost-effective and environmentally conscious option to borrow other people’s bricks at adult groups has revived her interest. “I love following instructions,” she says, “I love colourful bricks, basically. I love building things.”Tim Stone, a 35-year-old decorator, renewed his love for Lego after quitting smoking during Covid and buying himself a racing car set. While constructing a brick-based Nintendo Game Boy console, he explains how he joined the London Afol (Adult Fans of Lego) group to make new friends. “I got really bored. I had a load of buddies that would just go out drinking.” Now, Stone takes part in collaborative builds late into the night with more than 20 other Afol members.View image in fullscreenTim Stone working on his Lego Nintendo Game Boy console.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianThere are dozens of Lego fan groups across the UK. Jordan Wiltshire, 32, is a member of GertLUG, a “Lego user group” based in Bristol. He became conscious of the cost and began to wonder if Lego was a “sensible” purchase. When a friend bought him a Lego Star Wars Tie Fighter for Christmas when he was 26, things slotted back into place.He calls Lego his “personality”, and is a strong advocate against ageism related to the hobby. “Why can’t we play with Lego?” he asks. “Some people might say it’s for kids but there are so many of us and we all have different things we love about it.”Wiltshire, who builds his own Lego creations, says he enjoys the “sense of accomplishment”: “It’s a way I can be creative and actually be quite good at it.”There are other purported benefits to playing with Lego, such as improved mental health. Nick Bright runs Brighton Bricks, an adult Lego group that meets monthly, and says: “It’s therapy by stealth, you don’t even realise you’re helping your wellbeing.”View image in fullscreenWork on a Lego mosaic in Brighton.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianLike many adult fans, the 51-year-old rediscovered Lego later in life. He recalls the product that revived the habit: “It was the Haunted House Monster Fighters set. It was one of those moments where you go ‘Yeah, this is me’.” He shares his love for Lego with his nine-year-old son and 80-year-old mother. His home collection is large and admits “my wife maybe thinks I have too much”.View image in fullscreenNick Bright, who runs Brighton Bricks: ‘It’s therapy by stealth, you don’t even realise you’re helping your wellbeing.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThere are plenty of gateways into the hobby through collaborations with the likes of Disney, Dune and Fortnite, but Bright warns that one downside is that “there are a lot more bigger, expensive sets and there is a fear of missing out”.Bright prefers to follow the guide of a Lego set’s printed instructions, but has many friends whose constructions come from their own imagination. “We’re all doing the same thing, but we are all doing it differently,” he says. “What I love about Lego is that there’s no wrong way to build it.”He believes the creativity displayed through MOCs – an enthusiast term meaning “my own creation” to describe original builds – shows that Lego is much more than a children’s toy.“It’s just like how someone can do knitting and pottery – it’s an art form.”Regardless of people’s reasons to love Lego, its adult fanbase shows the company won’t be hitting a brick wall any time soon.Explore more on these topicsLegoHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Iain Stirling looks back: ‘I was worried about doing the Love Island voiceover, but it opened doors I thought would close’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The comedian on being a weird emo teen, the audition he didn’t show up for and why he was jealous of Rob Beckett
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The comedian on being a weird emo teen, the audition he didn’t show up for and why he was jealous of Rob Beckett
Content: FlashbackFamilyIain Stirling looks back: ‘I was worried about doing the Love Island voiceover, but it opened doors I thought would close’The comedian on being a weird emo teen, the audition he didn’t show up for and why he was jealous of Rob BeckettHarriet GibsoneSun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComedian Iain Stirling in 2001 and 2026, recreating a shot of him lying on his bed as a teenagerIain Stirling in 2001 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Grooming: Tori Ball. Archive photograph: courtesy of Iain StirlingBorn in Edinburgh in 1988, Iain Stirling is a comedian, actor and writer. He studied law at the University of Edinburgh while starting his standup career. He won a children’s Bafta for his work on CBBC alongside sidekick puppet Hacker T Dog and has narrated UK Love Island since 2015 and Love Island USA since 2022. He co-wrote and starred in the sitcom Buffering, and currently hosts true crime podcast Murder They Wrote with his wife Laura Whitmore with whom he has two children. Series two of Iain Stirling’s Roast the Internet will return toComedy Centralon 7 September.This must have been taken at the weekendas I’m wearing a Blink-182 T-shirt and baggy jeans. I wouldn’t have been allowed to look like that during the week. I lived this double life in my teens: I wore an outfit like this at school once and was told I was a “sweatie” – an emo – and that I’d let the school down. I was on the football team and things were tribal back then. But on a Saturday, when I was back from violin practice, I could dress how I wanted. Under the bed is an empty bottle of Irn-Bru, and there’s a remote control for the TV that I’d watch Pokémon on, all of which sums me up at this age.The first part of my life was spent on an estate in Liberton, a suburb of Edinburgh, before we moved to a bungalow in a little cul-de-sac just outside the city. My family was small – just me, my parents and my sister, and very few relatives. My memories of living here were that it was quaint, safe, quiet and insular.I was never the funniest person in my friendship circle, but I was obsessed with comedy. I started going to the fringe when I was 12. By the time I was 14, I formed a sketch group with a friend called Just So Ever Slightly. Influenced by Monty Python and Little Britain, there was often a three-minute blackout between sketches while we got into different outfits. Our jokes were fairly adolescent – I’d wear a wig and a dress and pretend to be a female weather reporter with inflatable boobs. It relied on a lot of innuendo – “Long, hard, cold fronts,” etcI’d watched so much live comedy that as soon as I began doing standup I felt I had a natural swing for it. I never told anyone at school what I was doing in my spare time, but they found out in the end. In my 20s, a few people from school came to see me and ruined it, probably on purpose. One of them found a drill in the venue and started threatening people in the audience with it. It was pretty mad, but it was how we were brought up – we were told to stay in our lane. People from where I was from weren’t meant to perform shows at the fringe – we were the ones serving pints behind the bar.double quotation markBack then, diversity on TV was: ‘We can still hire a white guy, just not a posh one’It wasn’t until law school that I felt I had permission to approach comedy with ambition.Susan Calmanwas a massive influence; she and her wife were lawyers. They took me under their wing – Susan would tell me which gigs to do, and her wife would tell me what law books to read. My degree was prestigious and it was the first time teachers filled me with confidence. At my school, if a kid said they wanted to be a footballer, the teacher would reply: “What about postman?” Containing us was the goal. University was a different environment. I wouldn’t have thrown myself into standup if it wasn’t for that experience.I was doing a gig at the Comedy Storewhen someone from CBBC asked if I’d be interested in auditioning. My standup was not kid-friendly, and I’d never heard of standups doing children’s TV, let alone presenting it, so I thought it was a wind-up. I didn’t show up, went back to my hostel in Leicester Square and thought nothing of it. They got in touch again, and this time I paid attention. I remember being in the audition room and hearing that someone called “Chris Ramsey” [now co-host of podcast Shagged. Married. Annoyed] was meant to be up for the job, too, but hadn’t shown up. So I got it. It was all very serendipitous.I was working on a show about kids training dogs to do tricks when my voice got spotted forLove Island. The dogs gig was given to me by a producer friend who sold it to me as: “A day’s work, maximum, but I’ll say it’s four so we can go on the piss for a couple of days in London afterwards.” I said yes, not realising it would get sent to someone at ITV, who happened to be looking for a voiceover for a new reality series. Apparently, they wanted someone who wasn’t from the south. Back then, diversity was: “We can still hire a white guy, just not a posh one.”I was initially reluctant to accept the job. Although I was skint, I was also worried that if I did Love Island, I wouldn’t get a Radio 4 series or interviewed by broadsheets. In fact, the opposite happened. Love Island became a cultural cornerstone and opened doors I thought would close. The culture was changing in comedy too – whereas traditionally you’d have to earn your stripes on the circuit and then get to go on a panel show, comedians were starting to get more visible through non-traditional routes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe narration I did with my writing partner Mark [Busk-Cowley], who is also Scottish, met with some resistance at first. Jokes such as “This date is awful, so if you want, Ice Road Truckers is on Channel 5 at the minute” didn’t get a great response from the people up top. Eventually, they came round to our sense of humour, and now they let us do what we like. I still get my voice recognised more than my face. If I don’t speak, generally I can still go under the radar.Standup and author Susan Calman: ‘Comedy is an industry full of weirdos – I found my people’Read moreI was aware of Laurafor yearsbefore I met her. In 2012, Rob Beckett got a presenting gig on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! NOW! and I thought: “What a lucky bastard. Not only has he got this cool job, but he’s presenting with this really hot girl.” We then met a few times, through being part of the ITV family, and I was struck by her incredible personality and energy. She is amazing at standing by what she believes in. By comparison, I am such a people pleaser. As a comedian, and as someone who did not fit in as a kid, I’ll often do whatever it takes to be liked. Meanwhile, Laura has this ability to be liked but also never compromise who she is. Has she inspired me? I definitely am more willing to speak my mind on political or socio-economic matters, subjects I might have shied away from in the past. But I still spend too much time worrying about how I might inconvenience someone in some way.While 13-year-old me was preoccupied with the stresses of belonging, he had a huge creative imagination. I’ve been doing this job for such a long time, and I’ve learned most of the tricks of the trade, so comedic uniqueness is harder to come by now. I wish I could go back to that blank slate and borrow some of his weirdness. But he’d be over the moon if he knew what was about to happen to him. And fucking delighted with the car I drive.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackPhotographyComedy CentralLove IslandComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: My car had been towed and my kids had no shoes, then a man made a wonderful offer | Life and style | The Guardian
description: ‘Can you help me?’ I asked. ‘I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes’
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: ‘Can you help me?’ I asked. ‘I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes’
Content: Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreenComposite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyKindness of strangersLife and styleThe kindness of strangers: My car had been towed and my kids had no shoes, then a man made a wonderful offer‘Can you help me?’ I asked. ‘I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes’Read more inthe kindness of strangers seriesGabrielle Eirew, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 20.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the first things we did after moving from the UK to Vancouver was buy a car. Unfortunately, I didn’t acquaint myself with the new road rules quite as quickly.Which is to say, I didn’t know you aren’t allowed to park on busy streets after 3pm in Vancouver. Unaware and in a carefree summer mood, I parked outside an ice-cream shop and took my barefoot children in for a treat. We emerged a short time later, sticky and splattered in drops of raspberry, mint and chocolate, and found my car wasn’t there.We were so fresh toCanadathat we were still staying in a hotel. So I headed out on foot, one kid under each arm, towards our accommodation. When I reached the concierge desk of the valet parking place out the front, I frantically turned to the nicely dressed man standing there and launched into explaining our situation.The kindness of strangers: I was a young, solo tourist when a taxi driver became aggressive – then two men stepped inRead more“Hi, can you help me? I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes. I’m sorry about the ice-cream, but can you help me get to wherever the towing place is?”He answered yes, of course, he was happy to help. After I badgered him about whether he’d have car seats for the kids, he said that we best get going, as he had to be back by 5pm. When I asked why, he replied, “Well, I’ve got a flight to catch.”At that moment I realised this nicely dressed man was not, in fact, a hotel employee.We laughed as he clarified he wasn’t a member of the concierge, just a regular guy waiting for his car. I refused to let this man spend his time driving us around, and instead got a cab to the towing place.But his wonderful offer – made so casually, as if it were no trouble at all – had a huge effect on me. Moving to a different country where you know no one can be frightening, but his generosity made me feel so welcome.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. They will only be seen by the Guardian.What is your email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsLife and styleKindness of strangersCanadaAustralian lifestylefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years on | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Protester Tess Asplund on the photo that made headlines, and why she sees it as a sign of the change in Sweden today
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Protester Tess Asplund on the photo that made headlines, and why she sees it as a sign of the change in Sweden today
Content: Tess Asplund challenges a 2016 neo-Nazi parade in Borlänge.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamyView image in fullscreenTess Asplund challenges a 2016 neo-Nazi parade in Borlänge.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamySwedenA lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years onProtester Tess Asplund on the photo that made headlines, and why she sees it as a sign of the change in Sweden todayAshifa Kassamin StockholmSun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised, standing in the path of hundreds of uniformed neo-Nazis on parade in 2016, and it made headlines across the globe.At the time, it was held up as a symbol of the resistance to the far right. But 10 years on, as Sweden gears up for elections in which the far right isexpected to emerge as the second most-voted-for party, the woman in the photo sees it as a sign of the bewildering change that has gripped the Scandinavian country.“Ten years ago, people would say: ‘Oh we dislike the far right, theSwedenDemocrats, we despise Nazis,’” said Tess Asplund, 52. “And now, they’ve become normalised. It’s like, what happened?”Woman who defied 300 neo-Nazis at Swedish rally speaks of angerRead moreHer comments hint at the recent reshaping of Swedish politics, where the far right – once a pariah –has steadily marchedinto the halls of power. “I’m sad, afraid and ashamed of Swedish citizens,” said Asplund in an interview at a cafe in central Stockholm. “It’s pure racism.”Ahead of a general election on 13 September,polls suggest that the centre-left opposition has a leadover the ruling rightwing coalition, meaning a change of government could be on the cards.But the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, is expected to garner the second-most votes in the country. In the 2022 elections, it also came second,paving the way for it to play a supporting role in a minority-run coalition.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Sweden Democrats party leader Jimmie Åkesson listen to him at an election campaign event in Huddinge on 18 August.Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesThe party haslong been dogged by accusations of harbouring violent racistsand swastika-wearing Nazi sympathisers. It has used its leverage in government toconsistently target migrants, including asylum seekers, as well as Muslims, ushering in ultra-restrictive migration policies and a discourse that routinely disparages the millions of people from around the world who have made Sweden their home and seek to contribute to it.Earlier this year, the Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, mused that if his four-party coalition won the upcoming election, the far rightcould enter government,in what was seen as a watershed moment for Swedish politics.It was a sharp contrast to the Sweden that Aspland had stood up for on 1 May 2016. She and scores of others had travelled to the central Swedish city of Borlänge to rally against a planned march by the Nordic Resistance Movement, one of the country’s largest neo-Nazi groups.As she faced off against them, her act of defiance was caught on camera by the photographer David Lagerlöf of Expo, the anti-racism foundation in Stockholm.It soon went viral, with Swedish media likening it to another iconic image of resistance:a 1985 photo in which photographer Hans Runesson captured a woman taking aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö.View image in fullscreenA woman takes aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö in 1985.Photograph: Hans RunessonMedia requests poured in from around the world. In Sweden, people began stopping Asplund on the streets, thanking her for her gesture, though she also grappled with a stream of online harassment and death threats on her home telephone line.For Asplund, who has spent much of her life campaigning against racism, it was a sobering frontline encounter with the far-right spectrum of Sweden, which ranges from the extremist Nordic Resistance Movement, which in 2024 wasdesignated as a terror group by the US, to the Sweden Democrats, who have long worked to make over their image.A 2023 studynoted that the presence of the two groups, both of which have shared roots in their militant opposition to immigration, probably works to bolster their causes by keeping issues of immigration and integration on Sweden’s political agenda.Or, in the words of Mohammad Aluaudt Allah, a Syrian refugee who was kicked unconscious on a street in central Stockholm last year, the politicians who blame immigrants for all of the country’s issues have “created a sense of impunity for violent Nazi groups”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“They may feel that they are being given permission to exercise their hatred and attack us,” he told the newspaper Dagens Nyheter.The view was echoed by Asplund. “The Nordic Resistance Movement, they’re kind of small now, we don’t hear so much about them any more,” she said. “They don’t have to be big because Sweden Democrats are big, so they’ve got people doing their work in the government. The Nazis are in the shadows.”The resulting rhetoric had then been amplified by some in media, she said, pointing to those who had uncritically swallowed the far right’s blaming of all social and economic ills on migration.What had emerged was a hardened Sweden, one where, for example, dozens of young people who had lived their whole lives in Swedenhad been deportedto their parents’ countries of birth after they failed to meet the increased earnings thresholds for migrants. “Thirty years ago, we would be on the street fighting against this. Now it’s like, ‘That’s sad for him or her.’ It’s a shift that really scares me,” she said.“If Olof Palme were alive today, he would turn over in his grave,” she added, citingthe assassinated former leader of Sweden’s Social Democratic party, who is credited with many of the progressive policies long associated with Sweden, from the robust social welfare system to a pro-refugee discourse that welcomed those escaping dictatorships and war.She noted, however, that her disappointment and shame did not extend to everyone in Sweden. “We are many, many people here fighting for human rights and against racism,” she said.View image in fullscreenPolice intervene against Tess Asplund during the neo-Nazi parade in 2016.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamyBut in some ways, the photo – hailed in 2016 for capturing one of the conflicts of our time – seemed to pit Palme’s Sweden against the march of the far right.In the years since, Asplund despaired that it may have been the far right who had emerged victorious.“I’m afraid and heartbroken because when I speak to people they’re like, ‘Oh for God’s sake, forget that. It was 20 years ago that there were Nazis and skinheads, now it’s gone,’” she said. “They’ve normalised it. It’s not my safe Sweden any more, it’s not the Sweden that I’m used to.”This article was amended on 30 August 2026 to correct the spelling of Tess Asplund’s name in a picture caption.Explore more on these topicsSwedenThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionDevolutionCities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?John HarrisLabour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get startedSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareApart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons whyAndy Burnhamseems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with theEnglish Devolution and Community Empowerment Actpassed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift thatthe Whitehall PR machineis hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.One changebecame clearearlier this year, and now looks like it willbe turbocharged. By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts.These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne,Minehead, Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to aHouse of Commons library briefing, qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will includeWiltshire, Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took itsfirst stepsto joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades,finally agreedto become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer governmentpostponed mayoral electionsin Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring the State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news thatplans for new, larger police forces are being delayedbecause their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDevolutionOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourSomersetWiltshirecommentShareReuse this content

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live on | Ed Vulliamy | The Guardian
description: When I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia today, says Ed Vulliamy, an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian
Author: Ed Vulliamy
Headline: When I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia today, says Ed Vulliamy, an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian
Content: Supporters of the deceased Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladić display and light flares in Novi Sad, Serbia, 27 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of the deceased Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladić display and light flares in Novi Sad, Serbia, 27 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersOpinionRatko MladićRatko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live onEd VulliamyWhen I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia todaySun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTShareMen age and die, but in the Balkans, time stands still and is stuck. General Ratko Mladić,who died in prisonin The Hague on Thursday aged 84, remains a hero in the Republika Srpskastatelet – the Serbian half of dismembered Bosnia that he carved out with ahurricane of violence between 1992 and 1995– and in Serbia itself.Too many Serbs in whose name Mladić carried out his mass murder of other ethnicities – mainly Muslim Bošniak and Roman Catholic Croats – adore him and mourn his passing.Since Bosnia’s war ended, Mladić’s portrait has adorned posters, gable ends, mantelpieces and football fans’ flags. Supporters of Red Star Belgrade marked his death at a match against Viktoria Plzeň on Thursday night with banners reading: “General: Eternal glory. Thank you.”Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik extended his condolences to the Mladić familyand paid tribute: “Republika Srpska will not forget his role, just as it has not forgotten it to this day. A man has died who was the commander in the struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people here, a commander who led the honourable army of Republika Srpska from the first day of its establishment. A man who demonstrated his human and military character.”Conversely, in the 30 years since the war ended, there has been scant apology from Serbian quarters to those people, most of them Muslims, who survived Mladić’s massacres, and no reckoning. Au contraire: across Republika Srpska, hatred of what remains of “the other” and for federal authority in the capital of Sarajevo is palpable and quotidian. A friend writes to me from Bosnia: “We’re still living with the legacy every day. Listening to Republika Srpska, to Dodik, to [Serbia’s president] Vučić, the same old lies, the same old denial.” There is mass collective amnesia, denial of or – nonsensically – justification for what was done.‘We know what is happening, we cannot walk away’: how the Guardian bore witness to horror in former YugoslaviaRead moreMourners who gather annually at the mass cemetery of victims of theSrebrenica massacreof some 8,000 men and boys in July 1995, and for commemorations at concentration camps, are routinely harassed by police and onlookers. It is made clear to Muslims and Croats who have dared to return to Republika Srpska in the north-west and east of the bitterly divided country that, if they could, the Serbs would do it all again.Mladić had a singular, and singularly nasty, squint. You can see it in the footage of him as he prepared the Srebrenica massacre, and in photo portraits that abound this weekend. For very many, it was a death sentence; for me, it was a stab across a courtroom at the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague as Itook the witness stand in 2012to testify against him. Having delivered that terrifying gaze, Mladić never met my eyes again during a half day of evidence from the ground of atrocities committed by those under his command. He sent a shiver of fear down the spine of anyone near him, and he knew it.Mladić was the military wing of an unholy trinity: at its apex, Serbia’s then president, Slobodan Milošević, resurrected the insane idea of a “Greater Serbia”, a form of nationalist fascism whereby wherever the Serbs lived, only Serbs would live – everyone else would leave or die, and every vestige of their culture and religion (Muslim or Catholic) would be erased. His political co-commander in Bosnia wasRadovan Karadžić,president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic.Milošević died while on trial at The Hague; like Mladić, Karadžić was convicted of genocide and other war crimes and remains jailed –surreally, on the Isle of Wight.If Milošević and Karadžić were dangerously deranged, Mladič was bloodthirstily effective. He was the killer,the “Butcher of Bosnia”. To invoke and invertHannah Arendt, if the others were the evil of banality, Mladić was the real thing: the banality of evil.Mladić was a military more than an ideological man, a career officer in the Yugoslav army. He knew what he was doing. Transcripts of the Bosnian Serb assembly submitted to The Hague by an historian at the University of Michigan, Robert Donia, show Mladić expressing concern in 1992 that the political leadership was setting goals that would be hard to achieve. “We cannot cleanse, or sift with a sieve, so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how … Mr Karadžić would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide.” And so it was – at Srebrenica at least, according to The Hague tribunal – and as a good military commander, Mladić obeyed his political masters and enforced his own orders.Mladić was convicted at The Hague in 2017. The media talked about “closure” for his victims. Wishful nonsense: there is no “closure”, nor can there be as long as the Serbs celebrate this creature.Most discussion of Mladić since his passing has inevitably invoked Srebrenica, the infamous massacre. There is the TV footage of him smirking, knowing what was to come. But it was not only Srebrenica. Srebrenica was the most egregious war crime, but it was a denouement: more than 55,000 Muslims and 7,000 Croats had already been killed in other places over those three years, and two million had fled their homes.Foca and Višegrad(sites of rape camps for the indulgence of Mladić’s soldiers); Rogatica, Vlasenica and Sokolac; Bjeljina and Brcko, Kozarac, Sanski Most, Ključ … the list goes on.The siege of Sarajevocounted 11,541 deaths, including 1,600 children.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMladić achieved most of what he set out to do. The “international community” granted the Bosnian Serbs a large part of what they killed, raped, tortured and burned for with theDayton peace agreement, signed in 1995. There was baffling agreement from the Muslim-led government, apparently more anxious to establish its own sectarian fiefdom than unite the republic in a war that the Bosnian army was – actually, finally – winning by that summer (in a counteroffensive that put Mladiċ’s soldiers to flight, liberating territory then returned at Dayton to Republika Srpska).Mladić succeeded in persecuting a very Bosnian, casually convivial interpretation of Islam into something more identitarian and polemical. In the absurd waltz of aspirant accession to the EU, Serbia leads the Balkan queue, ahead of truncated Bosnia, despite Belgrade’s open allegiance and subservience to Russia.Above all, Mladić has succeeded in death, as he did in life, because of the adoration he still commands. His mission to establish an ethnically “pure”, fascistic Greater Serbia remains a dream, anda plan. Through public celebrations, he continues to terrorisethe lives of those mostly Muslims and a few Croats brave enough to return to live under the insignia of those who mass murdered their families.Mladić’s funeral will probably tell us more than his death. Several Serbian government officials and ministers urge a “state and military funeral, and day of mourning”. The president, AleksandarVučić, says he will leave arrangements to the general’s son, Darko, who is of the faith. If Darko decides on full national honours, that is what will happen. Mladić is dead, but lives on.Ed Vulliamy is an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian and ObserverDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Why is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Senatorial candidate James Talarico, a former vegan, eats barbecue during his election campaign in June 2026.Photograph: The Dallas Morning News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSenatorial candidate James Talarico, a former vegan, eats barbecue during his election campaign in June 2026.Photograph: The Dallas Morning News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesOpinionVeganismWhy is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur?Emma BeddingtonUS republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the waysSun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.23 EDTShareCool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble,tofu-eating wokeratito dangerous radicals unfit for public office.Politico reportsthat US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,”Trump warnedof Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is“neither man nor woman”.)Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretarydescribed him on Xas “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowadrew heatfor merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”.It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does Americaactually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official responseto “vegan accusations”(“accusations” – the word you’d use for say,corruptionorsexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’sfirst indictment” (despitemany years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime).Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”.Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office.Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle.And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome.Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of thelandmark 2018 studyon the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes,concludedthat excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”.Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
