title: Italy may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?
Content: ‘Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionItalyItaly may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there?Dave SchillingThe move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 15.57 EDTShareImagine driving in Italy, with its narrow, cobblestone streets and scooter enthusiasts. I find it hard enough todrive in Los Angeles, a city designed specifically with the automobile in mind. I’d probably squash a pedestrian or two trying to navigate Italian roads.The modern world is just too hectic for the ancient streets of Europe, so Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can:outlawing texting in crosswalks. The Italian government’s updated draft of its highway code proposes fines of €75 or more for anyone caught sending a DM, updating their LinkedIn, finishing Wordle on the fifth guess, or anything else phone-related that might make them miss an oncoming metal projectile. I’m sure most people will risk the slap on wrist to get that message off, but it at least sends a signal to the Italian people that paying attention to traffic is actually kind of important.Distracted pedestrians aren’t just a problem inItaly, though. If I’m turning right on a red light, chances are there will be someone inching slowly toward the intersection with their thumbs furiously smashing against the glass of their iPhone, oblivious to the fact that I am planning to drive into the parcel of land they are currently occupying. It’s not just that this behavior is dangerous. It’s alsodeeply annoying. I’m forced to pay attention for both of us, like I’m a guardian angel or the arbiter of whether you, the clueless phone person, live or die. Sure, I might briefly get off on the power trip of having such authority over our mutual safety, but I’d much rather be thinking about where to have dinner instead of how long I should wait to honk at the drooling simpleton preventing me from turning.Distracted Italian pedestrians who cross road while on phone could be fined under new codeRead moreI applaud the Italian government for their forward thinking. Actually, I think it’s time we criminalize more small annoyances. Such as …Using a ringtoneSomeone please explain to me why anyone bothers with leaving their ringer on. We are decades past the era when, for a dollar, you could buy that Crazy Frog song and impress your friends every time you got a call. Now, it’s just pure sonic detritus, clogging up our ears with aural poison – bleeps, bloops, pings and plops. When AMC Theaters tells an auditorium full of grown adults to silence their phones before a movie, all I can think is: “Unless they’re an on-call heart surgeon, their phone should always be silent.”Fine amount: $200Interrupting me when I’m not done talkingI understand and accept that I have a lot to say. I make my meager living from writing, so pontificating just comes naturally to me. Sometimes, I wish it didn’t. But most of the time, what I’m saying is pretty important and you should be listening. Not waiting for your turn. I just listened to you try to captivate me with a treatise on gender roles in Christopher Nolan’s films. I respected you, even if I didn’t want to. Either let me finish or you’re fined!Fine amount: $200Not pushing in your chair when stepping away from a table at a restaurantWould you like to see the server at your favorite Olive Garden location break their tibia because you left your chair in the middle of a walkway? If that’s what you think of our restaurant industry workers, I’ve got a mind to go outside to my patio and bang on some pots and pans like it’s Covid lockdown to thank everyone carrying a plate of shrimp scampi who has to avoid rude customers. When you get up from your table, push in your chair. It takes two seconds and it could save a life … and a plate of delicious pasta.Fine amount: $250Riding an electric scooter on the sidewalkI would like to remind everyone that scooters from companies such as Lime and Lyft explicitly say to not ride these vehicles on the sidewalk. The sidewalk is called a sidewalk because it, much likeNancy Sinatra’s boots, was made for walking. A motorized conveyance doesn’t belong on the sidewalk, especially ones that actually can get some real speed behind them. Use the bike lane, for God’s sake. Or take the bus. Or anything else, really. It’s just beyond dangerous to be tooling around on a scooter while people are trying to go about their business.I mean, what if I’m looking at my phone and texting? Shame on you, scooter guy.Fine amount: $500Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsItalyOpinionEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: As a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriage | Nicholas Purcell  | The Guardian
description: Care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway
Content: Despite bitterness and distance, many marriages contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out, writes Nicholas Purcell.Photograph: Prostock-studio/AlamyView image in fullscreenDespite bitterness and distance, many marriages contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out, writes Nicholas Purcell.Photograph: Prostock-studio/AlamyThe modern mindMarriageAs a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriageNicholas PurcellCare and attention, the fundamentals to keep relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anywayThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.19 EDTShareI’ve killed every garden I’ve neglected, which is all of them: bring me a struggling houseplant and watch it die. But bring me a struggling marriage and I will sometimes encourage it back to life. Other times, when the conditions are right, by which I mean when something is wrong, I will kill it. Intentionally. Or, in more professional language, I will advise it to end. Not every plant gets to flower. Not every marriage should be saved.I have come to realise that care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway. I call them cactus marriages: alive, but I couldn’t tell you how.Jess* and Pete* came to see me: they had raised their kids and always turned up for their jobs – at least with work someone writes down what is required of you. Neglect, it turns out, takes longer to kill a marriage than it does a garden. When couples remember how to be loving, the cactus thrives, and sometimes it even flowers, which surprises everyone, including me.But not every struggling marriage I see is a neglected cactus. Sometimes the soil has gone sour. And sometimes the roots have been severed, intentionally, and no water reaches a severed root. From across the room, neglect and its harder cousins, soured and severed, look the same: quiet and unhappy. Up close, the difference is everything.Sour soil looks like Diane* and Thomas*, married more than 30 years, whose fighting had become a script neither could stop performing. She raised her voice. He corrected her grammar. She brought up his breath. A trade economy where no one wins. There was no innocent party in that room.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsUnderneath, this is mechanical failure. Contempt has become the default; the repair cycle – the small, ordinary apologies healthy couples make without noticing – has broken down and nothing is ever absorbed. But sour soil can be sweetened. Good gardeners do it all the time.This is the marriage I fight for because it so nearly wasn’t necessary; if only they had come in sooner, before the habit hardened into the marriage’s personality. Despite bitterness and distance, these marriages often contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out. And the honest news is that they are probably repairable if both are committed, and the equally honest news is that the window does not stay open for ever.I am burnt out from emotionally supporting my husband. Should I leave him? | Leading questionsRead moreThe severed root marriage is different. This marriage houses a person clinicians have names for: narcissist, abuser, controller, none of which quite closes over the thing itself: a way of being that depends on the other not fully having a self, let alone flourishing. These are the marriages you won’t see on TV shows like Couples Therapy: the erosion of a life that’s hard to capture on film. The soured marriage saddens me; this one disturbs me.The marriage with two people behaving badly worries me less than the marriage with one person doing real harm. Here the question is not how to love better. It is when to leave.An ordinary-looking couple came to me, Michael* and Liz*. It had begun small enough to mistake for love: his need to know where she was. He counted the seconds it took her to answer his texts. The tracking devices came next. Before long he was throwing her against walls, and worse. I challenged Michael privately: is your behaviour making your marriage more or less likely to last? His head turned to me, his breathing slowed and his eyes went black, the light stopped coming back out of them. I hesitate to use the word evil, but I’ve sat with it, there isn’t a better one. It is the look of someone who does not care whether you are alive, or whether they are the reason you stop being.This is not a relationship with a problem, the relationship is the problem. This marriage’s continuation requires one person’s diminishment, one person’s harm. To stay is a form of self-erasure. For anyone inside one, couples therapy is the wrong tool entirely. When only one person is being hurt, calling it “our relationship issues” launders the harm, and can keep a person in danger for years while they wait to become a better communicator.Almost everyone inside a marriage like this does the arithmetic and gets it wrong, not because they are foolish, but because the sums are rigged. The cost of leaving is concrete: money, housing, the children and even shame. The cost of staying is paid invisibly, in instalments of health and the self that keeps getting smaller. And the children, so often the reason given for staying, are there, absorbing what a husband is and what a wife is, and how one is allowed to treat the other.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo let me say it plainly, because this kind of marriage depends on it never being said plainly: some relationships must be left.But leaving is not the same as safe. The part people rush past, because it’s frightening to hear: the time around leaving is often when this kind of partner is most dangerous. Which is exactly when you need a safety plan, a domestic violence service, a friend or counsellor who knows the whole truth, not the version that’s easiest to say out loud.Liz left Michael. She survived. He repartnered.Sometimes I advise couples to end their marriage.*All clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. The Domestic Violence hotline is 1800 RESPECT.In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.orgNicholas Purcell is a relationship psychotherapist based in Adelaide. He is writing Raising Love, on why our theory of love is broken – and what an active one looks likeExplore more on these topicsMarriageThe modern mindRelationshipsFamilyDomestic violencePsychologycommentShareReuse this content

title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Content: The OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AIGene MarksSmall business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what worksSun 30 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTShareOne thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many casessquandered– by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.An AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene MarksRead moreWhat works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.Small businesses are watching. And now doing.A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.Big companies have also begun to discover theastronomical computingcosts that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companiesthrow away billonson large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.For months, onearnings callsand investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring,only to hirethose same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman,recently admittedthat their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)US small businesscommentShareReuse this content

title: How young women can learn to better wield economic power | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects
Content: Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. The results proved remarkable.Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreenGroups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. The results proved remarkable.Photograph: MBI/AlamyEconomics viewpointWomenHow young women can learn to better wield economic powerHeather StewartProject in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospectsSun 30 Aug 2026 10.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.06 EDTShareWomen making their way in patriarchal societies down the ages have always had to wield their meagre economic power deftly.New evidencefrom a fascinating research project in Zambia suggests that’s a skill that can be learned.A team of female US academics have been gathering data for more than a decade, which shows that teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects.Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks – delivered by local young women who had completed their schooling and had been closely involved in developing the curriculum.Follow-up analysis suggests the girls who took these lessons are continuing to reap economic benefits, more than a decade later.Measured against a control group, who were given “empowerment” classes by the same coaches, but without the negotiation work, the young women tended to stay in school longer; were more likely to graduate from college; and less likely to marry a much older man.Britain is paying the price for failing to invest in its young people | Richard PartingtonRead moreProf Corinne Low, whose day job is teaching economics at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, has been involved in the project from its inception. She says back then that the Zambian government was interested in understanding what was preventing girls from attending secondary school.Low and her colleagues carried out focus groups, suspecting they might hear that girls found school boring. Instead, participants told them they were keen to attend, but unable to convince their parents or other relatives to pay the fees.“There was misunderstanding in the relationships that they had – it would be, ‘I know that my son is going to help support me,’ or, ‘my son is going to look out for the family, but my daughter, she’s going to get into trouble with boys.’”That convinced Low and colleague Nava Ashraf that the girls could benefit from similar negotiating skills to those taught, in a very different context, to sharp-elbowed MBA students in the US.The most important insight in the six two-hour classes, she says, is that instead of seeing the person you’re negotiating with as an enemy, a more successful approach is to understand their perspective, and tackle problems together.“We really emphasised this sort of understanding somebody else’s interests; understanding somebody else’s problems,” she says.It’s an idea that would be familiar to former trade union negotiators Louise Haigh and Angela Rayner, now two of the most powerful women in the UK government.“You can’t just go in and tell these girls: ‘You have to stay in school.’ You need to give them tools that are actually going to change the outcomes here,” Low says.Perhaps counterintuitively, given the ultimate aim is female empowerment, the content of the curriculum also leant heavily on the need for respecting the reality of existing hierarchies – for now at least.“In Zambia, there was a lot of generational hierarchy and it was really important to show respect for parents. We talked to the girls and said: ‘If you’re going to approach your parents to ask them for something, what are some of the ways you show respect?’ And they said: ‘Oh well, I might kneel down, and I might address them formally, and I might wear a traditional wrapper – a chitenge.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The irony is, right – what kind of empowerment programme is teaching girls to kneel down?” she laughs. But she adds: “The reality is that these girls do not have the power in their household and we can’t pretend that they do.”Subsequent surveys showed the girls’ parents felt their relationships had improved. “The parents recorded that the girls were more respectful, were more likely to do chores around the household, that they were more understanding,” Low recalls.She and her colleagues are now working towards a 15-year follow-up with that original cohort, now women in their 20s; but their approach has since been incorporated into the Zambian curriculum, and replicated in several other countries.Most recently – and strikingly –the NGO Free to Runhas been using an adapted version of the material in online classes that have recently reached about 1,200 girls in Afghanistan, whose lives and opportunities have been brutally curtailed by the Taliban.While almost all prospect of economic advancement for them is blocked, Sana Mahmud, the charity’s global programmes manager, says the curriculum is helping young women to manage their mental health, and to achieve small freedoms in the grim context of the regime.“It’s a very useful skill inside the household to negotiate with parents, even if it’s small things like permission to visit a friend,” she says.And she adds: “Sometimes the young women would leave their homes to go out in the market or do errands, and some of them have even been stopped by members of the Taliban to ask: ‘Why are you here? What are you doing?’ and we realised that the skill of negotiation is probably the best for them to safely talk about what they’re doing, why they’re there.” The course is taught by four Afghan women, and feedback from participants has been “amazing”, Mahmud says.Of course, the wider economic and political system matters far more than each woman’s success in navigating her way through it, and the situation inAfghanistanis bleak. We should all be working towards a world in which the patriarchy is – as the placards and pin badges have it – smashed.But giving more girls skills that might help them further their own interests in the world as it is today seems a wise investment in that future.Explore more on these topicsWomenEconomics viewpointWomen in the boardroomGenderZambiaEconomicsAfricaAfghanistancommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the rise of Germany’s AfD: mainstream parties must deliver a bolder response | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The far right is close to winning a state election for the first time since the second world war. A different economic approach is needed to combat it
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The far right is close to winning a state election for the first time since the second world war. A different economic approach is needed to combat it
Content: Police officers guard a counterprotest during an Alternative für Deutschland campaign rally in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers guard a counterprotest during an Alternative für Deutschland campaign rally in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersOpinionGermanyThe Guardian view on the rise of Germany’s AfD: mainstream parties must deliver a bolder responseEditorialThe far right is close to winning a state election for the first time since the second world war. A different economic approach is needed to combat itSun 30 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe early autumn has become a time of foreboding and angst in German politics. In the eastern states that have become strongholds for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, it has regularly made headline-grabbing advances in September elections. Only the refusal of mainstream politicians to form coalitions with one of Europe’s most extreme movements has kept it out of power.This year, the lights are flashing red. Next weekend, when voters in Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots, thesignsare that the traditional firewall may not be enough. In polling, the AfD is currentlyscoringabove 40% in the state, which could win it enough seats to govern on its own. Compared with the last election in 2021, its support has doubled; backing for the closest challenger, the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has tumbled by almost 15%.View image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ ShutterstockThose are startling and alarming figures. Since the second world war, none of Germany’s 16 Länder have been governed by the far right, and in office the AfD would exercise substantial powers over education, policing and culture. The Saxony-Anhalt party – which wasclassifiedas a threat to democracy by the security services – haspledgedto fully exploit them. The party’s manifesto proposes policies such as the segregation of refugee children in separate schools (in violation of EU law), a nationalist curriculum that would shift the focus away from the Nazi period, and the championing of the “normal family” over “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles”.Whatever the outcome next weekend, the AfD’s sustained lead innationalpolls suggests a reckoning is at hand for mainstream parties. Postwar politics in Germany has, for obvious reasons, been founded on a horror of extreme nationalism and a focus on consensus and compromise. But more than one in four voters currently back a party that hasdiscusseda programme of mass “remigration”, which could include passport-carrying citizens deemed to have a “non-German” background.This stark reality has led tosuggestionsthat the taboo on cooperation with the AfD should be dropped, on the basis that exposing the party to the practical realities of governing would reveal the emptiness of its populist promises. That would be a strategy born of desperation and one carrying great risks, not least for the minorities at the sharp end of the experiment. But there is little doubt that despiteattemptsto ape the far right’s draconian stance on immigration, the political approach being pursued by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government is not working.As elsewhere in Europe, support for the far right is mostconcentratedin the ailing industrial regions that were once a source of pride and identity, as well as prosperity. Yet as the country suffers from the double whammy of Chinese competition and US protectionism, Mr Merz’s focus on tax cuts, welfare reform andraisingthe retirement age is signally failing to address the crisis afflicting Europe’s largest economy.While campaigning in 2018 to become leader of the CDU, the chancellor pledged to halve the AfD’s vote. Support for it has instead doubled. Mr Merz’s own popularity ratings are at a record low for any chancellor, while his coalition partner, the Social Democratic party, is faring just as badly in the polls. A vote next weekend freighted with ominous symbolism will send yet another message to a failing political class that it needs to rethink its priorities.Explore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightFriedrich MerzeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution
Content: A rare-earths mine in China. ‘Last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war … by the curbing of rare-earth exports.’Photograph: Imaginechina Limited/AlamyView image in fullscreenA rare-earths mine in China. ‘Last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war … by the curbing of rare-earth exports.’Photograph: Imaginechina Limited/AlamyOpinionCritical mineralsThe Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chainsEditorialOutsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solutionSun 30 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, Chinablocked exports of key rare earths to Japanin a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about70% of rare-earth miningglobally and 90% of separation and processing.Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, hasalready jumpedbecause of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.The 17 metals known as rare earthsare far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing arecostly, complexand often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedlyflowing to Asiabecause of the lack of domestic demand. While“Big shovel”is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worthless than $6bn globallylast year.Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it wouldspend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chainsas a “Manhattan Project”for rare earths. Othersquestionthe strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular,Brazil, raising grave concernabout the ecological impact. Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them frommining wasteor runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive.Earlier this year, the USlaunched a critical minerals coalitionwith 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland.Stockpilesof essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to thebiggest facilityoutside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals isunder discussion. But many fear that European countries are movingtoo slowly. That must change.Explore more on these topicsCritical mineralsOpinionMiningChinaEuropean UnionDonald TrumpEuropeeditorialsShareReuse this content

Content: One reader says improving public transport outside cities and towns would enable more people to experience the countryside.Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreenOne reader says improving public transport outside cities and towns would enable more people to experience the countryside.Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFWalkingLettersMaking the British countryside more accessible and inviting to allReaders respond to an article by John Harris on the diversity of hikers in the Peak DistrictSun 30 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareWhat a joy to read John Harris’s piece on the cultural changes taking place in rural areas (Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England, 23 August. title: Why solar bonds are a bright idea | Solar power | The Guardian
description: Letter: A financial model that could cut the cost of installing solar panels for many homeowners is welcomed by Alexis Abramson
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: A financial model that could cut the cost of installing solar panels for many homeowners is welcomed by Alexis Abramson
Content: ‘A household that can pay for solar upfront saves money from day one.’Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A household that can pay for solar upfront saves money from day one.’Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesSolar powerLettersWhy solar bonds are a bright ideaA financial model that could cut the cost of installing solar panels for many homeowners is welcomed byAlexis AbramsonSun 30 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTShareThe UK proposal to use “solar bonds” to make rooftop solar more affordable is a smart solution to a fundamental problem: the rising cost of capital (Cut cost of loans for solar panels on UK homes, ministers urged, 21 August).A household that can pay for solar upfront saves money from day one. For everyone else, high-interest financing can consume much of those savings and ultimately deter people from installing the technology. A solar bond structure changes that equation: investors receive a modest, guaranteed return, and homeowners get access to cheaper capital. Because the loan is attached to the property rather than the individual, there’s no issue if the person moves.The model is worth considering in the US too. Leases and power purchase agreements already let homeowners install solar with no money down, and green banks in states like Connecticut and New York offer below-market loans. But leases mean homeowners never own the system, forfeiting long-term savings, and even the best green bank loans are attached to the borrower, not the home. A solar bond wouldn’t replace these tools; it would fill the gap they leave.The bond mechanism itself isn’t a stretch – it’s similar to the state and municipal bonds already financing infrastructure, just retail-facing and earmarked for solar. The bigger challenge is repayment. The UK can tie the standing charge on a national energy bill, while the US has thousands of utilities with different rate structures. That makes a federal programme harder, but a state-by-state approach is realistic.The need is growing. The 30% residential solar tax creditexpiredat the end of 2025, as did the federal Solar for All programme. States that build this now won’t just be filling a financing gap; they’ll be shaping what energy independence looks like over the next decade.Alexis AbramsonDean, Columbia Climate School, USExplore more on these topicsSolar powerEnergyRenewable energyEnergy billsHousehold billslettersShareReuse this content

title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Simon Nieder on the global efforts needed to curb the threats posed by AI. Plus letters from Dr Anthony Harris and David Kyler
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Simon Nieder on the global efforts needed to curb the threats posed by AI. Plus letters from Dr Anthony Harris and David Kyler
Content: ‘AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control.’Photograph: pingingz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control.’Photograph: pingingz/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)LettersAI’s worst disasters will arrive unannouncedDr Simon Niederon the global efforts needed to curb the threats posed by AI.Plus letters fromDr Anthony HarrisandDavid KylerSun 30 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareTimothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.Dr Simon NiederChesterfield, DerbyshireProf Jonathan Michie (Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’sperceptronof 1957, to theDartmouth workshopof 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.Dr Anthony HarrisEmmanuel College, CambridgeIn his article about regulating AI (I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention aninternational effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at theinaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governancein Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillanceA fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.David KylerSaint Simons Island, Georgia, USHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The lost art of guilt-free relaxation on Sundays | Happiness | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article about le dimanche français, the French Sunday, being the secret to happiness
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article about le dimanche français, the French Sunday, being the secret to happiness
Content: ‘Sunday was the same day of the week for everyone. That made a difference. The whole atmosphere was quieter.’Photograph: AnnaStills/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Sunday was the same day of the week for everyone. That made a difference. The whole atmosphere was quieter.’Photograph: AnnaStills/Getty Images/iStockphotoHappinessLettersThe lost art of guilt-free relaxation on SundaysReaders respond to an article aboutle dimanche français,the French Sunday, being the secret to happinessSun 30 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTShareWhat Polly Hudson describes asle dimanche françaisis almost a description of the very British Sundays of my youth (Is a French Sunday the secret to a healthier, happier life?, 23 August). Sundays were days of guilt-free relaxation. There was time to enjoy the company of family, and sometimes close friends, with no time constraints.We enjoyed a good book (not a heavy one), an afternoon film on TV, board games, cards, or a gentle stroll for the pleasure of it rather than as part of a keep-fit regime. And let us not forget time to peruse the Sunday newspapers. Children got bored and learned how to entertain themselves, a skill today’s hard-pressed parents underestimate as they struggle to ensure Sundays are packed with activities.There were no home computers and shops were closed, as were cinemas, swimming pools, theme parks and even pubs in certain parts of the country. This was occasionally frustrating, but more usually an advantage, removing the temptation to feel like one ought to be doing something, thus enhancing a guilt-free mindset. It was wonderful.Importantly, it was the same day of the week for everyone. That made a difference. The whole atmosphere was quieter.So what changed? My impression is that the whole rhythm of the week changed with Sunday trading. I’m not sure a younger generation would even recognise the phrase. Oh, were it possible to go back.Old-fashioned Sundays were greeted with relief and the expectation of relaxation. No pressures, no guilt, time to just be. They were indeed rejuvenating – and necessary.The economy probably couldn’t withstand the country going back to shops closing on a Sunday. Perhaps what we need is a youthful social media influencer to promote reclaiming a nationwide “old-fashioned Sunday”. No posting on Sundays though.Siân DudleyIvybridge, DevonI’m French and I was happy to read an article about the beauty of the French Sunday. But for most people I know, including myself, it’s not necessarily a day for lazing around. The beauty of it lies in the fact that it is a day when shopping is not an option because the stores are usually closed, except for bakeries in the morning. That forces people to do other things such as take a walk in the forest, play a board game or share an extended meal.It is a day for enjoying what you have at hand rather than longing for more things that you believe will make you a happier person, but that distract you from the genuine joys of life.I’m not in any way immune to the appeal of mass consumption, but I do enjoy being forcedly taken out of its reach by the existence ofle dimanche français, which I can confirm no one calls it.Benjamin LescoffierAnnecy, FranceI have lived in France for five years and it took a bit of getting used to French Sundays – no nipping out to the supermarket in the afternoon as they are all closed. The village boulangerie is open all day, thankfully, and therôtisseurwho sells his roast chickens from a little stall outside the bakery does brisk business – better be there early. It’s a day for visiting friends and family or entertaining, but entertaining made easy with the chicken already prepared by therôtisseur.Carolyn DyerLézan, FranceWe have lived half the year in France for over 10 years. That the French cherish Sundays for relaxation is accurate, but you have omitted the major Sunday event:le déjeuner. This is typically a six-hour event beginning atmidi. Families and friends gather at home or at a local restaurant to share a multicourse meal, an abundance of wine and marathon conversations.I have marvelled at how the children sit attentively at the table, skilfully juggling utensils as each course arrives. They eat what is served for adults, and participate in the conversation like their elders. The meal is consumed slowly – leaving time in between courses to exchange news and stories.By about 6pm, as the event closes, one need only return home for a siesta. This is why nobody does anything and nothing gets done on Sundays in France.Kathleen GallagherBainbridge Island, Washington, USI remember the songLes enfants s’ennuient le dimanche, sung by Charles Trenet in the film L’Argent de poche by François Truffaut. It described exactly these Sundays, which at the time were not only a French phenomenon, but found in a lot of other European countries.In Austria, where I was born and have lived for the past 65 years, that’s still the case, thank God. No open shops, maybe a lie-in, late breakfast, then lunch with wider family (grandparents, old aunts) or an outing somewhere close to home.I also remember my grandmother tut-tutting when she saw the neighbour’s laundry still on the line on a Saturday evening.Church is definitely not so much on the agenda. I have just come home from a lovely afternoon with my children and grandchildren, spent at the races in a spa town just outside Vienna. Oh what fun we had!Brigitte Strohmeier-HoferWiener Neustadt, AustriaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
