title: Welcome to Ozball, the low-key story of a low-key England summer | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ollie Robinson’s metronomic medium-nip represents the new age – sometimes, you just get the heroes you need
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Ollie Robinson’s metronomic medium-nip represents the new age – sometimes, you just get the heroes you need
Content: Ollie Robinson and his England teammates succesffully appeal for the wicket of Mohammad Rizwan lbw.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOllie Robinson and his England teammates succesffully appeal for the wicket of Mohammad Rizwan lbw.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEngland v Pakistan 2026AnalysisWelcome to Ozball, the low-key story of a low-key England summerBarney Ronayat Lord'sOllie Robinson’s metronomic medium-nip represents the new age – sometimes, you just get the heroes you needSun 30 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareEach age makes its own heroes. Two hours from the end of the final day of the second-last Test at the fag‑end of the post‑Bazball summer, the cheer from the Lord’s crowd at deep fine leg had something pointed about it, a crackle of event glamour.Ollie Robinson turned as he ambled back and raised an arm in gladiatorial salute. “Oh Ollie Ollie, Ollie Ollie Ollie Ollie Robinson” was the response from a scattered, woozy swell, again with something arch and transgressive in it, the smell of anti-hero.What are you rebelling against, Johnny? What have you got?Also, if you really want to know, buzzword culture and enforced fitness regimes. Sometimes, you just get the heroes you need.Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue roll over Pakistan to give England series winRead moreMoments earlier, with the Lord’s clock at 3.59pm, Robinson had struck Shan Masood on the front pad and stood with his arms out, bellowing plaintively, the appeal of a man who really, really wants to get back for Call the Midwife and a peri-peri chicken throb-box meal deal.From the start this had been a Test that was less about what was going to happen, more just the question of when. Still, there was drama here, and confirmation of an extraordinary turnaround this summer for the bad boy of metronomic medium-nip.Robinson took four of the nine wickets needed to complete England’s 2-0 series win 45 minutes before the close. In doing so he took his own tally to 23 at eight across the two home Test series. Here it is then, the new age, replacement, in double-quick time, for the previous new age. Welcome to the summer of Ozball.Robinson was irresistible again en route to his four for 24, rumbling in from the Nursery End, bulky and quietly menacing, like a wardrobe rolling gently down a hill. It is all so simple in outline. The easy, high action, the perfect seam release, head up, already feeling the pitch in his fingertips, seeking out that zinging, fizzing contact. Stump to stump, every millimetre of movement in play. Simple. You try doing it.As we enter the new age, perhaps we need a new kind of absurd absolutism, a world where the managing director of England cricket makes a passionate speech about needing a battery of slow-medium-nip bowlers, or thumps his palm and declares thatnotdoodling it in with the keeper up to the stumps has absolutely no place in Test cricket.The one shame here was that Robinson ended on 99 Test wickets, taking them now at the astonishing average of 19. He really does deserve a nickname by this stage. The Butcher of Margate. The Sussex Strangler. Perhaps a variation on the great fast‑bowling monikers. White Drizzle. Whispering Chronic Illness. The Hove Stopping Train. Pace Like Air Conditioning.Plus, once Robinson gets to that hundred-wicket mark he will be officially the greatest Test bowler since the first world war. Kind of. OK, not really. But the numbers are still mind-boggling.The main case for Robinson-as-GOAT is simple enough. No pace bowler since the 19th century has ended their career with 100 wickets at a lower average. And yes, others have got to that mark at a similar rate, but Robinson is 32, he’s not got to have any real decline. This is him.Either way he can now claim to be an all-time Test great, and nobody can really argue, or why even bother with the numbers? Odd to think Robinson was dropped a few games back because Rob Key likes pace, along with some not‑being‑the‑right-kind-of-guy stuff. He’s very good. Get the best out of him. That’s the job.Here Robinson took the new ball in the fourth innings, and just kept on looming up to the stumps like a weather front barreling in off the Ramsgate coast. There was an amusingly forthright send-off for Abdullah Shafique, knocked over by an unplayable nipp‑backer, the kind of delivery where the batter’s shape makes the moment, turned around, playing for logic, the actual line, and getting instead magic, weirdness, parallax error.View image in fullscreenSaud Shakeel’s classy innings of 97 lifted some of the gloom for Pakistan at Lord’s.Photograph: Jay Patel/SPP/ShutterstockAt that point Robinson had six for 13 in the match, and you thought, well, why not 13 for 13? Would Pakistan actually score another run here? In the end a total of 194 was built around a splendid 97 from Saud Shakeel, who played beautifully, all swivel‑pulls and courtly, kneeling cover drives, the kind of shot that brings a digestive mid-afternoon gurgle from the crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOtherwise it was another slow-burn day in a slow-burn summer, a day for asking, what does it mean, why this, why here? Lord’s on an autumn Sunday will do this to you. The entire Lord’s industrial complex is full of places that feel like jarring tautologies. Lord’s Museum. Lord’s Gin Bar. Lord’s Picnic Garden. It’s fine. You can just say “Lord’s”. What else is it but a gin-soaked picnic museum? You might as well make a sign saying welcome to the Lord’s red-trousered men assembly point, the Lord’s cultural ossification hub.There is an issue here with the dominance of bowling, and above all a certain kind of bowling. Earlier in the day Mohammad Abbas could be seen kneeling at the edge of the square and kissing the reddish scrub of the Lord’s outfield, a beautiful spectacle, a man giving thanks to the god of crap Test pitches, in praise of shit-tip Jehovah, spirit guide of his own remarkable Test figures.Joe Root urges England to celebrate Pakistan series win in ‘sensible, grown-up way’Read moreThis is obviously unfair. Abbas is a brilliant bowler and a lovely guy. He’s on the honours board. He gets his wickets at 22, and in the best way, all brain, craft and skill. It is a method that has become very now. Look up the top nine lowest career bowling averages since the end of the 19th century and four of those nine have appeared in the past six years.These are: Robinson, Kyle Jamieson, Scott Boland and Axar Patel. All brilliant bowlers. All with the same basic method: fizzed straight stuff to Test batters who can’t deal with it. Look back over the summer of Ozball, and Abbas, Robinson and Matt Henry together have 45 wickets at 12, keeper stood up, front pads blowing up, crowd gripped by the spectacle of low-level apocalypse.Test cricket should be a bowler’s game. It is even more this with data analysis, raised seams and format confusion for batting techniques. As Ian Chappell said recently on the Grade Cricketer, there is very little financial incentive to become a great Test batsman now, no way we’re ever getting another Graham Gooch spending three winter months just working out how to defend his front pad.Maybe Bazball was right. Maybe we just need flat, quick pitches you can score on. Otherwise it’s Ozball, the age of high-craft jag and nip, and Test matches that become a race to the end, in more ways than one.Not that anyone minded much here, on a day where that Robinson redemption arc was confirmed as the low-key story of a low-key summer.Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Marcus Rashford’s Manchester United return feels like a marriage of convenience | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: A lack of offers and problems in finding a replacement may be behind the move, but that does not mean it cannot work
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: A lack of offers and problems in finding a replacement may be behind the move, but that does not mean it cannot work
Content: Marcus Rashford in action at Old Trafford for the first time since December 2024.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenMarcus Rashford in action at Old Trafford for the first time since December 2024.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester UnitedAnalysisMarcus Rashford’s Manchester United return feels like a marriage of convenienceWill Unwinat Old TraffordA lack of offers and problems in finding a replacement may be behind the move, but that does not mean it cannot workSun 30 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe first chant of the match was for Marcus Rashford, Manchester United’s returning rogue son, the one banished for 18 months, first to the Midlands and then Catalonia. Every football fan loves an academy product who has risen up the ranks, from scrawny child to getting 76,000 off their seats. Rashford is one of these, living out the dream of everyone inside Old Trafford and they are willing to forgive but want something in return.Not since 7 December 2024 has Rashford been seen in red at Old Trafford. Then it was as a substitute forlornly trying to turn things around in an eventual 3-2 defeat by Nottingham Forest. His relationship with Ruben Amorim was already deteriorating, the second head coach to have become irritated with Rashford. After loans with Aston Villa and Barcelona, everyone is surprised to see him back; it feels like a marriage of convenience because of a lack of offers and securing a replacement was deemed complex.Fernandes fires hat-trick as Manchester United fight back to thrash IpswichRead moreAt Hull, Rashford came on at the break for Patrick Dorgu after a dispiriting 45 minutes but floundered down blind alleys as he tried to spark a listless team into action. The truth is, Michael Carrick needs someone of Rashford’s experience and quality to be at the forefront of this latest attempt of building a successful era. He cannot have any off-field misdemeanours or sulking on the pitch when things are tough.Carrick is more willing to put an arm around the shoulder, understanding of the pressures that come with playing for United. That is increased when the situation is dire, being behind at home against a promoted club a week after being beaten by another. It is a test of character, one United have failed too often in recent times.Rashford’s ability has never been doubted: this is someone who did not look out of place at Barcelona and spent the summer playing for his country at the World Cup. In the buildup to the tournament, he went away and worked privately, inviting former teammates to help him to train in Miami, showing a dedication to his craft.At 28, he should be a leader and Carrick is giving him the opportunity to be one. United have the teenagers Shea Lacey and JJ Gabriel waiting for opportunities, and Rashford is someone they can learn from, having witnessed more than most. He started brightly against Ipswich on the left wing, with United eager to target Dara O’Shea on that side. Rashford can go either way, pushing past a defender to reach the byline or cut in. He tried both, creating dangerous situations with his crossing but without a striker capable of finding the finish.While Bruno Fernandes, rightly, takes the headlines with his hat‑trick, everyone knows United cannot rely on one man, however influential he may be. Following Fernandes’s example has not always been part of the Rashford playbook but seeing his influence on a team should offer some inspiration for the England international to reach the levels he and United expect. Rashford was certainly not at his best but his head remained high, making runs into dangerous areas, even if the chances of reaching the ball were somewhat forlorn.View image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes (right) could be an inspiration to Marcus Rashford.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APFinishing without a goal or assist when five were scored may irk Rashford but reputations cannot be rebuilt completely in 80 minutes. Willingness needs to be the bare minimum because it will be a long season for United and everyone will need to play their part. On another day, Bryan Mbeumo would not have turned Rashford’s cross on to the bar from a yard out or his saved shot would have beaten the goalkeeper.Against Hull, barely a clearcut chance was created as United fired blanks, but on Sunday, 33 shots were attempted, 11 of those on target. It was a display of greater intent, energy and productivity, but a long way from flawless as Ipswich were given chances to capitalise on. One reason United were able to cause problems in the second half was down to Rashford and Mbeumo being relentless, occupying defenders and, ultimately, tiring minds and legs with United in the ascendancy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Really pleased with Marcus, I am sure it was nice for him to be back and start games and be involved in a good performance,” Carrick said. “I thought he did particularly well in not easy circumstances. I thought he did all round good and will only get better.”Michael Carrick hails Manchester United’s grit after rout of IpswichRead moreRashford is United’s No 9 in squad number only, as Carrick is opting to use Benjamin Sesko from the start. When the Slovene is fully fit, a different dimension will be added to the attack, a player used to finishing crosses, which will help Rashford – and others – to thrive. After a year alongside Robert Lewandowski, Rashford is used to having a clinical finisher waiting for service and having an out-and-out striker would benefit him.Even if few expected Rashford and United to continue their alliance, they are back together. Harmony is not completely restored but both have shown they can make things work,; the affection is evident. The good times and the bad are remembered by both, from the debut goals against Midtjylland to the fallout with Amorim, Rashford’s United story is a rich tapestry, spanning his entire life, and it is not over yet.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMarcus RashfordIpswich TownanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Mikel Arteta ‘begging’ Premier League to expand 20-man matchday squads | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: The Arsenal manager wants the Premier League to allow bigger matchday squads to bring the competition in line with Serie A and La Liga
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: The Arsenal manager wants the Premier League to allow bigger matchday squads to bring the competition in line with Serie A and La Liga
Content: Mikel Arteta believes larger matchday squads will help with players’ mental wellbeing.Photograph: Ian Stephen/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta believes larger matchday squads will help with players’ mental wellbeing.Photograph: Ian Stephen/Every Second Media/ShutterstockArsenalMikel Arteta ‘begging’ Premier League to expand 20-man matchday squadsArsenal manager says dropping players ‘affects wellbeing’Serie A allows 25-player matchday squads and La Liga 23Sam CunninghamSun 30 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal have asked thePremier Leagueto increase the size of matchday squads, with Mikel Arteta saying the current system is detrimental to player welfare. Top‑flight clubs can name 20 players for games, including a minimum of three homegrown players. In Spain’s La Liga, clubs can name a matchday squad of 23, while Italy’s Serie A allows 25.Arsenal have competed on multiple fronts in recent seasons. Last year, as well as winning the Premier League, they reached the finals of theChampions LeagueandCarabao Cup, as well as the quarter-finals of the FA Cup. With pressure increasing on the football calendar and players facing more matches, Arteta sees no reason why English teams should operate with smaller squads than those from other European leagues.Who was given the toughest fixtures in the Champions League draw?Read more“I’ve been begging the Premier League if we can extend those numbers just for the welfare of the players, which is the most important thing, because I think every squad needs more than 20 outfield players, ideally, to sustain the level of demand in international games that we have,” Arteta said, as he prepares for the champions’ trip to Aston Villa on Monday night. “But these are the rules, and within the rules we have to play. We need to be very close to the players to explain those situations in the right way, for everybody to feel important, because they will be.”Clubs can register a squad of 25 senior players – those aged over 21 – for the season, with at least eight homegrown. As a result, five senior players registered for the season miss out each game. Arteta has said it can be difficult to tell players they are not involved and that the news can negatively affect their wellbeing.“The question has to be to the players. What do they want? If they raise their hands and say: ‘No, I prefer to stay at home and not travel,’ I think we have an issue because then they don’t love what they do, which is the matchday,” he said. “But I’m sure that if you ask the players, everybody would like to be part of the squad on matchday, because that’s the way that they can fulfil themselves.“Otherwise you have to tell somebody: ‘You are not even part of this matchday,’ and that’s really tough. And it doesn’t help anybody. It doesn’t help the club. It doesn’t help the valuation of the player. It doesn’t help the player feel part of something. It’s a real issue that has a really simple solution.”Arteta added: “And all the clubs, because I’ve done the research with all the top clubs in Europe, we are not different to anybody. Most of them, 90% of them, they have more players than us. So we are going to have to deal with that.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetaPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Transfer roundup: Ollie Watkins completes move to Al-Hilal from Aston Villa | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: The England forward Ollie Watkins has completed a move from Aston Villa to Al-Hilal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The England forward Ollie Watkins has completed a move from Aston Villa to Al-Hilal
Content: Ollie Watkins has completed his switch to Al-Hilal.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenOllie Watkins has completed his switch to Al-Hilal.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PATransfer windowTransfer roundup: Ollie Watkins completes move to Al-Hilal from Aston VillaEngland forward’s exit continues busy summer for VillaNews follows Emiliano Martínez moving to ChelseaAssociated PressSun 30 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAl-Hilal have signedOllie WatkinsfromAston Villa, ⁠the two clubs announced on Sunday, as the 30-year-old striker ended a successful ⁠six-year spell with ⁠the ​Midlands club where he became their top scorer in the Premier League. The England international, who had ​two years left on ‌his Villa contract, has moved for a reported £51m.Watkins ‌signed a three-year contract asAl-Hilalacquired ‌a proven goalscorer after he scored 21 goals in all competitions last season, including five goals in the Europa League as he helped deliver a European trophy to Unai Emery’s side.However, an ‌exit was on the cards before the transfer window closed, with Emery revealing the ​striker had apologised for making himself unavailable for the club’s Premier League opener, a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.Watkins scored 91 Premier League goals for Villa and 108 ⁠in all competitions since arriving from Brentford for £28m in ​2020. The striker is among ​a string of departures from Villa ​in the ‌close season following ​the ​exits of key players such as Morgan Rogers and Emi Martinez to Chelsea –the latter moving on Sunday– Ezri Konsa to Arsenal and Youri Tielemans to Manchester United.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Roma have stepped up their Serie A challenge with the acquisition of two captains, midfielderMarten De Rooncoming over from Atalanta and centre-backLeonardo Balerdijoining from Marseille. The 35-year-old De Roon evolved into Atalanta’s skipper after a decade spent in Bergamo over two spells. He will reunite with Roma’s manager Gian Piero Gasperini, who formerly coached him at Atalanta.And the former Serie A MVPRafael Leãohas completed a €38m transfer from Milan to Galatasaray. The Turkish side confirmed a deal for the Portugal winger, signing him to a four-year contract with a net salary of €10m per season.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowAston VillaAl-HilalSaudi Pro LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea hold off Brighton in 4-3 win but remain chaotic under Xabi Alonso | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Cole Palmer eventually made the home win safe after Brighton rallied from 3-0 down, with João Pedro scoring at both ends
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Cole Palmer eventually made the home win safe after Brighton rallied from 3-0 down, with João Pedro scoring at both ends
Content: Cole Palmer (right) continued his fine start to the season with what proved to be a vital fourth goal for Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersView image in fullscreenCole Palmer (right) continued his fine start to the season with what proved to be a vital fourth goal for Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersPremier LeagueChelsea hold off Brighton in 4-3 win but remain chaotic under Xabi AlonsoJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeSun 30 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the fullness of timeChelsea’s surrender against Brighton in Aprilmay be seen as the turning point. The humiliation accelerated Liam ­Rosenior’s demise and forced the Stamford Bridge hierarchy into a ­reckoning leading to the appointment of Xabi Alonso, a shift in ­transfer ­strategy, the birth of the JP Morgan front three and the end of ­Robert Sánchez’s time in goal.For now, though, the argument that Emiliano Martínez is the final piece in the jigsaw seems a touch ­premature. With seven goals scored and five conceded while winning their first two league games, it is not hard to see whereChelseaneed to improve in order to sustain a title challenge. They have to be savvier when ahead, and although the good has so far outweighed the bad Alonso could do with his side not dropping their guard when they have the ­opposition on the ropes.Alonso’s cool disappeared as ­Chelsea’s focus dipped after they went 3-0 up against an injury‑hit Brighton inside 32 minutes. ­Stamford Bridge was anxious when a João Pedro own‑goal cut the ­advantage to one just after the hour. Alonso was ­shouting at his bench and it was only when Cole Palmer scored with 16 minutes left that calm was restored.View image in fullscreenXabi Alonso has won his first two league games as Chelsea manager, but neither have been what you would call relaxing.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersNot for long, mind you, given that Brighton still managed to grab a consolation through Pascal Gross deep into added time.It was that kind of game, Martínez conceding three despite playing well on his debut after joining from Aston Villa for £7.5m. “We can hurt teams,” the Argentina goalkeeper said. “At the back, we need to bring the goals down.”Alonso agreed. Chelsea have been thrilling in transition – they beat Fulham with 37% possession last Monday and had only 26% against Brighton – but they must tighten up when they visit Arsenal next Sunday.Equally, few sights will be more captivating this season than Palmer combining with João Pedro and ­Morgan Rogers in attack. Palmer looks refreshed after a summer off and Chelsea will be dangerous when games turn into shootouts. They have so many ways to score. The hope is that there will be more stability with Martínez in position.Alonso did not hesitate to start Martínez, even though the ­Argentinian lacks match ­practice and joined on Friday. “He felt ready,” Alonso said of Martínez, the first 30‑something player to start for ­Chelsea since ­Thiago Silva in May 2024. “We will feel his ­presence because he has this charisma, this aura to influence.”Chelsea, again in a 3-4-2-1 system, are getting serious. Sánchez was not even on the bench against his old side and needs to leave. There was a huge ovation for Martínez before kick‑off and it was followed by the focus switching to Brighton’s No 1 in the fourth minute, a handling error from Bart Verbruggen allowing Roméo Lavia to put Chelsea ahead after Mats Wieffer had cleared a João Pedro header off the line from a corner.It was a lovely moment for Lavia. It was four years to the day since the Belgian’s last goal, against Chelsea coincidentally enough. His luck with injuries is hopefully turning.View image in fullscreenRoméo Lavia was on hand to punish Bart Verbruggen’s early handling error and put Chelsea 1-0 up.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesLavia starting his second consecutive league game was important with Chelsea light in midfield. Moisés Caicedo limped off after coming on in the second half, Reece James started on the bench and Enzo ­Fernández was off ­pining for a move to ­Manchester City, so Malo Gusto moved in from right wing-back to partner Lavia.Chelsea’s selection issues were nothing compared to Brighton’s problems, though. Fabian Hürzeler did not use the absence of Jack Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Georginio Rutter, Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh as an excuse, but it had an impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea were rampant. Rogers ­continued his fine start after joining from Villa, creating the second goal with a powerful surge away from Luka Vuskovic in the 14th ­minute. Brighton were caught cold by a throw‑in and Rogers crossed for Pedro Neto to score.Linked with a move away this summer, Neto has been repurposed by Alonso as a wing-back and was bright. João Pedro missed a chance after strong pressing from the ­Portugal international. The away end jeered but João Pedro converted his next opportunity, when a Rogers flick sent Jorrel Hato flying down the left to set the former Brighton striker up.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro rather summed up Chelsea’s start under Xabi Alonso with a goal, an assist and an own goal.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesChelsea’s mistake was thinking it was over. Brighton responded before half‑time, Malick Yalcouyé ­volleying in after Martínez made a brave block from ­Charalampos ­Kostoulas. “They showed belief in their quality,” ­Hürzeler said of his players.The German thought Brighton deserved more. Chelsea were wobbling when João Pedro diverted a Gross cross past Martínez. Diego Gómez then lashed a shot wide and Martínez denied Olivier Boscagli the equaliser.Alonso needed his big players to step up. Palmer, who had earlier sidefooted over from close range, delivered when he took a João Pedro flick and bent a shot past Verbruggen. Chelsea will be anything but dull.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueChelseaBrighton & Hove Albionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 10: London City Lionesses | London City Lionesses | The Guardian
description: The Ballon d’Or winner Putellas leads an influx of superstar names at London City Lionesses with the aim of bridging the gap to the very best in the WSL
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: The Ballon d’Or winner Putellas leads an influx of superstar names at London City Lionesses with the aim of bridging the gap to the very best in the WSL
Content: Mary Earps is one of London City Lionesses’ big name signings. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesBallon d’Or winner Putellas leads influx of superstar names at independent club aiming to bridge gap to very bestBySuzanne WrackSun 30 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:4th (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wrack’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:6thProspectsTrying to figure out what London City will look like this season, or where they will finish, is nigh on impossible.Eight players have come inas the owner, Michele Kang, bids to continue her drive towards the top of the Women’s Super League and there are some superstars in that group, among them the two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas.The WSL debutants finished a respectable sixth last season, but were 22 points adrift of the top three. Evidence suggests Kang will be ruthless if the team do not meet her expectations – despite a strong start to the 2025-26 campaign, Jocelyn Prêcheur was sacked as manager shortly before Christmas and replaced by Eder Maestre.Wholesale changes to teams hoping to break into the top three have proved costly in the past. The hope will be that the level of the players coming in will help London City develop into a side capable of securing Champions League football and challenging for the league. What is clear is that Kang’s spending and ambition is playing a big role in bringing some of the biggest players in the world to the WSL.Mapi León said of her: “Everything counts when you make this kind of a decision, and of course, she was an important part because seeing another woman doing so much to help women’s sports and women’s football grow, I think it’s impossible not to value that. I think it’s something very powerful.”Graphic showing London City Lionesses’ finishing position the past five seasonsOff-field pictureLondon City’s accounts for 2024-25 showed an operating loss of £10.6m and the effect of their big spending before their first season in the WSL, and even bigger spending this summer, will show in future filings. The 2024-25 loss was more than 10 times their £902,000 revenue in that period. Critically, there is a need to grow the fanbase and, with no men’s club supporter pool to draw from, London City will have to be inventive.The manager‘People think I’ve vanished’: Mary Earps on signing for London City and feeling forgottenRead moreMaestre was appointed in January having previously managed UD Tenerife in Liga F, guiding them to sixth. Maestre’s contract runs until 2028, but he cannot rest on that given Kang’s high expectations. The 42-year-old has shifted the way London City play and a host of new signings could prove fruitful in his system.Star signingMary Earps, León and Kadidiatou Diani have arrived from Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona and Lyonnes respectively, but it isthe recruitment of Putellasthat has rocked the WSL. The 32-year-old spent 14 years at Barcelona, helping them to the top of the women’s game, in the process becoming a talismanic figure. Putellas is far from past her prime and had the pick of clubs worldwide when deciding to leave Spain. Her recruitment was a statement of intent from Kang.View image in fullscreenThe 32-year-old Alexia Putellas has plenty to offer London City Lionesses.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockStat attackLondon City made more Opta-defined defensive errors that led to goals and conceded more penalties than any other team in the WSL last season. Elene Lete saved one penalty and the players in front of the 24-year-old goalkeeper need to make her life easier.Graphic showing London City Lionesses made the most errors leading to goals and conceded the most penalties in 2025‑26Set for a breakthroughSuperstars have come through the door this summer, meaning Nicole Anyomi is one that has slipped under the radar and could go on to make a big impression. Anyomi is a little bit of an unknown to UK audiences having played all her club football in Germany. The forward scored 60 goals in 130 games for Frankfurt in five years. She also has four goals in 34 games for Germany.Alexia Putellas: ‘I’m hungry to win, to fight with my teammates for victory’Read moreWhat they say“I’m going to bring to the project whatever the project needs from me, so I’m 100% committed. I’m hungry to win, to be better day after day, to fight with my teammates for the victory” –PutellasWhere are they playing their home games?Hayes Lane in Bromley is far from an ideal ground for such an ambitious club given the 5,150 capacity. The medium- to long-term goal is to upsize, but space for a ground in and around London is limited. Before any move, however, London City need to increase their fanbase.On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27London City LionessesWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar shares picture from hospital after Vuelta-ending crash | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar, who had to withdraw from the Vuelta after a fall, shared a photo of himself from hospital, while Enric Mas has extended his lead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tadej Pogacar, who had to withdraw from the Vuelta after a fall, shared a photo of himself from hospital, while Enric Mas has extended his lead
Content: Tadej Pogacar posts an Instagram story on Sunday morning from his hospital bed.Photograph: tadejpogacarView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar posts an Instagram story on Sunday morning from his hospital bed.Photograph: tadejpogacarVuelta a EspañaTadej Pogacar shares picture from hospital after Vuelta-ending crashSlovenian awaiting surgery on collarbone after fallMas extends overall lead by winning ninth stageAgence France-PresseSun 30 Aug 2026 12.13 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar, who was dramatically forced towithdraw from the Vuelta a Españaon Saturday after a heavy fall, has shared a photo of himself from hospital accompanied by the Bee Gees’ song Stayin’ Alive.Pogacar, the clear leader of the Vuelta until his crash, greeted followers on his Instagram account with a photo showing him in a hospital bed wearing a neck brace. The Slovenian five-time Tour de France winner could also be seen with a plaster near his right eyebrow, as well as on his right hand, which he held in his usual gesture of raising his index finger and little finger.The UAE Team Emirates rider soundtracked the photo with the 1977 upbeat disco anthem, appearing to be in good spirits as he awaits surgery on his collarbone.Quick GuidePidcock dedicates mountain bike world title to TarlingShowTom Pidcock dedicated his victory to the late British cyclist Fin Tarling on Sunday after winning the mountain bike cross-country world title for the second time.Tarling, whose brother Josh and Pidcock were Netcompany Ineos teammates in 2023, died in a crash with a vehicle at a race in Portugal earlier this month at the age of 19.'I don’t have much words to be honest, it was a hard road here after the Tour,' said an emotional Pidcock, who finished ninth at July’s Tour de France. 'I want to dedicate this win to Fin Tarling, to Josh. Seeing him start the Vuelta was pretty incredible, so I dedicate it to him and his family.'Agence France-PresseWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Pogacar crashed on Saturday during the eighth stage of the Vuelta, just over 30km from the finish line in the Valencian town of Xeraco, a stage that was initially expected to be transitional. The 27-year-old had been leading by a massive 3min 50sec a week into the race, and was the overwhelming favourite for victory in his attempt to complete a career clean sweep of the three Grand Tours.According to the medical report provided by his team, Pogacar was “diagnosed with a concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture, a stable C7 cervical fracture, and multiple abrasions”. UAE’s statement added that there were “fortunately, no other major injuries and no neurological fallout”. The team has not specified how long Pogacar will be out of action, but it seems unlikely he will be fit to defend his world title in late September in Canada.Once racing resumed on Sunday, the home rider Enric Mas extended his lead by winning stage nine. Mas beat Britain’s Oscar Onley in a two-man sprint finish to enlarge his advantage over the four-time former winner Primoz Roglic, who finished in third 12sec behind.View image in fullscreenEnric Mas crosses the line to win stage nine.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesRoglic now trails Mas by 1min 18sec, with Austria’s Felix Gall, who shipped 18sec in finishing fourth, third overall at 1min 39sec. Onley, who leads the best young rider category, moved up a place to fourth at 2min 20sec as the former winner Sepp Kuss tumbled three places to seventh overall after coming home 1min 44sec behind Mas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Now I understand Tadej – the red jersey gives you wings,” smiled Mas, who said that he felt in the form of his life. “The team was 10 out of 10, we controlled the situation really well and I felt good in the finish.”Mas’s victory on the 187.4km mountainous stage from Villajoyosa to Alto de Aitana, ended his Spanish team Movistar’s five-year win drought at their home Grand Tour. Monday is the first rest daty of this year’s race, with the Vuelta resuming on Tuesday with a hilly 187.5km run from Alcaraz to Elche de la Sierra in south-east Spain.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: All-time great Aaron Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin stacked LA Rams | Los Angeles Rams | The Guardian
description: Aaron Donald, one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams
Author: Tom Lutz
Headline: Aaron Donald, one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams
Content: Aaron Donald played 10 seasons for the Rams before his initial retirement.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APView image in fullscreenAaron Donald played 10 seasons for the Rams before his initial retirement.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APLos Angeles RamsAll-time great Aaron Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin stacked LA RamsLos Angeles were already Super Bowl favoritesDefensive tackle was 10-time Pro Bowler with Rams35-year-old aiming to win second Super Bowl in LATom LutzSun 30 Aug 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAaron Donald, one of thegreatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams.During a 10-season career with the Rams, who drafted him with the 13th overall pick in 2014, Donald was a three-time defensive player of the year and an eight-time first team All-Pro. Hewon a Super Bowl with the Ramsat the end of the 2021 season beforeannouncing his retirement in March 2024at the age of 32.Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI saysRead moreThe 35-year-old returns to a stacked Rams roster who were already betting favorites to win the Super Bowl this season. The team includes reigning MVP Matthew Stafford at quarterback and the reigning defensive player of the year, Myles Garrett, who Los Angeles acquired in a tradewith the Cleveland Browns in June.ESPN reportsthat Donald will earn $20m in his one-year deal, which could rise to $30m with bonuses.Rumors had circulated that Donald would return after the trade for Garrett. Rams head coach Sean McVay had undergone a “very strict, regimented process that was similar to what he did when he played” to see if he was still able to play in theNFL. McVay said the 10-time Pro Bowler had been “outstanding” during a workout with the Rams this summer.If Donald can replicate anything close to the form he showed during his peak – when he was arguably the greatest defensive tackle of all time – he will form part of a formidable line with Garrett, who set the NFL single-season sack record in 2025.Donald, who was listed at 6ft 1in and 280 lbs when he retired, is small for a defensive tackle but during his first spell with the Rams he made up for his lack of size with his extraordinary athleticism and work rate. He ended his career with a franchise record 111 sacks.If the Rams do reach the Super Bowl this season, they will play on home turf at SoFi Stadium, the venue for their championship victory in February 2022. The Rams start their season on 10 September against their NFC West rivals, the San Francisco 49ers.Explore more on these topicsLos Angeles RamsNFLWest CoastUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Calvert-Lewin cancels out Schade’s opener as Leeds salvage point against Brentford | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Dominic Calvert-Lewin rescued a point for Leeds in a 1-1 draw at Elland Road after Kevin Schade’s clever finish had given Brentford a first-half lead
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Dominic Calvert-Lewin rescued a point for Leeds in a 1-1 draw at Elland Road after Kevin Schade’s clever finish had given Brentford a first-half lead
Content: Dominic Calvert-Lewin is in the right place at the right time to steer the ball into the net.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin is in the right place at the right time to steer the ball into the net.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueCalvert-Lewin cancels out Schade’s opener as Leeds salvage point against BrentfordAaron Bowerat Elland RoadSun 30 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese nascent moments of the new season can often provide false hope but, as both sets of players shook hands after what was indisputably the correct result at Elland Road, it was difficult not to imagine we had just witnessed a contest between two sides that should have lofty ­ambitions for the months ahead.Leeds andBrentfordwere vic­torious on the opening weekend in differing circumstances. Leeds crafted a hard-earned but ultimately deserved win at Nottingham Forest, while Brentford Tottenham. Time will tell what the ceiling of both these sides is but, as they each continued their unbeaten starts here, hopes should be high.This was a thoroughly ­entertaining game but it was also an occasion in which both managers, as well as the players, displayed their importance to their respective clubs.Managers are scrutinised at every turn but Daniel Farke and Keith Andrews both excelled here. Both have had question marks as to whether they were the right man to take their team forward: Andrews when he was surprisingly appointed just over a year ago, and Farke in the difficult early stages of last season.Andrews’s tactical nous was at its peak in the first half. He nullified the Leeds back five and his team led at half-time and probably should have been more than a single goal in front. Kevin Schade’s wonderful flick to turn home a Keane Lewis-Potter cross was the least the visitors deserved.However, Farke showed his own tactical flexibility at the break. The German was under immense pressure last November and at real risk of losing his job before a move to a back five away at Manchester City proved the catalyst to transform Leeds’s season. He did the reverse here, going back to a four and matching Brentford in the second half to great effect.Spearheaded by the impact of Ao Tanaka and Lukas Nmecha, both on as substitutes, the hosts were the stronger of the two sides after half‑time. They ultimately got the equaliser their play deserved when ­Nmecha’s shot across goal was prodded home by Dominic Calvert-Lewin to ensure it would be a point apiece, and four from the first two for both sides.The early evidence overall? Leeds and Brentford should both be ­looking upwards this season. “It’s definitely a good point,” Farke said. “It was a very difficult and complicated game like we expected. Brentford were ­excellent in the first half and deserved to be in the lead, but I’m so proud of our reaction.”His side struggled to get to grips with Brentford’s shape in the first half. Ethan Ampadu and Anton Stach were overrun in midfield, with the visitors’ three of Vitaly Janelt, ­Mamadou ­Sangaré and ­Mikkel Damsgaard ­running riot. James ­Trafford was called into action on multiple occasions, with smart saves to deny Igor Thiago and Schade.Such was the strength of Brentford’s momentum that a goal felt inevitable. It duly arrived as half‑time approached when Lewis-Potter’s cross caught the Leeds backline off‑guard and Schade, with his back to goal, turned the ball home expertly to silence Elland Road.As mentioned, perhaps the ­biggest gripe at that stage was that ­Brentford’s lead wasn’t greater. “I thought we could have done more in the first half,” Andrews said.“We could have tested Trafford more but we were outstanding. The storm was always going to come and they were forced into ­making changes they haven’t done for quite some time.”Those changes were pivotal. The back five was abandoned, with Leeds adding Tanaka as an extra man in midfield. It provided an instant impact, with the balance of play shifting the way of the hosts. James Justin forced a clever save from Caoimhín Kelleher before Dan James, on as a substitute, arguably could have done better after being set free on halfway.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn contrast, Brentford were struggling without as much space in the middle, with Igor Thiago cutting a slightly isolated and frustrated ­figure. The Leeds supporters, sensing the momentum was now with them, were beginning to come alive – as were their team. Just like in the first half, a goal was starting to feel more like an inevitability than a possibility.Farke tweaked things further, with ­Nmecha pro­viding direct support for Calvert‑Lewin, and the duo combined with 11 ­minutes ­remaining. Nmecha dragged a shot across goal to leave Kelleher flat‑footed, with Calvert‑Lewin ­poking into the empty net for his first of the season.A draw was the least Leeds deserved. Both sides showed their ambition by pushing for a winner, though they cancelled each other out in the final moments to underline further that these are two teams who should think positively about what lies ahead.Chelsea v Brighton, Leeds v Brentford, Sunderland v Fulham: Premier League – liveRead moreView image in fullscreenKevin Schade stretches to reach Keane Lewis-Potter’s cross and flicks the ball home with the outside of his boot.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLeeds UnitedBrentfordmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Sunderland’s Wilson Isidor applies the finishing touch to sink Fulham | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Substitute Wilson Isidor scored in a 1-0 win over Fulham that gave Sunderland their first points of the season
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Substitute Wilson Isidor scored in a 1-0 win over Fulham that gave Sunderland their first points of the season
Content: Wilson Isidor strikes in the 75th minute to give Sunderland the three points.Photograph: Colorsport/Bruce White/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWilson Isidor strikes in the 75th minute to give Sunderland the three points.Photograph: Colorsport/Bruce White/ShutterstockPremier LeagueSunderland’s Wilson Isidor applies the finishing touch to sink FulhamLouise Taylorat the Stadium of LightSun 30 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the final whistle Álvaro Arbeloa provided a study in pensiveness while Régis Le Bris simply looked relieved. For protracted periods an almost palpable fear of losing formed the subtext of a match decided when two of theSunderlandmanager’s ­second-half substitutes, Habib Diarra and Wilson Isidor, combined for the latter to score.Isidor’s goal not merely supplied Sunderland with their first win of the season while leaving Arbeloa’s side pointless, but also ended his side’s 17‑year run without aPremier Leaguehome victory against Fulham.Calvert-Lewin cancels out Schade’s opener as Leeds salvage point against BrentfordRead more“It wasn’t our day for sure,” said Marco Silva’s successor, whose team were confounded repeatedly by Sunderland’s outstanding central defender Nordi Mukiele.“We need to improve many things, for sure, especially the energy and the attitude.“It was a tough game for us. Sunderland were better for many ­minutes. It’s not easy here. If you want to come to Sunderland and play the way you want to, then you need the right mentality. We need to show more energy and fight for every ball.”Le Bris was a little happier, ­saying: “We didn’t create enough.Fulhamwere well organised but we had a good balance to manage the transitions. We had to be smart. It’s a question of balancing risk and organisation.”The tone of a cagey, risk‑averse first half dominated by Fulham’s ­cautious low block was raised, albeit sporadically, by a typically indus­trious central-midfield performance by Sunderland’s Noah Sadiki.The visiting gameplan seemed all about ouncing on the counterattack but the Democratic Republic of the Congo international extinguished so many potential visiting fires that Fulham’s sole real chance during the opening 45 minutes involved Josh King finding himself confounded by geometry as he miscued a tightly angled opening conjured by Alex Iwobi. Otherwise the home goalkeeper, Robin Roefs, was left pretty much undisturbed.That apart, a slightly nervous impasse endured. Despite dominating possession, Sunderland’s attacking edge proved anything but serrated, leaving Bernd Leno severely underemployed in Fulham’s goal.It all left both Le Bris and Arbeloa with much to ponder at the interval. If the watching Sunderland owner, Kyril-Louis Dreyfus, required a reminder as to precisely why Le  Bris is so keen to sign a specialist right winger and another striker before the transfer window’s closure he received it.View image in fullscreenWilson Isidor salutes the fans after scoring.Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesAt least Sunderland’s manager had the excellent Mukiele restored to his backline following injury. The former Paris Saint-Germain defender’s importance on Wearside was, not for the first time, underscored as, early in the second half his tremendous sliding challenge blocked Gonzalo García’s path to a near certain goal following Sander Berge’s stellar through pass.“I was really impressed with Nordi and I told him this,” Le Bris said. “Nordi showed us today that he’s a great player.”García, meanwhile, had scored twicein his first two gamessince joining Fulham from Real Madrid but found Sunderland’s rearguard difficult to decode. Nonetheless, ­perhaps sensing that the visitors were ­gaining a slight initiative, Le Bris made a ­double substitution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn came Diarra and Isidor for the hitherto largely ineffective Nilson Angulo and Brian Brobbey. Within minutes Sunderland should have been ahead after Enzo Le Fée played a beautiful, first-time ball across goal.It seemed easier for the on-rushing Isidor to score than miss but, somehow, he ended up striking the base of a post and, in the technical area. Le Bris was left sinking to his knees in disappointment after making a premature celebratory leap as the delivery left Le Fée’s boot. “It was such a good chance,” he said. “It was such a shame.”Poor Isidor looked mortified but redemption beckoned. Just moments later he surged onto another fabulous low dispatch across the box – from Diarra this time – and atonement arrived as his high-velocity shot whizzed past Leno.Diarra and Isidor had succeeded in breathing new life into Sunderland’s suddenly much more dynamic press – not to mention capitalising on ­Fulham’s high defensive line – but the former’s cameo was to prove short‑lived after an injury necessitated his replacement by Chris Rigg.No matter, he and Isidor, had already done just enough. “Habib is so, so intense,” Le Bris said. “He and Wilson changed our press, it was tactically the same just with 20-30% more energy. But the most important thing is, as we saw this afternoon, that the core of this group are very good.“The players are all in. You can’t play at this level if you’re not all in and well connected with the project of the club. If we can add one or two signings that can help this group then we’ll do it. But I have trust and con­fidence in this squad.”How Arbeloa must wish he could say the same.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSunderlandFulhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Iceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaign   | Iceland | The Guardian
description: Well-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across Europe
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Well-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across Europe
Content: An EU flag at a gathering in Reykjavík on referendum night.Photograph: Marco Di Marco/APView image in fullscreenAn EU flag at a gathering in Reykjavík on referendum night.Photograph: Marco Di Marco/APIcelandIceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaignWell-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across EuropeAnalysis: Definitely no or maybe yes – what tipped the Icelandic referendumMiranda Bryantin ReykjavíkSun 30 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoters inIcelandhave ⁠rejected ⁠a government proposal ​to reopen ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU after a closely fought referendum campaign that divided the country against a backdrop of global volatility.After a long and anxious night for those on both sides of the debate, the no camp ended up with 52.8% of votes on Sunday morning and the yes camp with 47.2%. Voter turnout was high at 82.5%.The vote was held in the shadow of repeated threats by Donald Trump to invade or acquire neighbouring Greenland. Although Iceland is a Nato member, supporters of EU membership said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats towards the smaller, Arctic island.At a press conference the prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, said the campaign had “raised the debate in Iceland to a higher level” while acknowledging that there were aspects that “could have been done better”.View image in fullscreenKristrún Frostadóttir speaks to reporters on Sunday after the result.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersGiven how close the outcome was, she said, it was important to respect the views of yes voters. But she said: “It is quite clear that this matter will not move forward under this government.”She said the government would wait to decide on whether to submit a parliamentary resolution formally withdrawing its EU membership application. Iceland originally applied in 2009 after the financial crash but pulled out of talks in 2013, saying it could not go any further without a referendum.There will be disappointment in Brussels, which had been keen to welcome a wealthy new member and appeared willing to compromise with Iceland on thorny issues such as fishing to facilitate its accession.The yes campaign had argued that joining the EU could offer greater security amid war in Ukraine and the Middle East, and given the US president’s unpredictable attitude towards the Arctic.But the no campaigners’ warnings that EU membership would threaten the country’s sovereignty and fishing waters turned the vote in their favour.View image in fullscreenPeople wave an Icelandic flag at a referendum-night event organised by the no campaign.Photograph: Halldor Kolbeins/AFP/Getty ImagesTheir victory quickly attracted the attention of anti-EU leaders. The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen wrote on X: “At a time when some are pushing for greater federalism and the transfer of sovereignty to the European Commission, this vote reminds us that another Europe is possible, a Europe of free, sovereign nations cooperating voluntarily on matters of common interest.”Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, wrote: “Congratulations to Iceland on voting to keep their independence.”The ‌government in Reykjavík had framed its membership plan as a “now or never” moment, and Kristrún told voters earlier in August that a no vote would put all EU speculation aside.On Sunday, she told RUV that she hoped the vote would not leave the nation divided.Kristrún, who spoke at public meetings around the country in the final weeks in support of yes, said: “I don’t experience this as hurt. I know some people have been in a state of shock, but now I’ve sat with a large group of people across the country and people are completely open to different outcomes.”She acknowledged that many people in Iceland, particularly from rural areas, had concerns about the potential impact on agriculture, fisheries and natural resources of joining the EU. “I promise that we will handle these issues well and keep these concerns in mind,” she said.View image in fullscreenA boat leaving the harbour in Reykjavík on Sunday after the vote.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersThe vote exposed a stark divide between rural and urban areas, with the capital, Reykjavik, the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people where a majority supported yes.The government had pledged to hold a referendum on whether to reopen the accession talks when it came into office, with Kristrúntelling the Guardianat the time that it was a “necessary step forward”. After Trump renewed his threats to invade Greenland at the start of this year and amid a greater global focus on the Arctic, the government announced that the referendum would be brought forward.Hulda Þórisdóttir, a politics professor at the University of Iceland, said she was not surprised by the result given the tone of the latter stages of the campaign, with misinformation spreading and the considerably bigger financial resources of the no campaign.“No won due to a combination of factors: a strong feeling that the EEA [European Economic Area] is all we need, a sense of Icelandic exceptionalism, economic self-interest and a lot of misinformation among the least engaged – for example, ‘I don’t want my son to have to join the EU army,’” Hulda said. “But very importantly, it seems clear to me that the no campaign was much, much better funded.”Reaction from Brussels was muted. António Costa, the European Council president, told Kristrún on Sunday the bloc “fully respects the democratic choice” of the island’s voters not to resume EU membership talks, a spokesperson said. “Iceland remains one of the EU’s closest and most trusted partners,” said the spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsIcelandEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ghislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn conviction, experts say | Ghislaine Maxwell | The Guardian
description: The Jeffrey Epstein associate’s apparent last hope would be a Hail Mary from Donald Trump – a presidential pardon
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: The Jeffrey Epstein associate’s apparent last hope would be a Hail Mary from Donald Trump – a presidential pardon
Content: A document included in the US Department of Justice release of the Jeffrey Epstein files shows a photo of Ghislaine Maxwell in 2019.Photograph: Jon Elswick/APView image in fullscreenA document included in the US Department of Justice release of the Jeffrey Epstein files shows a photo of Ghislaine Maxwell in 2019.Photograph: Jon Elswick/APGhislaine MaxwellGhislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn conviction, experts sayThe Jeffrey Epstein associate’s apparent last hope would be a Hail Mary from Donald Trump – a presidential pardonVictoria Bekiempisin New YorkSun 30 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGhislaine Maxwellseems to be all but guaranteed to have run out of legal avenues to challenge her conviction for her involvement inJeffrey Epstein’s abuse of girls and young women with perhaps her lingering hopes of freedom resting on a pardon from the Trump administration.Paul Engelmayer, a Manhattan federal court judge, last weekrejectedMaxwell’s contention that her constitutional rights were violated at trial and sentencing for her crimes. “Maxwell’s claims are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous,” Engelmayer wrote in his ruling on the former British socialite’s legal gambit.Engelmayer also rejected Maxwell’s claim that new evidence, which she said came to light during Epstein Files Transparency Act disclosures, did not support her allegations of constitutional violations. “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings,” he ruled.Maxwell’s family said in a statement that Engelmayer’s ruling was “marked by a tone of sarcasm and disdain that, in our view, undermines the appearance of impartiality and invites scrutiny of the judge’s conduct”. They also said Maxwell “will continue to pursue every available legal avenue” for relief.Legal veterans said, however, that Maxwell had virtually exhausted all her court-based routes. With Maxwell apparently running out of legal pathways, many have wondered whether Donald Trump will at some point deliver a Hail Mary – apresidential pardon.“She’s exhausted her direct appeals. Now she’s trying to collaterally attack the conviction, which is very difficult to do,” said Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor who founded the law firm West Coast Trial Lawyers.“I don’t know what world she lives in,” Rahmani also said. “Her only chance of ever seeing the light of day before her sentence runs is a presidential pardon.”Rahmani explained Maxwell’s recent rejected request was different from her supreme court effort – which was based on claims that a decades-old non-prosecution agreement with south Florida federal authorities shielded her from prosecution. The supreme court bid failed when the justices declined to review that appeal.Maxwell could ask the second circuit court of appeals to review Engelmayer’s ruling, but that is a request, not a surefire opportunity to be heard, said Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor now practicing white-collar defense at the firm Dykema.“Ordinarily, you either have to get a certificate of appealability from the trial court that denies your motion or your petition, or you can get it from the appellate court,” he said, noting Engelmayer did not grant such a certificate. “I would assume what she’s going to do is seek a certificate of appealability [from] the second circuit.”The second circuit, however, will see Engelmayer’s decision and his denial of this certificate. “It seems unlikely that she is going to get a certificate of appealability from the second circuit court of appeals meaning that in essence, her legal avenues are going to be dead,” Chutkow said“This decision should bring Ghislaine Maxwell’s campaign to escape accountability to a final close. A jury heard the evidence and convicted her. The court of appeals affirmed her conviction. The supreme court declined to intervene,” said Spencer Kuvin, an attorney at Goldlaw who has represented dozens of Epstein survivors. “Now, after thoroughly reviewing her latest claims, Judge Engelmayer has found that the evidence of her guilt was overwhelming and that her arguments were largely frivolous, procedurally barred, and based upon speculation, distortions and outright falsehoods.”Given that Engelmayer’s ruling virtually shuts the door on future efforts per longtime attorneys, attention has once again shifted to a presidential pardon or commutation from Trump, who has been saddled with ongoing Epstein and Maxwell controversies since taking office again.‘Politically, a pardon would be catastrophic’Trump vowed while campaigning that his administration would release all Epstein documents, but his justice department repeatedlymissedcongressionally mandated disclosure deadlines, and some allege that some files remain secret. Trump, who socialized with Epstein before the latter’s Florida state court soliciting conviction, has maintained that he never engaged in inappropriate conduct.The White House, when asked for comment on the pardon issue, pointed to two statements. When Trump was asked if he had ruled out a pardon, he said: “I haven’t even thought about it, I mean, I haven’t thought about it for months.”“Maybe I haven’t thought about it at all,” Trump alsosaid. “But I don’t talk about that. I don’t rule it in or out, I don’t even think about it.”“Politically, I think it would be catastrophic,” said Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who is the executive director of Principles First. “You run on releasing the Epstein files. Then when documents are released, they’re limited and heavily redacted. Then you turn around and call the entire controversy a hoax. And after all of that, you pardon Jeffrey Epstein’s closest associate? While claiming to be the president who protects women and children?“That would be incredibly difficult to defend,” she added.Rahmani explained that there is a formal pardon process. A request would go to the justice department’s pardon attorney who, in turn, makes a recommendation. That said, “the president sort of marches to the beat of his own drum,” Rahmani said – Trump could just grant it.“There is a very, very, very slim chance it happens at all,” Rahmani added. If it did, however, Rahmani said he would expect it to happen when Trump’s presidency wraps, not before the midterms.“Even though the president is very unpredictable, I just can’t see it … It would be career suicide. But again, he obviously doesn’t care.”Maxwell’s family said legal routes must be exhausted before making a pardon application. They said to the best of their knowledge, there isn’t an application to theTrump administration.For advocates, presidential clemency would deal an immense blow to survivors.Lauren Hersh, a former prosecutor who is the CEO of the non-profitWorld Without Exploitation,said: “After listening to so many survivors and hearing the devastating harm caused by Ghislaine Maxwell, I can’t imagine anybody would give the idea of a pardon a moment’s thought. It would be totally egregious.”Asked about a pardon, Thomas Massie, a Republican Kentucky congressman who co-sponsored the bipartisan Epstein Files Transparency Act, said in a statement: “I’m adamantly opposed to it. [Todd] Blanche already inexplicably and inappropriately moved her to a country club prison with no new information or indictments of coconspirators.”Julie Roginsky, whofiledsexual harassment lawsuits against Roger Ailes, the former Fox News CEO, and co-founded the survivors advocacy non-profitLift Our Voices, said an act of clemency would be a “monumental slap in the face” for survivors. But she did not rule it out.“She already got a sweetheart deal by being moved not just into Club Fed, but by being given privileges that nobody else in her position would be given,” Roginsky said, referring to Maxwell’s controversial transfer to a low-security prison.Roginsky also pointed to Blanche’sinterviewof Maxwell, which the now attorney general conducted while he was the justice department’s second-ranking official. “I think we already understand that the fix is in for her, and I don’t know whether she had some sort of guarantee that once the president is on his way out, as one of his last acts of commutation, he will commute her sentence or just give her a full pardon,” Roginsky said.“Nothing would surprise me.”Explore more on these topicsGhislaine MaxwellJeffrey EpsteinLaw (US)Donald TrumpTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Recruiter places ‘phoenix’ firm into liquidation just months after repurchase erased millions in debt | Business | The Guardian
description: New company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administrator
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: New company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administrator
Content: PRG went into administration last September owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyView image in fullscreenPRG went into administration last September owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyBusinessRecruiter places ‘phoenix’ firm into liquidation just months after repurchase erased millions in debtNew company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administratorSimon GoodleySun 30 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA recruitment executive who was allowed to buy back the assets of his bust company in instalments, despite it accumulating almost £3m of debt, has placed his new business into liquidation after falling behind with promised payments to the administrator.The news is the latest event to raise questions about the practice of “phoenixism”, accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts.The tactic, which is legal, is often justified by supporters who argue it can save jobs and help secure some returns for creditors – although HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) estimates it costs the UK taxpayer hundreds of millions of pounds a year.Premier Group Recruitment went into administrationin September 2025 owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC, which had begun enforcement proceedings against the company.The recruiter’s assets were acquired three days later by a new company, PGGBR Ltd, founded by Andrew Woosnam, Premier’s 99% shareholder, who made an initial £10,000 payment and promised to transfer a further £600,000 via monthly £25,000 instalments over the following two years.Despite a seemingly positive start for the new business – which offered its consultants an “all expenses paid”trip to Las Vegas for hitting their targets– the company quickly fell behind with its promised repayments, causing the administrators tofile an updateon its struggles with Companies House in March.On Sunday,filings at Companies House said PGGBR had appointed a voluntary liquidator.Woosnam, who had received a £1.2m director’s loan from the defunct Premier and had taken dividends out of the company totalling almost £2m since 2022, is also understood to have made a series of redundancies at the new business in July that industry sources said equated to at least half his staff. The company’s website, which now appears to have been taken down, listed a management team of 12 people.Sources with knowledge of the job losses also suggested that those affected had not been paid and that Woosnam was planning to launch another new company to take his recruitment business forward.Companies House records show that in June the businessman changed the name of a business he founded a year ago from PGUSA to PGREC.The problems at Premier chime with long-running questions concerning the efficacy of allowing connected parties to buy back their bust businesses by promising future payments – deferred considerations, in the industry jargon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResearch has suggested that poorer outcomes tend to occur in insolvencies where the assets are acquired by connected parties paying via future instalments.For example, research by the University of Wolverhampton, for theUK government’s 2014 Graham review, concluded: “The failure rate of a connected party sale increases from 15% of all cases without deferred consideration to 37% when deferred consideration is introduced. Generally, when deferred consideration is present, whether or not a connected sale is also present, the failure rate rises considerably.”Similar results were published bya 2018 studyfunded by the EU. It concluded: “When the sale was to connected purchasers, there was a significantly higher risk of buyer mortality.”Woosnam has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsBusinessAccountancyCorporate governanceHMRCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man arrested over fatal stabbing of British woman in Germany | Germany | The Guardian
description: Rosenheim police detain 27-year-old German man after woman, 31, killed outside train station early on Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rosenheim police detain 27-year-old German man after woman, 31, killed outside train station early on Sunday
Content: The train station in Rosenheim, in south-east Germany.Photograph: Peter Kneffel/DPA/APView image in fullscreenThe train station in Rosenheim, in south-east Germany.Photograph: Peter Kneffel/DPA/APGermanyMan arrested over fatal stabbing of British woman in GermanyRosenheim police detain 27-year-old German man after woman, 31, killed outside train station early on SundayAssociated PressSun 30 Aug 2026 09.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been detained in Germany on suspicion of the fatal stabbing of a 31-year-old British woman in Rosenheim early on Sunday morning, local authorities said.According to Rosenheim police, the woman, who was attacked at the city’s train station, was taken to a nearby hospital where she died from serious injuries.Federal police officers who were called to the scene detained the suspect immediately after the stabbing.Police identified him as a 27-year-old German man from the nearby county of Fürstenfeldbruck. He was expected to be brought before magistrates on Sunday.In line with German privacy rules, police did not release the names of the victim or the suspect and said they were still investigating the circumstances and motive behind the crime.They asked any witnesses to come forward and asked whether anyone had seen an argument or a physical altercation at the train station between Saturday night and the early hours of Sunday.Explore more on these topicsGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: South West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis shows | Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Friends of the Earth finds greatest sewage discharge in Devon, Cornwall, Dorset and Somerset
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Exclusive: Friends of the Earth finds greatest sewage discharge in Devon, Cornwall, Dorset and Somerset
Content: Exmouth beach in Devon. South West Water recorded 666 pollution incidents or warnings in 2025.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyView image in fullscreenExmouth beach in Devon. South West Water recorded 666 pollution incidents or warnings in 2025.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyWaterSouth West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis showsExclusive: Friends of the Earth finds greatest sewage discharge in Devon, Cornwall, Dorset and Somerset‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollutionPippa NeillEnvironment reporterSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth West Water is doing more harm to the environment than any other water company in England, according to new analysis, with more sewage discharged in Devon, Cornwall, Dorset andSomersetthan anywhere else.Friends of the Earth analysed water companies’ environmental performance in six categories: sewage spills, water quality at bathing sites, pollution incidents or warnings at bathing sites, severity of sewage pollution at bathing sites, the percentage of rivers rated below the standard for good ecological health, and the affordability of bills.South West Water, which operates across Devon,Cornwalland parts of Dorset and Somerset, was among the top three worst performers in four out of the six categories.The water company had the highest total duration of sewage spill events since 2024, averaging 574,323 hours annually. Severn Trent andYorkshire Watercame second and third respectively but were outstripped by South West Water, by almost 200,000 spill hours.Group expands legal claim over South West Water sewage pollutionRead moreSouth West Water’s designated bathing sites also recorded the most pollution incidents and warnings, with 666 recorded in 2025 alone.There are 157 official bathing sites in South West Water’s catchment. If a site is designated, the Environment Agency will monitor water quality during the bathing season to protect people’s health.A spokesperson for the company said: “We manage more than a third of England’s designated bathing waters, so improving water quality is a huge priority for us. We’re already seeing progress, with storm overflow spills down 17% and spill duration down 25% over the past year, despite significantly higher rainfall across the region. We’re also on track to meet new Environment Act bathing water standards by 2030, five years ahead of the national deadline, showing the impact of record investment across the south-west.”View image in fullscreenGyllyngvase beach, Falmouth. Friends of the Earth said South West Water’s 1.8 million customers faced some of the highest water bills at £726 annually.Photograph: Hugh Hastings/GettyAlongside this poor environmental performance, Friends of the Earth said South West Water’s roughly 1.8 million customers faced some of the highest water bills at £726 annually. Since 2024, they have had the second biggest increase in England, with bills rising by 39%.Southern Wateris responsible for the most expensive water bills in England and the biggest increase since 2024, with £281 added to the average bill in that period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories.
