Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSewage released into England’s rivers and seas nearly 300,000 times last yearRead moreKierra Box, a water campaigner at Friends of the Earth, is calling on the government to bring forward a robust clean water bill that sets out a “meaningful plan for restoring the health of the UK’s rivers and seas”.She said: “People have had enough of hearing ministers say they’ll fix the problem, only to bring in measures that superficially address the issue. If we’re to end the sewage scandal once and for all, we must see the government committing to a complete overhaul of our water system.”A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.“The government recognises that we need to build on our reforms which banned bonuses so our water system works for the public. That’s why we are driving forward the biggest overhaul of the water sector in a generation, with new legislation to give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible.”Friends of the Earth is also calling on the government to nationalise water companies. Sources recently told the Guardian that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, wasconsideringripping up insolvency laws to make it easier to bring key utilities such as water companies under public control. However,the Times reportedthat Burnham had shelved plans to put Thames Water into administration amid concerns about the cost and the legal risk involved.Defra said Thames Water remained financially stable, but the government stood “ready for all eventualities, including applying for a special administration regime if that were to become necessary”.A Water UK spokesperson said: “No sewage spill is ever acceptable, and we are working to end them as fast as we physically can. That’s why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works.”Explore more on these topicsWaterEnglandWater industryPollutionDevonCornwallDorsetnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollution | Water | The Guardian
description: Checking for sewage spills has become as normal as checking the weather forecast, say swimmers on East Sussex beaches
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Checking for sewage spills has become as normal as checking the weather forecast, say swimmers on East Sussex beaches
Content: Keeping your head above water: Brighton beach had two sewage alerts issued in August.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKeeping your head above water: Brighton beach had two sewage alerts issued in August.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWater‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollutionChecking for sewage spills has become as normal as checking the weather forecast, say swimmers on East Sussex beachesSouth West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis showsPippa NeillEnvironment reporterSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m furious,” says Jo Armstrong, 75, sitting onBrightonbeach with her daughter and granddaughter.Armstrong lives in Lewes, a town 8 miles from Brighton, and usually goes swimming in nearby Seaford inEast Sussexevery day. But over the past week the water there has been too polluted to swim. “Brighton beach was the only place that stayed clean,” she says.In the weekFriends of the Earthranked the UK’s water companies for their environmental damage, and news of further sewage leaks emerged, the Guardian headed to Brighton beach to talk to swimmers. According topublic data, a sewage alert was issued twice at the beach in August, and 158 alerts recorded overall in 2025.View image in fullscreenJo Armstrong usually likes to swim in the sea in East Sussex every day.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“There’s a tiny bit of rain and then the sewage comes, I just don’t understand it. It’s extraordinary that we can’t have clean beaches,” says Armstrong.This summer England has enduredrecord-breaking heatwavesduring which scores of people have spent time on beaches and rivers. In Brighton, the state of the country’s water is an issue on many people’s minds.Hildi Mitchell, 55, runs a programme calledPool to Pier, where she teaches pool swimmers to swim safely in open waters. Increasingly, she is finding that pollution is stopping people from taking the leap to the sea.“There are swimmers who have swum with us in the pool all year round but won’t come out in the sea in the summer because they’re worried about becoming ill,” she says.View image in fullscreenHildi Mitchell teaches pool swimmers to swim safely in the sea in Brighton.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWhen it comes to the safety of the water, checking for sewage spills has become as important as checking the weather and tidal patterns. “I would love to be able to swim anywhere, rather than thinking about trying to avoid pollution,” Mitchell says.‘Forever chemicals’ surge during pilot of Thames Water plan to combat droughtRead moreThrough Pool to Pier, Mitchell offers free workshops to children from families on low incomes. “These families already have limited things they can do in the summer to keep their children active, healthy and entertained.Swimmingshould be something that’s free and available to local families, but it’s not and that’s really sad.”Greg Veros, 59, has lived in Brighton for 22 years and swum all his life, but after falling ill due to what he believes was sewage pollution a few years ago, he now spends more time at Brighton’s outdoor swimming pool than he does in the sea.“I’m an enthusiastic swimmer, I can’t get enough of it,” Veros says. He used to have to skip his daily swim if there was a rainstorm or a sewage scare, but now the pool has given him an alternative. “It’s the best thing to have happened to Brighton,” he says.View image in fullscreenGreg Veros has switched to swimming in Brighton’s outdoor pool after he fell ill, he believes, from swimming in the sea.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianBut for Mitchell, there is nothing that can replace swimming in the sea.“It’s about freedom. You’re not constrained by the black line on the pool. Nobody’s in your lane, you’re not worried about getting in anyone’s way. It’s a place where you can just swim in the way you want to swim,” Mitchell says.Anna Field, 54, moved to Brighton so she could swim regularly, but, like Mitchell, she says checking for sewage spills is as important as checking the weather. There have been several times when she has come down to the beach and could smell the sewage, although this has been less common this summer amid the dry weather. When pollution stops her from swimming, it’s a bit like not being able to walk in the park because it’s raining, “except with this, you feel people [are] to blame”.View image in fullscreenAnna Field and her husband, Jim, take the plunge in Brighton. Field checks for sewage spills before she goes for a swim.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianShe is more angry than sad. “I absolutely love being in the ocean. It’s got its own personality, you look out of the window in the morning and it’s a different colour from yesterday or on some days it will tell you, no, you’re not coming in today,” Field says.“Swimming is such a nice thing for people to be able to do and it’s public, anyone can go in – it would be a real shame if that was less accessible.”Explore more on these topicsWaterBrightonOceansPollutionEast SussexSwimmingFitnessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Prosecutors consider charges against officers involved in spycops scandal | UK news | The Guardian
description: More than 100 undercover officers spied on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over decades
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: More than 100 undercover officers spied on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over decades
Content: Twelve former police officers are under consideration by the CPS.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTwelve former police officers are under consideration by the CPS.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianSpycops scandalUK newsProsecutors consider charges against officers involved in spycops scandalMore than 100 undercover officers spied on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over decadesRob EvansSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProsecutors are examining whether to bring criminal charges against 12 former police officers who were involved in spying on political groups.The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) is examining a file of evidence that the officers may have committed wrongdoing while working in controversial undercover operations.It follows a police investigation into Mark Kennedy, an undercover officer who infiltrated environmental and leftwing groups for six years.Kennedy is a key figure in the spycops scandal. He deceived a number of women into intimate relationships while concealing from them that he was a police spy. The total number is unknown, but is believed to be in double figures.Prosecutors are considering whether to authorise charges against the other officers under the offence of misconduct in public office. However, details of the alleged wrongdoing have not been made public.Kennedy was one of 139 undercover officers who spied on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over more than four decades.If the CPS decides to launch a prosecution of any of the 12 officers, it would be the first time that any officer involved in the undercover operations, which lasted between 1968 and at least 2010, were criminally charged with any kind of wrongdoing that had not been authorised by their managers.The spycops scandal has revealed that the undercover officers committed a range of misconduct. These included regularlydeceiving women into sexual relationships, lying in court proceedings when they appeared in their fake identities, and stealingthe identities of dead children.Like the other undercover officers, Kennedy adopted a fake identity to infiltrate environmental groups such asEarth First! and Climate Campbetween 2003 and 2009. He transformed himself from an ordinary police officer into a long-haired, tattooed protester. He worked for the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, one of two squads that infiltrated undercover officers into political groups.He had a six-year intimate relationship with a social justice campaigner, known as Lisa Jones. Through her owndetective work, she uncovered his real identityin 2010.This exposure led to the outbreak of the spycops scandal and was the first in a string of revelations, which has over time disclosed the scale of misconduct.These led to the long-runningpublic inquiry, which hasbeen examining the activities and management of the undercover officers.It also led to the police setting up a number of their own internal investigations into alleged criminal behaviour by individual officers.One of these, known as Operation Montrose, examined the conduct of Kennedy and others.Police have previously said Operation Montrose wasexamining whether Kennedy had conducted “inappropriate sexual relationships”while undercover.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInitiated in 2015, the investigation has been run under the auspices of the NationalPoliceChiefs’ Council (NPCC).I was lied to by a police spy. The inquiry promised the truth but we’re far from it | Kate WilsonRead moreThe NPCC confirmed that it had sent a file of evidence relating to Kennedy and 11 other police officers to the CPS. The nature of the alleged wrongdoing by the other police officers is unclear.Kennedy had a two-year relationship with Kate Wilson, a campaigner. She won a landmark victory in 2021, when judges in a tribunal decided that police had grosslyviolated her human rights.The judges concluded that senior officers in charge of Kennedy “either knew of the relationship, chose not to know of its existence, or were incompetent and negligent in not following up” clear and obvious signs.Covert surveillance filesshowed how the police secretly monitored and recorded her personal activities during the relationship. They recorded how Wilson and Kennedy frequently stayed together, visited her parents’ house, and went on holiday.They chronicled trips the couple made to the cinema, a museum and a concert, as well as a visit to the college where she had studied.Kennedy’s lawyer said he did not wish to comment.Explore more on these topicsUK newsSpycops scandalPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Researchers find Britain’s 11th-century ‘Conquest Man’ was Scandinavian – but did he land with the Norman army? | North of England | The Guardian
description: It’s ‘plausible’, though more likely the Humberside resident was one of many immigrants to Viking-controlled Danelaw
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: It’s ‘plausible’, though more likely the Humberside resident was one of many immigrants to Viking-controlled Danelaw
Content: A reconstruction of Conquest Man by the Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University.Photograph: Liverpool John Moores UniversityView image in fullscreenA reconstruction of Conquest Man by the Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University.Photograph: Liverpool John Moores UniversityNorth of EnglandResearchers find Britain’s 11th-century ‘Conquest Man’ was Scandinavian – but did he land with the Norman army?It’s ‘plausible’, though more likely the Humberside resident was one of many immigrants to Viking-controlled DanelawNicola DavisScience correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the most consequential showdowns in the history of the British Isles, the Battle of Hastings is seen as the foundational event of the Anglo-Saxons’ conquest by their Norman enemy across the Channel.But researchers who have put flesh on the bones of one man who lived through the turmoil of the era are learning more about the fighters who may have belonged to neither side.Dubbed Conquest Man, a skeleton of an unknown male was buried atSt Peter’s church in Barton-upon-Humber, with previous analyses revealing the oak used to make his coffin came from a single tree felled in 1079 – probably when the man died.But while this and other details are clear – he died in his 50s or 60s, was of stocky build, had multiple healed fractures and stood just 5ft 1in tall – his origins are not.According to English Heritage’s head curator of collections, Kevin Booth, who has been leading the project, questions remain over whether the man was even a Norman or Saxon.“He’s likely neither, and we shouldn’t be shocked by that,” Booth said.View image in fullscreenKevin Booth lays out the skeleton at St Peter’s church in Barton-upon-Humber, north Lincolnshire.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/English HeritageThe new work – which has not been peer-reviewed – was produced by researchers at Historic England, the Francis Crick Institute, the British Geological Survey, the University of Southampton and the Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University.The results helped the team produce a reconstruction of Conquest Man’s face, suggesting he had thin lips, a receding hairline and a frank gaze.View image in fullscreenThe man died in his 50s or 60s, was of stocky build and stood 5ft 1in tall.Photograph: Liverpool John Moores UniversityAccording to analyses of the man’s DNA, he had substantial continental ancestry, while studies based on his skull shape suggest he had Scandinavian origins.Levels of strontium isotopes in his teeth are compatible with someone living in the Barton area, while levels of oxygen isotopes suggest he may have spent time in a colder region during adolescence.And though the man was interred in the cemetery of a pre-conquest church that had been transferred to Gilbert De Ghent, one of William the Conqueror’s knights, his grave goods indicate a Scandinavian influence, with applewood staffs placed by his side.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A fascinating discovery’: research challenges Battle of Hastings narrativeRead moreWhile it is possible Conquest Man came from Barton, Booth said the most likely explanation is that he arrived from Scandinavia – a situation that would not be surprising given pre-conquest Barton would have been in the heart of the Viking-controlled territory known as the Danelaw, with the River Humber providing access to the sea.“Our man was born into a world where one king ruled England, Denmark, Norway and parts of Sweden. That pretty much continued through to 1042. The exchange through the Humber and other east coast ports must have been commonplace,” said Booth.“That our man could have come across in early adulthood within this common North Sea territory makes a lot of sense.”However, there is another possibility. “It’s entirely plausible that our man comes in through Pevensey beach in 1066,” said Booth, noting it is also plausible the man came to Normandy from Scandinavia, whether because of family connections or trade, or simply in search of a life.“It’s just perhaps … not the most likely account,” he said. Indeed, the report from the new work stresses it would be “a step” to place Conquest Man with the victorious Norman army.“While the dukedom of Normandy (land of Northmen) had itself been formed through the intermingling of Danish incursion and settlement in the 10th century, by the mid-11th century that connection and movement of peoples between (largely Denmark) and Normandy seems to have all but ceased,” the report says.Booth added the work highlights that the events of 1066 were not in isolation, but noted the year was exceptional in putting a final break in the long-lasting connections between Scandinavia and, particularly, the east coast of England.“Our man grows up in a different world but manages to navigate his way into the new reality,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNorth of EnglandAnthropology (Science)HeritageAnthropology (Education)featuresShareReuse this content

title: UK asks banks for feelgood stories about keeping out dirty money | Financial sector | The Guardian
description: City firms tapped for case studies to try to convince global watchdog that London has cleaned up its act
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: City firms tapped for case studies to try to convince global watchdog that London has cleaned up its act
Content: Police escort an arrested man and carry away evidence after a dawn raid on a property in east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenPolice escort an arrested man and carry away evidence after a dawn raid on a property in east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyFinancial sectorUK asks banks for feelgood stories about keeping out dirty moneyCity firms tapped for case studies to try to convince global watchdog that London has cleaned up its actKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government is asking bankers and lawyers to provide feelgood stories about how they blocked dirty money from entering the UK, as ministers try to prove the UK’s money-laundering controls are working.The Treasury’s call for evidence is meant to illustrate that the UK has upped its game when it comes to preventing financial crime, particularly since its last dismal assessment by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) global crime watchdog in 2018, which fuelled allegations that London had becomea hub for “dirty money”.“To build the strongest possible picture of system-wide effectiveness,” thegovernment call for evidence said, “we are looking for real-life examples with clear, demonstrable results that illustrate how the UK’s anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and sanctions frameworks operate effectively in practice.”JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon warns UK chancellor not to hike taxes on banksRead moreThe government is rushing to collect those examples before it submits its own evidence packet to the taskforce in October. The watchdog’s assessment team will then visit the UK for an on-the-ground review next summer.But the UK faces an uphill battle to prove the City has made substantial changes, and are staying alert to new threats including asurge in AI-fuelled investment fraudand the growing popularity of cryptocurrencies, which can help shield the source of transactions.Last year, the National Crime Agency estimated that £100bn is being laundered through or within the UK every single year, with City firms providing legal and financial services for fraudsters, human traffickers, the illegal drug trade and other types of organised crime. The UK’s national risk assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing has alsoclassed the UK legal sector as “high risk”for every one of its assessments since 2017.“As the UK approaches its next FATF mutual evaluation in 2027, the pressure on its anti-money laundering (AML) regime is intensifying,” the rating agency Moody’s said in a report published earlier this year. “Billions are spent each year in the UK on supervision with hundreds of firms refused entry to the financial system following due diligence, yet an estimated £100bn is still laundered annually.”Moody’s added: “When FATF examiners arrive in the UK, they may ask how much of that risk is really being reduced by the UK’s controls, intelligence and enforcement, and how quickly.”The first phase of the next FATF review will allow the UK government to submit its own evidence, outlining how effectively the country handles and prevents money laundering and other financial crime.The Treasury is asking City firms to share any cases, from 2022 onward, showing how they dumped, or refused to take on, potentially high-risk clients. That is on top of cases where a company’s intervention later led to a state investigation or prosecution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government has also asked companies for any examples where they discovered red flags for financial crime in customer profiles, and how this ended up changing the types of clients the firm was willing to take on.A Treasury spokesperson said: “We take firm and coordinated action across government and industry to crack down on economic crime. We have introduced new strategies, enhanced enforcement capabilities and increased funding designed to disrupt those seeking to abuse the UK economy.“As you would expect, the government regularly engages with industry on this - and preparations for the FATF assessment in 2027 are no different.”Explore more on these topicsFinancial sectorCorporate governanceTax avoidanceHMRCNCA (National Crime Agency)CrimeCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Statins can reduce dementia risk by up to 15%, long-term study suggests | Dementia | The Guardian
description: The cholesterol-busting drugs are more effective the earlier in life they are taken, 15-year research project indicates
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: The cholesterol-busting drugs are more effective the earlier in life they are taken, 15-year research project indicates
Content: The number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenThe number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PADementiaStatins can reduce dementia risk by up to 15%, long-term study suggestsThe cholesterol-busting drugs are more effective the earlier in life they are taken, 15-year research project indicatesAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichSun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStatins can lower the risk of dementia by 15%, and the earlier in life they are taken the higher the chances of avoiding the disease, a 15-year study suggests.The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.Now research presented in Munich at the world’s largest heart conference suggests that the cholesterol-busting drugs could dramatically reduce the risk of people developing dementia.In the largest study of its kind, more than 132,000 people in Denmark were tracked by researchers between 2006 and 2021.Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men.The findings were presented on Sunday at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), and simultaneously published inthe Lancet Regional Health Europe journal.Prof Isabel Goncalves, a member of the ESC communication committee, who was not involved in the research, hailed the findings. “Because statins are widely available and inexpensive, the findings are potentially important,” she said.Statins are already one of the most commonly used drugs in the world. The drugs reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels in the blood, which can lead to plaque buildup in arteries and increase the chance of heart attacks, strokes and heart disease. But statins could also help protect the brain in the long term.Experts believe this is because there is strong evidence that high LDL cholesterol can increase people’s risk of developing dementia, by hardening or narrowing blood vessels that supply the brain.LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) drives plaque formation, and the resulting disruptions to the brain’s blood supply can increase the risk of dementia.Previous research from the Lancet dementia commissionsuggested addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, could prevent or delay 45% of dementia cases.“Detecting and treating high levels of LDL-C from midlife is one such highlighted risk factor,” said Dr Tummas Ternhamar, from Copenhagen University hospital, who presented the results of the new research at the conference.All those in the 15-year study had type 2 diabetes. But Ternhamar said the findings strengthened the idea that one day everyone might be offered statins as part of a package of measures – such as staying physically active and eating well – to reduce their risk of dementia.View image in fullscreenStatins, which reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels in the blood, are one of the most commonly used drugs in the world.Photograph: Darren Lehane/AlamySpeaking to reporters in Munich, he said: “Our study supports the idea that dementia risk is best addressed by targeting several factors at once, and that cholesterol may belong on that list.“The Lancet commission already takes that multicomponent view, recommending that high LDL cholesterol be detected and treated from midlife. What our findings also add is that timing matters within that – acting early looks better than acting late.”Among the 132,585 people followed by Ternhamar and his colleagues, 2.7% went on to develop dementia.Compared with no statin initiation, early statin treatment was associated with a 15% lower relative risk of dementia over 10 years. Late statin initiation was associated with a 10% lower relative risk of dementia over 10 years.Ternhamar said experts were investigating exactly why statins might lower the risk of dementia.“Statins effectively lower LDL cholesterol and protect against atherosclerosis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases,” he said. “This may in turn protect against cerebrovascular atherosclerosis, ischemic stroke, reduced blood flow, and damage to brain tissue, offering a plausible link to explain our findings.”Dr Honorine Lebraud, a senior partnerships manager at Alzheimer’s Research UK, who was not involved in the research, said: “This observational study adds to growing evidence linking cardiovascular health and brain health. It reinforces the fact that what is good for the heart is good for the brain.Study finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 yearsRead more“More work is needed to show a direct link between statins and reduced dementia risk. This study offers important clues about how cholesterol and cardiovascular health influence dementia risk, while also showing where future research should focus.”Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, said it was important to remember that this was an observational study, which meant it could show an association but cannot prove that statins themselves reduced the risk of dementia.“That said, there is evidence from trials that do show that statins reduce the risk of dementia so the findings in this study are certainly plausible.”Explore more on these topicsDementiaStatinsAlzheimer'sMental healthMedical researchHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nasa space telescope launches after surviving Trump budget cuts | Nasa | The Guardian
description: Searching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope begins million-mile journey from Florida launchpad
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Searching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope begins million-mile journey from Florida launchpad
Content: NASA launches powerful new space telescope from FloridaNasaNasa space telescope launches after surviving Trump budget cutsSearching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope begins million-mile journey from Florida launchpadRichard Luscombein MiamiSun 30 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA $4.3bn space telescope thatDonald Trumptried to kill has lifted off from Florida as Nasa embarks on the next stage of its quest to unlock the secrets of the universe.The Nancy Grace Roman spacetelescopesurvived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts, and began a million-mile journey into deep space from a launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center on Sunday morning. .Sunday’s launch marked “an endpoint for the engineers, ⁠but it’s a starting point for the scientists,” Julie McEnery, the telescope’s senior project scientist, told reporters, including Reuters, at a post-launch news conference.“It feels like I’m on the edge of a precipice, and we’re just about to set a foot off into the unknown.”Searching chiefly for exoplanets and clues about planetary formation, it is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes in the annals of Nasa’s storied history of space exploration.But as next-generation equipment almost 10 years in the making, the Roman telescope, named for the space agency’sfirst chief of astronomy, who died in 2018, is many times more powerful than Hubble and will work to enhance the output of its stablemates, both of which continue to operate.View image in fullscreenAstronomer Nancy Grace Roman, Nasa’s first chief of astronomy.Photograph: NASA/APAccording to Nasa, its 300-megapixel infrared camera will give Roman the same sharpness and resolution as Hubble, but with a field of view at least 100 times larger. The agency says each image will capture a patch of sky about 1.5 times bigger than the apparent size of a full moon.Roman also contains a specialized instrument known as a coronagraph that blocks glare from stars and makes it easier to photograph planets around them in detail.Nasa said it expected the images would reveal “giant worlds that are older, colder, and in closer orbits than the hot, young super-Jupiters direct imaging has mainly revealed so far”.Roman’s destination is Lagrange point 2, a “parking spot” in space about one million miles from Earth, where it will operate in the same complex sun-Earth orbit as Webb, though the two telescopes will remain far apart.It is not entirely a successor to Hubble and Webb, which were launched in 1990 and 2021, respectively, but was designed to support and advance their missions, while making discoveries of its own.View image in fullscreenTechnicians connecting the inner and outer segments of Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on 25 November 2025, at Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.Photograph: Jolearra Tshiteya/NASA/APNasa said Roman’s large panoramas would “uncover interesting targets that Hubble could follow up on using infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light to offer a more comprehensive view”, while Webb “can then use its larger mirror and more powerful vision to deliver even more detailed, ultra-sharp observations”.Roman, meanwhile, can view regions around objects Hubble or Webb observe “to offer context”. Its imagery, which Nasa expects will first come in early 2027 after months of calibration and tests in the telescope’s final orbit, will be made immediately public, allowing the agency, professional researchers and amateur astronomers an unprecedented opportunity for analysis.“From objects in our outer solar system and exploding stars, to growing black holes and galaxies by the billions, very little will be beyond Roman’s reach,” Nasa said in anonline explanationof the telescope’s initial five-year mission, which could be extended to 10.“Roman will pair a large field of view with crisp infrared vision to scan vast, deep swaths of sky. This flagship mission is designed to help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, and planets outside our solar system.”McEnery, Nasa’s senior project scientist for the Roman mission, said the need for it was conceived at the end of the last century, although it was only in 2016 that Nasa began the development stage, and 2020 before it finally approved the entire project and commenced construction.“One of the motivations for Roman was the discovery that our universe is not just expanding, but that expansion is accelerating,” she said inan interview on Thursdaywith Sophia Roberts, an astrophysics video producer at Nasa’s Goddard space flight center in Maryland.“It’s like if you were to throw a ball in the air, and instead of the ball coming back down, it just keeps shooting away. There’s something really fundamental that we don’t understand about the nature of our universe itself, and Roman is purpose-built to address and provide the data that we need to address these questions.”If the US president had his way, Roman would never have made it to the launchpad. A 2025 White House proposal for what analysts said would be “extinction level cuts” to Nasa’s science budget, including the axing of the Roman project, wasroundly rejectedin January by Congress, which restored the agency’s 2026 funding level to $24.4bn.Seemingly undeterred, the Trump administration istrying againfor the 2027 fiscal year, seeking a 23% reduction in Nasa’s overall budget to $18.8bn, and a 46% chop for science projects that thePlanetary Society saidwould lead to the termination of more than 50 missions.The launch of Roman marks the final flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket, which Elon Musk’s company is phasing out along with its smaller Falcon 9 rockets to concentrate onStarship, its versatile new workhorse that is planned to eventually carry humans to Mars.Explore more on these topicsNasaSpaceFloridaDonald TrumpTrump administrationSpaceXAstronomynewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman, 22, killed and five injured in shooting at Swiss rave  | Switzerland | The Guardian
description: Manhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday
Content: A poster advertising the rave where the shooting took place.Photograph: Harold Cunningham/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA poster advertising the rave where the shooting took place.Photograph: Harold Cunningham/AFP/GettySwitzerlandWoman, 22, killed and five injured in shooting at Swiss raveManhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of SundayReutersSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA manhunt is under way inSwitzerlandafter a 22-year-old woman was killed ⁠and five people were injured, ⁠some seriously, in a ​shooting at a rave in the northern town of Aarau, local police have said.In the attack in the early hours of Sunday at a techno party at a covered horse-racing track, an Italian woman died from her injuries at the scene, authorities said. All those caught up in the shooting were residents of Switzerland and in their 20s.Police appealed to the public for any images of the incident and said large areas of the town had been cordoned off in the search for one or more attackers.“We have no definite information about who is behind ​the attack,” a police spokesperson, Bernhard Graser, told Reuters. “We don’t know if it’s one, if ‌it’s several people, if they are on ‌the run by vehicle or on foot.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers patrol a street in Aarau on Sunday.Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPAA 34-year-old witness ‌who asked for anonymity said he heard shots shortly after the music stopped at 2.30am on Sunday, which he initially mistook for fireworks.Some took cover behind a DJ booth and one woman hid behind a refrigerator but was hit in the back by a bullet and bled to death despite efforts to revive her, he said.“It’s just incredibly tragic. She was young,” he said. “That something like this could happen in Aarau, at a local event, ‌is simply unimaginable. I still can’t really process it.”As a precaution police have increased their presence beyond the town – which is about 50km west of Zurich and 30km south of the German border – but Graser said there were indications the shooter or shooters were no longer in the immediate area.View image in fullscreenPolice secure the area around the Schachen racing track after the shooting.Photograph: Michael Buholzer/Keystone/AP“But we still have a lot of police here in the area, in the town of Aarau, in the whole state, to make sure that we could get them if they’re still ⁠around,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReuters footage showed armed officers patrolling the area, police convoys moving through the ​streets and armoured vehicles parked near the ​crime scene.Organisers of the annual rave said they ​were shocked and heartbroken ‌by the incident. “A rave should ​always be a place ​of joy and love, never a place where people are killed, injured, or left in fear,” they said.Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership inEuropealthough violent shootings are rare and it approved tighter gun control rules in 2019.The text of this article was amended on 30 August 2026. Aarau is west of Zurich rather than north, as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsSwitzerlandEuropeGun crimeItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city | Sudan | The Guardian
description: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts
Content: Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSave the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSudanPeople fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge cityMore traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirtsRachel Savagein JohannesburgSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.The UN saysmore than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figurescitedby Save the Children.“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.View image in fullscreenTens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeidlast week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSFdescended into open conflict.Since then,about 11.3 million peoplehave been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, areat risk of famine.Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range fromtens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have beenmassacred by the RSF in El Fasherover two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.View image in fullscreenThe damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesA surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in Juneled the UN to warnthat the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according toEmergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.View image in fullscreenConditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”Explore more on these topicsSudanAfricaRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: On long road back from Brexit, north-east’s recovery rides on survival of Nissan’s ‘shining star’ plant  | Nissan | The Guardian
description: Operating at only half its capacity, Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland factory seeks deal with China’s Chery as it battles Brexit threats
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Operating at only half its capacity, Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland factory seeks deal with China’s Chery as it battles Brexit threats
Content: A Turntide employee works on a pancake motor, also known as an axial flux motor, at the company’s Gateshead factory.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Turntide employee works on a pancake motor, also known as an axial flux motor, at the company’s Gateshead factory.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianNissanOn long road back from Brexit, north-east’s recovery rides on survival of Nissan’s ‘shining star’ plantOperating at only half its capacity, Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland factory seeks deal with China’s Chery as it battles Brexit threatsJasper JollySun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a factory in Gateshead, engineers carefully wind metal wires around iron cores to go in electric motors. Here, workers produce a smaller “pancake motor”, which generates higher torque than conventional versions for supercars or construction equipment.These workers form part of north-east England’s automotive industry, which has experienced a long line of political disruptions, fromMargaret Thatcher’s efforts to attract international investment, through Brexit and now Andy Burnham’sreindustrialisation strategy.Across the Gateshead factory, which is owned by Turntide, more people are readying tools to assemble 2.5-tonne prototype battery packs for Hitachi’s hybrid trains, also to be built in the north-east.The busy factory is just one example of the ripples that have spread out from the centre of the area’s automotive industry, theSunderlandcar factory 15 minutes down the road owned by Japan’s Nissan.Turntide’s business would not be here without its bigger automotive neighbour. Hyperdrive, one of the businesses combined into US-owned Turntide, secured its firstbatteriesfrom a factory supplying Nissan. The smaller company shows why governments court big manufacturers: they bring stable jobs and can also spark growth in the local economy.Yet the situation is not so positive across the local industry. Four decades after opening in 1986, Nissan’s underutilised Sunderland plant is hoping to build cars for China’s Chery. The deal, which is still not confirmed, came at just the right time for Sunderland’s workers, with the plant operating at barely half its capacity and facing a series ofBrexitthreats to its export-led model.Nissan maps out deal to build cars for China’s Chery at its Sunderland plantRead moreThe Nissan factory opened as the keystone ofThatcher’s investment drive. In Sunderland those efforts are mostly seen as a success: the first Bluebird from the plant takes pride of place in the city’s museum. The factory produced 507,000 cars in 2016, just shy of the 510,000 made in 2012, and it was seen as the carmaker’s most efficient plant internationally.Andy Palmer, who was Nissan’s global chief operating officer before leaving to lead Aston Martin in 2014, said the plant was “the shining star globally forNissanin the manufacturing world”.View image in fullscreenTechnicians work on the Nissan Juke and Qashqai production line at the Nissan factory in Sunderland.Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/GettyYet it still had to fight to survive. Nissanclosed its other European plant in Spainin 2020 (later selling it to Chery). That survival was “no mean feat”, Palmer said, and came “in spite of everything else” that it had to deal with.Brexit threatsThe list of challenges faced by the global car industry over the past decade is long, with the pandemic and subsequent supply chain chaos, increased protectionism and the rise of Chinese competitors – all while finding cash to invest heavily in electric technology. But Sunderland’s automotive industry in particular became a symbol of a difficulty specific to Britain’s companies: Brexit.The Brexit vote triggered a decade of political turmoil in the UK, and huge uncertainty for carmakers over whether the Conservative government would pursue a “no deal” exit that would have led to the overnight imposition of tariffs on the UK’s largest export market. Nissan was eventuallygranted £61m in secret state aidto invest in new models, followed by another £101m in late 2022.The no deal outcome – seen as a catastrophe by most exporters – was averted but car exporters still have to cope with twin Brexit threats this year. The first is from EU rules of origin that say electric cars made in Britain must contain batteries made in the UK or EU to avoid paying tariffs, and vice versa. The rules wereincluded in the 2020 Brexit dealto spur manufacturers to secure British and EU batteries rather than relying on Chinese imports. However, many of the battery projects have collapsed, leaving the industry short of European supply.Nissan sources batteries from the next-door gigafactory run by Chinese-owned AESC, but the rules also require crucial cathode materials inside the cells to be sourced from Europe. That may prove too hard, so the automotive industry in the UK and EU is pushing for the latter to extend the rules of origin deadline for a second time. But some industry insiders do not expect an extension until as late as December, as the EU uses it for leverage in negotiations.Car industry pressing EU for further delay to Brexit EV tariffsRead moreThe second threat is from the EU’s separate Industrial Accelerator Act that will limit public procurement and subsidies to cars “made in EU” in an effort to protect carmakers from China. Factories in Britain will be locked out under the current draft. British and EU companies (who own most of the UK’s car factories) have called for the UK to be included in the rules. Nissan, which declined a request for an interview, has privatelywarned the government that Sunderland’s future was at risk.“It’s not a slam dunk that Nissan will survive,” Palmer said. “If made in Europe excludes the UK then I think it’s existential for Sunderland. Sunderland will die.”David Bailey, a professor of business economics at the University of Birmingham, said: “Brexit keeps bringing up these uncertainties. The world is changing, and the EU responds to that, and that affects the UK.”Electric shocksThe big carmakers in the UK are also lobbying hard on another issue the government is considering: watering down electric vehicle targets, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. The existing rules mean battery cars make up 80% of sales from high-volume manufacturers, but Burnham’s government this month announced thenew target could be as low as 50%.Nissan was an electric pioneer and hasinvested heavilyto build its new electric Leaf and Juke crossover SUV models. Yet the company will welcome lower targets after reportedly shelving development of an electric Qashqai, wary of lower-than-expected demand for battery cars around the world. It has also set its sights onselling new petrol cars beyond 2035, when they are due to be banned.View image in fullscreenA Nissan Leaf comes off the production line at the Sunderland factory.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSome analysts believe carmakers trying to delay the shift to electric are signing their own death warrants by ceding the market to Chinese competitors. Colin Walker, the head of transport at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a thinktank, said: “Embracing this new technology represents the best chance that manufacturers have to survive and thrive in an electrified world. Pushing increasingly obsolescent technologies will only hasten their demise and would be a recipe for factory closures and mass redundancies.”A Nissan spokesperson said it was “committed to a fully electric future” and that the mandate “must align with real-life consumer EV demand to ensure a gradual transition to full zero-emission vehicle sales while supporting the competitiveness of UK automotive manufacturing”.Nissan is undergoing a painful restructuring process worldwide, with the chief executive, Ivan Espinosa,closing seven factories and cutting 20,000 jobs.If confirmed, Nissan will build cars for Chery, a part-state-owned Chinese carmaker that also makes the Omoda and Jaecoo brands. Nissan would still own the plant and employ the workers and would be able to use its spare capacity – it only managed 273,000 cars in 2025.Some experts think there is little chance of Chery confirming the deal if the Brexit issues are not resolved. Yet the Unite union is pleased, arguing it would keep volumes up, thus preserving jobs.For Turntide, the north-east ofEnglandstill offers what it needs to try to grow its business. David Orgill, Turntide’s vice-president of global operations, said: “Why not here? Why not in the north of England? The supply chain is fantastic up here.”Turntide’s US parent company, backed by Bill Gates’s Breakthrough Energy Ventures, BMW and Amazon, combined three UK businesses with the aim of expanding sales. It is expecting surging demand for its pancake motors (which are known as axial flux motors because of the different arrangement of their internal magnets). Based on talks with carmakers and construction equipment companies, it wants to expand production to 12,000 motors a year by 2028.View image in fullscreenTurntide workers on the production line in Gateshead.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“We’re expecting to grow significantly in the next 18 months,” Orgill said. “We’re actually able to pull back a lot of the capability and manufacturing back into the UK.”The survival and success of the Nissan plant is seen as politically crucial in the north-east and at Westminster, which partly explains why the government is indeed preparing to weaken the mandate further.Kim McGuinness, the Labour mayor for the north-east, said Nissan was a key part of the region’s economic plans. She said that despite the political disaffection, Sunderland was thriving, with significant investment in improving the city centre, as well as extra public transport, such as extending a metro line from the city (which lies to Nissan’s east) to Washington, the town to Nissan’s west.Centre forward: Sunderland sets sights on a revival by bringing homes and jobs to its inner cityRead more“In the north-east, we all know that factory is absolutely fundamental to our regional economy, but also [to] the position of the country in the automotive industry,” she said, adding that it acted as an anchor for the broader supply chain. “This is what the north-east does very well – that clustering effect”.McGuinness is hopeful that devolution will help to attract more manufacturing jobs and assuage the “left behind” feeling that drove the Brexit vote and the subsequent rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, which won control of Sunderland council in May’s local elections. The Reform branch in Sunderland did not respond to requests for an interview.McGuinness said: “People like me can give local residents more say. I believe that is the way that we combat Reform.”Even if the Chery deal is confirmed, the north-east’s automotive industry faces a long road to get back to its heyday when Nissan was producing half a million cars. Yet it has got through tricky situations before.“I admire the plant for surviving,” said Prof Colin Herron, an automotive expert at Newcastle University. “The resilience of the people at that factory is incredible. Now they’re entering a new phase.”Explore more on these topicsNissanAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorBrexitSunderlandNorth of EnglandEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s what saved me’: Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance on the prison drama workshop that brought them together | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performing
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: A masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performing
Content: Brothers in arms … Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanView image in fullscreenBrothers in arms … Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanTheatreInterview‘That’s what saved me’: Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance on the prison drama workshop that brought them togetherJN BenjaminA masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performingSun 30 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDarren Raymond doesn’t remember having any significant interest in acting when he was growing up. And when he metMark Rylancefor the first time, on Christmas Eve 2004, he had never heard of the multi-award winning actor. These days, things are very different: Raymond is the artistic director of Intermission Youth, the London-based arts charity and theatre, and is directing his friend Rylance in the lead role of Tartuffe (Remixed), Raymond’s adaptation of the Molière play, which opens at London’s Marylebone theatre this week.It’s fair to say neither could have anticipated they’d still be in touch this long after their initial meeting. “Unlikely companions” is a tired cliche by this point, but that doesn’t make it any less true to say that on the surface, the two had very little in common. Raymond was a young twentysomething raised on an inner-city housing estate and serving a prison sentence at HMP Brixton. Meanwhile Rylance was twice his age, a successful professional actor, and artistic director of Shakespeare’s Globe. Nevertheless that meeting, at a Shakespeare workshop in the prison, turned into a professional connection, which soon evolved into a solid friendship.double quotation markIn terms of my debt to Shakespeare, my debt to all the great teachers I had, this is it – this will be it until the day I dieMark RylanceRylance has been a supporter of Intermission, the charity Raymond set up 20 years ago – which helps to transform the lives of young people aged 11-30+ through theatre – since the very early days. Its flagship programme takes 80 trainees a year for a regular schedule of masterclasses, pastoral support and professional performances. In a 2008 interview on Radio 4, Raymond mentioned the positive impact of his and Rylance’s Christmas Eve meeting and how it inspired his vision for Intermission. Rylance was listening, and was prompted to visit the theatre’s headquarters at St Saviour’s Church in Knightsbridge. “I was really knocked out by it, the production was everything I’d been looking for,” Rylance says of the performance he saw. We’re speaking today at Intermission’s temporary base at Omnibus theatre in Clapham – the organisation has struggled to secure a suitable permanent home since being asked to leave the church in 2019.Intermission’s output is why Rylance thinks it holds such a critical place in the context of the industry. It offers free-of-charge, rigorous, professional-standard training that produces high-quality results. For many, particularly those from working-class backgrounds, such an opportunity would be otherwise unaffordable. Rylance firmly believes in giving back, but in the current climate his preference is to invest in grassroots arts initiatives over major institutions. For him, that feels more impactful. “I don’t support my drama school, I don’t support the Globe any more, or the RSC,” he says. “In terms of my debt to Shakespeare, my debt to all the great teachers I had as a young person, this is it for me – this will be it until the day I die.”View image in fullscreenDarren Raymond in rehearsals for Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorRaymond’s own debt to Shakespeare started with that workshop he reluctantly attended while in prison. He was confused when his friend told him he’d signed them both up for drama classes, but saw it as an excuse to get more time out of their shared cell. On the day of the workshop about 20 prisoners were greeted by Dr  Bruce Wall, co-founder of the London Shakespeare Workout – a charity that uses work by major cinematic, musical and choreographic writers and thinkers, along with Shakespeare, to promote confidence and relationship-building among its participants.Casting his mind back to the first session with Wall, Raymond and his friend didn’t know what to expect. “This guy’s come in, like, ‘Drama!’, all flapping hands and flamboyant. I dunno how he got away with that because it’s just him and there’s 15 to 20 inmates in there. All serious inmates.” The group was initially hesitant, but Wall’s upbeat energy proved irresistible – the enthusiasm soon spread. Raymond remembers an exercise where participants were given a line of Shakespeare’s text and had to respond using their own words. The group reacted to Raymond’s contribution with a chorus of oohs and aahs. “When I look back, that was a really profound moment in my life because it was the first time I knew my words could have any kind of impact. When I left the session, Bruce said: ‘Well done, I thought you were excellent.’ I don’t know if he said it to everybody – probably did. But it meant something to me.”double quotation markI didn’t know what an audition was. But I went, met him, done the audition – and then they cast me as OthelloDarren RaymondBack in their cell, Raymond and his friend were energised by their first drama workshop experience. “Normally we’d be talking about how to get one back over the system, but that day we were talking about Shakespeare,” he remembers. Wanting to replicate that feeling, he returned every week, eventually becoming an advocate for the group – encouraging others to get involved, petitioning the prison to keep the initiative going when it was under threat of closure, and even declining relocation to a lower category prison with fewer restrictions as well as privileges such as home visits, knowing that the move would mean he’d no longer be able to attend. Nobody had ever turned down a move to a “D-Cat” prison before, the governor told him, adding: “You must be really into this drama thing!”Raymond’s commitment earned him the opportunity to represent the prison in a poetry convention, where he first met Rob Gillion, an actor turned reverend who maintained an active interest in the life-changing power of the arts. “For some reason there was a lot of clergy present, I don’t know why. I remember [Gillion] showing a real interest in my story, but I didn’t think anything of it,” he says. He didn’t know it at the time, but that was the beginning of his artistic journey.View image in fullscreenDarren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanAt one of the final Shakespeare sessions Raymond attended, he met Rylance, who was guest-facilitating the session along with his late wifeClaire van Kampen. The group had been told Rylance was an acclaimed actor and the artistic director of Shakespeare’s Globe – “nobody knew what the Globe was!”, Raymond laughs. He describes his first impression as an anticlimax: “He’s come in with his shorts and sandals, looking like some dishevelled guy off the road. None of us really paid any mind to his stature. Nobody knew any Shakespeare, and that was a good thing – it made the playing field more even.”Rylance remembers that first meeting well. “It was a small workshop, with just four young men,” he says. “Each had learned a soliloquy and I listened to them. There was a definite marriage of what’s mortal and immortal, because of the interweaving of their own language right next to Shakespeare. The Shakespeare stuff will live as long as humanity lasts on the planet, but the mortal lives of these young people brought alongside the immortal, is very thrilling and delightful to me. That’s what was happening with those four guys that day”.The exercise was a revelation for the group. “We could talk to him very quickly” recalls Raymond, “and that was testament to how he came to us in the room. The way he spoke to us about Othello … it was riveting listening to these stories because he related it to us and the situation we were in and the lives we were living. At the end of it, he said: ‘Look, we don’t have to revere this work in the way people make you think you need to. Use whatever you want from it – take whatever you want and use it however you want.’ That’s what I do now. That’s what saved me.”Some time after his release from HMP Brixton, Raymond received an out-of-the-blue call from Wall – an invitation to audition for London Shakespeare Workshop’s national tour of Othello. “I really didn’t know what it meant. I didn’t know what an audition was really, I didn’t know what a UK tour was. But I went, met him, done the audition – and then they cast me as Othello.” Rehearsals took place at St Saviour’s Church, where Gillion was the resident vicar.View image in fullscreenMark Rylance and Blanche Williams in rehearsals for Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorThe relationship between Raymond and Gillion would be transformative – “I was really inspired by Rob, he was a role model to me,” Raymond says. They stayed in touch following the end of the tour, and when Gillion later took a sabbatical to do some international travelling, he asked Raymond to move into the vicarage and keep an eye on the place while he was away. With hindsight, he realises they both knew the vicarage probably didn’t need anybody to look after it but rather the “favour” was a calculated act of kindness in the knowledge that a young Raymond would have been too proud to accept the help he needed. In 2006 Gillion invited him to run Intermission theatre.Staging full productions has always been part of Intermission’s regular activity. Over the years Raymond has adapted 15 Shakespeare plays, each time weaving contemporary issues into the classical texts in order to demystify the language and make the pieces feel more relevant for a new generation of actors. The upcoming production of Tartuffe (Remixed), however, is the company’s biggest production to date, and a rare instance of a cast that brings together Intermission graduates and actors who have taken other, sometimes more traditional routes into the industry.double quotation markThis feels like a natural path forward for me as I try to figure out a new story to my lifeMark RylanceRylance wasn’t sure if he’d return to do any more theatre. “This is the first time I’ll be directed by Darren. First time back in the theatre since my wife has died, too.” Van Kampen passed away in early 2025 after being diagnosed with cancer. “When you lose your wife of 35 years – I keep thinking of wonderfulJoan Littlewoodwho, when she lost Jerry Raffles, stepped out of that theatre and never stepped in any theatre again. And that’s a temptation – but it’s like when you think you have a death wish but its not that you want to kill yourself – but you want to kill a certain way you’ve been living.”Returning to stage acting feels like part of a ritual of remembrance for his wife, who was also a passionate supporter of Intermission’s work: “It was something we gave money to, something we supported. And so this feels like a natural path forward for me as I try to figure out a new story to my life. What’s the story of my life without her?”For Rylance, Intermission is part of the journey of his life, and he’s not alone. When it comes to the organisation’s impact, there have been many success stories that have come from the training programme. The actor Tosin Cole graduated from the very first Intermission cohort in 2009, and has since worked consistently across TV, film and theatre. His CV includes series regular roles in Hollyoaks, Doctor Who, and most recently as the lead in Supacell on Netflix. “I never really had aspirations to become an actor,” he says. “It was just a cool thing to do on a Saturday.” It was going to Intermission that helped him not only realise his talent but also supported him to develop the tools he needed to take advantage of the opportunities that came his way.Asked what he thinks he would be doing if he wasn’t an actor, Cole laughs heartily as he says “Boy!”, elongating the short syllable as he diverts his gaze. That’s south London speak for let’s not even go there. Does he think there are still challenges facing young people who want to pursue a career in acting? “For a start, we need a lot more different types of stories from different types of cultures. [As Black people] our history is rich and full of those stories, and we are capable of telling them.”He’s also an advocate for more spaces like Intermission’s original venue to exist, lamenting the loss of the city’s youth clubs and adventure playgrounds. “That place was super special. It’s sad now when you’re in Knightsbridge and you walk past and see the place vacant.” The church has since been converted to a luxury home and was on the market for £35m last year. “Look at any artist or musician that’s come from an inner city and a lot of their skill and their success has come from resources being accessible. A lot of talent came out of the youth clubs where things were free.”“But every success is relative, right?” says Raymond. While he’s keen to note the commercial success of Cole and others, he also wants to spotlight the young person “who came to me from a youth offending team and was no question on the road to prison, or death. Now they have a job and a family. They’re not acting or working in the industry, but that’s also success to me.” For Raymond, the definition of success isn’t limiting, it’s expansive.Tartuffe (Remixed) is atMarylebone theatre, London,4 Septemberto 24 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreMark RylanceShakespeare's GlobeMolièrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning? | Movies | The Guardian
description: Its moguls are ripe subjects for drama, and there is huge anticipation for forthcoming features The Social Reckoning and Artificial. But other projects have failed as the film industry is increasingly colonised by IT empires
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Its moguls are ripe subjects for drama, and there is huge anticipation for forthcoming features The Social Reckoning and Artificial. But other projects have failed as the film industry is increasingly colonised by IT empires
Content: What’s not to like? … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenWhat’s not to like? … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyAutumn arts preview 2026MoviesBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Its moguls are ripe subjects for drama, and there is huge anticipation for forthcoming features The Social Reckoning and Artificial. But other projects have failed as the film industry is increasingly colonised by IT empiresTom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereSteve RoseSun 30 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iknow there are easier enemies to make,” tech reporter Jeremy Allen White tells his colleague in a recent trailer for The Social Reckoning. “The mafia would be an easier enemy to make,” comes the reply. They’re talking about Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, but they might as well be discussing big tech as a whole. As The Social Reckoning promises to underline, it’s become clear that these people are not on our side – “us” being the whole of humanity except billionaire tech overlords and their mates. But for an industry that loves a clear-cut baddie, Hollywood has barely landed a blow on the tech industry. Now it finds itself in mortal danger of being absorbed by it. Is it too late to fight back?The Social Reckoning’s predecessor,The Social Network, showed how this kind of thing is done. It was pacy, buzzy and full of weirder-than-life characters – not least the young Zuckerberg, portrayed by Jesse Eisenberg as an obnoxiously smart mogul-in-the-making, whose mission to connect the world stood in stark contrast to his own social deficiencies. Directed by David Fincher and co-written by Aaron Sorkin, it was also a commercial and critical hit, winning three Oscars. But a big part of what made The Social Network work, and makes its sequel such a threat, is that it was about the actual, real-world Silicon Valley, which is where a lot of recent entertainment has gone wrong.View image in fullscreenGlobal dominance … (from left) Ramy Youssef, Cory Michael Smith, Steve Carell and Jason Schwartzman in Mountainhead.Photograph: Macall Polay/APIn the years since, we’ve had a lot of underwhelming satire featuring fictionalised tech moguls. Jesse Armstrong’sMountainhead, for example, with its quartet of broligarchs carving up the world from on high. Or the various bonkers tech titans inDon’t Look Up(Mark Rylance),Knives Out: Glass Onion(Ed Norton),Alien: Earth(Samuel Blenkin) orThe Circle(Tom Hanks). These films obliquely caricatured real-life figures such as Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Jobs, but why go for veiled satire when the real Silicon Valley is so full of drama, incident and deeply weird, often terrible, now globally notorious personalities?The Social Reckoning certainly has a lot to work with: in the 16 years since the original, all manner of social, emotional and political harm has been laid at the doors of Meta/Facebook, while Zuckerberg himself has only become more weird/terrible/notorious – and therefore ripe for impersonation. Jeremy Strong, replacing Eisenberg, must fancy his awards chances. Written and directed by Sorkin, the sequel focuses onwhistleblower Frances Haugen(Anora’s Mikey Madison), who leaked details of the company’s machinations to the press. Courtroom drama, verbal sparring, a bit of social justice grandstanding – it looks very much in Sorkin’s wheelhouse.View image in fullscreenBig-screen bound … OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) speaks  virtually during an  AI conference in Sydney earlier this year.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPAnother ripped-from-the-headlines drama holds similar promise, but also highlights the real-world perils of tackling big tech head-on. Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial dramatises the real-life saga of OpenAI, and again, it’s a juicier story than any fiction, focusing on shifty CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield) and the many enemies he created along the way, including Musk (Ike Barinholtz –perfect casting) and the OpenAI board (Monica Barbaro, Cooper Hoffman and Yura Borisov, among others), whose efforts to oust Altman famously backfired. The script was described as “the Social Network on steroids”.But life didn’t like being imitated by art. In June this year Artificial’s producers, Amazon MGM Studios, suddenlydropped the completed movie, saying they felt it would be “better served if it were released by a different studio”. A few months earlier, Amazon and OpenAI had entered into a $50bn “strategic partnership” to “develop customised models available to power Amazon’s customer-facing applications” – which sounds like the world’s least exciting movie, but also points to inevitable synergies between tech and entertainment. Indie distributor Neon eventually stepped in, and is now releasing Artificial in early 2027.It’s too late to talk of a takeover – most Hollywood studios are wholly or partly tech companies already: Amazon, Apple, Sony, Netflix. But big tech is coming for the rest, and its pockets are very deep. On the macro scale, there is the fraught $110bn takeover of Warner Bros by Paramount, which is currently beingheld up in US courts. A large chunk of the money is coming via Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, whose personal wealth peaked at over $400bn, but has plummeted since. Disney made a $1bn investment andentered into a licensing agreementwith OpenAI last year, and even hot indie label A24 has entered intoa $75m “research partnership”with Google’s AI division DeepMind. If you’re looking for arealportent of change, news leaked last week that Gwyneth Paltrow is allegedly tohost a private, “off the record” dinnerat her Hamptons home in honour of Altman.View image in fullscreenElon running … a still from Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APIf this were a simple matter of Hollywood coming under new management, that would be showbusiness as usual, but the tech takeover could be having a chilling effect on what does and doesn’t get made.
