Many of Hollywood’s tech moguls – Ellison, Altman, and Amazon’s Jeff Bezos – are cosy with the Trump administration, which has not flinched from exerting its influence over media and entertainment. That could explain why not only did we nearlynotget to see Artificial, we alsodidget to seeMelania, the brazen puff-piece documentary on the first lady, for which Amazonshelled out $40m. How many other tech stories are no longer being greenlit in this new climate? In 2024, for example,Netflix announced Thumblite, a new show led by Rosamund Pike billed as a “Silicon Valley House of Cards” – but it somehow never got off the ground.But not even big tech calls all the shots. Elon Musk used his X pulpit to rant against Christopher Nolan’s “woke” Odyssey, for example, but everyone ignored him and went to see it anyway. Now Musk could be getting a taste of his own medicine: pugnacious film-makerAlex Gibneyhas a four-hour documentary on him premiering at the Venice film festival, which promises to “reframe the story of the tech titan as the 21st-century reincarnation of the confidence man”.Meanwhile, Zuckerberg’s Meta has just resolvedanotherlandmark casein the US over its allegedly harmful products, agreeing to a $17bn settlement – so you could say they’re already laying the groundwork for part three to the Social Network/Reckoning franchise.Explore more on these topicsFilmAutumn arts preview 2026Social networkingThe Social NetworkAaron SorkinMark ZuckerbergSam AltmanLuca GuadagninofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Bridge review – a funny, furious odyssey through occupation | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistance
Content: Witty … Writer and actor Alaa Shehada.View image in fullscreenWitty … Writer and actor Alaa Shehada.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Bridge review – a funny, furious odyssey through occupationAssembly George Square studios, EdinburghWriter and actor Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistanceMark FisherSun 30 Aug 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the simplicity of the task that gives this story heft. Recalling his formative years in the West Bank, actor and writer Alaa Shehada is asked by his mother to go on a bus journey that would take a couple of hours in any other part of the world.His mission is to deliver a plastic jerry can filled with the family’s home-pressed olive oil to his aunt in Jordan. His obstacle is the 180m crossing point known variously as the Dignity Bridge, the Allenby Bridge and the King Hussein Bridge, depending on your political standpoint.In this follow-up toThe Horse of Jenin, Shehada describes the journey with a cartoonist’s eye for human detail and a campaigner’s ear for injustice.With broad physicality, he takes on a cast of characters from the self-aggrandising taxi driver who picks him up to the smothering old lady who sits next to him on the bus and the cold-eyed Israeli teenagers who man the checkpoints. The heat is stifling, the air conditioning is ineffectual and the level of bureaucracy staggering, with each passenger laden with an all-or-nothing litany of passports, receipts and tickets.Shehada is a witty performer, brimming with life, but his tale is one of constant humiliation. This is the only way for West Bank Palestinians to reach the outside world, yet they must face arbitrary closures, endless queues, random arrests and disempowering regulations. After hours of indignity, they dream of their own international airport.Co-written and directed by Sam Beale for the Palestine Comedy Club, The Bridge is a tamer, more focused piece than The Horse of Jenin, but is no less urgent. For Shehada, the olive oil is not just a gift but a symbol of a violated land that isbeing bulldozed by settlersto this day. A story performed with fun is driven home with fury.AtAssembly George Square studios, Edinburgh, 30 August, thenBush theatre, London, 28 October–11 NovemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mere Mortals review – a dazzling, maddening ballet for the AI age | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: San Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s box
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: San Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s box
Content: Supple, sprightly, puckish … Wei Wang in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSupple, sprightly, puckish … Wei Wang in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMere Mortals review – a dazzling, maddening ballet for the AI ageEdinburgh PlayhouseSan Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s boxLyndsey WinshipSun 30 Aug 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is a spectacular show. Literally, it is full of spectacle: as much a visual extravaganza as it is a concert, as it is dance – and a gloriously maddening piece of dance at that. The dancers are as impressive as you’d expect fromSan Francisco Ballet, the US’s oldest professional ballet company, and the splashy concept is bold: artistic director Tamara Rojo commissioned choreographer Aszure Barton, composer Sam Shepherd (AKA electronic producer Floating Points) and multidisciplinary artists Hamill Industries, their starting point being the myth of Pandora’s box, transposed to the current world of AI technology and what unknowns we might be unleashing.Hamill Industries, who used some AI in their creation process, unleash something transfixing on a giant screen above the stage: morphing, pulsating pixels that look like lava or the surface of the sun. It’s intoxicating, easily dragging attention away from the dancers’ bodies (this may be the whole point – more on this later). Those dancers appear en masse in strict manoeuvres at driving tempo. Are they an army of mortals, gods, automatons or lines of code? Who knows. But they are moulded into large-scale moving images by Barton just as Pandora is moulded from clay in the best bit of integration between the digital and physical worlds, countless hands crafting this first woman out of dust.View image in fullscreenFuture shock … Wei Wang (left) and Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBarton is a magpie of a choreographer, always unpredictable, classical virtuosity sewn in among countless other ideas in unstoppable phrases. Jennifer Stahl as Pandora is an impressive creation, for sure, and Wei Wang is great: supple, sprightly, puckish. He represents Hope, although you wouldn’t know that without doing a bit of research. Choreographers are not duty-bound to enact a narrative; the Pandora tale is merely a creative trigger, they’d say, but in a story with such clear dramatic beats, and such a clever contemporary parallel, it does seem a waste to essentially throw that away.There are a few scenes where humans come to the fore, with black-clad dancers just about visible against a black backdrop: Prometheus (Joseph Walsh) and Epimetheus (Harrison James) being competitive brothers who hug and shove in one motion; a pas de deux for Pandora and her husband in which Barton’s unconventional choreography steers clear of romantic tropes and their bodies make uncommon shapes that fold in on each other.View image in fullscreenWild … Mere Mortals at the Edinburgh international festival.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianShepherd’s score is really impressive, a hybrid of electronics and orchestra (played live by the Royal Scottish National Orchestra). It’s full of drama and contrast, tension, propulsive urgency (hints of Stravinsky) and fascinating textures: slippery strings, woozily lurching or ricocheting arpeggios.At the moment that presumably represents the opening of the box (or the AI floodgates), the screens go into hyperdrive, vomiting up dazzling imagery. Then they go dark and we’re left with only bodies, a new world – black catsuits swapped for fabulous, shining gold. Precious bodies – is this the idea? Or mere robots? What the dancers do – how they relate, how they move – doesn’t really change between the two worlds. There’s no choreographic revelation. No judgment, it seems. Perhaps an exhortation to stop being distracted by the sparkly baubles of the AI gods and notice the real people in front of you. Or perhaps no moral at all, just a wild sensory experience, and the strangest non-ending, with the most human thing of all – feeling – frustratingly absent.AtEdinburgh Playhouseuntil 30 August, thenSadler’s Wells, London, 9-12 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceEdinburgh festivalFestivalsFloating PointsSan Francisco BalletreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘After I had my cat stolen, I would listen to Funkadelic and cry and cry’: Jennifer Herrema’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The Black Bananas singer knows all the words to Rapper’s Delight and relates to AC/DC, but which song reminds her of a heartbreaking theft?
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The Black Bananas singer knows all the words to Rapper’s Delight and relates to AC/DC, but which song reminds her of a heartbreaking theft?
Content: ‘I listen to the Gap Band when the roosters are crowing in the morning’ … Jennifer Herrema.Photograph: Bunny BiskitView image in fullscreen‘I listen to the Gap Band when the roosters are crowing in the morning’ … Jennifer Herrema.Photograph: Bunny BiskitHonest playlistMusic‘After I had my cat stolen, I would listen to Funkadelic and cry and cry’: Jennifer Herrema’s honest playlistThe Black Bananas singer knows all the words to Rapper’s Delight and relates to AC/DC, but which song reminds her of a heartbreaking theft?Priya ElanSun 30 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withVan Halen’s Runnin’ With the Devil. I was five or six and I went to visit my cousin Tommy who was much older. He was on a hockey team and we went to see them practise before the game and they had Runnin’ With the Devil on really loud. I was like: “Wait, what’s this?!”The song I do at karaokeYou Shook Me All Night Long by AC/DC. Me and Brian Johnson – my voice has that thing, you know?The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI still remember the full 12-inch version of the Sugarhill Gang’s Rapper’s Delight – I did it this morning! That’s a record my dad got me. He loved dancing to it.The song I can no longer listen toMeet on the Ledge by Fairport Convention. Partly because of the tragedy of Sandy Denny. But also because I listened to it over and over at a really depressing time.The song that changed my lifeWhen I first heard Lou Reed’s Satellite of Love on the radio it sounded so different and weird to me. It really imprinted on me.The best song to play at a partyLet It Whip by Dazz Band. The way it starts, it sounds just like the way a party starts.The song that gets me up in the morningI listen to the Gap Band’s Gotta Get Up when the roosters are crowing and it’s really early in the morning. It’s a song I can listen to without getting inside my head.The first single I boughtI had braces on my legs when I was a baby and then later I went with my dad to a shoe shop, Buster Brown, to buy some Mary Janes. I loved those patent leather party shoes. Then my dad went and got me Mary Jane by Rick James. I didn’t know what Mary Jane meant, but my dad did.The song I want played at my funeralFree Bird by Lynyrd Skynyrd. I’m a big fan. The lyrics are gorgeous and it’s appropriate. I don’t think I’m going to die anytime soon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best song to have sex toI never put on music or anything like that. But if I was going to choose something that’s got a chill vibe it would be Memory Motel by the Rolling Stones.The song that makes me cryFunkadelic’s I Miss My Baby. My cat Callie was stolen by the post lady and I would listen to that song and cry and cry. She was suspended from the postal service. But I never got my cat back.Black Bananas’ new album,Bad Bunch,is out on Friday.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dom McGovern: Prize Hog review – a sharp standup who is sure to go stellar | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Chicken Shop Date co-writer gives a gossipy, erudite account of his relationship with how he looks in this assured debut
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The Chicken Shop Date co-writer gives a gossipy, erudite account of his relationship with how he looks in this assured debut
Content: Smooth … Dom McGovern.Photograph: Kit McCarthyView image in fullscreenSmooth … Dom McGovern.Photograph: Kit McCarthyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewDom McGovern: Prize Hog review – a sharp standup who is sure to go stellarPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe Chicken Shop Date co-writer gives a gossipy, erudite account of his relationship with how he looks in this assured debutBrian LoganSun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a fringe noticeable for the polish even of its rookie standups, here’s another debut showing no signs of callowness. The co-writer ofChicken Shop Date with Amelia Dimoldenberg, you wouldn’t bet against Dom McGovern being a TV fixture soon, such is the smoothness – and good humour – characterising this account of the Hounslow man’s troubled relationship with his body. So are we talking about men’s mental health? Not if McGovern has anything to do with it. His scepticism of that phenomenon, and the performative (straight) male vulnerability it entails, forms one amusing section of his show.There’s precious little emoting or “trauma comedy” at play in Prize Hog, which doesn’t soft-soap McGovern’s difficulties with body dysmorphia and bulimia, but doesn’t over-dramatise them, either. They’re all just fodder for his sharp and gossipy chat with the audience, about a recent trip to Brazil (suboptimal destination for travellers already unconfident about their looks), and about Jesus and his unhelpful dieting example. Brought up in an Irish Catholic family, McGovern couldn’t ignore the influence of that “ripped little twink on the cross” – but 00s slimming culture cast a darker pall. At least until he undergoes therapy, under the charge of a South African counsellor rejoicing in the name Wendy Christmas.Tom Towelling Teaches You to Knit review – quirky yarns and a pop quiz in mathsRead moreAll this will be Christmas come early for fans of urbane and camp comedy, of the type practised before him byTom Allenand others. McGovern loves to flash his erudition, and his crowd-work is less duty, more infectious delight. It’s a show that will particularly connect with fellow children of the early 00s, with its running jokes about Jedward and invocation ofGillian “You Are What You Eat” McKeith.McGovern, and many of his generation, developed fraught relationships with how they looked. But this is less a tale of self-loathing than of McGovern’s journey back to full (whisper it) mental health: the friends he makes in group therapy, the dubious politics of his therapist. Mixed blessing it may be for a man ill at ease with his looks, but I’d guess we will soon be seeing McGovern a lot more often.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. title: Oslo Philharmonic/Gražinytė-Tyla/Kopatchinskaja review – weapons-grade charisma and anarchic delight | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Patricia Kopatchinskaja hurls herself into Stravinsky’s Violin Concerto, while conductor Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla brings precision and intensity to Prokofiev
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Patricia Kopatchinskaja hurls herself into Stravinsky’s Violin Concerto, while conductor Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla brings precision and intensity to Prokofiev
Content: Force to be reckoned with … Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts the Oslo Philharmonic at Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenForce to be reckoned with … Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts the Oslo Philharmonic at Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouClassical musicReviewOslo Philharmonic/Gražinytė-Tyla/Kopatchinskaja review – weapons-grade charisma and anarchic delightRoyal Albert Hall, LondonPatricia Kopatchinskaja hurls herself into Stravinsky’s Violin Concerto, while conductor Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla brings precision and intensity to ProkofievFlora WillsonSun 30 Aug 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are the violinists whose instruments seem barely relevant, their tone appearing to emanate mysteriously from the ether. And there are the violinists whose music-making is audibly rooted in the physical contact between fingers, bow and string.Patricia Kopatchinskajais among the latter – and Stravinsky’s 1931 Violin Concerto is an ideal expressive fit for this full-body performer.In her latest Proms appearance, Kopatchinskaja hurled herself into each of Stravinsky’s movements with a kind of anarchic delight. No double-stopped chord was too outrageously far-flung, no moto perpetuum passage too fiddly, no filigree descant too stratospheric. Her tone was by turns ferocious and honeyed. Bowing came in harsh wedges, glistening cascades of spiccato and generous ribbons of velvet legato. The fiendish details were all there – indeed, the sharp angles and wild lurches of the third movement began to verge on mannerism. But Kopatchinskaja’s intensity was balanced by theOslo Philharmonic’s diffidence. Their passages of neoclassical chugging were nonchalant, the wind and brass solos characterful but subtly detached, Stravinsky’s witty echoes and reworkings of Bach made achingly cool.View image in fullscreenFerocious and honeyed … violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja (centre) plays Stravinsky’s 1931 Violin Concerto.Photograph: BBC/ Chris ChristodoulouKopatchinskaja was not, in other words, this concert’s only source of weapons-grade charisma. ConductorMirga Gražinytė-Tylawas a stiller, steelier presence on the podium than at her last Proms appearance in 2021. But she remains a communicative force to be reckoned with. After a performance of the Norwegian national anthem to commemoratethe death of King Harald, Gražinytė-Tyla conjured an instant change of atmosphere inØyvind Torvund’s Symphonic Poem No 1: Forest Morning. The opening’s twitters, peeps, gurgles and blips – some synthesised, most instrumental – were a delicate tapestry in sound. The louder moments that followed were brief and minutely controlled, the whole inhabiting an intriguing uncanny valley of near-tonality.After the interval, excerpts from Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet invited close listening to more familiar material. At one extreme, there was the violence of the opening’s cataclysmic orchestral shriek and the vicious tattoo heralding Tybalt’s death; at the other, sudden sentimental tenderness for Friar Lawrence and the almost inaudible violin shivers that began Juliet’s funeral. Throughout, Gražinytė-Tyla commanded high-definition playing from the Oslo Philharmonic – rendering this sometimes densely scored music utterly lucid.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicRoyal Albert HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Waterboys review – Steve Earle joins a gloriously unruly return to Fisherman’s Blues | Music | The Guardian
description: The Nashville singer-songwriter is among the guests joining Mike Scott for a sprawling, exuberant revue that finds new life in the Waterboys’ rootsy past
Author: Peter Ross
Headline: The Nashville singer-songwriter is among the guests joining Mike Scott for a sprawling, exuberant revue that finds new life in the Waterboys’ rootsy past
Content: Intense … Mike Scott of the Waterboys at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIntense … Mike Scott of the Waterboys at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianMusicReviewThe Waterboys review – Steve Earle joins a gloriously unruly return to Fisherman’s BluesOVO Hydro, GlasgowThe Nashville singer-songwriter is among the guests joining Mike Scott for a sprawling, exuberant revue that finds new life in the Waterboys’ rootsy pastPeter RossSun 30 Aug 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is strange. A Waterboys gig, but something else, too: the first night of the Fisherman’s Blues Revue. Which is what, exactly? Inspired by the Rolling Thunder Revue, the wild tour in which Bob Dylan performed alongside a troupe of guest stars, Mike Scott’s version is a way of digging into the rootsy music he and his band were making in the mid-1980s, some of which emerged on the classic Fisherman’s Blues. The aim of this show is not a faithful play-through of that album, which Scott has said he would find dull, but a “reigniting” of its spirit.The fire is lit with an opening half-hour of favourites: A Girl Called Johnny is notable for the legs-akimbo keytar heroics of Brother Paul Brown. Scott gives him a shout-out and promises “a few other miscreants and villains yet to join us”. Chief among them is Steve Earle, who takes the stage after the interval. Ursine and magnetic, the mandolin looks like a toy in his hands as he sings Copperhead Road and others from his songbook. It feels, for a while, like a Steve Earle set dropped into a Waterboys gig, rather than a blending of the two. The wonderful exception is And a Bang on the Ear, Scott’s fond chronicle of lost loves.Reworked as a duet, Earle contributes new verses that seem to refer to his own romances: “Sandy was just 18 when I took her for my wife/I believed we’d be together all the seasons of my life”. It works beautifully. Not everything does. The show is too long, pushing three hours including the interval, and the room is too big. The Stolen Child, that shivery setting of a Yeats poem, is not heard to advantage in an arena. Yet there is an exuberance and intensity in the performances, especially the playing of fiddler Steve Wickham – veteran of Fisherman’s Blues – which threatens to tip over into transcendence. A closing Will the Circle Be Unbroken sends the audience out into the night having experienced something better than nostalgia: artists weaving a new tapestry from the bright threads of their past.At the3Arena, Dublin, 5 September and theO2, London, 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicThe WaterboysPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet Chronicles | Elizabeth Jane Howard | The Guardian
description: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off?
Author: Louisa Young
Headline: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off?
Content: Elizabeth Jane Howard in 1962.Photograph: Ronald Dumont/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElizabeth Jane Howard in 1962.Photograph: Ronald Dumont/Getty ImagesElizabeth Jane Howard‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet ChroniclesThe author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off?Louisa YoungSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, andKingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983).Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex.The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since.As each one came out I tore through them: not just because Jane was brilliant and I was a fan, but also because she was my aunt. My grandmother, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, had been Jane’s mother-in-law: mother of Peter Scott and of my father Wayland Young. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. It put my smoky-voiced, glamorous aunt and me in a peculiar overlap: she, in her 60s, was writing a fictional version of the actual life she had lived, and I, at 29, was writing a putatively factual version of the same things, though they had happened before I was born.double quotation markThrough the mirrors of her fiction, I recognised people and situations, saw hints of truth about my own family’s mysteriesThat was my first book; the last Cazalet novel was to be Jane’s last. I was so ready to sit at her feet, listen to her stories, to “carry her reticule”, as she put it, when she went to literary festivals. In her beautiful house in Bungay, Suffolk, where she lived with her brother Colin, known as Monkey, we talked about everything. How funny life is, how circular! We gossiped about people I’d never met, from decades before my birth. Jane gave me one version; Monkey gave me another. She loved me, I think, at least initially, for my dad’s sake, and because I was a young woman, becoming a writer.Through the mirrors and veils of her fiction, I recognised people and situations, saw hints of truth about my own family’s mysteries. In reality, Kathleen Scott and 19-year-old Jane had not got on at all – it was a hurried and frightened wartime marriage, a failure immediately. In the Cazalet books, Kathleen is fictionalised as Zee and comes across as an absolute monster, who threatened to kill Jane/Louise.View image in fullscreenPaul Rhys, Lesley Manville, Anastasia Hille and Hugh Bonneville in the 2001 BBC TV series The Cazalets.Photograph: John Rogers/BBCBut my father adored his mother: “She was always saying she was going to kill people!” he said. “It was a turn of phrase … but the wrong one for Jane then.” My own mother had been secretary to Peter (fictionalised as Michael Hadleigh), and had lent the penniless Jane money to leave him. Both the real people and the characters in the books, only in their twenties, overlapped during and after the war in west London, where I lived. The past seemed so close, and so far away. And of course it’s always fascinating to think of your parents’ generation being young, and messy.I read the volumes avidly as they came out, and ran back to her wanting to ask, “Jane, is that real? Was that true?” But these can be hard questions, and impertinent.Fictionis meant to be emotionally true, not factually. “True in spirit,” she told me. At the same time as she protected her own version, she wanted to protect those she loved. This curious palimpsest gives the fiction an astonishing extra tension, as those who have read her memoir, Slipstream (2002), or the biography by Artemis Cooper (A Dangerous Innocence, 2016) can testify.The Cazalet Chronicles are often described as a comfort read, both because they contain servants and food and clothes, and because they provide such a deeply complete fictional world for escaping into from an unsatisfactory real one. But being upper-middle-class doesn’t protect the characters from rape, child abuse, incest, abandonment, suicide, divorce, concentration camps, war, fear, loss, cancer or death. They are sometimes seen as somehow lighter than her earlier, more literary works, but she didn’t think they were, and they’re not: I’ve read them many times now and each time they get darker. Their surge of popularity during Covid makes perfect sense to me: the characters, like the rest of us during the lockdowns, were restricted by events beyond their control. They couldn’t go where they wanted; they couldn’t be with who they wanted to be with, they were constrained and scared and bored. And, in the main, they survived. Which is always reassuring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markCan these three novels count as mine, when I’ve broken into her world to write them?When something works, we want more of it. I always wanted more Cazalets. Chroniclesshouldgo on. But it never crossed my mind to imagine I could pick up Jane’s mantle. Until it did – which was as a PS in a “What Next?” email of my own to my agent. I was suggesting a long list of bad ideas, and then at the end: “Or I could always try to continue the Cazalet Chronicles”. It was a joke! Jane was a great writer. Who would dare face the ranks of devotees, still so dedicated and protective? Or launch into the continuity perils of 500,000 words?I realised it wasn’t such a terrible idea when Jane’s daughter, my cousin, gave her blessing. I found a message from Jane telling me a novel of mine was “a triumph”. My agent was all for it. We went to Jane’s own publishers, and worked with some of her editors. There would be three volumes, we decided. One would just be silly – why wake everybody up for that? – and more than three was too far ahead to see.I read the books again, thinking about how I would do it. Loose ends trailed before me, begging to be picked up. Pitfalls beckoned. The unsettling incestuous romance between half-siblings Juliet and Neville needed closure. Villy, Louise’s mother, was a victim of being a 20th-century woman as well as being a bad mother. Mainly because she had to have all her teeth out, I wanted her to have a better ending than just being dumped and her four children disliking her. Virtuous, kind Rachel, who for years didn’t even realise she was a lesbian, deserved better too (I am regularly accosted by young gay women wanting to know what I have planned for her, because it had better be good). And then there is the great unresolved issue of Louise’s abandoned son, Sebastian, who was too close to home in reality for Jane to address in fiction. And look, there’s my fictionalised grandparents, Zee and The Judge; there’s fictionalised Dad, here called Hugo, disguised as a cousin for propriety’s sake. It was these novels that told me how much Jane had loved Dad. Alas, she had him die in the War, and this is not the kind of saga where he can come back to life played by a different actor. (In reality he had six children and a sixty-year marriage, and lived till 2009.)It did seem to me that the characters were all still there, their lives continuing, just off-stage. The fifth Cazalet book, All Change, ends at Christmas 1958. I was born three months later. I was there! The idea that their lives might be up to me and my imagination was intoxicating, trepidation-inducing and inspiring. It’s not about inventing things to happen to them: they are already in full flow. I am chasing after them with a notebook. I make it seamless for the reader by continuing Jane’s elegant structure of tessellated sections, each from one person’s point of view, but I do allow the way I write, my generation’s use of language, to bring things forward in time, as time itself moves forward.I’m now the age Jane was when she was writing this fictionalised account of her life. Can these three novels count as mine, when I’ve broken into her world to write them? I’m not sure that’s answerable. But equally, what a circle it is, from writing about the young girl Jane in my biography of my grandmother, to the picking up of her baton now, after her death, beyond her knowledge. By bringing these characters on, of necessity I make them mine. Because this isn’t a pastiche, an imitation, or a homage. It’s a living story. The family chronicle rolls on through time in reality as it does on the page. I might even put it in a book …The Golden Hours, the sixth volume of the Cazalet Chronicles, is out on 3 September. To order a copy go toguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply. Move on Up, the seventh, will be published in September 2027.Explore more on these topicsElizabeth Jane HowardFictionAutobiography and memoirKingsley AmisMartin AmisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was miserable for a lot of this century’: Stewart Lee on divorce, his adoption and the twisted children’s poem that explains his life | Stewart Lee | The Guardian
description: After a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: After a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?
Content: Stewart Lee in Abney Park cemetery, Stoke Newington, London. Portraits: Sophia Spring/The Guardian. Grooming: Celine Nonon at Arlington ArtistsView image in fullscreenStewart Lee in Abney Park cemetery, Stoke Newington, London. Portraits: Sophia Spring/The Guardian. Grooming: Celine Nonon at Arlington ArtistsStewart LeeInterview‘I was miserable for a lot of this century’: Stewart Lee on divorce, his adoption and the twisted children’s poem that explains his lifeZoe WilliamsAfter a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?Sun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStewart Lee is somewhat fretfully tidying his kitchen. Nothing is exactly where he left it two months ago to go on tour. Plus, he says, “I’ve come back with a load of records that need to be alphabetised, and that’s really stressing me out.” His house is miles from minimalist – posters everywhere, for spaghetti westerns, avant-garde Welsh harpists, the Fall (who he said in aninterview in 2005 were the love of his life) – but if anything was an inch out of place, he’d notice. He puts things away with theatrical flourish, like a guy doing an impression of a guy who needs things just-so, for the comic effect of how absolutely impossible that guy would be, but at the same time, it’s funny because it’s true.In the show he’s been away for,Stewart Leevs the Man-Wulf, he – a 58-year-old lefty – enters into breakneck dialectic with toxic masculinity in werewolf form (age unknown). “Things have got worse in the 18 months I’ve been doing it,” he says. “I need to really amp the werewolf up. He would be much more explicitly racist and homophobic and transphobic now. But you don’t want people to be really upset in the room.” It feels quite a 2026 dilemma, being unable to even satirise the right without causing the distress it lives for.Then he went with his girlfriend to a treehouse in Scotland he found on Airbnb, but was surprised to find it was an “actual treehouse – to get out of it, you went down a slide”. He gestures vaguely at himself, as if to ask, “Can you imagine me going down a slide?”, although the answer – looking at his skater-boy aesthetic, record‑label T-shirt, shorts – is, in fact, yes. “It was quite good. You couldn’t really cook there. It had a bed.”double quotation markAfter my divorce I’m in the whole house rather than one bit of it. So I’m one of life’s winners. Look at all these posters I can put up. It’s greatView image in fullscreenLee at the grave of comedian and actor Herbert Campbell in Abney Park cemeteryHe was there to join his half-sisters, who “had instructions to put their father’s ashes – I didn’t know him, really – in a river in the west of Scotland where he used to go fishing”, he says, “and they invited me. The actual village was the location base of The Wicker Man. So I went and looked at its feet, which are still in the cliff.”What, the Wicker Man’s feet are still in the cliff? I ask, since it seems impossible. The film came out in 1973 – those feet are the same age as I am (53) and made of wicker.“Yeah. You’d have to know what you were looking for.”His other project is Pea Green Boat, a book based on theshow he devised in 2001, which became a pared‑downradio version of itself in 2004, and has come back to life a quarter of a century later thanks to some surreal and engrossing illustrations by David Waywell. It’s a retelling of The Owl and the Pussy‑cat by Edward Lear in which – spoiler alert – the mince that the owl eats at the end is actually the deceased cat, rotting in a bag. To introduce it, if such a simple thing were possible, Lee has written a candid essay about the state he was in when he first wrote it.One minute he was on the brink of screenwriting success, and the next his toilet had broken down and he was shitting in plastic bags that he left in bins in Finsbury Park, north London, the next morning. Can all that possibly be true? “In fact,” he says, gesticulating emphatically, “it was about 500 yards that way when I lived above a shop, where I had to shit in the bags. It’s funny – after my divorce, I’ve ended up living so close to where I lived in the 90s. But I’m in the whole house rather than one bit of it. So I’m one of life’s winners. Look at all these posters I can put up. It’s great.” He and the comedian Bridget Christie married in 2006, separated in 2021. They have two children, who are 15 and 19, and appear to be the platonic ideal of amicable divorcees. For a while he dated the comedian Rosie Holt, who heworked on a show with, but he is now seeing somebody else.The introductory essay concludes with a thought Lee absolutely must mean, because it’s poignant enough that it would choke him if he didn’t. “Never really having thought Pea Green Boat had meaning as such, it’s obvious to me as an older man what it’s about. We drift through life. We impose our hopes and desires on others, hopes and desires of which they are often unaware, or care not to reciprocate, or cannot reciprocate in the way we would wish. And then we die. Alone. But the journey to that ultimate destination can be beautiful, full of weird sights and strange creatures. And we should not wish it to be any other way.”But what slings and arrows of the past 25 years taught him that?He describes his “road to Damascus moment at 16”, when he saw a comedian supporting the Fall: “Before that, I thought you had to be a confident performer. I thought you had to run around like Ben Elton. Ted Chippington was silent and still to the point of having almost no presence whatsoever. A quarter of the audience would be in tears, and everyone else was really annoyed.” Lee was an immediate success in the 90s, on TV in adouble act with Richard Herring, out‑deadpanning each other; but the purer distillation of Stewart Lee-ness wasComedy Vehicle, which ran for four seasons on the BBC, from 2009 until 2016: half‑hour routines in front of a live audience, televised. Chris Morris script-edited and Armando Iannucci was an executive producer, and it was a high-water mark for the sheer art of comedy; incredible rigour and intellect and coherence, applied to the most ludic, surreal constructs. Later, he became the guy you read about politics (well, Brexit) if you wanted to keep yourself sane, and in his most recent tour, he is a guy nearing 60 whose intricate, absurdist satire has been out-absurded by the world around him, cracking open a new truthfulness that is both serious and incredibly funny.When Lee, less than a year out of university, in February 1990, won the Hackney Empire New Act of the Year, the judge (the comedy editor of City Limits, a huge tastemaker job back then) said, “That was great, mate. We need acts like you to get rid of all these Oxbridge wankers like David Baddiel,” Lee remembers now. “But I did go there” – he studied English literature at St Edmund Hall, Oxford – “and all the things I was supposed to get, Saturday Night Live, a paid gig at The Comedy Store, just disappeared.” In the 70s, if you were posh you might be the next Monty Python, “so you’d get a hearing. Whereas what we had was the misplaced arrogance and undeserved confidence that comes with having gone to a top university, but those doors were being gatekept. By people that wanted to be more fair, right?”View image in fullscreenLee in his show Stewart Lee vs the Man-Wulf.Photograph: Steve UllathorneBut what class is he, because he doesn’t read posh? He was adopted at the age of two, having spent his early life in foster care: “I know that I’m from the exact centre of society because the way that religious charities engineered adoption in those days was they were trying to place you in an entirely neutral environment.” His adoptive mum left school at 14, worked as a medical secretary, went to night school after she divorced his dad when he was four, worked her way up to being a GP practice manager. His dad was a rep for a cardboard company. He says of his birth father: “One of the few conversations I ever had with him was when he said an English degree was a colossal waste of time. I thought, ‘Well, actually, someone needs to know about Beowulf.’” Lee’s son is now studying English at uni; but he feels it’s becoming a luxury degree: “He’s relatively privileged. His parents have got two houses, and he can live in either one of them.” (Though this is not the typical take on being the child of divorced parents.)Lee’s route to Oxford came via a part-scholarship to Solihull, a private school, with the shortfall made up by “a masonic charity that provided educational help for orphans, waifs and strays. And I technically was an orphan, waif and stray, because I spent the first two years of my life in care.”double quotation markI’m not genetically connected to the world. It means you view it as otherHe didn’t give much thought to his origin story until he was about to become a dad himself, in 2006. “When Bridget was pregnant, I’m such a man, I thought, Oh, it’s quite hard work, isn’t it? I expect, if you had a baby, you would want to know what happened to it. Not even for me, but I thought I should find my mother just to tell her that I was all right. It opened a bit of a can of worms, really. But I’m in touch for 15 years or so now with my two half-sisters – my father’s children – and they’ve been great, I’m really glad I met them.”Not the half-sisters you’ve just been away with?“Yeah, they invited me to come.”So those were your birth father’s ashes?“Yeah. It’s interesting, when you’ve got nothing to go on, things seem hugely significant. Maybe that’s why I like The Wicker Man, because that’s where I’m from. My birth mother’s family can trace their roots back to leaving the village of Clonakilty in the west of Ireland during the famine. It’s famous for black puddings, which I really, really like.” The thinking around adoption has changed immeasurably since the 1968 Adoption Act. “Now, people view that as a very problematic start in life. Everyone in care for two years has post-traumatic stress disorder and we’re all drunk.” He’s still quite insistent that he was unscathed. When he was young, he read a “brilliant” book, Mister Fairweather and His Family, written as a tool to help adoptive children understand their origins. “It was about a bloke, and he was bored, so he got a cat. He was still bored, so he gets a dog, and he’s still bored, so he gets a wife. He’s still bored. And then they go, ‘Well, let’s get a baby’. That book is considered an absolute disaster now because it’s not child-centric. The baby isn’t supposed to be a pet for the parents. Anyway, I looked it up on Amazon, everyone was slagging it off, ‘This book ruined my life. I wanted to kill myself.’ And then there was one really good review of it. I thought, ‘That’s what I think. It’s a really nice little book with really nice pictures.’ And I’d written that review myself, 20 years ago, and forgotten.”Yet at the same time, what he describes is not an unscathed person. “Lots of comedians go, ‘We all do this, don’t we? Why do we all do this?’ Michael McIntyre, love him or hate him, is the king of that. Whereas what I do, I go, ‘Why doyoudo this? Why don’t you do what I do? Because I’m right.’ I think that’s partly through not being genetically connected to the world. It means you view it as other. I also think you view it as other if you’re a little bit on the spectrum, but that’s a hole that I’m not prepared to go down. Even though people have said I should.”View image in fullscreen‘We were ripped off in the way people in the music business are’ … Lee in 1998.Photograph: Julian Makey/ShutterstockLee’s 90s looked like living the dream – the successful double act with Herring, a TV series (Fist of Fun) – “but we were in a weird loop, the only way we could afford to do live work was if we were doing telly or radio. The last tour we did as a double act in 98 lost money, and the TV series didn’t get recommissioned, so it was just over, really.” He’d had mixed feelings about telly, anyway: “We were becoming much more like light entertainment, under pressure from the BBC, which wasn’t something I wanted to do.” But standup was his life, and his experience with a big comedy machine – where you’d always end up in debt no matter how big your crowds were, because comedy is always loss making – sounds as if it still stings. “We were only ripped off in the way that people in the music business are,” he says. But people in the music industry are ripped off royally.So by 2000, he was miserable. He’d stopped standup, about which he had a zealous perfectionism – “I’d gone to university, and I thought it was an incredible privilege. And I felt that I should ultimately try to do something with standup that was like a writer or someone creating a body of work” – and he was scratching a living reviewing music for Q magazine. Then he started working with Richard Thomas on Jerry Springer: The Opera.A few things have been lost about that musical and the controversy that followed: mainly how successful it was. It won a huge number of awards – Evening Standard, Critics’ Circle, Laurence Olivier, Theatregoers’ Choice – and musicals, when they fly, are career-defining. When the Christian right came after it, for blasphemy, it seemed almost like a curiosity – yes, there was a lot of profanity, it featured Jesus in a nappy, had zero respect for the crucifixion or any other sacred moments, but these were jokes-within-jokes, the butt of them never felt like Christianity at all. Legal actions brought against the BBC, for filming it, were given short shrift by the justice system. But, ultimately, the musical was brought down. Activists put pressure on local councils to pull it from theatres, a tour became impossible. For years, Lee was as likely to be approached in the street by someone wanting to know “Why didn’t you do it about Muslims?”, as by an obsessive fan. “Those people are still in play now,” Lee says. “Stephen Green, who was the self-styled reverend that led the campaign against it, was recently put up by thefake grassroots organisation Restore Trustto be on the board of the National Trust.”It was an inflection point in Lee’s career, just not in the way he’d have planned. “After that, I thought, right, things can get banned. You can be stopped from saying things. So it’s quite important that the things you say are worth saying. I didn’t becomeMark ThomasorLenny Bruceovernight. I did just start to think, there should be something important in this.”Even at his most political, Lee’s routines are never agitprop, being too surreal, resisting interpretation, not colouring within the lines; but for years, since Comedy Vehicle,when he takes an issue head‑on, it’s been magisterial. Hisimmigration monologue(“Bloody Indians, coming over here, inventing us a national cuisine … bloody French, coming over here, doubting transubstantiation …”) – “That’s become my parrot sketch.” He traces its origins to being in the car, listening to then-Ukip politician Paul Nuttall “say a really stupid thing about Bulgarians, so I went home, listened to the programme on catch-up, transcribed it, and the whole thing was done in half an hour. Whereas some things take years.” There’s a bit that’s resurfaced recently, sinceRod Liddle died: “It was basically 20 minutes of me, trying to talk about him, but I keep getting distracted by bits of food on his clothes. Loads of people didn’t know who he was, either, which made it even funnier – this long routine about a man nobody had heard of, with suet on himself. I remember one of those rightwing papers said the whole point of the routine was that the foods were working class. So I despised the working class. But, actually, I was thinking about things that were quite oleaginous: Angel Delight, pork pie jelly. It never would have occurred to me that it was a class warfare statement.”Brexit reradicalised him, and out of that came his Observer column, which was and remains a completely unparalleled display of what comic polemic can do (he now writes acolumn for The Nerve, an online magazine funded by Carole Cadwalladr and others. “What I learned from that was that you couldn’t afford to leave room for doubt about what you meant, because if you did, bad faith actors on the right would take legal action. You can’t be funny in the same way. You have to make sure that the sentence is bulletproof.”He now looks at the comics and personas his children “would call ‘edgelords’”, at Jeremy Clarkson, “suddenly going, ‘Oh, everything’s died in my farm. I spent a quarter of a century saying climate change was not worth worrying about, and only snowflakes cared about it.’ Dave Chappelle has started saying, ‘When I was taking the piss out of trans people, I didn’t mean for you to restrict their rights and kill them.’” Doing gigs in Colchester, he went to Wivenhoe, “the hippy town of Essex”, which now has a Reform council. “A councillor had said to a woman I know there, a lesbian, ‘Oh, withdrawing funding for Pride is coming from head office. We don’t feel like that. Don’t worry about it.’ But they’re still enacting the policies. And I expect, at the risk of committing the nuclear option, there were probably Nazi officials saying that to Jews in the 30s. ‘You’ve got to wear this badge, don’t worry about it, it’s coming from Berlin.’ All those people that played with that stuff – congratulations. The world’s on fire. Trump’s showing no sign of withdrawing from fossil fuels, there are councils where they’re literally enacting policies against LGBTQ+ people and removing references to climate change from council literature. So you’ve won, haven’t you? Is that what you wanted?”When Stewart Lee is out and about now, “pretty much everyone that stops you” – he always says “you” when he means “me” – “is really nice. They say it’s important to them, because they feel that no one talks about the things they’re interested in. They say they’ve watched me for a long time, or that they were going to kill themselves and they laughed their way out of it. Someone online said that I attracted an insular cadre of pseudo-intellectual, prematurely bald middle-aged men. I thought, ‘Yeah, that’ll do.’ I wish more women would come, though. I think it’s sort of perceived as something women wouldn’t like.”I think women think it’s going to be laced with references that they don’t get, I offer. Then there’s a bit of a pause.“I do joke about that,” he says eventually. “When I say, ‘You can’t come if you haven’t read this book’, that is supposed to be a joke.” Then he says, out of nowhere: “I think I was miserable for a lot of this century. It’s not really anyone’s fault.” He says it so matter-of-factly I have to double check.What, this century now?“Yes, the whole of the 21st century, until a few years ago. I like my kids, my kids are good fun.”double quotation markThe idea of leaving a legacy is entirely spurious because there’s obviously no future for humanityView image in fullscreenReturning to Pea Green Boat, he says: “The Owl and the Pussy-cat seems to be about a pair of characters of indeterminate gender, going to a place where normal laws are suspended, where a cat can marry an owl. I think it’s about the tragedy ofLear’s own life [he could never live openly as a gay man]. When I read it now, having lived a life, it’s also a little bit about me. I don’t really seem equipped to do certain sorts of things in life.”What kind of things?“That owl doesn’t know how to deal with another person and ends up eating their decomposing corpse out of a bag. There’s something in that about a failure to relate to people.”You don’t really think you can’t relate to a person?“Why do you end up choosing the life you’ve got? I spend most of my life on the move on motorways. I know a lot of people had a bad time in lockdown, but when I couldn’t do that any more, I found it really difficult.”So being on the road was an escape hatch from intimacy, and once you lost it, you found yourself unequal to the overall task?“Well, yeah. Not up to the job.”Mindful that he’ll be 60 soonish (in just over 18 months), he wants everything he’s done to be compiled into “some kind of physical media package, 13 DVDs with the same spine design, numbered”. It sounds kind of modest, but important. “Partly why I went round the bend in the mid part of this century, between about 2005 and 2015, was because I wrote about 15 hours of standup in eight years. No one’s ever done that. And now I think I’d like to at least show that I did that. Although the idea of leaving a legacy is entirely spurious because there’s obviously no future for humanity.”Hang on, I say, you say you went round the bend between 2005 and 2015, and you went round the bend in Covid?“Yeah, different. Worse.”So was there a period between 2015 and 2020 when you were the right side of the bend?“No.” He smiles. It’s funny because it’s true.Pea Green Boat by Stewart Lee, illustrated by David Waywell, is published by Ebury on 3 September (£16.99). To buy a copy for £15.29, go toguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsStewart LeeComedy (Stage)TV comedyComedy (Culture)TelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Messina mystery: theft of Renaissance art from Sicilian museum leaves investigators baffled  | Art theft | The Guardian
description: How did thieves pull off robbery of Antonello da Messina’s 15th-century masterpiece – and why did they leave part of it behind?
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: How did thieves pull off robbery of Antonello da Messina’s 15th-century masterpiece – and why did they leave part of it behind?
Content: Three panels of Antonello da Messina's 1473Polittico di San Gregorio(San Gregorio Polyptych) were stolen from the Museo Regionale Accascina in Messina.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersView image in fullscreenThree panels of Antonello da Messina's 1473Polittico di San Gregorio(San Gregorio Polyptych) were stolen from the Museo Regionale Accascina in Messina.Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/ReutersArt theftMessina mystery: theft of Renaissance art from Sicilian museum leaves investigators baffledHow did thieves pull off robbery of Antonello da Messina’s 15th-century masterpiece – and why did they leave part of it behind?Lorenzo Tondoin MessinaSun 30 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt about 8.47pm on the evening of 15 August, while tens of thousands of worshippers filled the streets of central Messina for a religious festival, at least two men cut through the fencing surrounding the regional museum, located a few miles to the north on the outskirts of the Sicilian harbour city.Capitalising on the fact that the streets around the museum were unusually quiet, the men forced open a side door with a crowbar, gaining direct access to a display case containing the five surviving panels of the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina’s polyptychPolittico di San Gregorio, his most important work, and a small double-sided painting. Undisturbed,they removed the works from the buildingand fled.View image in fullscreenThe double-sided panel depicting the Madonna and Child with Christ in Pieta, attributed to Antonello da Messina, at the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina.Photograph: Elisabetta Baracchi/EPAThe heist – one ofa series of high-profile theftsfrom European institutions in recent years – has left investigators baffled. Investigative authorities have said very little on the record, but sources speaking anonymously to the Guardian and local media,as well as art historians who know the building intimately, say lots of elements don’t add up, except one: the date chosen by the thieves.“If there is one day out of the 365 in the year that a thief would choose to carry out a robbery in Messina, it would be 15 August, the day of the Vara procession,” said an investigator close to the inquiry. Founded in 1535, the religious event takes place in Messina on 15 August, the day of Italy’s nationalFerragostopublic holiday. At its centre is a 14-metre pyramidal float depicting the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. More than 150,000 people pack into the city centre, hundreds of police are deployed, and major roads and squares are closed.View image in fullscreenThe thieves’ point of entry to the museum remains unclear.Photograph: Danilo Arnone/Reuters“The city’s outskirts are almost deserted that day,” said Lelio Bonaccorso, a graphic novelist, illustrator and Messina-based art expert who has collaborated with the regional museum. “Those who stay home are mostly elderly people, for whom the August heat and huge crowds can pose a health risk.”According to investigative sources speaking to local media,two masked men entered the museumwearing motorcycle helmets, possibly aided by two accomplices who remained outside as lookouts.The exact point of entry into the museum’s grounds remains under investigation, but one line of inquiry is that the thieves came in via an adjacent apartment block.View image in fullscreenThe thieves are believed to have escaped through the museum’s outer fence, where they abandoned two of the five panels of the San Gregorio Polyptych.Photograph: Lorenzo Tondo/The GuardianAfter cutting through the fence, the thieves are believed to have headed straight for a side door, one of the few entrances that, according to investigative sources, was not fitted with an alarm system.“This is where one of the first mysteries emerges,” said Valentina Certo, an art historian affiliated with the University of Messina. “CCTV shows the raid lasted just two to three minutes. How did the thieves remove all five panels so quickly, and know the door was not alarmed?”Investigatorssuspect the thieves may have had inside help. TheAnsa news agencyreported that a museum employee was under investigation over alleged inconsistencies about the alarm system, thoughpolice sourcesdismissed the report.“Law enforcement always looks for an insider connection when it comes to museum thefts,” said Christopher Marinello, a lawyer and the chief executive of Art Recovery International. ‘‘It’s just a sign of good investigative work. How did the criminals get past the guards, the alarms, the cameras? There is always an assumption that the thieves must have had inside help, even if it is eventually proven otherwise.”View image in fullscreenThe museum, known as MuMe, houses some of Sicily’s finest archaeological and Renaissance and baroque treasures.Photograph: Danilo Arnone/ReutersWhile the door used by the thieves may not have been alarmed, Antonello’s polyptych was protected by a security system designed to trigger an alert at the slightest movement.Investigative sourcestold La Siciliathat the alarm sounded as expected. According to police sourcesspeaking to the TG La7 news programme, one guard allegedly told investigators he heard it and switched it off, believing it was a false alarm.The theft was discovered by a woman who noticed something unusual on a low wall outside the museum about 10 minutes after the theft.In a recording shared with the Guardian,she told police: “There are museum paintings in the street, as if someone stole them and left them here. They’re large and worth a lot of money.”Inexplicably,two panels from the polyptychwere left on the wall. “They had not been thrown to the ground, but carefully propped up,” said Bonaccorso. ‘‘Why go to the trouble of dismantling a five-panel work and then abandon two of them outside the building?’’skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Museo Regionale Interdisciplinare, often shortened to MuMe, houses some of Sicily’s finest archaeological and Renaissance and baroque treasures, including two Caravaggios. The Italian painter spent several months in Messina in 1609, painting The Raising of Lazarus and The Adoration of the Shepherds before moving to Palermo, where he painted the Nativity with St Francis and St Lawrence.View image in fullscreenThe Raising of Lazarus and The Adoration of the Shepherds by Caravaggio.Photograph: Lorenzo Tondo/The GuardianThat work wasstolen from the Oratory of San Lorenzoin 1969 and has never been recovered. Investigators have long suspectedmafia involvement, and it remains on the FBI’s list of most wanted stolen artworks.Shortly after the Antonello theft,Messina’s chief prosecutortold Rai that mafia involvement could not be ruled out – a familiar line in Sicily in investigations into major art thefts.‘‘Given the location of theft and Hollywood stereotypes, I can understand why people are considering mafia involvement,” said Marinello. “However, in my view, even the most hardened local mafioso would never desecrate Messina in this way.”The stolen work is no ordinary painting. Originally composed of six panels and created for the Monastero di San Gregorio, it is the only work by the Sicilian painter never to have left his home city, and it survived the 1908 earthquake that devastated Messina, killing about half its population. Some local people saw it as embodying a kind of rebirth in a city repeatedly scarred over the centuries by earthquakes and then by the bombs of the second world war.View image in fullscreenInside the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina.Photograph: Lorenzo Tondo/The GuardianOpposite the artwork’s display case is an emergency exit that investigators believe the thieves may have used to leave the building. It leads towards the wall where two panels were abandoned and, beyond that, the strait dividing Sicily from Calabria on the Italian mainland.Investigatorshave not ruled out an escape by speedboat, a theft to order or a ransom demand. But selling such a famous, incomplete work would be extremely difficult.“How would an evil collector display it?” asked Marinello. “It would have to remain hidden. These thieves will soon discover the paintings are ‘radioactive’ – and will never bring them the millions they expected.”For now black panels cover the space where the polyptych sat, as if mourning the loss.“Here we have a saying,” said Bonaccorso. “We are like the phoenix. We always rise from the ashes of the catastrophes that have struck our city. This theft is not a tragedy like an earthquake, but another wound for Messina. Yet we will rise again this time too.”Explore more on these topicsArt theftItalyPaintingMuseumsEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for ages
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for ages
Content: Kismet, London SE1: ‘Soothing, filling and hearty.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKismet, London SE1: ‘Soothing, filling and hearty.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewKismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant reviewThe first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for agesGrace DentSun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleATurkish-Cypriotmeyhane, which translates roughly as “wine house”, has slotted in upstairs atthe Globe Tavern in Borough Market, south London. Any cab driver worth his salt will bend your ear over the fact that this is “where Bridget Jones lives”, which might be a bit confusing if you’ve booked in to eatkuzu şiş(lamb neck kebabs) and to knock back a couple of rakis with a fermented turnip juice chaser.ThatBridget Jonestrivia, by the way, is completely true: the upstairs space at the Globe was used as the heroine’s gaff in that famous film franchise. Now, however, when you climb the staircase up toKismet, an old, slightly eerie and flickering TV by the restaurant entrance begins to tell a very different tale. This is chefKeiran Mustafa’s very personal tribute to his family’s homeland and the community they built in London. Mustafa was the opening head chef at BiBi,to my mind one of the best restaurants in London, and before that he worked at industry stalwartsChez Bruceandthe Harwood Arms.View image in fullscreen‘One of the best things being served anywhere at Borough Market right now’: Kismet’satom(strained yoghurt) with chilli butter.Mustafa’s partner in this new venture isDom Hamdy, the smart-cookie restaurateur behindCrispin,Bistro FreddieandCanal. The result is structured and very chic bedlam that’s lovable and edgy in equal measure. On a midweek lunchtime not long after opening, chaotic Turkish jazz gives way to Turkish techno on the speakers as the grill in the open kitchen roars and glasses of Karmen’s Diren white wine at £8 a pop slide down rather too easily for the lunchtime crowd. Mustafa tells us that our table is where the weekly live music sets up. I haven’t sat that close to a PA since I was on a cross-channel ferry eating chips beside the bingo caller, and I’m sure that Kismet in full swing will be just as choppy.The dining space is split into two rooms, all dark wood and white tablecloths, with lace over the windows and walls the colour of a 70-a-day Rothmans smoker’s lounge. Those walls are also festooned with Mustafa’s childhood photos, including one of his mum as a waitress in a long-gone restaurant.The menu, meanwhile, is soothing, filling and hearty, with all manner of Turkish favourites. There’sgirit ezme, or white cheese with walnut, dill and mint, andsigara boregi(feta rolled up inyufkapastry and deep-fried). There’s a grill, too, of course, blasting out the fragrant smells of beef and lambköfteandtavuk şiş(chicken thigh kebab). The cooking leans heavily, if not decadently, on lashings of strained yoghurt, chilli butter, good olive oil and tahini – six of the nine cold meze are built on one or other of them. But don’t expect a great deal of spicy heat because this is more about comfort and coddling. Kick back with a basket of warm, pillowy bread that’s begging to be pulled through someatom(strained yoghurt) in a red pool of chilli butter.View image in fullscreen‘Properly great’: Kismet’s grilled monkfish with yoghurt and chilli butter.In fact, that very humble-sounding atom with bread might well be one of the best things being served anywhere in Borough Market right now. I ate two whole baskets to myself, which finally killed off my ambition to be Victoria’s Secret’s most elderly thong model. Damn it, give me warm carbs. We ate monkfish straight off the mangal, which at £30 is the most expensive dish on the menu (the meze start at £6). To begin with, I was a little concerned that we’d never finish it and it would be a huge waste of fish, but no, it’s properly great: expertly grilled, succulent, and served with yet more yoghurt and chilli butter. The lamb neckkuzu şişwas likewise incredibly juicy, and we ate it with hand-cut fried potatoes that were unmistakably shallow-fried – proper staying-at-your-gran’s-house chips. Braised green beans were soft but fibrous, beautifully seasoned and the sort of beans that make you want to sell your house and move to the sun whenever you’re on holiday. A £14 plate of fried liver with onion salad lent some iron to proceedings, with a side of velvety and not-remotely bitter braised swiss chard.View image in fullscreenKismet’s baklava is ‘glossy and teeth-chatteringly sweet’, just as it should be.Over tiny glasses of tea and glossy, teeth-chatteringly sweet pistachio baklava, we picked at a pistachio ice-cream that was much, much less sweet than the pastries, and therefore balanced them beautifully. You must order both, and we asked for the bill without an ounce of regret for our overindulgence.Kismet will not make my confused definition of a meyhane any easier, nor will the Turkish-Cypriot community be in full agreement over whether it’s at all like one in Istanbul, either. What’s undeniable, however, is that Mustafa and Hamdy have come up with something that’s unique in its own right: the first genuinely cool, weird thing to have happened in Borough for ages. They’re only signed up to be here for a year, so go before that telly gets turned off.KismetUpstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London SE1 (no phone). Open lunch Weds-Sun noon-2.30pm (3pm Sun); dinner Tues-Sat 5-10pm (9.30pm Tues & Weds). From about £40 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsTurkish food and drinkMiddle Eastern food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Make your bed – and be ruthless: 14 expert rules for a clean, healthy, happy home | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Is your place crying out for some TLC? Housekeepers reveal how to keep it looking its best – and when it’s OK to let standards slip
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Is your place crying out for some TLC? Housekeepers reveal how to keep it looking its best – and when it’s OK to let standards slip
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Prostock-Studio/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Prostock-Studio/Getty ImagesThe expertsLife and styleMake your bed – and be ruthless: 14 expert rules for a clean, healthy, happy homeIs your place crying out for some TLC? Housekeepers reveal how to keep it looking its best – and when it’s OK to let standards slipSarah PhillipsSun 30 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLife is busy and there is only so much time to spend cleaning and tidying. What are the non-negotiables of a well-managed home? Here, housekeepers share their tips and hacks for making a chaotic house feel more orderly.Run a tight shipThere are four elements to a well-run home, according to Matt Church, AKAMr Housekeeping, from Maldon in Essex. These are keeping the place “clean, tidy, decluttered and organised,” he says. “I call myself a housekeeper because it’s not just cleaning. Cleaning is one element, but some cleaners wouldn’t tidy, empty bins, make beds, put laundry away or organise cupboards. They are all jobs I get involved with.” People laugh about tidying before the cleaner comes, but they are different things entirely, Church says.“When you take on somebody’s house, a lot of it at the beginning is about listening,” says Georgie Cutbill, who runsThe Bruton Housekeeper, a household management service in Somerset. “People have very particular ideas about what they want, so you’ve got to get into their headspace.” Cutbill has found herself in all kinds of surprising scenarios, from organising parties involving miniature donkeys to sourcing Tadelakt [Moroccan lime-based plaster] specialists. “No two days are the same,” she says.Lisa Williams is head of housekeeping atThe Grand hotel in Yorkand chair of theUK Housekeepers Association. During the pandemic, when hotels were closed, Williams worked in hospitals and learned a great deal about using chemicals to avoid infection transmission.Guests expect to check in to a room that is spotless, but “obviously you’ve got your time constrictions,” says Williams, explaining that it is not the same as cleaning a home. “You have to clean 11 rooms within an eight-hour day. And obviously, if guests don’t check out on time, that can put tremendous pressure on you.” Sometimes things get broken or there is other damage to a room: “We appreciate that guests sometimes can be sick, but they don’t always tell you. It’s great if guests can be honest, because then we can deal with it straight away. If it’s left there all night and all day, it’s harder to get out.”At home, Williams says it helps to have a regular cleaning routine that you stick to, otherwise you are constantly “chasing the dirt”.Always make your bedView image in fullscreen‘There is nothing nicer than a fresh bed.’Photograph: Richard Drury/Getty Images“It makes a massive difference when you go to bed for the bed to be made,” says Church. “It can make a bedroom feel a lot tidier than it is.” Should you do it as soon as you get up? “Yes, in your own home,” says Church. “It’s the last job I do before I leave a client, because if you make the bed and then you start dusting the light fittings above it, you end up with dust all over the sheets, so I make the bed last.” How often should you change the sheets? “Once a week is good,” says Church, but more frequently is preferable in hot weather. Sam Hodges, who ownsHectic Housekeepersin Hastings, suggests twice a week if you have pets that sleep with you.“There is nothing nicer than a fresh bed,” says Williams. If you’re in a hotel for a long stay, your bed might be changed as frequently as every other day. At home, weekly is fine, he says. “I keep my bed fresh. It’s important to remember to vacuum it too.” She also recommends giving mattress toppers a good shake because they can get flattened. Bed linen for the hotel is ironed but Williams says she only does this at home if she has guests, divulging a useful hack if you can’t be bothered: “If you put water in a spray bottle and lightly spray it and pull the bed tight, after a half an hour or so, the creases come out. That’s what we do for photoshoots if duvets have slight creases.”Williams says she can’t resist putting chocolates on the pillows of guests at her home, although she draws the line at swan-shaped towel arrangements.Never leave dishes unwashedWashing the dishes and putting them away is an absolute must if you want your home to appear well ordered, says Church. He doesn’t own a dishwasher and has a baby, so this can be quite a struggle: “You can spend all night getting the kitchen clean, then the next morning it is a complete mess again.”Ensure your home smells amazingYou’ve got to have a tidy kitchen, agrees Cutbill, which “feels and smells clean”. Cutbill recommends using candles or putting wood oil on surfaces for a more subtle scent. Using good-quality cleaning products also makes a massive difference, she says.“When somebody walks into your house, it’s about that first impression,” agrees Williams, who swears by plug-in diffusers for a fragrance that makes an impact.Hodges takes an empty spray bottle with her on jobs and will put some of her client’s fabric conditioner in it with water and spritz it round the house: “The smell is amazing and it lasts.”Have a sparkling bathroomView image in fullscreenA spotless bathroom is a must.Photograph: brizmaker/Getty Images/iStockphotoWilliams says the bathroom is her number one priority: “If you’ve ever got people coming round, make sure your bathroom’s spotless.”Church is of the view that toilets should be cleaned daily: “not a deep clean but a bit of bleach.” Hodges doesn’t do bleach, opting for eco-friendly alternatives instead. “For limescale, white vinegar or elbow grease usually goes down quite well.” Hodges says that she recently discovered that a pumice stone and water can be used to effectively remove tough limescale from some surfaces.Don’t forget to leave products on long enough to work their magic, says Hodges. “When people are cleaning their own homes, it’s a quick spray, then they wipe it off. Instead, “Let it sit – then you are saving yourself so much hard work from having to scrub it off.”Keep the fridge under controlView image in fullscreenRemove things that have been lurking at the back of your fridge.Photograph: Posed by model; Kentaroo Tryman/Getty Images/MaskotWith a fridge, “if you see an obvious stain, get at it as soon as you can, or it will set and become like glue,” says Church.
