Regularly cleaning the fridge has the benefit of revealing things that are lurking at the back of shelves that you may have forgotten about, says Church. “I clean it weekly or just whenever I have got a cloth in my hand,” says Cutbill, adding: “You cannot beat a freshly washed cloth or tea towel.”Don’t let laundry languishView image in fullscreenHang washed clothes on the line as soon as possible.Photograph: Johner Images/Getty Images/Johner RF“Don’t leave things in the washing machine too long,” says Church. “Hanging it up straight away can mean you don’t need to iron as much.”“The laundry room gets left behind in my home,” says Cutbill, “but not in my clients’.” She says the key to washing management is strategically placed laundry baskets, getting washed clothes out on the line if possible, then folding everything and putting it away in a timely manner. “Otherwise,” says Hodges, “it will end up on that dreaded chair or table in the bedroom, and it will be there for three weeks, and no one puts it away.”Keeping on top of the laundry is about doing a little and often, continues Hodges. “Sort clothes before washing and don’t overload the machine or it won’t wash properly,” she says.If you do one job, make it the floorsView image in fullscreenBrushing and mopping the floor regularly makes a world of difference.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesA clean floor can make a world of difference, says Church, who starts at the “top of a room and does the floors last”. Cutbill is constantly mopping her own floor because she has three dogs who bring filth from the garden inside. “I regret it from a cleaning point of view, but I don’t regret it because they are very lovely.” She keeps a good brush to hand at all times to deal with dog-related detritus. “I brush most days, then mop regularly to keep it fresh and clean.”Don’t forget to clean your vacuum cleaner, says Hodges: “I spray the inside of the Henry with fabric freshener, so the room gets a nice smell. And with my Shark, once a week I’ll take the sponges out and I’ll hand-wash them with a washing pod or fabric conditioner.” This then releases a pleasant scent when vacuuming.Rediscover the lost art of dustingView image in fullscreenDiluted washing-up liquid works a treat when cleaning blinds.Photograph: ronstik/Getty Images/iStockphoto“Make sure all areas are dusted,” says Williams. Factor in time for “periodically cleaning blinds and curtains. You need to do them weekly or monthly.” Hodges puts an old sock on her hand like a puppet with some diluted washing-up liquid on it to run across dusty slatted blinds. “Don’t spray the actual blind. Spray the sock and then just run your hand along after you’ve given it a dust. It’s so much easier to clean.”Struggling to remove a stain? Think CHATChurch explains that this stands for: chemical, heat, agitation and time, a concept developed by the German chemistHerbert Sinner in the 1950s. “If you’re struggling with cleaning something, if you increase one of those it should do it,” says Church. For example, “you could be using the wrong chemical, it might need hotter water or to be scrubbed differently or for longer.”Be ruthlessView image in fullscreenWhen decluttering, decide what you want to keep, rather than what you want to put back.Photograph: Posed by model; Cicy/Getty Images“When decluttering, chuck out anything you haven’t used for a year,” says Cutbill. “Find somebody who is going to give it a home because a lot of these things can have a second life.” Cutbill swears by local WhatsApp groups for rehoming unwanted goods, and charity shops.“I like to get everything out and into the centre of the room,” says Church. “If you are just picking things up around you, you’re dealing with little fires everywhere.” With everything in the middle, it is easier to decide ‘What do I want to keep?’ and ‘What do I want to put back?’ Enlisting a friend can help you to be more ruthless: “When you pick something up yourself and you’re holding it in your hand, you can make up a hundred excuses as to why this is sentimental. But if someone else is holding it and saying, ‘Do you need this random booklet?’ or whatever it is, you are more likely to say ‘no’.”“Small wins quickly build momentum,” says Hodges. “Pick a corner and start from there. Work your way around until you’ve completed the room. It doesn’t have to be done in one day.”Keep toys on rotationView image in fullscreenAvoid leaving all the toys out at once.Photograph: Posed by model; Lacheev/Getty Images/iStockphoto“Children get bored of the same toys and overstimulated when there’s too much out,” says Church. Rotating which toys are accessible every few days “helps to keep the room less cluttered – particularly helpful in smaller homes.”Treat tradespeople with respectView image in fullscreenOffer tradespeople a regular cuppa.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty ImagesOn choosing good tradespeople, Cutbill advises to “go with your gut instinct. And really take the time to get to know them. You’ve got to invest in your people.” Offering regular cups of tea is crucial. If you are fortunate enough to have someone to help at your home, communication is key, says Church: “Don’t be afraid to tell them what you want done because every house is different and what is a priority for you is often different to someone else.”Know that it is OK to let standards slip sometimesChurch says he can get quite stressed when people come to his home, “because I feel as if they expect mine to be perfect. But I work about six days a week, so when I get home, I’m quite tired of cleaning, and I’ve got a one-year-old – we do our best.”“I’d love to live in a well-organised home,” says Hodges, “but the truth is, it’s definitely not spotless 24 hours a day. Being busy and doing everyone else’s homes, it’s not usually the top of my list. There’s always a washing pile or a cup appearing from nowhere: things mysteriously migrate from one room to another. I think the saying is ‘the cleaner needs a cleaner’, and it’s very true.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe expertsHomesHotelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ProCook outdoor pizza oven review: a budget-friendly model that brings the pizzeria home | Pizza | The Guardian
description: This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people
Content: The flame game: the gas-powered ProCook is a ‘capable, compact and versatile pizza oven’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe flame game: the gas-powered ProCook is a ‘capable, compact and versatile pizza oven’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterPizzaReviewProCook outdoor pizza oven review: a budget-friendly model that brings the pizzeria homeThis no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most peopleThe best pizza ovens – testedOoni Koda 2 reviewRachel OgdenSun 30 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe market forpizza ovenstends to be dominated by a handful of specialist brands, so it can feel like a gamble to buy from a lesser-known manufacturer or a retailer that offers a wider range of goods.The ProCook outdoor pizza oven is no gamble, though. It’s every inch a capable, compact and versatile pizza oven, despite being just one product in an offering that includes pretty much everything from storage jars to squeegees.This outdoor pizza oven conforms to ProCook’s usual direct-from-manufacturer pricing. Coming in at a comparatively reasonable RRP of £249, the oven punches far above its weight in terms of functionality. As well as foldable legs for storage, it has room for 12in pizzas and a manual rotating stone for more even cooking. Turn the stone as the pizza bakes for an evenly blistered crust or simply adjust it as needed. At 12kg, it’s also light enough to take to a friend’s house or on a camping trip.View at ProCookHow I testedView image in fullscreenTest slice: one of the veggie pizzas cooked at 350C to caramelise the toppings.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianI tested the ProCook in the same way I test otherpizza ovensfor the Filter. As well as assessing the quality of the cook by making pizzas with different toppings – cheese and tomato at about 430C; a slow-cooked veggie pizza at 350C with onion, pepper and tomato to caramelise and soften the topping; and a salami pizza at about 400C – I rated the oven for ease of assembly, overall use, lighting, temperature control and storage. I also recorded heat-up times, although, as it was tested in cooler months, these may be longer than in the warmer months.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenRound here: the ProCook’s rotating stone sits on its own turntable.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView at ProCookThe ProCook outdoor pizza oven is cheaper than similarly sized models, but you’ll need to invest in aninfrared (IR) thermometerfor the best results. In tests, the oven heated from cold to 430C in about 25 minutes, which is about average for a compact gas-powered oven, and the rotating stone that sits on its own turntable doesn’t have much impact on heat-up times either way.The rotating stone has no raised edges, which means that you’ll need to be fairly accurate when launching pizza. Any other dishes you cook in the oven, such as chicken or fish, will also need to fit on the round stone.ProCook doesn’t offer much in the way of accessories. There’s no cover, but there is a great-valuepizza peelfor just £10.ProCook outdoor pizza oven specificationsDimensions:43.2 x 65.5 x 31.2cm (WDH) / mouth 35 x 10cm (WH)Maximum capacity:stone diameter 32cm (working capacity, 12in pizza)Features:manual rotating stone, control dial ignitionFuel:gasSpare parts:control knob, rotating knob and fixing nutWeight:12kgWhat we loveView image in fullscreenFire away: the salami-topped pizza was declared ‘best on test’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianFor what is effectively a budget-friendly model, the ProCook outdoor pizza oven gets all the basics right. It lit first time via the built-in ignition, but can also easily be lit with a match should this fail. I especially liked that there was no need for a turning peel – a utensil that helps you turn the pizza in the oven – and that the rotating stone is powered by hand, making the whole thing pleasingly low-tech, with no need for batteries or recharging.Some of the pizzas I made burned at the corners, but this is because the bought dough I tested with (for consistency) was shaped into rectangles, rather than circles. Overall, pizzas cooked well, although with less rise than I’ve achieved in pricier ovens. This was most noticeable on the cheese and tomato pizza. I also found thicker toppings needed a lower temperature and longer cook, with some of the vegetables remaining firm while others began to char. The salami-topped pizza was the best of all, with evenly melted cheese and just a slight singe on one edge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat we don’t loveView image in fullscreenControl freak: the rotating stone is turned using a dial on the side of the oven but for controlling gas … head to the rear.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThe dial for the rotating stone sits at the side of the pizza oven, relegating the control for the gas to the rear. This means you can’t see the flame as you light the oven and adjust the heat. You may need two people – one on the gas control, and one watching the oven’s flame size as it’s altered.Another drawback is the size of the oven’s mouth. It’s relatively narrow and short, with the space becoming even tighter around the stone. This makes launching and retrieving pizza trickier than with rival models such as my overall favourite, theGozney Arc Lite, and theOoni Koda 2. On the plus side, if you later invest in a bigger oven, the ProCook will at least mean you’ve honed some serious pizza-launching skills.Warranty, repairability and longevityThe ProCook outdoor pizza oven comes with a two-year guarantee, with spare parts also available via customer services once it’s out of warranty. Sadly, the rotating stone cannot be replaced if it becomes damaged or breaks. Despite being an outdoor oven, ProCook’s instructions advise storing it indoors, out of harsh weather conditions, such as heavy rain, strong winds and direct sunshine.ProCook outdoor pizza oven: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenMelting moment: ‘a smart buy for beginners’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThe ProCook is my favourite budget pizza oven. The combination of good design and low price makes it a smart buy for beginners – and those who’d rather spend big on toppings for their next pizza party. It might not deliver the wow results of more expensive ovens, nor come with lots of fancy features, but unless you plan to cook pizza regularly, it’s unlikely you’ll miss them.Another point to bear in mind is that this is very much just a pizza oven. Unlike those models that double up as versatile outdoor ovens, this ProCook model offers limited space on the stone for roasting pans, slow cooking in ambient heat, and sizzling side dishes – so if you want to experiment with a wider range of dishes, this probably isn’t the oven for you.However, if pizza is what you want most of the time – and who doesn’t? – the ProCook outdoor pizza oven is an excellent choice for families, busy households and anyone keen to master homemade pizza.View at ProCookFor more:The best pizza ovens in the UKOoni Koda 2 reviewThe best BBQs and grills – testedRachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she is less successful at assembling and repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of appliances while her garden has seen a succession of pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters put through their paces. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failedExplore more on these topicsPizzaThe FilterFoodHomesGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make key lime pie – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: The indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy steps
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: The indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy steps
Content: Felicity Cloake's key lime pie.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's key lime pie.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make key lime pie – recipeThe indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy stepsFelicity CloakeSun 30 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeautiful as the Florida Keys are, with average August temperatures topping 30C and with hurricane season looming, I think I’d rather enjoy their most famous culinary export in the calm of our own more temperate isles (well, usually, at least). Cool and creamy, with a refreshingly sharp, citrus tang, this is the perfect make-ahead dessert for any bank holiday festivities.Prep20 minCook15 minChill3 hr+Serves6For the base75g butter, or coconut oil, plus extra for greasing200g digestive biscuits(about 13)1 pinch saltFor the filling4-5 limes4 egg yolks400g tin condensed milkFor the topping (optional – see steps 8 and 9)300ml whipping or double cream1 tbsp icing sugar1 A note on the biscuitsIn the States, this would involvegraham crackers, which are sweeter and more crisp than our digestive biscuits. The latter do make a decent substitute, but feel free to swap in any other biscuits you like the idea of with lime (I suspect ginger nuts would be rather good).View image in fullscreen2 Start on the pie crustHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and lightly grease a 20cm tart tin – not too shallow a one, ideally, and preferably loose-bottomed if you’re planning on taking the pie out of the tin to serve. Crush the biscuits to a fine crumb, either using a food processor or by wrapping them in a clean tea towel and whacking with a rolling pin.3 Pack the crust into the tinMelt the fat in a microwave or a small saucepan – butter is the classic choice, but I like the flavour of coconut oil here – then stir into the crumbs with a pinch of salt. Tip into the tin, use your hands to press down the mix into an even crust across the base and up the sides, then press down again with the base of a glass.4 Bake, then coolBake the crust for about 15 minutes, until it’s dry to the touch, then take out of the oven and leave to cool (though not mandatory, this step will give a crisper crust that holds together much better upon slicing, so it’s worth turning on the oven for).5 Wash and zest the limesView image in fullscreenKey limesare a distinct variety of thin-skinned, aromatic citrus that are hard to get outside the Americas. Happily, though not an exact match, this recipe works just as well with standard limes, especially if you use the zest as well as the juice. Scrub the fruit under hot water, then finely grate the zest into a large bowl.6 Juice the limesSqueeze the juice from the zested limes into a jug until you have about 120ml, straining out any pips as you go. Add the egg yolks to the zest bowl (the whites make a lovely meringue topping, if you’re looking for a way to use them up: see step 9 for a suggested recipe to replace the cream).View image in fullscreen7 Beat the egg yolks and zestBeat the yolks and zest for a couple of minutes with a whisk, electric beaters or a food mixer until the mixture thickens and turns pale green, then stir in the condensed milk. Beat in the lime juice – the mix should be shockingly tangy and sweet; chilling will mute the lime flavour, so add more juice, if you like – then pour the filling into the cooled biscuit shell.8 Chill, then top with creamChill for at least three hours, until set. If you’re planning on topping your pie with cream, whisk this and the sugar in a large bowl until the mix holds soft peaks, then dollop on top of the set filling. Garnish with extra slices of lime, if you have them, or some grated lime zest, and serve.View image in fullscreen9 … or top with meringueIf you prefer a meringue topping (and to use up some excess egg whites into the bargain) – for the sweet toothed only! – whisk two of the egg whites to soft peaks, then beat in 115g sugar a tablespoon at a time, until the mix is glossy and holds its shape. Beat in half a teaspoon of vinegar or lime/lemon juice, then spoon on top the pie. Brown briefly with a blowtorch or under a hot grill before serving.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassAmerican food and drinkDessertBakingFruitEggsCakefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘My ex wouldn’t even kiss me during sex. Marcus is happy to take his time’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Camille had bad experiences with men, so when she met Marcus they took things slowly. Now sex is a shared joy
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: Camille had bad experiences with men, so when she met Marcus they took things slowly. Now sex is a shared joy
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘My ex wouldn’t even kiss me during sex. Marcus is happy to take his time’Camille had bad experiences with men, so when she met Marcus they took things slowly. Now sex is a shared joyHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 30 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCamille, 65double quotation markMarcus will go down on me for as long as it takes. He has a gentle touch and is an amazing kisserI met Marcus onGuardian Soulmatesnine years ago. I had been divorced for eight years, and getting back out there had been tough – I had a hard time finding a genuine man. We messaged back and forth about our shared love of films and discovered we only lived 10 minutes apart. He really took the pressure off our first date by writing: “If there isn’t a romantic spark, we can just be friends who watch films together at our local cinema.” But when we met, we both felt a connection.Even so, I decided to wait to have sex with him. I’d had bad experiences of sleeping with men, who would then disappear on me. Marcus was very respectful and patient.He’s taught me that it’s not all about penetration. In my previous marriage, the sex was check-listy and turn-takey. It felt like a routine task – done without care, interest or enthusiasm. My ex-husband wasn’t very nice to me. I found it hard to understand how he expected me to sleep with him when we weren’t in a good place. Sometimes we would have sex and not even kiss. Marcus is happy to take his time, and go down on me for as long as it takes for me to orgasm. He has a gentle touch and is an amazing kisser.double quotation markThe other day, I dressed up in only a leather jacket and high boots and Marcus took racy photosWe still live in our separate homes, near one another. It works well for us because from Monday to Thursday I am often overwhelmed by my stressful job and don’t have the capacity for sex. Fridays are the best time for us. I’ll ask him: “Do you fancy having sex?” He always says yes, I never feel rejected. In the past, I dressed up in sexy underwear for my ex and he just laughed at me. The other day, I dressed up in only a leather jacket and high boots and Marcus took racy photos of me.We spend weekends at each other’s houses and prioritise our sex life. My kids are grown up and out of the house, so it’s a different experience to be able to walk around the house naked with your boyfriend. He often compliments my body. When I was young, I was super slim. Now I’ve put on a bit of weight but it’s encouraging that Marcus is always telling me how good I look.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: I’ve got feelings for a teacher at my children’s school. What should I do? | Family | The Guardian
description: Crushes can feel freeing because they operate outside everyday life, but does that mean you should act on them?
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Crushes can feel freeing because they operate outside everyday life, but does that mean you should act on them?
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyI’ve got feelings for a teacher at my children’s school. What should I do?Crushes can feel freeing because they operate outside everyday life, but does that mean you should act on them?Annalisa BarbieriSun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’vebeenmarriedfor20 years and have two children.By most measures, our marriage is stable and successful.Butlately I have found myself developingstrongfeelings fora teacher at my children’s school. While our interactionsthere are limited, we also attend a weekly non-school activity. What began as casual conversation has becomemuch more significant in my mind. I find myself looking forward to seeing them, thinking about our conversationslater, and wondering what might have been if we’d metin different circumstances.They are married with childrentoo. Nothing inappropriate has happened, and neither of us hasacknowledged any romantic feelings. However, I cannot shake the sense that there may be a mutual connection.I am struggling with what these feelings mean. Are they evidence that something is missing in my marriage, orsimply the result of encountering someone new afteryears with the same partner? Is this a genuine connection that deserves attention, ora fantasy thathas never been tested by real life?Most importantly, what should I do next? I don’t want to hurt my wife, my children, thisperson, or their family. Yet pretending these feelings don’t exist hasn’t made them disappear.The first thing to address is your use of the pronoun “they”. This makes me wonder if it’s a man or a woman you’ve developed feelings for. If it’s the former, and you’ve lived as a heterosexual man thus far, and that’s what your wife believes, then you need to be really honest with yourself and then your wife about what this all means beyond the crush.I went to psychotherapist Mark Vahrmeyer, who said: “It’s a romantic idea that once we have found the right person we should only ever desire them. In reality, that’s not how desire works. You can love your wife, value your marriage and still find yourself drawn to someone else. The existence of the feeling does not in itself mean your marriage is failing, or there is something wrong with you.”Neither is it an instruction to do something about it other than wonder what this is trying to tell you.“A crush,” said Vahrmeyer, “can be harmless and even enjoyable. It can feel like something private within the constraints of a committed life. The difficulty begins if you start feeding it, seeking signs that it is mutual, creating more contact or treating the fantasy as though it were already a relationship.”double quotation markInfatuation can make the unfamiliar seem vivid, but that does not mean it would survive realityReal-life, long-term relationships, as you know, have to deal with a lot of everyday-ness. Crushes operate outside that and can feel freeing and heady.This “imagined relationship”, said Vahrmeyer, “is largely untested. You know this person only through limited, favourable circumstances, not through the demands and compromises of everyday life. They can become almost anyone you need them to be. Infatuation can make the unfamiliar seem vivid and the familiar seem dull, but that does not mean the unfamiliar would survive reality any better.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA childhood sexual abuse allegation has rocked our family – what should we do?Read more“You do not need to deny the feeling, but nor should you test whether it is mutual,” advised Vahrmeyer. “Seeking signs, creating more contact or disclosing your attraction would begin to turn fantasy into action. The task is not to repress the desire, but to contain it: to think about what it may be telling you while taking responsibility for the boundaries that protect everyone involved.”Whether this feeling is mutual, or for a man or a woman, I would heavily counsel against you doing anything about it. Starting a relationship with a trusted “other” at your child’s school will have deep and long-lasting effects, not least for your children.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.Explore more on these topicsFamilyAsk Annalisa BarbieriRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroad | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: Some young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countries
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: Some young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countries
Content: Arianna Marie and Zwiwe Dlamini teach English in South Korea.Photograph: Courtesy Arianna Marie and Zwiwe DlaminiView image in fullscreenArianna Marie and Zwiwe Dlamini teach English in South Korea.Photograph: Courtesy Arianna Marie and Zwiwe DlaminiWork & careersMeet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroadSome young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countriesJenna ZazaSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA year ago, Arianna Marie, 25, was struggling to control the students in her Florida elementary school classroom.She was living with her parents to save on rent and quickly feeling her passion for teaching dry up, even though it was her first job since graduation.“I was extremely burnt out,” Marie said. “We had a teacher shortage, so all of my classes were overcrowded.”When her district wanted to transfer her to a new school, she looked for opportunities abroad. Through an English-language teaching job inSouth Korea, Marie is now living in Daegu, a city in the south-eastern part of the country, with enough pay and benefits that she can save and travel.How to find a career you love – for gen Z and everyone else: ‘You don’t want your life’s compass to be dread’Read moreThe fact that it’s the home to K-pop and K-dramas doesn’t hurt – and in a striking shift, she’s rediscovered her love for the job. “I never have to crack down on behavior issues, and both students and teachers respect me so much,” Marie said. “I actually get to focus solely on teaching.”Marie is part of a program by the South Korean government that is placing native English speakers with a college degree and Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) certificates with local public schools, as itincreases spendingon education. Benefits include free housing, flight reimbursements, healthcare and monthly salariesstarting at about $1,400.Graduating with a college degree in the US no longer comes with the stability it once guaranteed. Since the Covid pandemic, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has beenhigherthan the overall unemployment rate.For those who have a job, earnings have beenrising slowerthan the pace of inflation. New entrants in US public service jobs like teaching areincreasingly leaving the profession, citing low pay and high stress.Other countries, including Japan and Taiwan, are similarly investing in full-time English-language teachers, attracting young workers with benefits they would be hard-pressed to find in their home countries.Gen Z is spreading the word. Some English-language teachers have garnered thousands of followers onTikTokandInstagram, showing audiences their lives abroad. Marie has been keeping track of her travels, and documenting some of her classroom experiences, on herInstagram account.The TEFL Institute, which issues TEFL certification courses that accredit English-language teachers, notes that the English-language teaching market wasvaluedat $95bn in 2026, with more than 2m TEFL jobs available worldwide. The market is expected to reach $181bn by 2034, and the Asia-Pacific region isgrowingthe fastest.View image in fullscreenArianna Marie.Photograph: Courtesy of Arianna MarieAs the US federal government hasguttedthe Department of Education, American public school teachers, who areoverwhelmingly female, are especially feeling the pull to overseas jobs.But the phenomenon isn’t exclusive to Americans, or teachers. Zwiwe Dlamini, 28, was spiraling into a deep depression working as an administrative assistant in Durban,South Africa.“I’ve always been behind the desk, gathering minutes, gathering meetings, working for CEOs and it was just extremely draining,” Dlamini said.Though she knew that finding a better job at home would be difficult – the youth unemployment rate in South Africa isnotoriously high, at almost 70% – Dlamini still quit her job. After six months of job searching, she knew she would have to look elsewhere.After she applied to the same program as Marie, she ended up in Incheon, the north-west South Korean city, as an English-language teacher. The free housing and low monthly expenses have allowed her to start paying off her debt while having enough savings to travel and plan for a master’s degree.“One year ago, [I] could not have imagined the position I am in today,” Dlamini said. “I couldn’t afford food and had [accumulated] debt, so paying it off now and still [experiencing] life to the fullest – I am actually so grateful.”View image in fullscreenZwiwe Dlamini.Photograph: Courtesy of Zwiwe DlaminiJohn Bentley, co-founder of the International TEFL Academy, which offers TEFL certification courses, noted that interest in teaching English abroad particularly soared after the 2024 presidential election.“With a difficult political and economic situation, we see gen Z turning to TEFL,” he said. “A lot of people go with the intention of staying for just one year. What happens is they fall in love with the country or experience and stay three [or] four years, or even much longer.”This tracks with a broader trend of Americans who increasingly say that they want to migrate. Last year, a Gallup pollfoundthat 40% of US women said they would move abroad if given the chance.Marie said her South Korean classroom, which she shares with another teacher, is worlds apart from her former classroom in Florida, where she would handle more than 20 kids on her own.“We always say that teaching is extremely undervalued in the US, but here you can tell how much they do value it,” she said. “The students are more receptive when I correct them and have so much respect for me as a teacher.”Explore more on these topicsWork & careersUS work & careersYoung peopleSouth KoreaUS personal financeTeacher shortagesTeachingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tuscany’s treasured islands: five to explore | Tuscany holidays | The Guardian
description: Want to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free Giannutri
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Want to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free Giannutri
Content: Cannelle beach on Giglio.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCannelle beach on Giglio.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty ImagesTuscany holidaysTuscany’s treasured islands: five to exploreWant to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free GiannutriFrancesca LombardoSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScattered between the Tuscan coast and Corsica, the seven islands of the Tuscan archipelago offer a striking contrast to mainland Tuscany. All are part of a protected national park, but each has its own character – some are lively, others tiny and sparsely inhabited. Montecristo and Gorgona are only accessible via strictly limited guided tours, but here’s a brief guide to the highlights of the other five.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Guardian GraphicsElba: theall-year-rounderAs Italy’s third-largest island, and with a year-round community, Elba is the archipelago’s main tourist hub, blending Napoleonic history with rugged landscapes, lively seaside towns and fine beaches. It is famous for Napoleon’s brief 1814 exile at thePalazzina dei Mulini, but its history runs much deeper, with 16th-century Medici fortifications to defend against pirate raids around the coast, and medieval hill towns, some standing on sites occupied since Roman times, inland.Beach lovers tend to divide between the white-pebble coves of Sansone and Capo Bianco near the largest town, Portoferraio, in the north, and the golden sands of Fetovaia and Cavoli in the south-west beneath Monte Capanne. Marina di Campo on the south coast is a favourite for watersports, and windsurfing and sailing schools are popular in many resorts, from Procchio in the north to Lacona in the south.View image in fullscreenThe Medici fortifications in Portoferraio on Elba.Photograph: Stevan ZZ/ShutterstockHikers can explore the 36-mile (58km)Grande Traversata Elbana,crossing the island from Cavo in the north-east to Pomonte or Patresi on the west coast, passing along mountain ridges and through traditional villages. Usually completed in three or four days, it’s best tackled in spring or autumn.Where to eat:In Portoferraio,Ristorante da Gianniis a favourite for handmade pasta, seafood and traditional cuisine. Try the house speciality, orecchiette with prawns and courgettes. In Marina di Campo,Da Pieroserves seafood-focused dishes right on the beach.Where to stay:Near Fetovaia,Hotel Montemerlo(doubles from about £88 B&B) offers a relaxed, eco-conscious stay among olive groves. In Marina di Campo,Hotel Punto Verde(doubles from about £90 B&B) is a charming family-run hotel near the beach. On the west coastHotel Gallo Nero(doubles from £79) is a family-run hotel overlooking Capo Sant’Andrea Bay. In an 18th-century building in Portoferraio’s historic centre,Indarsena(doubles from £86 B&B) is 10 minutes’ walk from several beaches.Getting there:Ferries from Piombino to Portoferraio take about an hour withToremar,MobyorBlu Navy.Giglio:the charmingisleView image in fullscreenThe village and harbour of Giglio Porto.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyAt just 21 sq km, Giglio is small but has three villages, secluded coves, an extensive coastline and a landscape of historic terraced vineyards. Access for private vehicles is heavily restricted during August, with exceptions for longer stays, which helps preserve its peaceful atmosphere, while buses and taxis link the harbour, villages and beaches, so a car-free holiday is easy.From Giglio Porto, trails lead to hidden coves and hilltop viewpoints, while the medieval lanes ofGiglio Castello, a fortified 12th-century hilltop village, are perfect for an aperitivo and an evening stroll.Beaches have distinct characters. Campese,on the north-west coast, is the largest, with reddish-gold sand and views of the 16th-century Torre del Campese. Cannelle, in the east, offers pale sand and crystalline water, while farther north, Arenella combines golden sand, granite boulders and clear water for snorkelling.Where to eat:In Giglio Porto,Ristorante Doriais a seafood favourite with a sea-view terrace (tryspaghetti alla chitarrawith sea urchin and toasted breadcrumbs). In Campese,Da Zio Meinoofferscucina povera(peasant cooking) such aspancotti di mareandspaghetti alle vongole e alla bottarga(with clams and cured mullet roe).Where to stay:On a hillside overlooking Giglio Porto,B&B La Vela(doubles from £87 B&B)is a small guesthouse with maritime-themed interiors. On a headland above Campese Bay,Le Poste di Simplicio(doubles from £100 B&B) is a family-run B&B with sweeping sea views.Getting there:ToremarorMaregiglioferries run from Porto Santo Stefano to Giglio Porto in about an hour.Capraia:a wild hikers’paradiseView image in fullscreenCapraia is best explored on foot.Photograph: Arkanto/AlamyLocated just over 20 miles (33km) north-west of Elba, Capraia is one of the archipelago’s most remote islands. Largely car-free, with few roads, it is best explored on foot along mule tracks winding between sea cliffs, hidden coves and 16th-century Genoese fortifications, although taxi boats and a bus provide limited transport.Highlights include the red rock formations ofCala Rossa, theGenoese fortress of San Giorgioand the 16th-centuryTorre dello Zenòbito.Beaches are few, but swimmers can cool off at Cala San Francesco, hike to Cala del Ceppo and Cala dello Zurletto, or take a taxi boat to Spiaggia della Mortola, one of the few sandy stretches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere to eat:In the main village, the fixed menu atIl Carabottinochanges according to what the local fishers happen to bring ashore, whileIl Pigghiolotakes a more contemporary approach, reworking island flavours in dishes such as squid parmigiana and cod croquette.Where to stay:Accommodation is limited, butLa Mandola Eco Hostel(doubles from £70 room-only) near the port is a restorative basecamp for walkers, beachgoers and divers, with a sheltered saltwater pool. In Capraia village,Il Saracino Boutique Suitesis a small, characterful retreat with sea views (doubles from £130 B&B).Getting there:The ferry from Livorno takes 1 hour 45 minutes withToremar.Pianosa:the protected isleView image in fullscreenThe harbour on Pianosa, where visitor numbers are strictly limited.Photograph: Fabiano Sodi/AlamyDaily visitor numbers to Pianosa are restricted, helping preserve the island’s fragile environment and tranquil atmosphere. You can either buy a ticket on the limited ferry service or join an authorised guided excursion.Roman remains (including early Christian catacombs) and abandoned prison buildings from when the island served as a penal colony offer glimpses of its history. And the restoredCasa dell’AgronomoandMuseo delle Scienze Geologiche e Archeologicheexplore its agricultural, geological and archaeological heritage.Guided walks, cycling and kayak excursions are among the best ways to explore. Swimming is restricted to Cala Giovanna, an easy walk from the small port and historic village, to help safeguard the marine ecosystem.Where to eat:Da Brunelloin the small harbour village is Pianosa’s only cafe/restaurant, with a focus on fresh fish and vegetables grown on the island.Where tostay:Close to the cafe and run by the same management, the island’s only accommodation,Albergo Milena(doubles from £95 half-board) offers simple rooms in a historic building.Getting there:There are authorised excursions from Elba withAcquavision(45 minutes), and limitedToremarferry services run from Piombino to Pianosa (about three hours).Giannutri:the roadless retreatView image in fullscreenA Roman column on the beach at Cala Maestra on Giannutri.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyWhile Elba hums with holidaymakers and Vespas, this tiny, car-free limestone crescent, where scent-heavymacchiaslopes into ink-blue waters, offers a radical detox from modern life.With only one restaurant-cafe, which also functions as a small grocery shop, day trippers are advised to bring their own water and lunch. Most people swim at Cala Spalmatoio and Cala Maestra, while much of the coastline forms part of a protected marine reserve renowned for its diving and snorkelling. A guided tour of aRoman villalinked to the Domitii Ahenobarbi family is a must.Where to eat:La Vela Giannutri, the island’s only dining option, focuses on seafood dishes, from tuna tartare tospaghetti alle vongole.Where to stay:Accommodation is limited to the family-runA Casa Diana(doubles from £123 B&B), with simple rooms and sea views, and a scattering of holiday rentals.Getting there:Maregiglioruns ferries from Porto Santo Stefano, or there are seasonal excursion boats (taking about an hour). In summer, Maregiglio also operates excursions andmini-cruisesbetween Giglio and Giannutri.Explore more on these topicsTuscany holidaysItaly holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New payment set up? Get in touch! The bank scam where your ‘bank’ is the scammer | Scams | The Guardian
description: Impersonation scams – where callers or texts claim to be from trusted entities such as banks, HMRC or even the police – are rife … and growing
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Impersonation scams – where callers or texts claim to be from trusted entities such as banks, HMRC or even the police – are rife … and growing
Content: The phone pings and it’s your bank asking you to hand over your bank card.Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe phone pings and it’s your bank asking you to hand over your bank card.Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyScam watchScamsNew payment set up? Get in touch! The bank scam where your ‘bank’ is the scammerImpersonation scams – where callers or texts claim to be from trusted entities such as banks, HMRC or even the police – are rife … and growing‘I’ve £80k in the account, here’s my pin’: turning the tables on scammersHilary OsborneSun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour phone pings and it’s a message from your bank about a new payment being set up on your account. If you do not recognise the transaction, it says, you should get in touch. There’s a number for you to call.The person on the other end of the line tells you that your account has been compromised by scammers. They need details from you so they can help protect your money. Before you know it, they are giving you details of a safe account to transfer your savings to, or asking you to hand over your debit card so it can be replaced.Scam texts, this one purporting to be from Santander, often drop in company names that could be familiar to persuade the recipient they are genuine.Photograph: HandoutImpersonation scams suh as this are rife - and costly. Figures from Lloyds bank show that fraudsters posing as representatives of trusted organisations – including the police, banks, HM Revenue & Customs and phone providers – stole 10% more from its customers in the year to the end of June than in the previous 12 months.While the number of its customers reporting a scam has fallen by 3% this year, the average sum taken rose by 10% to £3,516.Meanwhile, Santander says more than £3m has been stolen from its customers through bank impersonation scams so far this year, with an average loss of £6,000.Because the messages are being sent out randomly, the scammer could claim to be from a company you have no financial relationship with. But if a text or phone message does include your bank’s name, it is likely to stop you in your tracks.What it looks likeIt might be a call or email, but it usually starts with a text, says Elaine Ross, head of fraud analytics at Nationwide building society. “A lot of people are more sceptical about people calling them than they are about getting a message,” she says.double quotation mark‘If something doesn’t look or sound right, trust your instincts. Stop, check and contact your bank directly using a trusted number.Chris Ainsley, SantanderThe text says that a payment has been set up to someone from your account and asks you to take action if you don’t recognise, or did not make, the transaction. Recent messages seen by Guardian Money show criminals saying that people have paid a specific person or business.View image in fullscreenScam texts are often for high value amounts to lure the recipient into taking action, with the option to replyPhotograph: Scam text message for Money section/Handout“The value will be a high value, and it will be a person the victim doesn’t know,” Ross says.In some cases the message will give you a number to call, in others it will ask you to reply ‘Y’ if it was you, and ‘N’ if it wasn’t. “As soon as you press ‘N,’ they will call you back and say they are from Nationwide’s security team or the police. That puts people into a panic,” she says.Once they have you on the phone, they will attempt to persuade you to move cash or hand over your cards - or both – for your own protection.‘Friday afternoon fraud’: warning for UK homebuyers on bank scamsRead moreWhat to doIgnore any message that is from a mobile phone number and not your bank.Chris Ainsley, head of fraud risk management at Santander UK, says: “If something doesn’t look or sound right, trust your instincts. Stop, check and contact your bank directly using a trusted number.”Use the number on the back of your card to contact your bank if you are concerned.Hang up and call back if you are on a call that you become suspicious about. Ross says that when Nationwide contacts people to warn them about scams, “we expect customers to say ‘I’m going to call you back’ – if they are worried during a call, we would absolutely encourage them to do that”. That might mean joining a queue to get through, she says, but it will be worthwhile.Find out what tools your bank or building society has in place to help you detect and avoid scams. At Nationwide, for example, if you are speaking to someone claiming to be from the building society, you can now check via its app that it is a genuine call: open and go to the “more” section, then tap “call checker”.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchConsumer affairsConsumer rightsBanks and building societiesLloyds Banking GroupBankingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump | Mark Carney | The Guardian
description: The Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprised
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: The Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprised
Content: Mark Carney has challenged Donald Trump in recent trade talks between Canada and the US.Illustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs Mims/GettyView image in fullscreenMark Carney has challenged Donald Trump in recent trade talks between Canada and the US.Illustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs Mims/GettyThe Sunday readMark Carney‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with TrumpThe Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprisedLeyland Ceccoin Toronto,Heather StewartandKalyeena Makortoffin LondonSun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareMark Carney stood before a walnut-veneered lectern, his face drawn tight, as he announced that talks with Canada’s biggest trading partner had collapsed. “Last spring, I warned thatAmerica is trying to break usso that they can own us,” he said. “And I promised: that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”For years, the former central bank governor had worked hard to calm markets. Now, he was asking Canadians to accept uncertainty and confrontation.Near the end of the press conference last Saturday, a reporter made reference to the sombre, combative tone of the speech: “Why does it feel like todayMark Carneyis going to war?”The prime minister paused.“We were attacked. You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said. “We got attacked.”The unlikely transformation of an economist and central banker with no prior electoral experience into a powerful global politician has bucked precedent and expectations. But Carney has settled into the role he warned was necessary for the country, that of a wartime leader standing up to an erratic and vindictive adversary who seems hellbent on subjugatingCanada.After trade negotiations with the US broke down, the two sides traded recriminations and made good on threats to impose new tariffs on each other. In his latest act of petty antagonism, Trumpsigned an executive orderon Thursday directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.But Carney, in walking away from the proposed deal, did what few other leaders have done: dared Trump and the US to test his nation’s resolve.“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” he said.‘He was pretty doggedly determined’For those who have worked with the demanding – and, at times, temperamental–central banker, such a calculated refusal to accede to a bad deal comes as little surprise.Carney was raised in Canada’s western prairies, and his story – of an outsider gradually working his way into, and eventually reshaping, powerful institutions – offers clues to a man unwilling to accept the terms set by others.“He was pretty doggedly determined,” said one person who worked alongside Carney when he was serving as UN special envoy for climate action in 2021.View image in fullscreenMark Carney with the then chancellor of the exchequer, Rishi Sunak, at the UN Climate Change Conference (Cop26) in Glasgow in 2021Photograph: ReutersWhen trying to convince banks to sign up to climate pledges, Carney could turn on the charm. “He was pretty diplomatic, when dealing with people that he knows he’s got to influence,” his former colleague said.But it has been no shock to see Carney standing up to Trump on the world stage. “It doesn’t surprise me … and I think it’s because of that determination and that unwillingness to back down.”Carney was not always so sure-footed. When he was handpicked as governor of the Bank of England in 2013 by the then UK chancellor, George Osborne, Carney’s hard-driving approach was not a natural fit with the venerable institution in London’s Square Mile. When he arrived, it still had pink-uniformed, top hatted guards at the entrance.The traits acquired during his days at Goldman Sachs have continued into his tenure as prime minister. He remains an early riser, a dedicated runner and demands that ministers know their files front to back, according to those who work with him. Media have also reported that staff are expected to dress in formal business attire and documents are to be written using British spelling – to thefrustration of Canadian linguists.View image in fullscreenMark Carney when he was governor of the Bank of Canada in 2010 at a House of Commons committee meeting on Parliament Hill in Ottawa.Photograph: Blair Gable/ReutersWhile Carney’s career in a string of powerful institutions reflects a sharp, analytical mind, his tenure at the Bank of England telegraphed that the wonkish economist was also willing to become political when necessary.When Carney overhauled the Bank’s communications strategy,introducing “forward guidance” to show its thinking about future interest rates, it was not immediately embraced as a success.The senior Labour MP Pat McFadden – now a cabinet minister – accused the Bank under Carney of baffling investors and the public with mixed messages about the future of interest rates.View image in fullscreenCarney speaking at Oxford University’s Sheldonian Theatre in October 2015 about Britain’s EU membership.Photograph: Getty ImagesIn October 2015, with the referendum looming on whether Britain should leave the European Union, Carney used a speech at Oxford University to underline the benefits to the UK of the “economic and financial openness” that came with membership.With theeurozone debt crisisa recent memory, Carney also highlighted the increased risk of financial instability that membership of the EU implied; but Brexiters seized on his positive comments as an unwarranted intervention in a highly politicised topic.The row deepened when Carney suggested Brexit might plunge the UK into recession. Bernard Jenkin, the Conservative director of the leave campaign wrote to the governor, urging him to butt out.Carney’s replydisplayed the same relish for a fight that has been evident in his handling of Trump. “Dear Mr Jenkin,” his letter began, “I am responding to your letter to dispel immediately the numerous and substantial misconceptions it contained.” He went on to accuse the veteran MP of “a fundamental misunderstanding of central bank independence as enshrined in statute”.View image in fullscreenMark Carney delivering the Bank of England’s quarterly inflation report in London in May 2016, warning that a Brexit vote would negatively affect the UK economy.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAIn the event, there was no Brexit recession, something many economists attributed partly to the Bank’s robust response, including rapid interest rate cuts and quantitative easing (the emergency bond-buying scheme used during the global financial crisis).Charles Randell spent five years on the board of the Prudential Regulation Authority, which Carney chaired after becoming Bank of England governor. “I’m sure if you ring around enough people who worked with him at the Bank, you’ll find people who will say that he had his shortcomings,” Randall said. “But with time to reflect on my experience … he’s one of the most impressive people I’ve ever worked with.”Randell, who was then the chair of the Financial Conduct Authority, said that even behind the scenes, Carney was a “very serious person, very analytical, very driven” and “very careful about how he communicates”.“On the morning after the Brexit vote in 2016 … he went in front of the cameras to reassure financial markets that the Bank was ready to deal with any of the consequences of that decision,” he said. “It was a masterpiece in strategic messaging.”View image in fullscreenCarney speaking after Britain voted to leave the EU in London on June 2016.Photograph: Reuters Tv/Reuters‘Compliance will not buy safety’Joseph Steinberg, a professor of economics at the University of Toronto, said that while during the Brexit debate, Carney “did not shy away from trying to tell kind of the hard economic truths”, he had not spoken much about the economics of the current US trade war.“In public, he is leaning pretty heavily on the sovereignty angle. It is clear that he privately is probably thinking about the​​ cold, hard economics of an incredibly tenuous situation.”Carney’s decision to retaliate against the US has caused some economists, including Steinberg, to point out that Canada will take a far more painful blow than the US.For the first time in his career Carney is fully beholden to a wary public, a reality that underscores the clashing of two personalities: the technocrat who understands the economics, and the politician who must contend with the political costs of compromise.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump meets with Mark Carney in the Oval Office.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA“At the moment, Canadians are likely to be extraordinarily intolerant of making any kind of concessions to the US whatsoever, even if they are in our economic best interest,” he said.In January, Carney warned people at Davos that “compliance will not buy safety” in a world increasingly dominated by hegemonic powers. While it never mentioned Trump, his speech was seen as a thinly veiled critique of the US president’s aim to abandon longstanding alliances and reshape the world to his advantage.25:51How did Trump get so rich? | Politics Weekly AmericaOne of Carney’s prescriptions – forging deep relations with like-minded “middle powers” and restructuring to lessen reliance on former allies – has already taken shape in Canada, at a speed and degree to which the pollster David Colettodescribedas a “wartime-footing government without a war”.“It’s a government organised around an external threat that’s willing to suspend its own party’s orthodoxies, centralise power to move fast, and measure itself in outcomes rather than values,” he wrote.Carney abandoned many of the policies of his predecessor Justin Trudeau, including his carbon and electric vehicle mandates. He has also fast-tracked large projects, including an oil pipeline, and invested tens of billions more into defence.View image in fullscreenCarney waving to supporters at a victory party in Ottawa, after he won Canada’s election on 28 April 2025.Photograph: Dave Chan/AFP/Getty Images“The public has hardly blinked,” Coletto said in an interview. “Mark Carney’s approval rating has just sustained itself through this entire period.”“When [Carney] first became prime minister, I was sceptical that a central banker would be able to respond to public opinion because that is the opposite of their job,” he said. “But I’ve been surprised with his nuanced read of the country. He’s been adept at being not just politically effective but in holding his support together through a trying time. This suggests there’s little value in underestimating his political instincts.”Polling shows that Carney remains the leader Canadians trust most to steer the country through economic uncertainty. But the prime minister has also embraced a role that would once have seemed almost incongruous: asking a country vastly smaller and less powerful than its neighbour to stand its ground.He said in his recent address: “Canadians don’t submit to the weather – we thrive in it. We don’t wait to see which way the wind is blowing. Or surrender ourselves to the waves to be storm-tossed by events.“We set our own course. We make our own weather. In Canada, we are masters in our own home, from coast to coast to coast.”

title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?  | Society | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needs
Author: Paul Sagar
Headline: Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needs
Content: Illustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianThe big ideaSocietyCould this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needsPaul SagarSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse.In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle.What the government needs is big, innovative ideas. We should look to history for inspiration, while also absorbing the lessons of past mistakes.How about national service – but instead of entering the military, recruits are pledged to the NHS? Eye-catching, but ultimately not right, at least not in that form. Forcing young people to do work they’d prefer not to, when there isn’t even an enemy at the gates, will only lead to bad results. Indeed, the army has already learned this: compulsory recruits in the postwar period were typically unmotivated and incompetent; a drag rather than a boost to the military’s performance.double quotation markSince I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in careBut that’s a crude precedent. We can take more relevant inspiration from elsewhere. For example, young men in Austria who do not wish to serve in the military can instead opt for health or social care work; many end up driving ambulances. The trade-off is that they do nine months instead of six. In Norway, conscientious objectors were, until 2012, able to perform “civilian national service”, working in community settings such as primary schools or nursing homes, and accruing points towards university entry for doing so.Thinking along similar lines, how about this? The government offers recent school leavers a deal: 50% off their total university fees if they first spend a year volunteering in social care. (You could even up the ante: 100% off if they commit to two years; full back pay with a bonus if they stay in the profession.)There are many reasons to take this proposal seriously. First, it is not just social care that is in crisis. University funding is, too. Right now, UK universities are panicking because student enrolment fees no longer keep them in the black. But at the same time, undergraduates are being presented with eye-watering loan bills and interest rates at levels that make capital repayment much harder. We are rapidly approaching a cliff edge. The government is going to have to fix the system one way or the other. Why not do something innovative and radical at the same time?The overall maths might work surprisingly well. If uptake is sufficiently high, the state gets an enormous amount of free (in the short term) labour to offset the costs of lost loan revenue. If that sounds exploitative, remember that it would be in the interests of young people themselves (in the longer term) because they would leave university with a heck of a lot less debt.But the upsides go beyond just money. At the moment, unscrupulous agencies too often rely on low-paid migrant labour, ignoring the linguistic and caring skills required do a safe and competent job. A scheme like this would open up a new pool for recruitment – of eager-to-learn young people at the start of their careers.Of course, they would have to undergo proper training and would only get the discount if they complete the programme to a certified high level. Along the way, some would discover that care work can be deeply rewarding; that the current stigmatisation of this kind of employment just doesn’t tally with reality.I know, because since I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in care. I am lucky to be with avery good agency, which only employs highly competent and conscientious staff (from all over the world). I have seen up close just how rewarding and dignified care work can be. Sure, there are some icky parts to looking after a man who can’t go to the toilet by himself. But all my care workers take real pride in helping me live as close to a normal life as possible. Of course, they’re not on footballers’ wages. But they get a very visible amount of life satisfaction from helping me find mine.One of the most interesting care workers I’ve met was covering holiday earlier in the summer. Originally from Ireland, she had just finished a two-year master’s degree at King’s College London (by coincidence where I teach, in a different department). She is now a qualified dietitian, who in future will be working in hospitals. But until she makes that transition she is spending a year with my spinal agency, after having been employed as a care worker in Ireland for two years prior to her degree. It’s a job she finds deeply rewarding.I am confident that if we incentivised UK students to try social care before university, many would consider rejoining once they had graduated. This would help to reduce wider stigma around care work as the preserve of poor, often vulnerable migrant workers, assumed to be doing it only because no one else will.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLook, I’m neither a government accountant nor a policy expert. Perhaps when we’ve crunched the numbers, it just doesn’t work. But from where I’m sitting this has the potential to be a win-win of the sort that could define the Burnham administration. All the scheme needs is a name, and there’s an obvious one for the taking: “Care First”.Dr Paul Sagar is a reader in political theory at King’s College London.Further readingLabours of Love: The Crisis of Care by Madeleine Bunting (Granta, £9.99)The Courage to Care: Nurses, Families and Hope by Christie Watson (Vintage, £10.99)Who Caresby Emily Kenway (Headline, £12.99)Explore more on these topicsSocietyThe big ideaSocial careWelfarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city | Sudan | The Guardian
description: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts
Content: Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSave the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSudanPeople fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge cityMore traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirtsRachel Savagein JohannesburgSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.The UN saysmore than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figurescitedby Save the Children.“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.View image in fullscreenTens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeidlast week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSFdescended into open conflict.Since then,about 11.3 million peoplehave been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, areat risk of famine.Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range fromtens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have beenmassacred by the RSF in El Fasherover two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.View image in fullscreenThe damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesA surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in Juneled the UN to warnthat the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according toEmergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.View image in fullscreenConditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”Explore more on these topicsSudanAfricaRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign
Content: Ontario premier Doug Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign near Grimsby, Ontario, after Trump’s order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersView image in fullscreenOntario premier Doug Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign near Grimsby, Ontario, after Trump’s order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersDonald TrumpCanada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalatesMeanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America signEdward HelmoreSun 30 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald TrumpandCanadacontinued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.0:54Ontario premier unveils Lake Ontario sign in response to Trump’s ‘Lake America’ order – videoWith talks to resolve the tradedispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.View image in fullscreenLake Ontario renamed as Lake America on US-facing Google Maps.Photograph: Google MapsLake Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or ​how the rest of the ‌world refers to the ‌lake”, Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names”.Google had done similarly in Trump’sexecutive orderfor the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Google Map users in the US fornow seethat body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery forwhich he has shown a penchant.He posted one such video of anarmy of Canada geesewith Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America.
