He published another of himselfkicking over a Lake Ontario signand replacing it with Lake America while he danced in hisdistinctive wayto a soundtrack of the Village People hitYMCA, which he hasincorporatedinto his public appearances for years.Across the US’s northern border, Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, replied with a two-stories-high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.He appeared on Sunday on the ABC News program This Week and remarked that Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming order was like “something out of Saturday Night Live,’” the famous NBC sketch comedy show.“No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford said. “It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.Trump on Sunday afternoon published a social media post declaring “Canada to be the worst”.“I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” Trump also wrote, referring to the ongoing US-Canada trade war.Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpCanadaAmericasUS politicsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez defends ‘endless’ benefits of her oil deal with Trump | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Deal that will reportedly see US take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil has provoked outrage in her country
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Deal that will reportedly see US take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil has provoked outrage in her country
Content: Delcy Rodríguez claimed the deal would help her country become ‘an energy powerhouse’.Photograph: Presidency of Venezuela/EPAView image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez claimed the deal would help her country become ‘an energy powerhouse’.Photograph: Presidency of Venezuela/EPAVenezuelaVenezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez defends ‘endless’ benefits of her oil deal with TrumpDeal that will reportedly see US take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil has provoked outrage in her countryTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVenezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’shighly controversial energy dealwith Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”Trump announces new US oil agreement with VenezuelaRead moreTrump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.View image in fullscreenOil platforms and pumpjacks at Lake Maracaibo in north-western Venezuela.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersOn Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “One of the things I am going to do with the VenezuelanOilis fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied.”Trump added: “The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”Hours after seizing Maduro on 3 January,Trump warned Rodríguezshe would face an even worse fate if she failed to toe the US line. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump said.Details of the agreement – struck during months of secret talks – remain sparse but it will reportedly see Washington take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.The South American country has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn. Rodríguez said the deal involved 17 “strategic oilfields” where it was hoped more than 1.5m barrels could be produced each day.But the deal has provoked outrage, both among members of Venezuela’s opposition and within the Chavismo political movement of which Rodríguez is part.Speaking on Friday, one prominent opposition figure, who asked not to be named, called the agreement “a massive land grab” by a “rapacious, mafioso United States”.View image in fullscreenProtesters affiliated with Chavista groups and social movements of the Anti-Imperialist Popular Front march in Caracas on Saturday to oppose the oil deal.Photograph: Mario Flores/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockWriting on X, Rafael Ramírez, the former head of Venezuela’s state-owned oil company PDVSA, accused Rodríguez’s administration of “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the homeland” with the “neocolonial” transaction. “They are handing over 65bn barrels of our reserves to the United States. That has never happened in Venezuela, and I think nowhere else in the world,” Ramírez added inan interviewwith the newspaper El Nacional.On Saturday, dozens of leftwing protesters marched through Caracas with banners reading: “We are neither a colony, nor a back yard” and “Yankees go home!”Critics of the agreement shared an ironic meme on social media suggesting the state oil company’s name should be changed from PDVSA to “PDUSA”.In her broadcast, Rodríguez, the daughter of a Marxist guerrilla who spent years denouncing “imperialist” attempts to snatch her country’s oil reserves, countered claims she was surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power. She thanked Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, for striking the deal but added: “There is something that must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains the ownership and sovereignty over its resources.”“We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” claimed the politician, whose country was plunged into authoritarian rule and one of the world’s worst peacetime economic crises during Maduro’s 13-year rule.The deal represents an astonishing U-turn from Rodríguez and the socialist, anti-imperialist political movement she and Maduro inherited from Hugo Chávez after his death in 2013.In one 2024 speech, footage of which circulated on social media after Friday’s announcement, Rodríguez lambasted the Venezuelan opposition, accusing it of seeking to surrender the country’s oil, natural gas and gold reserves to its “masters” in Washington.View image in fullscreenA fuel station in Caracas. The deal has provoked outrage among opposition figures in Venezuela.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesLast September, as the US tightened the screws on Maduro, Rodrígueztold the New York Times: “The Pentagon always had a strategic objective of obtaining Venezuelan reserves.”The deal will reportedly involve the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which channels funds into projects seen as important for national security. It will also involve a private company owned by Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial UK-based tycoon who has emerged as a key intermediary between theTrump administrationand Rodríguez.Opposition politicians fear the deal will scupper attempts to recover Venezuela’s democracy and hold fresh presidential elections. Maduro is widely believed to have stolen the last vote, in 2024, and Rodríguez has deflected questions about a future election, saying vaguely that it will happen “some day”. Trump has also said Venezuela is “not really ready” for elections.Writing on X, the opposition leader Juan Pablo Guanipa, said: “The only way to truly reactivate the Venezuelan economy in the long term and make this agreement benefit both parties is through a free election that leads to a representative government, clear rules of the game, rule of law, and institutions that allow our resources to be managed transparently and for the benefit of the nation.”Without that, the energy deal was like “a skyscraper [built] on pillars of clay”, Guanipa added.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaDelcy RodríguezAmericasUS foreign policyOilTrump administrationDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75 | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday
Content: Indigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenIndigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPBoxingAustralian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine had a heart attack on SundayWarning:Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images and names of Indigenous Australians who have diedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSun 30 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, aged 75.The father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine had a heart attack on Sunday.Born in Baryulgil, near Grafton in northern New South Wales, Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions, challenging for the world middleweight title against Argentina’s Carlos Monzon in 1974, in a bout stopped in the seventh round.View image in fullscreenTony Mundine with former boxer and activist Rubin ‘Hurricane’ Carter in 2010.Photograph: Lee Besford/AAPMundine leaves a significant boxing legacy. Anthony was an IBO middleweight and WBA super-middleweight world champion, whose son Rahim won his fourth career fight from as many professional bouts on the Gold Coast only last week.Anthony Mundine posted a tribute to his father on social media, saying he was returning home for his funeral after travelling to Saudi Arabia.View image in fullscreenAnthony Mundine spars with Tony during a training session at his gymnasium in Redfern in 2013.Photograph: AAP“I don’t know what to say, I’m broken,” Anthony posted.“Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul.“I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.View image in fullscreenNBA star Clyde Drexler with Tony Mundine during a basketball clinic for the Aboriginal community at Mundine's gym in Redfern.Photograph: Tim Cole/AAP“Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength gonna miss you Tonza, there’s only one Tony Mundine.”Through a career in the middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight divisions, Tony Mundine recorded 80 wins – 64 from knockouts, 15 losses, and one draw.Explore more on these topicsBoxingIndigenous AustraliansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cash settlements on home insurance claims leaving vulnerable Australians short-changed, Asic says | Insurance (Australia) | The Guardian
description: Corporate regulator finds insurers settling most claims with cash rather than by managing repairs or rebuilding, warning of ‘unfair outcomes’ for homeowners
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Corporate regulator finds insurers settling most claims with cash rather than by managing repairs or rebuilding, warning of ‘unfair outcomes’ for homeowners
Content: Asic reviewed a sample of home building insurance claims from Cyclone Jasper, which hit far north Queensland in December 2023.Photograph: Brian Cassey/AAPView image in fullscreenAsic reviewed a sample of home building insurance claims from Cyclone Jasper, which hit far north Queensland in December 2023.Photograph: Brian Cassey/AAPInsurance (Australia)Cash settlements on home insurance claims leaving vulnerable Australians short-changed, Asic saysCorporate regulator finds insurers settling most claims with cash rather than by managing repairs or rebuilding, warning of ‘unfair outcomes’ for homeownersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniSun 30 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHome insurers are overwhelmingly paying cash to settle claims, leaving Australians to foot blowouts in repair costs for their cyclone-damaged homes.The corporate regulator is calling for “realistic” bigger payouts, warning the practice could cause “unfair outcomes” for people already in vulnerable positions.In a report released on Monday, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) found many homeowners were being paid based on a single quote from insurers’ favoured builders.Asic commissioner Alan Kirkland said homeowners were then left to find tradespeople, oversee repairs and pay for unexpected costs and damage, all issues that would otherwise have been handled by insurers.“The easy option for insurers can be the expensive one for homeowners,” Kirkland said.“If the amount falls short, consumers can be left shouldering the cost of repairs and paying the difference out of their own pocket.”A spokesperson for the Insurance Council of Australia said cash settlements could give customers flexibility and control over their own repairs. They said the industry had improved since Cyclone Jasper and focused on ensuring settlements were clearly explained and understood.Asic reviewed a sample of home building insurance claims fromCyclone Jasper, which hit far north Queensland in December 2023.It looked at the companies that it said accounted for most of the home insurance industry: Insurance Australia Group (IAG), AAI, QBE Insurance, Allianz Australia and Sure Insurance.Car owners should challenge insurers on steep price hikes and ‘call their bluff’, Asic saysRead moreAsic said insurers professed to prefer to settle claims by managing repairs or rebuilding, not by paying cash. The review found none of the five were systematically recording why claims were being settled with cash.Cash settlements were used in more than 63% of final claims. IAG and Allianz each used full or partial cash settlements in more than 80% of cases.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailMost cash settlement offers were based on just one quote and most of those were from insurers’ preferred suppliers, the review found.Asic said it was concerned the quotes may not be high enough to cover customers’ repair costs, as customers may not be able to get the discounts given to insurers.In one case, an insurer’s preferred builder provided a quote at a 40% discount and the insurer paid out that cheaper quote in cash. When the customer asked the builder to repair their home for that cash amount, the builder refused.Some insurers applied extra pay to account for their suppliers giving the insurer a discounted quote but none had consistent systems in place to do so, the review found.Insurers rarely provided consumers enough information to determine if cash was their best option. Three insurers did not tell consumers their policies permitted them to change their mind after accepting cash settlements, though two later told Asic they had begun clearly informing consumers of their rights.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFour of the five insurers had flawed approaches for identifying and assisting vulnerable customers, the report found.While the report did not identify any breaches of legal obligations, it said insurers would clearly comply with the rules if they ensured cash settlement offers were based on market prices, not discount rates.Insurance and CPI graphThe costs of construction and repairs have soared in recent years, with a resulting surge in home insurance costs.Finity, an analytics company, has found home insurance premiums rose 51% in the five years to October 2025.Insurance prices generally rose 4.2% in the year to July, faster than inflation of 3.5%, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Wednesday.While Rick waited for his insurance payout, mushrooms sprouted in his flooded Victorian home. He’s not aloneRead moreAsic earlier this month advised car owners to challenge their insurers and shop around for better deals after findinginsurers were failing to clearly justify their steep increases to premiums.Complaints about home building insurance have returned to highs not seen since 2022-23 due to insurers’delays in handling claims.The Insurance Council of Australiahas foundthe climate crisis and increasing incidence of extreme weather has nearly tripled total costs for insurers.In a 2025 report, it estimated extreme weather had generated $4.5bn worth of claims each year on average in the 2020s.Explore more on these topicsInsurance (Australia)AsicBusinessNatural disastersConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summit  | Pacific Islands Forum | The Guardian
description: Solomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: Solomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa
Content: Pacific Islands leaders and delegates arrive at Palau International Airport ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPacific Islands leaders and delegates arrive at Palau International Airport ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesPacific Islands ForumPacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summitSolomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and SamoaKrishani Dhanjiand Australian Associated PressSun 30 Aug 2026 03.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeveral leaders have pulled out of a thePacific Islands Forumleaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.The Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”,according to the ABC.Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and hisVanuatucounterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the Cop31 climate summit in November and a pre-Cop31 summit to be held inFijiand Tuvalu in October.He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.”Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive.Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the“Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader.“In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeekdaysSign up toAfternoon UpdateOur Australian afternoon update breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region.Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit.Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country.Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties.Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration.Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit.“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.“So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them.“We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.”Explore more on these topicsPacific Islands ForumPacific islandsSouth PacificFijiSamoaVanuatunewsShareReuse this content

title: Renee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help search  | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Missing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of Nepal
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Missing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of Nepal
Content: Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China on Saturday.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China on Saturday.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterRenee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help searchMissing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of NepalFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCait Kellyin KathmanduSun 30 Aug 2026 02.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations.“Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them.“And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.”View image in fullscreenRenee, an Australian, was travelling in Nepal and is now missing.Photograph: GoFundMeLike many of the missing Australians, Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away.Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s.Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said.“And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.”A map showing the flood zone in NepalRenee’s family understand how dire the situation is, and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived. But until they know for certain, they would hold hope, she said.“Everyone’s very realistic. We know how bad this was and where she was. But until they find her, everyone’s got this little slither of hope that maybe she’s stuck somewhere and can’t get out, or she’s injured.Families balance hope and despair in race to find survivors in Nepal as 41 Australians still missingRead more“I’ve been looking through pictures trying to identify someone or see her. But we understand the reality of this situation.”Like most Australians, Renee had come to Nepal on a pilgrimage. Spry said her sister was a “deeply spiritual” person who loved to help people.“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” she said.“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”The family of Michael Keats, an Australian who had been near the Tibet-Nepal border when flash flooding began, confirmed his death in posts to social media on Sunday.Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram he had been on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash that had been a “dream for many years”.“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted then to know God, and to merge with the divine.”He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Captain and crew arrested after at least eight die in northern Cyprus ferry disaster – as it happened | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: An estimated 237 people have been rescued but 18 are missing after accident off the coast of northern Cyprus
Author: Yohannes Lowe
Headline: An estimated 237 people have been rescued but 18 are missing after accident off the coast of northern Cyprus
Content: 15.18 EDTNorthern Cyprus ferry disaster - key developments so farHere are the main updates from the last few hours:The death toll has risen to “at least 8”, with 18 people still missing.Ünal Üstel, the north’s Turkish Cypriot prime minister, told Turkish state broadcaster TRT that 237 people have so far been rescued.Survivors have described a blast which went off at the vessel’s bowbefore the catamaran-style ship rolled over.The captain and seven other crew membershave been arrestedand are in custodyThe captain was allegedly among the first to abandon ship, according to witnesses who spoke to local media.The boat was sailing from the port of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu inTurkey, when the disaster occurred about 4 nautical miles (7.5km) off the coast.Three children rescued from the sea were in intensive careon Sunday.The ferry has “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres (1,686 feet)”, according to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus’ transport ministerShare

title: Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Nathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspension
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Nathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspension
Content: Nathan Cofnas said in a post on X he was grateful to Ghent’s rector ‘for allowing me to stay’.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixView image in fullscreenNathan Cofnas said in a post on X he was grateful to Ghent’s rector ‘for allowing me to stay’.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixJason ArdayJason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchNathan Cofnas told by Ghent University to work remotely as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspensionChris OsuhSun 30 Aug 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProf Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.Cofnas, an American academic, wassuspendedfrom his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution earlier this month pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed that it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.The US ambassador toBelgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been controversial. In May, the university’s philosophy departmentalleged to the institution’s leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise”for his role researching “the future of liberalism” and that he had a “far-right agenda”.In July Cofnas accused Arday, a University of Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging also that there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August.View image in fullscreenJason Arday was found dead on 14 August. He was accused of plagiarism by Cofnas.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianWhite, aDonald Trump supporter, donor and fundraiser, had called Cofnas’s suspension “truly unacceptable”, calling earlier this month for De Sutter to rescind it immediately.On Friday, White wrote on his personal X account: “I just saved Belgium from a complete global media meltdown and well deserved spanking by @elonmusk and everyone by resolving the UGHENT Cofnas matter – quite quickly.”The previous night, Cofnas thanked White and the US state department for “defending American values” on X, adding: “It was beyond my imagination that such a person would take an interest in the fate of a postdoc. The Ambassador responded with great support which helped to bring about a just outcome.”Cofnas has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, and was reportedly among bloggersrecommended to the Palantir founder Peter Thielby a “race science” researcher.Cofnas has also hit out at Trump and Maga in his writing, while claiming the US president’s executive orders against diversity, equity and inclusion in the US were a “cause for celebration”.In a piece in April last year he said the Republican party had “degenerated into a low-IQ cult of personality”.Hitting out at Trump’s tariffs, he said the effect “will be to halt the American economic juggernaut, discredit the anti-woke movement, pave the way for a leftwing populist … [and] stop the right’s momentum in other countries”.In October, he wrote: “The right simply does not have the human capital to retake the institutions and run them effectively. The vast majority of intelligent, psychologically stable, and public-spirited Americans remain left and woke. The Trump administration’s war on universities, science, and data has only reinforced smart people’s identity as leftists.”Asked by the Guardian if he stood by previous criticisms of Trump and Maga, Cofnas said: “I voted for Trump three times and I am still a registered Republican. I strongly criticised some Maga policies, particularly tariffs. There are other Maga policies that I support, such as interventions on behalf of free speech.”Ghent University said it did “not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding this matter … ongoing preliminary disciplinary inquiries must be allowed to proceed calmly, independently and with full respect for the rights of all those involved”.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayBelgiumUniversitiesEuropeHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least eight dead and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Authorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted for
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Authorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted for
Content: Survivors arrive onshore after being rescued from the capsized boat off Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSurvivors arrive onshore after being rescued from the capsized boat off Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.Photograph: ReutersCyprusAt least eight dead and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern CyprusAuthorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted forHelena Smithin Athens,Angelique Chrisafisand agenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least eight people have died and 18 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said.The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for.“Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish ​Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy ‌at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister.The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from footage of rescued passengers.Photograph: Reuters TV/ReutersThe port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people ⁠and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey.Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence.“We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian.Location mapHours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.”Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.Video footage from the scene showed people wearing life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel. When the ship capsized, passengers clung to its overturned hull.The Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation reported the boat was new and that when it began taking in water four miles from the coast, the captain had told the passengers to put on lifejackets.View image in fullscreenA rescue helicopter winches up a passenger.Photograph: Reuters TV/ReutersErhürman told CNN’s Turkish channel he was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life.He said: “The ship capsized. It has sunk in an area where the water is 514 metres deep. So far, we have reached 244 people.”Speaking from the crisis centre set ⁠up in the area, he said: “There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... We are extremely saddened. Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort.”A source close to Erhüman said the ferry was a popular means of travel between the mainland and the island for Turks working in northern Cyprus.“It’s much cheaper than the plane and only fakes a few hours. A lot of Turkish citizens use it to travel and see their families back home,” said one official requesting anonymity. “You could say that a lot of the passengers were poor. It’s all just so very sad.”Four coastguard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, local officials said.With Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsCyprusTurkeyWater transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman, 22, killed and five injured in shooting at Swiss rave  | Switzerland | The Guardian
description: Manhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday
Content: A poster advertising the rave where the shooting took place.Photograph: Harold Cunningham/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA poster advertising the rave where the shooting took place.Photograph: Harold Cunningham/AFP/GettySwitzerlandWoman, 22, killed and five injured in shooting at Swiss raveManhunt under way after Italian dies from her injuries in the town of Aarau in the early hours of SundayReutersSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA manhunt is under way inSwitzerlandafter a 22-year-old woman was killed ⁠and five people were injured, ⁠some seriously, in a ​shooting at a rave in the northern town of Aarau, local police have said.In the attack in the early hours of Sunday at a techno party at a covered horse-racing track, an Italian woman died from her injuries at the scene, authorities said. All those caught up in the shooting were residents of Switzerland and in their 20s.Police appealed to the public for any images of the incident and said large areas of the town had been cordoned off in the search for one or more attackers.“We have no definite information about who is behind ​the attack,” a police spokesperson, Bernhard Graser, told Reuters. “We don’t know if it’s one, if ‌it’s several people, if they are on ‌the run by vehicle or on foot.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers patrol a street in Aarau on Sunday.Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPAA 34-year-old witness ‌who asked for anonymity said he heard shots shortly after the music stopped at 2.30am on Sunday, which he initially mistook for fireworks.Some took cover behind a DJ booth and one woman hid behind a refrigerator but was hit in the back by a bullet and bled to death despite efforts to revive her, he said.“It’s just incredibly tragic. She was young,” he said. “That something like this could happen in Aarau, at a local event, ‌is simply unimaginable. I still can’t really process it.”As a precaution police have increased their presence beyond the town – which is about 50km west of Zurich and 30km south of the German border – but Graser said there were indications the shooter or shooters were no longer in the immediate area.View image in fullscreenPolice secure the area around the Schachen racing track after the shooting.Photograph: Michael Buholzer/Keystone/AP“But we still have a lot of police here in the area, in the town of Aarau, in the whole state, to make sure that we could get them if they’re still ⁠around,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReuters footage showed armed officers patrolling the area, police convoys moving through the ​streets and armoured vehicles parked near the ​crime scene.Organisers of the annual rave said they ​were shocked and heartbroken ‌by the incident. “A rave should ​always be a place ​of joy and love, never a place where people are killed, injured, or left in fear,” they said.Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership inEuropealthough violent shootings are rare and it approved tighter gun control rules in 2019.The text of this article was amended on 30 August 2026. Aarau is west of Zurich rather than north, as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsSwitzerlandEuropeGun crimeItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaign   | Iceland | The Guardian
description: Well-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across Europe
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Well-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across Europe
Content: An EU flag at a gathering in Reykjavík on referendum night.Photograph: Marco Di Marco/APView image in fullscreenAn EU flag at a gathering in Reykjavík on referendum night.Photograph: Marco Di Marco/APIcelandIceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaignWell-funded no camp prevails, winning 52.8% of votes and gaining plaudits from Eurosceptic figures across EuropeAnalysis: Definitely no or maybe yes – what tipped the Icelandic referendumMiranda Bryantin ReykjavíkSun 30 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoters inIcelandhave ⁠rejected ⁠a government proposal ​to reopen ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU after a closely fought referendum campaign that divided the country against a backdrop of global volatility.After a long and anxious night for those on both sides of the debate, the no camp ended up with 52.8% of votes on Sunday morning and the yes camp with 47.2%. Voter turnout was high at 82.5%.The vote was held in the shadow of repeated threats by Donald Trump to invade or acquire neighbouring Greenland. Although Iceland is a Nato member, supporters of EU membership said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats towards the smaller, Arctic island.At a press conference the prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, said the campaign had “raised the debate in Iceland to a higher level” while acknowledging that there were aspects that “could have been done better”.View image in fullscreenKristrún Frostadóttir speaks to reporters on Sunday after the result.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersGiven how close the outcome was, she said, it was important to respect the views of yes voters. But she said: “It is quite clear that this matter will not move forward under this government.”She said the government would wait to decide on whether to submit a parliamentary resolution formally withdrawing its EU membership application. Iceland originally applied in 2009 after the financial crash but pulled out of talks in 2013, saying it could not go any further without a referendum.There will be disappointment in Brussels, which had been keen to welcome a wealthy new member and appeared willing to compromise with Iceland on thorny issues such as fishing to facilitate its accession.The yes campaign had argued that joining the EU could offer greater security amid war in Ukraine and the Middle East, and given the US president’s unpredictable attitude towards the Arctic.But the no campaigners’ warnings that EU membership would threaten the country’s sovereignty and fishing waters turned the vote in their favour.View image in fullscreenPeople wave an Icelandic flag at a referendum-night event organised by the no campaign.Photograph: Halldor Kolbeins/AFP/Getty ImagesTheir victory quickly attracted the attention of anti-EU leaders. The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen wrote on X: “At a time when some are pushing for greater federalism and the transfer of sovereignty to the European Commission, this vote reminds us that another Europe is possible, a Europe of free, sovereign nations cooperating voluntarily on matters of common interest.”Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, wrote: “Congratulations to Iceland on voting to keep their independence.”The ‌government in Reykjavík had framed its membership plan as a “now or never” moment, and Kristrún told voters earlier in August that a no vote would put all EU speculation aside.On Sunday, she told RUV that she hoped the vote would not leave the nation divided.Kristrún, who spoke at public meetings around the country in the final weeks in support of yes, said: “I don’t experience this as hurt. I know some people have been in a state of shock, but now I’ve sat with a large group of people across the country and people are completely open to different outcomes.”She acknowledged that many people in Iceland, particularly from rural areas, had concerns about the potential impact on agriculture, fisheries and natural resources of joining the EU. “I promise that we will handle these issues well and keep these concerns in mind,” she said.View image in fullscreenA boat leaving the harbour in Reykjavík on Sunday after the vote.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersThe vote exposed a stark divide between rural and urban areas, with the capital, Reykjavik, the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people where a majority supported yes.The government had pledged to hold a referendum on whether to reopen the accession talks when it came into office, with Kristrúntelling the Guardianat the time that it was a “necessary step forward”. After Trump renewed his threats to invade Greenland at the start of this year and amid a greater global focus on the Arctic, the government announced that the referendum would be brought forward.Hulda Þórisdóttir, a politics professor at the University of Iceland, said she was not surprised by the result given the tone of the latter stages of the campaign, with misinformation spreading and the considerably bigger financial resources of the no campaign.“No won due to a combination of factors: a strong feeling that the EEA [European Economic Area] is all we need, a sense of Icelandic exceptionalism, economic self-interest and a lot of misinformation among the least engaged – for example, ‘I don’t want my son to have to join the EU army,’” Hulda said. “But very importantly, it seems clear to me that the no campaign was much, much better funded.”Reaction from Brussels was muted. António Costa, the European Council president, told Kristrún on Sunday the bloc “fully respects the democratic choice” of the island’s voters not to resume EU membership talks, a spokesperson said. “Iceland remains one of the EU’s closest and most trusted partners,” said the spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsIcelandEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: US says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forces
Content: The islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). The strikes were the first known American attacks since July.Photograph: Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe islands of Hormuz (top), Larak (centre) and Qeshm (left). The strikes were the first known American attacks since July.Photograph: Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranUS strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in JordanUS says it attacked sites in Larak Island to prevent launch of sea mines, prompting Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guard to strike airbases in Jordan used by US forcesAgenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island,” a US official said on Sunday. “Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and ​would be met with a “response ‌and punishment” from ‌Tehran, Iranian state media reported.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreIn response, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.A spokesperson said the US would pay for the attack economically and militarily, according to the semi-official news agency Fars.Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US attack was ‌a drone strike.On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying that all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.The exchange of strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.The US said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway.Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening ​to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.The US andIsraelattacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now ⁠crossed its six-month mark.Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared“economic warfare” against Tehran.US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on ​Lebanon have killed thousands ​and displaced millions. Eighteen US service ​members have been killed in the conflict.The war has ​led to the ‌blockade of the ​strait of ​Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranIsraelStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnel  | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Total of 804 confirmed dead and more than 3,000 missing amid threat of fresh inundation
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Total of 804 confirmed dead and more than 3,000 missing amid threat of fresh inundation
Content: A woman carries belongings from her destroyed home in Devighat after the disaster in Nepal.Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman carries belongings from her destroyed home in Devighat after the disaster in Nepal.Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnelTotal of 804 confirmed dead and more than 3,000 missing amid threat of fresh inundation‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospitalAngelique Chrisafisand agenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 23.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescuers in Nepal andTibethave battled through leg-sucking mud amid the threat of fresh flooding to search for thousands of people still missing after a deadly wall of water swept through the Himalayan border zone, engulfing entire villages.The latest updates on Sunday put the number of missing at 3,048, including hundreds of foreigners. There was a total of 804 confirmed deaths acrossNepaland Tibet, and reports of some bodies swept downstream possibly as far as India.Nepal said it had begun the task of burying some of the hundreds of bodies after first taking DNA samples so that families could later reclaim them after identification and perform traditional funeral rites.The disaster, which struck the border on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse which sent a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said.Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the small, poor Himalayan nation was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said on Saturday.View image in fullscreenA vehicle drives past houses covered in mud in Baireni, in the Dhading district of Nepal.Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty ImagesMore than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Nepal said on Sunday that 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact in the country. It reported an updated death toll of 788 people.Chinese authorities on Sunday reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, of whom 261 were foreign nationals, including 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the US and 15 British citizens.In a breakthrough at the weekend, Nepal’s army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site, where more than 100 workers are believed to be trapped.The home minister, Sudan Gurung, said: “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside.”It is a race to reach the workers, who may still be alive inside the tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites. They are among 933 hydropower workers who are among the missing, according to Nepal’s disaster authority.View image in fullscreenSoldiers search for bodies as rescue operations shift into search and retrieval in Nepal.Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty ImagesNepal warned on Sunday of rising flood waters and urged rescue teams to exercise caution. “We have received information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa has increased further,” the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.Flood warnings were sent to people’s phones early on Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas hit by the floods.‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in NepalRead moreIn Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some people began returning to ruined homes to see what could be salvaged. Residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they had received since the initial floods.One resident, Govind Shreshta, told the Associated Press: “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain. It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mum. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”2:04‘I have lost everything’: survivors reflect after deadly flood in Nepal – videoThe government estimated Nepal’s reconstruction bill could run to billions of dollars.Officials in Nepal called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them in, saying bodies that had been in water could decompose at a faster rate.Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing. “All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told Agence France-Presse in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.”View image in fullscreenFirefighters conduct search and rescue operations along a river in Gyirong county in Tibet.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersIn Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake. A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area.In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning,desperately searchingfor news of missing loved ones.Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital noticeboard, clutching photographs and scanning lists of patients in the hope of finding them.Dil Maya Lama stood weeping near the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had travelled from Ramechhap, about 80 miles (130km) away.“I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she told the Associated Press. “There is no information about him.”Nelza Moktan sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa. “I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said.With Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaNatural disastersSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Rajendra Dawadi ordered students to higher ground with moments to spare after receiving warnings from upstream
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Rajendra Dawadi ordered students to higher ground with moments to spare after receiving warnings from upstream
Content: A mud-covered classroom at the Shree Bageshwori Madhyamik school, damaged in flash flooding in the Dhading district of Nepal.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APView image in fullscreenA mud-covered classroom at the Shree Bageshwori Madhyamik school, damaged in flash flooding in the Dhading district of Nepal.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APNepal-Tibet flood disasterHeadteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in NepalRajendra Dawadi ordered students to higher ground with moments to spare after receiving warnings from upstreamHarry CockburnSun 30 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA headteacher inNepalevacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way.Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream.Rajendra Dawadi, the headteacher of Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in NuwakotThis prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,”he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.”Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water.“If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.One student said Dawadi’s decision had saved their lives with moments to spare. Yunisha, 16, told reporters: “I, along with my friends, survived by just 10 seconds.”She described the children running up a muddy path to escape as water and debris inundated the town. “Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes,” she said. She was reunited with her family three days later.‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in NepalRead moreAt least 69 schools have been destroyed or damaged by the floods, affecting nearly 19,000 children, according to the charity Save the Children.In Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by the floods, a group of schoolchildren survived the disaster when they left their classroom for their lunch break.Others in the area escaped when teachers told them to quickly evacuate classrooms just before the waters came crashing in.The mother of one child told the Associated Press that teachers had warned students: “There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins. That’s how they managed to survive.”More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. The country said on Sunday 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people.The disaster, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region of the Himalayas on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris cascading downstream, the US Geological Survey said.Nepal’s foreign minister has called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the Nepali people had disproportionately become “major victims of climate change” despite having contributed a fraction of the planet’s fossil fuel emissions.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalNatural disastersSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifteen Britons among 261 foreigners missing in China after floods | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Total number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workers
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Total number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workers
Content: Chinese police take part in search and rescue operations near Gyirong port in Tibet on Sunday.Photograph: China Daily/ReutersView image in fullscreenChinese police take part in search and rescue operations near Gyirong port in Tibet on Sunday.Photograph: China Daily/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterFifteen Britons among 261 foreigners missing in China after floodsTotal number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workersRaphael BoydSun 30 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding inNepaland Tibet.Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border.‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in NepalRead moreThe 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons betweenTibetand Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US.Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border. Some were on a pilgrimage at the time of the flood, includingHemangini Jitendra Patel and Hema Sunil Amin, two sisters who were last seen on the Friendship Bridge on the border.The figure for missing Americans has been disputed by the US state department, which declared on Sunday that at least 85 US citizens were missing. The department’s spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said getting accurate information from the region had been difficult, “made even more so by the devastation and the remoteness that we see”.Chinese authorities have said at least 16 people have died on their side of the border. But there are concerns over a possible lack of transparency from the Chinese government, which has prevented footage of the floods from being shared in the country and may have downplayed the casualties.Police in Nepal said 794 people had been confirmed to have died there and at least 2,742 injured. Numerous areas remain at risk of fresh flooding and people who have returned to their homes have been told to remain alert and be prepared to evacuate again at short notice.View image in fullscreenArmy personnel conduct a search and rescue operation for flood victims along the Narayani River in Nepal’s Chitwan district on Sunday.Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty ImagesRescue efforts have been affected by the threat of landslides and dangerous weather as well as confusion over which side of the border victims had been on when the waters struck.Chinese state television reported that officials in Beijing, far better resourced than their Nepali counterparts, had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated more than 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts.Equipment and supplies have been airdropped to frontline workers, while Chinese soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing, CCTV said. The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had already travelled to the region.Numerous countries have pledged to help Nepal, including the US, which has offered $3.6m (£2.7m) in humanitarian aid, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households”, on top of $500,000 previously pledged, and Australia, which will donate more than $3m in assistance.Britain has committed £5m to Nepal and sent a rapid deployment team, which arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday.A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: “We are working around the clock to support British nationals and their families affected by the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border. We are coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities and have deployed consular support staff to the region to ensure British nationals can access support.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterTibetChinaNepalSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Relatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the dead
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Relatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the dead
Content: A Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianNepal-Tibet flood disasterDevastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homesRelatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the deadHannah Ellis-Petersenin DevighatSun 30 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys ofNepaland Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.Satellite image of Nepal showing location of DevighatDNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.Residents try to salvage belongings from their damaged homesIn an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.View image in fullscreenPeople searching for their belongings in their mud-damaged home in Devighat.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianEven in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnelRead moreThose who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.View image in fullscreenPeople in Devighat salvage what possessions they can from their damaged homes.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.View image in fullscreenMany returned to Devighat to pack up their belongings before leaving, never to return.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianIn the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsiaFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Number of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to 3,000 as bad weather hampers search | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Nepal requests foreign ⁠help in identification and storing of bodies, DNA testing and rescuing people from tunnels
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Nepal requests foreign ⁠help in identification and storing of bodies, DNA testing and rescuing people from tunnels
Content: Chinese crews conduct search and rescue operations in Gyirong, Tibet.Photograph: China News Service/GettyView image in fullscreenChinese crews conduct search and rescue operations in Gyirong, Tibet.Photograph: China News Service/GettyNepal-Tibet flood disasterNumber of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to 3,000 as bad weather hampers searchNepal requests foreign ⁠help in identification and storing of bodies, DNA testing and rescuing people from tunnelsVisual guide: how the deadly flooding unfoldedNew flood fears and a race to free group trapped in tunnelDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 29 Aug 2026 21.25 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 22.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePoor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal on Saturday as the search for thousands of missing people in areas devastated by catastrophic flash floods along the border withChinacontinued.The combined toll in Nepal andTibetrose to 691 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday.
