Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said late Saturday that the death toll had climbed to 675 with 2,498 people missing.‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in NepalRead moreMore than 3,700 people have been rescued inNepalso far.Seven bodies have also been recovered inIndiafrom rivers flowing from Nepal and are believed to be flood victims.The missing list includes 517 foreigners and 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.2:04‘I have lost everything’: survivors reflect after deadly flood in Nepal – videoA number of rescue workers are also missing, including 45 Nepali army soldiers and 40 police officers.When a Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time on Friday, they found “nothing but ruins”.Surveillance camera footage from the complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only ⁠on Friday were rescuers able to reach the area.Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign ⁠help in specialised and technical areas, but not in search and rescue. On ⁠Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage ​the rescue ​efforts on its own for ​now and declined foreign involvement.The areas in which Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing, rescuing people stuck in tunnels, and storing bodies for longer durations, the foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said late on Friday.View image in fullscreenPeople put up posters of missing family members at a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianKhanal said ​there was no ​need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.Nepal has requested that its neighbours, India and ​China, provide bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges have been destroyed.So far, India has sent three flights carrying about 60 tons of relief material to Nepal, including blankets, medicines, food and water purification tablets, ⁠and a specialised tunnel rescue team.China has also dispatched five tunnel experts from Tibet to Nepal for flood-related rescue work, Chinese state media reported, as the country called for emergency aid to be sent to disaster-hit areas and for international rescue cooperation.View image in fullscreenNepali army personnel rescue survivors from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPARescuers – including army personnel and police – have been clawing through mud and using drilling equipment to reach more than 100 people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa. More than 350 people have already been evacuated from the site under “extremely risky” conditions and the office of Nepal’s prime minister said the rescue effort had become “extremely challenging” due to adverse weather.Search and rescue operations were temporarily halted because of rain and fog but resumed on Saturday afternoon after the weather improved.Kawan Koirala, a rescue worker from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they had been struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud. “People want their family member’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them … you can see the mud,” he told Agence France-Presse, exhausted after an 18-hour shift.Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geohazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be ‌unstable and that more than 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.View image in fullscreenA woman salvages usable materials from her house deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: AFP/GettyIn Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of ​the highest national priority.In China,strict controls on the flow of informationfrom one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events. The BBC and New York Times have reported that videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s belt and road network linking the country to south Asia, with logistics zones and vehicle parks built there in the past decade.On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods – videoNepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, estimated the country will ⁠need $4-$5bn (£3-£3.7bn) for rebuilding. “This is just an ​estimate. Loss and ⁠damage is ​being assessed,” he ​said.More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.Some of the bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition and will need to be identified using DNA samples, Nepali officials have said.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaIndiaSouth and central AsiaNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’
Content: HMP Wormwood Scrubs in London. Offenders guilty of manslaughter, rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will not be eligible for early release.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHMP Wormwood Scrubs in London. Offenders guilty of manslaughter, rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will not be eligible for early release.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationPrisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release schemeCritics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 14.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention byAndy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were each jailed for 13 years over the killing of PC Harper, had been eligible for early release under the Sentencing Act until Burnham’s intervention.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PASpeaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?Read moreHarper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force,said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, butgovernment figuressuggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a reviewled by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for18% of those in prison.“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accusedLabourof avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationAndy BurnhamLabourUK criminal justiceCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Man killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tribute | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Robert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Robert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’
Content: Robert Guanco: ‘His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him,’ the church said.Photograph: gofundmeView image in fullscreenRobert Guanco: ‘His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him,’ the church said.Photograph: gofundmeWest SussexMan killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tributeRobert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’Harry CockburnSun 30 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 41-year-old manwho died after a large wooden sign fell at a Christian festival on Fridayhas been named as Robert Guanco, a pastor at a church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.A tribute from his church on Sunday described him as a respected pastor who was a “loving husband” and “a devoted and caring father”.Six other people were injured when the overhead sign fell at the Big Church festival (BCF) near Steyning in West Sussex, including four who were taken to hospital.Festivalgoers said they rushed to lift the heavy sign, which read “Everything’s Unmissable”, after it was blown over in the wind.Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne named Guanco, describing him as “our beloved brother, friend and pastor”, in a GoFundMe to help his family, who it said faced “unimaginable loss” following his death.It said: “Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love and his service to God will never be forgotten.”It added: “He was also a good friend, mentor and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers and encouragement, he touched many lives.“His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”View image in fullscreenOrganisers of the Big Church festival said they were ‘heartbroken’ by Guanco’s death.Photograph: BigchurchfestivalOrganisers of the BCF, billed as the UK’s biggest Christian festival, said they were “heartbroken” by Guanco’s death and cancelled the rest of the event.“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026, in which Pastor Robert Guanco tragically lost his life and others were injured,” they said in a statement.“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Particularly with the family, friends and church of Pastor Guanco as they process the immense grief of his loss.”They added: “We are working with the police, the Health and Safety Executive and others as they establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.”The festival opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday. The event, which includes worship, music and various performances, first took place in 2009.The archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” by the incident. “I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve,” she said. “I pray for those receiving treatment and the healthcare workers looking after them.“And I pray too for the other festivalgoers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.”Many people at the festival were first alerted to the tragedy when God TV announced that “due to unforeseen circumstances” the festival live stream had been paused.Sussex police’s Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said: “Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the man who died and all others who have been affected by this tragic incident.”He urged anyone among the “thousands of people” at the festival on Friday who had information or video footage to come forward.Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing | Far right (US) | The Guardian
description: ‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: ‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APFar right (US)‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for ReformHelena HortonSun 30 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump administration, the far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos may be wondering what lies ahead for him in his native country.The “alt-right” agitator, 41, made his name in the US by promoting Donald Trump and associating with his allies before the 2016 election.But now the Trump administration has unceremoniously dumped the former Breitbart News editorback in the UKafter he allegedly overstayed his visa. He has also made plenty of disparaging comments about the president, including that he is “firmly off the Trump train”.Those in the rightwing ecosystem in the UK say Yiannopoulos is now too extreme to find a prominent berth back home.The commentator started his career at the Daily Telegraph, where he wrote a controversial blog until 2011, when he started his own website, the Kernel. In 2014 he started working for the former Trump adviser Steve Bannon at Breitbart News, before moving to the US and promoting far-right causes.He left Breitbart after a controversy over a video in which he appeared tocondone sexual relationswith boys as young as 13. He later said “sloppy editing” and his “British sarcasm, provocation and gallows humour” had created the wrong impression and denied endorsing paedophilia.Since he left the UK,GB Newshas become the ascendant broadcast outlet of the right, but he is unlikely to find a place there. A source at the channel said: “We wouldn’t touch him with a barge pole, not in a million years. GBN had a few odd people to start with and we’ve got rid of them.”Yiannopoulos after his arrest by federal immigration agents in New Orleans.Photograph: Department of Homeland Security/ReutersOf the provocative positions that brought him notoriety in the US, the GB News source said: “He won’t make much money out of it here, he appeals entirely to an American audience. It’s a bigger country and you have a bigger pool of fruit loops.”There is a growing subsection of rightwing provocateurs in the UK who have been deemed too controversial for the main channels but have established niche brands of their own. The journalist Dan Woottonwas suspended from GB Newsafter a guest on his show made sexually inappropriate comments about a female journalist, andafter leavinghe now has his own channel.The former TalkTV host Mike Graham has also set up his own independent show. He wassackedafter the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on one of his social media accounts. Graham said the racist comment had been the result of his account being hacked.It is understood thatReform UKwill not accept him into its ranks. His former colleague at Breitbart, Raheem Kassam, is close to the party’s leader, Nigel Farage, and is in the UK for Reform’s national conference.Kassam, who is British but now lives in the US, claimed he was kept updated on the deportation of Yiannopoulos, who he accused of making “lurid and false accusations” against him.He added: “I got word last month that he was about to be deported. On Thursday night, I got a call. As overly dramatic as it may seem. ‘We got him. In Louisiana.’”The Maga influencer Laura Loomer has claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to immigration enforcement over his expired visa.View image in fullscreenLaura Loomer (front, centre) celebrates with Yiannopoulos at a congressional primary election night event in West Palm Beach, Florida, in August 2020.Photograph: Allen Eyestone/APOne political party that may accept Yiannopoulos isRestore Britain, which is led by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP who had a falling-out with Farage.Restore has accepted a number of characters viewed as too extreme for Reform, including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson.Yiannopoulos has praised Lowe, calling him “fantastic” and urging those on the UK hard-right to join Restore. He said “the rising generation of young British activists” all “support Restore” and has taunted Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, online, telling him “you’re gonna lose all your votes to Rupert”. The Guardian contacted Lowe to ask whether he would accept Yiannopoulos as a party member or adviser but did not receive a response.Kassam said: “He’s certain to resurface in Britain shortly. Perhaps as an adviser to Rupert Lowe, or perhaps as a contestant on some third-tier reality TV show.”Yiannopoulos used to have more political influence; he was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.He was deported to the UK on Friday, according to US authorities. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.In 2022, Yiannopoulosworked onKanye West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working one of the rapper’s companies.Last year, Yiannopoulossaidhe was “never going back home” because the UK needed a “mass deportation programme”.Yiannopoulos was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFar right (US)US immigrationFar rightGB NewsReform UKRestore BritainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayor | James Cleverly | The Guardian
description: Conservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Conservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’
Content: James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to stand for mayor of London.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenJames Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to stand for mayor of London.Photograph: James Manning/PAJames CleverlyCleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayorConservative hopeful says Sadiq Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Andy Burnham is ‘very anti-London’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 30 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJames Cleverly has pledged to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting that his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister.The former home and foreign secretary denied he had resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership.However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture war issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader.“I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor ofLondon, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio.“That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.”If he wins his party’s nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the last Tory candidate, Susan Hall. Shedrew criticismfor claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to getLondonback.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote.Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift and said he thought it unlikely the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said.Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to Cleverly’s2024 speechduring the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” Dilnot said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”View image in fullscreenSadiq Khan (centre) stacks shelves in a Sainsbury’s in London with Andy Burnham, the prime minister, and Pat McFadden, work and pensions secretary.Photograph: WPA/GettyProf Tony Travers, of the London School of Economics, said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” Travers said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe entrance of a Conservative big-hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan, who was first elected in 2016, will run for a fourth term, a question he has thus far avoided.AYouGov survey this monthfound that 56% of Londoners thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found that Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while other potential candidates in the Labour ranks include Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.“Andy Burnham just doesn’t get it,” he said. “He’s got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner.”Explore more on these topicsJames CleverlyMayoral electionsConservativesLocal governmentLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Recruiter places ‘phoenix’ firm into liquidation just months after repurchase erased millions in debt | Business | The Guardian
description: New company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administrator
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: New company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administrator
Content: PRG went into administration last September owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyView image in fullscreenPRG went into administration last September owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyBusinessRecruiter places ‘phoenix’ firm into liquidation just months after repurchase erased millions in debtNew company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administratorSimon GoodleySun 30 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA recruitment executive who was allowed to buy back the assets of his bust company in instalments, despite it accumulating almost £3m of debt, has placed his new business into liquidation after falling behind with promised payments to the administrator.The news is the latest event to raise questions about the practice of “phoenixism”, accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts.The tactic, which is legal, is often justified by supporters who argue it can save jobs and help secure some returns for creditors – although HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) estimates it costs the UK taxpayer hundreds of millions of pounds a year.Premier Group Recruitment went into administrationin September 2025 owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HMRC, which had begun enforcement proceedings against the company.The recruiter’s assets were acquired three days later by a new company, PGGBR Ltd, founded by Andrew Woosnam, Premier’s 99% shareholder, who made an initial £10,000 payment and promised to transfer a further £600,000 via monthly £25,000 instalments over the following two years.Despite a seemingly positive start for the new business – which offered its consultants an “all expenses paid”trip to Las Vegas for hitting their targets– the company quickly fell behind with its promised repayments, causing the administrators tofile an updateon its struggles with Companies House in March.On Sunday,filings at Companies House said PGGBR had appointed a voluntary liquidator.Woosnam, who had received a £1.2m director’s loan from the defunct Premier and had taken dividends out of the company totalling almost £2m since 2022, is also understood to have made a series of redundancies at the new business in July that industry sources said equated to at least half his staff. The company’s website, which now appears to have been taken down, listed a management team of 12 people.Sources with knowledge of the job losses also suggested that those affected had not been paid and that Woosnam was planning to launch another new company to take his recruitment business forward.Companies House records show that in June the businessman changed the name of a business he founded a year ago from PGUSA to PGREC.The problems at Premier chime with long-running questions concerning the efficacy of allowing connected parties to buy back their bust businesses by promising future payments – deferred considerations, in the industry jargon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResearch has suggested that poorer outcomes tend to occur in insolvencies where the assets are acquired by connected parties paying via future instalments.For example, research by the University of Wolverhampton, for theUK government’s 2014 Graham review, concluded: “The failure rate of a connected party sale increases from 15% of all cases without deferred consideration to 37% when deferred consideration is introduced. Generally, when deferred consideration is present, whether or not a connected sale is also present, the failure rate rises considerably.”Similar results were published bya 2018 studyfunded by the EU. It concluded: “When the sale was to connected purchasers, there was a significantly higher risk of buyer mortality.”Woosnam has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsBusinessAccountancyCorporate governanceHMRCnewsShareReuse this content

title: USDA reportedly shelves cyclospora research amid relocations and fund cuts | Cyclosporiasis outbreak (US) | The Guardian
description: Trump officials shuttering three projects on foodborne parasite, two defunded by Congress, Politico reports
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump officials shuttering three projects on foodborne parasite, two defunded by Congress, Politico reports
Content: Two projects were defunded earlier this year, and the third is ⁠due to be moved from Maryland to Iowa amid a broader USDA reorganization, Politico reports.Photograph: J David Ake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTwo projects were defunded earlier this year, and the third is ⁠due to be moved from Maryland to Iowa amid a broader USDA reorganization, Politico reports.Photograph: J David Ake/Getty ImagesCyclosporiasis outbreak (US)USDA reportedly shelves cyclospora research amid relocations and fund cutsTrump officials shuttering three projects on foodborne parasite, two defunded by Congress, Politico reportsReutersSun 30 Aug 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationis shuttering ⁠two of the three US Department of Agriculture research projects studyingcyclosporaafter the foodborne parasite has ⁠sickened tens of thousands of Americans during the summer, Politicoreportedon Sunday.The two projects were defunded byCongressearlier in the year, while the third is ⁠due to be moved in coming months from Maryland to Iowa as part of a broader USDA reorganization, according to the ⁠report.Although the third project remains funded, all scientists working on the ​parasite have declined to relocate ‌to Iowa, Politico reported, citing ‌people familiar with the plans and internal documents.US law to investigate foodborne illness outbreaks has been delayed for 15 yearsRead moreReuters could not immediately ‌verify the report.“None of the research has been disrupted, and research will continue without disruption,” a USDA spokesperson said, while pointing to Congress over the funding cuts.Congress did not appropriate funding for the two research projects that were being undertaken at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center ‌outside Washington DC for the 2026 fiscal year in the Agriculture Appropriations Act, the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The spokesperson ​added that the Agricultural Research Service is working with research leaders to ensure an orderly transition of the programs.Scientists researching foodborne parasites, including cyclospora, are retiring or leaving the USDA’s ARS rather than relocating or being reassigned to ⁠other projects, the report said.The Centers for Disease ​Control and Prevention has​recordedmore than 17,000 confirmedcyclosporiasis casesacross 48 states ​plus Washington DC, from 1 May to 24 August, making ​it one ​of the largest foodborne illness outbreaks in recent US history.At least 11,844 additional cases may require further investigation and analysis, the CDC said.Explore more on these topicsCyclosporiasis outbreak (US)Trump administrationFood safetyUS CongressUS politicsMedical researchnewsShareReuse this content

title: All-time great Aaron Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin stacked LA Rams | Los Angeles Rams | The Guardian
description: Aaron Donald, one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams
Author: Tom Lutz
Headline: Aaron Donald, one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams
Content: Aaron Donald played 10 seasons for the Rams before his initial retirement.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APView image in fullscreenAaron Donald played 10 seasons for the Rams before his initial retirement.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APLos Angeles RamsAll-time great Aaron Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin stacked LA RamsLos Angeles were already Super Bowl favoritesDefensive tackle was 10-time Pro Bowler with Rams35-year-old aiming to win second Super Bowl in LATom LutzSun 30 Aug 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAaron Donald, one of thegreatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams.During a 10-season career with the Rams, who drafted him with the 13th overall pick in 2014, Donald was a three-time defensive player of the year and an eight-time first team All-Pro. Hewon a Super Bowl with the Ramsat the end of the 2021 season beforeannouncing his retirement in March 2024at the age of 32.Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI saysRead moreThe 35-year-old returns to a stacked Rams roster who were already betting favorites to win the Super Bowl this season. The team includes reigning MVP Matthew Stafford at quarterback and the reigning defensive player of the year, Myles Garrett, who Los Angeles acquired in a tradewith the Cleveland Browns in June.ESPN reportsthat Donald will earn $20m in his one-year deal, which could rise to $30m with bonuses.Rumors had circulated that Donald would return after the trade for Garrett. Rams head coach Sean McVay had undergone a “very strict, regimented process that was similar to what he did when he played” to see if he was still able to play in theNFL. McVay said the 10-time Pro Bowler had been “outstanding” during a workout with the Rams this summer.If Donald can replicate anything close to the form he showed during his peak – when he was arguably the greatest defensive tackle of all time – he will form part of a formidable line with Garrett, who set the NFL single-season sack record in 2025.Donald, who was listed at 6ft 1in and 280 lbs when he retired, is small for a defensive tackle but during his first spell with the Rams he made up for his lack of size with his extraordinary athleticism and work rate. He ended his career with a franchise record 111 sacks.If the Rams do reach the Super Bowl this season, they will play on home turf at SoFi Stadium, the venue for their championship victory in February 2022. The Rams start their season on 10 September against their NFC West rivals, the San Francisco 49ers.Explore more on these topicsLos Angeles RamsNFLWest CoastUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ‘border czar’ denies Milo Yiannopoulos was deported quickly to spare him from ICE detention | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Tom Homan denies British far-right commentator, who was deported one day after arrest, got preferential treatment
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Tom Homan denies British far-right commentator, who was deported one day after arrest, got preferential treatment
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos pauses while speaking during a news conference in New York in February 2017.Photograph: Mary Altaffer/APView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos pauses while speaking during a news conference in New York in February 2017.Photograph: Mary Altaffer/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump ‘border czar’ denies Milo Yiannopoulos was deported quickly to spare him from ICE detentionTom Homan denies British far-right commentator, who was deported one day after arrest, got preferential treatmentEdward HelmoreSun 30 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House “border czar,” Tom Homan, denied on Sunday thatdeportingBritish far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment.Homan said it was his understanding that Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July.“He didn’t show up,” Homantold CNN’s State of the Union.“The judge ordered him deported. So, once ICE gets an order of deportation from a federal judge, their job is to execute that order, and that’s what they did.”Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UKRead moreHe added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.”Yiannopoulos’s removal one day after his arrest, when many others who have been deported had first endured lengthy detention center incarcerations, has prompted questions about whether he received preferential treatment in that respect. Homan said the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, was trying to speed up the deportation process.“Once a judge orders them out, rather than being in detention, waiting for travel documents and flight arrangements, we – ICE, along with the [border patrol] and [DHS] – [are] working really good on the efficiencies of the removal process,” Homan remarked.He continued: “As soon as we get an order removal, our goal is remove them as quick as possible, regardless of who they are. Get them out quick. Open those beds up for more detainees.”DHS had quickly publicized Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Thursday at an airport in New Orleans – where he may have travelled to attend a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West, on Friday at the city’s Caesars Superdome.Officials with DHS touted Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Friday. By Saturday morning, Yiannopoulos’s name was removed from a list of people in ICE detention, and DHS confirmed that he had been deported to the UK on Friday – one day after his arrest.“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a DHS release said, adding “The administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wingRead moreCNN host Dana Bash asked Homan if the rightwing influencer Laura Loomer had, as she claimed, tipped off ICE that Yiannopoulos’s permission to be in the US had expired.“A lot of people tipped ICE off,” Homan replied. “There are a lot of people who’s calling ICE, and she says she’s one of them. She probably was.“But bottom line is, it doesn’t matter. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge, and ICE’s job it to execute that order.”Loomer and Yiannopoulos – who had sanguinely cheered the Trump administration’s deportation efforts before his expulsion from the US – had publicly fallen out.Homan, meanwhile, denied that the Trump administration had made an example of Yiannopoulos to send a message. “We don’t deport people based on political affiliation,” he said.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS immigrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face ‘punishment’ from FCC | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Trump’s threat comes after host described success record of candidates whom president had endorsed as ‘mixed’
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Trump’s threat comes after host described success record of candidates whom president had endorsed as ‘mixed’
Content: NBC News’s Meet the Press host Kristen Welker.Photograph: Jim Bourg/ReutersView image in fullscreenNBC News’s Meet the Press host Kristen Welker.Photograph: Jim Bourg/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump says NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face ‘punishment’ from FCCTrump’s threat comes after host described success record of candidates whom president had endorsed as ‘mixed’Edward HelmoreSun 30 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump⁠on Sunday saidNBC’s Kristen ‌Welker – host of Meet the Press – should face “rebuke or punishment” from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).Welker, during a live segment for a local Washington, DC, affiliate, described the success record of political candidates whom the president had endorsed as “mixed”. The segment aired prior to Sunday’s edition of Meet the Press.Trump “is going to loom large over these midterms,” Welker remarked on that live shot. “He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries. He’s had some mixed results.”But Welker went on to mention Trump’s endorsement of appointed interim US senator Darline Graham, sister of her late predecessor Lindsey Graham, who was successful in her primary battle.Nonetheless, the president then took verbal aim at Welker with a social media post deriding her as the “Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of … Meet the Fake Press,” accused her of “purposeful inaccuracy” and warned that she would “be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”.The post also said that Trump hoped his appointed FCC chair Brendan Carr – and Carr’s colleagues on the commission – “take this Threat to our Country very seriously”.Once Meet the Press actually started on Sunday, a guest analyst on the showsaid“the single most important factor in who the Republican nominee will be in [the presidential election of] 2028 will be who Donald Trump endorses”.Trump is estimated to have made more than 300 endorsements that resulted in the recipient winning. In the election cycle leading up to November’s midterms, 214 of the 218 House candidates he endorsed winning their primaries, including all 24 Republican senate primaries.Meanwhile, in gubernatorial primaries, five of the 21 candidates he endorsed lost their primaries, among them Mike Lindell – who finished a distant second in Minnesota to state house speaker Lisa Demuth.The state’s supreme court on Saturday effectively confirmed Lindell’s 11-percentage-point defeat by rejecting his bid for a recount.“My Endorsements are stronger than ever,” Trump nonethelessmaintainedin a 23 August social media post. “There has never been anything close!”When taking aim at Welker on Sunday, beside touting Darline Graham’s victory, he mentioned Oklahoma gubernatorial hopeful Mike Mazzei’s Republican primary win.He had said days earlier that any of his endorsed candidates who lost were already faced with “impossible” races – but they had earned his support “out of loyalty”.How much power Trump’s endorsement carries has been a touchy issue for the president. On Friday, HBO Max talkshow host Bill Maher apologized to Trump for claiming that the president is winning “almost none of” his endorsements. Trump had sent Maher statistics making the president’s case that the talkshow host was wrong.Welker and Trump have a contentious relationship. In June, hewalkedout of an hour-long interview with the host after being asked, among other unpleasant topics for him, about having pledged “no new wars” during his successful run for a second presidency.He started war in Iran in late February alongside Israel, and Trump denied guaranteeing there would no wars if he were returned to the Oval Office.“You’re a one-sided crooked network,” Trump said at the time. “Let’s call it quits because I’ve had enough. Thank you, darling. Have a good time.”He added: “You ought to straighten out your press. A country can never be great with a dishonest press.”NBC on Sunday issued a statement saying: “Kristen is one of the best in the business, and we stand by her.”NBC News on 19 August hadpublished an article examining Trump’s endorsement record,saying in the story’s headline that the president’s “endorsement record takes a hit at the end of primary season”.Trump’s comments on Sunday about Welker were only the latest instance of him or his administration seeking to bring the weight of the FCC down on media outlets with whom he has become cross.In September 2025, Carr – appointed by Trump – reportedly put pressure on television station groups to pre-empt Jimmy Kimmel’s show as punishment for a comment that the ABC host, a frequent critic of the president, made in the wake of the assassination of conservative influencer Charlie Kirk. Two conservative-friendly broadcast groups, Sinclair and Nexstar,did so. And ABC opted to “indefinitely”pullKimmel’s show before he ultimately returned to the air a week later.Trump has also won private settlements from ABC and CBS totaling more than $30m during his second presidency.Earlier in August,ABC sued the FCC, arguing that it was being illegally targeted by the regulator after being forced to apply early to renew its eight local broadcast licenses. Among Republicans’ complaints about ABC are that its candidates are not given equal airtime on the daytime talkshow The View.“Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the network said in its lawsuit.NBC is licensed by the FCC to directly operate 11 local stations.Involving itself in broadcast outlets’ editorial decisions and constitutionally protected speech is beyond the mandate of the FCC, which was established in 1934.CNN media reporter and commentator Brian Stelter, who on Sunday first found the clip of Welker mentioning Trump’s “mixed record”,wrotethat the FCC “can’t punish Welker” because it has “limited power … by design”.But Stelter noted that Carr has been “responsive” to Trump in the past – and “it’s reasonable to think NBC will be targeted next”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpNBCUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroad | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: Some young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countries
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: Some young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countries
Content: Arianna Marie and Zwiwe Dlamini teach English in South Korea.Photograph: Courtesy Arianna Marie and Zwiwe DlaminiView image in fullscreenArianna Marie and Zwiwe Dlamini teach English in South Korea.Photograph: Courtesy Arianna Marie and Zwiwe DlaminiWork & careersMeet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroadSome young people are teaching in countries like South Korea as education funding is gutted and recent grads face a tough job market in their own countriesJenna ZazaSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA year ago, Arianna Marie, 25, was struggling to control the students in her Florida elementary school classroom.She was living with her parents to save on rent and quickly feeling her passion for teaching dry up, even though it was her first job since graduation.“I was extremely burnt out,” Marie said. “We had a teacher shortage, so all of my classes were overcrowded.”When her district wanted to transfer her to a new school, she looked for opportunities abroad. Through an English-language teaching job inSouth Korea, Marie is now living in Daegu, a city in the south-eastern part of the country, with enough pay and benefits that she can save and travel.How to find a career you love – for gen Z and everyone else: ‘You don’t want your life’s compass to be dread’Read moreThe fact that it’s the home to K-pop and K-dramas doesn’t hurt – and in a striking shift, she’s rediscovered her love for the job. “I never have to crack down on behavior issues, and both students and teachers respect me so much,” Marie said. “I actually get to focus solely on teaching.”Marie is part of a program by the South Korean government that is placing native English speakers with a college degree and Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) certificates with local public schools, as itincreases spendingon education. Benefits include free housing, flight reimbursements, healthcare and monthly salariesstarting at about $1,400.Graduating with a college degree in the US no longer comes with the stability it once guaranteed. Since the Covid pandemic, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has beenhigherthan the overall unemployment rate.For those who have a job, earnings have beenrising slowerthan the pace of inflation. New entrants in US public service jobs like teaching areincreasingly leaving the profession, citing low pay and high stress.Other countries, including Japan and Taiwan, are similarly investing in full-time English-language teachers, attracting young workers with benefits they would be hard-pressed to find in their home countries.Gen Z is spreading the word. Some English-language teachers have garnered thousands of followers onTikTokandInstagram, showing audiences their lives abroad. Marie has been keeping track of her travels, and documenting some of her classroom experiences, on herInstagram account.The TEFL Institute, which issues TEFL certification courses that accredit English-language teachers, notes that the English-language teaching market wasvaluedat $95bn in 2026, with more than 2m TEFL jobs available worldwide. The market is expected to reach $181bn by 2034, and the Asia-Pacific region isgrowingthe fastest.View image in fullscreenArianna Marie.Photograph: Courtesy of Arianna MarieAs the US federal government hasguttedthe Department of Education, American public school teachers, who areoverwhelmingly female, are especially feeling the pull to overseas jobs.But the phenomenon isn’t exclusive to Americans, or teachers. Zwiwe Dlamini, 28, was spiraling into a deep depression working as an administrative assistant in Durban,South Africa.“I’ve always been behind the desk, gathering minutes, gathering meetings, working for CEOs and it was just extremely draining,” Dlamini said.Though she knew that finding a better job at home would be difficult – the youth unemployment rate in South Africa isnotoriously high, at almost 70% – Dlamini still quit her job. After six months of job searching, she knew she would have to look elsewhere.After she applied to the same program as Marie, she ended up in Incheon, the north-west South Korean city, as an English-language teacher. The free housing and low monthly expenses have allowed her to start paying off her debt while having enough savings to travel and plan for a master’s degree.“One year ago, [I] could not have imagined the position I am in today,” Dlamini said. “I couldn’t afford food and had [accumulated] debt, so paying it off now and still [experiencing] life to the fullest – I am actually so grateful.”View image in fullscreenZwiwe Dlamini.Photograph: Courtesy of Zwiwe DlaminiJohn Bentley, co-founder of the International TEFL Academy, which offers TEFL certification courses, noted that interest in teaching English abroad particularly soared after the 2024 presidential election.“With a difficult political and economic situation, we see gen Z turning to TEFL,” he said. “A lot of people go with the intention of staying for just one year. What happens is they fall in love with the country or experience and stay three [or] four years, or even much longer.”This tracks with a broader trend of Americans who increasingly say that they want to migrate. Last year, a Gallup pollfoundthat 40% of US women said they would move abroad if given the chance.Marie said her South Korean classroom, which she shares with another teacher, is worlds apart from her former classroom in Florida, where she would handle more than 20 kids on her own.“We always say that teaching is extremely undervalued in the US, but here you can tell how much they do value it,” she said. “The students are more receptive when I correct them and have so much respect for me as a teacher.”Explore more on these topicsWork & careersUS work & careersYoung peopleSouth KoreaUS personal financeTeacher shortagesTeachingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Content: The OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AIGene MarksSmall business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what worksSun 30 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTShareOne thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many casessquandered– by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.An AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene MarksRead moreWhat works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.Small businesses are watching. And now doing.A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.Big companies have also begun to discover theastronomical computingcosts that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companiesthrow away billonson large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.For months, onearnings callsand investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring,only to hirethose same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman,recently admittedthat their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)US small businesscommentShareReuse this content
