title: Chelsea hold off Brighton in 4-3 win but remain chaotic under Xabi Alonso | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Cole Palmer eventually made the home win safe after Brighton rallied from 3-0 down, with João Pedro scoring at both ends
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Cole Palmer eventually made the home win safe after Brighton rallied from 3-0 down, with João Pedro scoring at both ends
Content: Cole Palmer (right) continued his fine start to the season with what proved to be a vital fourth goal for Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersView image in fullscreenCole Palmer (right) continued his fine start to the season with what proved to be a vital fourth goal for Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersPremier LeagueChelsea hold off Brighton in 4-3 win but remain chaotic under Xabi AlonsoJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeSun 30 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the fullness of timeChelsea’s surrender against Brighton in Aprilmay be seen as the turning point. The humiliation accelerated Liam ­Rosenior’s demise and forced the Stamford Bridge hierarchy into a ­reckoning leading to the appointment of Xabi Alonso, a shift in ­transfer ­strategy, the birth of the JP Morgan front three and the end of ­Robert Sánchez’s time in goal.For now, though, the argument that Emiliano Martínez is the final piece in the jigsaw seems a touch ­premature. With seven goals scored and five conceded while winning their first two league games, it is not hard to see whereChelseaneed to improve in order to sustain a title challenge. They have to be savvier when ahead, and although the good has so far outweighed the bad Alonso could do with his side not dropping their guard when they have the ­opposition on the ropes.Alonso’s cool disappeared as ­Chelsea’s focus dipped after they went 3-0 up against an injury‑hit Brighton inside 32 minutes. ­Stamford Bridge was anxious when a João Pedro own‑goal cut the ­advantage to one just after the hour. Alonso was ­shouting at his bench and it was only when Cole Palmer scored with 16 minutes left that calm was restored.View image in fullscreenXabi Alonso has won his first two league games as Chelsea manager, but neither have been what you would call relaxing.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersNot for long, mind you, given that Brighton still managed to grab a consolation through Pascal Gross deep into added time.It was that kind of game, Martínez conceding three despite playing well on his debut after joining from Aston Villa for £7.5m. “We can hurt teams,” the Argentina goalkeeper said. “At the back, we need to bring the goals down.”Alonso agreed. Chelsea have been thrilling in transition – they beat Fulham with 37% possession last Monday and had only 26% against Brighton – but they must tighten up when they visit Arsenal next Sunday.Equally, few sights will be more captivating this season than Palmer combining with João Pedro and ­Morgan Rogers in attack. Palmer looks refreshed after a summer off and Chelsea will be dangerous when games turn into shootouts. They have so many ways to score. The hope is that there will be more stability with Martínez in position.Alonso did not hesitate to start Martínez, even though the ­Argentinian lacks match ­practice and joined on Friday. “He felt ready,” Alonso said of Martínez, the first 30‑something player to start for ­Chelsea since ­Thiago Silva in May 2024. “We will feel his ­presence because he has this charisma, this aura to influence.”Chelsea, again in a 3-4-2-1 system, are getting serious. Sánchez was not even on the bench against his old side and needs to leave. There was a huge ovation for Martínez before kick‑off and it was followed by the focus switching to Brighton’s No 1 in the fourth minute, a handling error from Bart Verbruggen allowing Roméo Lavia to put Chelsea ahead after Mats Wieffer had cleared a João Pedro header off the line from a corner.It was a lovely moment for Lavia. It was four years to the day since the Belgian’s last goal, against Chelsea coincidentally enough. His luck with injuries is hopefully turning.View image in fullscreenRoméo Lavia was on hand to punish Bart Verbruggen’s early handling error and put Chelsea 1-0 up.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesLavia starting his second consecutive league game was important with Chelsea light in midfield. Moisés Caicedo limped off after coming on in the second half, Reece James started on the bench and Enzo ­Fernández was off ­pining for a move to ­Manchester City, so Malo Gusto moved in from right wing-back to partner Lavia.Chelsea’s selection issues were nothing compared to Brighton’s problems, though. Fabian Hürzeler did not use the absence of Jack Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Georginio Rutter, Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh as an excuse, but it had an impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea were rampant. Rogers ­continued his fine start after joining from Villa, creating the second goal with a powerful surge away from Luka Vuskovic in the 14th ­minute. Brighton were caught cold by a throw‑in and Rogers crossed for Pedro Neto to score.Linked with a move away this summer, Neto has been repurposed by Alonso as a wing-back and was bright. João Pedro missed a chance after strong pressing from the ­Portugal international. The away end jeered but João Pedro converted his next opportunity, when a Rogers flick sent Jorrel Hato flying down the left to set the former Brighton striker up.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro rather summed up Chelsea’s start under Xabi Alonso with a goal, an assist and an own goal.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesChelsea’s mistake was thinking it was over. Brighton responded before half‑time, Malick Yalcouyé ­volleying in after Martínez made a brave block from ­Charalampos ­Kostoulas. “They showed belief in their quality,” ­Hürzeler said of his players.The German thought Brighton deserved more. Chelsea were wobbling when João Pedro diverted a Gross cross past Martínez. Diego Gómez then lashed a shot wide and Martínez denied Olivier Boscagli the equaliser.Alonso needed his big players to step up. Palmer, who had earlier sidefooted over from close range, delivered when he took a João Pedro flick and bent a shot past Verbruggen. Chelsea will be anything but dull.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueChelseaBrighton & Hove Albionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Calvert-Lewin cancels out Schade’s opener as Leeds salvage point against Brentford | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Dominic Calvert-Lewin rescued a point for Leeds in a 1-1 draw at Elland Road after Kevin Schade’s clever finish had given Brentford a first-half lead
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Dominic Calvert-Lewin rescued a point for Leeds in a 1-1 draw at Elland Road after Kevin Schade’s clever finish had given Brentford a first-half lead
Content: Dominic Calvert-Lewin is in the right place at the right time to steer the ball into the net.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin is in the right place at the right time to steer the ball into the net.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueCalvert-Lewin cancels out Schade’s opener as Leeds salvage point against BrentfordAaron Bowerat Elland RoadSun 30 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese nascent moments of the new season can often provide false hope but, as both sets of players shook hands after what was indisputably the correct result at Elland Road, it was difficult not to imagine we had just witnessed a contest between two sides that should have lofty ­ambitions for the months ahead.Leeds andBrentfordwere vic­torious on the opening weekend in differing circumstances. Leeds crafted a hard-earned but ultimately deserved win at Nottingham Forest, while Brentford Tottenham. Time will tell what the ceiling of both these sides is but, as they each continued their unbeaten starts here, hopes should be high.This was a thoroughly ­entertaining game but it was also an occasion in which both managers, as well as the players, displayed their importance to their respective clubs.Managers are scrutinised at every turn but Daniel Farke and Keith Andrews both excelled here. Both have had question marks as to whether they were the right man to take their team forward: Andrews when he was surprisingly appointed just over a year ago, and Farke in the difficult early stages of last season.Andrews’s tactical nous was at its peak in the first half. He nullified the Leeds back five and his team led at half-time and probably should have been more than a single goal in front. Kevin Schade’s wonderful flick to turn home a Keane Lewis-Potter cross was the least the visitors deserved.However, Farke showed his own tactical flexibility at the break. The German was under immense pressure last November and at real risk of losing his job before a move to a back five away at Manchester City proved the catalyst to transform Leeds’s season. He did the reverse here, going back to a four and matching Brentford in the second half to great effect.Spearheaded by the impact of Ao Tanaka and Lukas Nmecha, both on as substitutes, the hosts were the stronger of the two sides after half‑time. They ultimately got the equaliser their play deserved when ­Nmecha’s shot across goal was prodded home by Dominic Calvert-Lewin to ensure it would be a point apiece, and four from the first two for both sides.The early evidence overall? Leeds and Brentford should both be ­looking upwards this season. “It’s definitely a good point,” Farke said. “It was a very difficult and complicated game like we expected. Brentford were ­excellent in the first half and deserved to be in the lead, but I’m so proud of our reaction.”His side struggled to get to grips with Brentford’s shape in the first half. Ethan Ampadu and Anton Stach were overrun in midfield, with the visitors’ three of Vitaly Janelt, ­Mamadou ­Sangaré and ­Mikkel Damsgaard ­running riot. James ­Trafford was called into action on multiple occasions, with smart saves to deny Igor Thiago and Schade.Such was the strength of Brentford’s momentum that a goal felt inevitable. It duly arrived as half‑time approached when Lewis-Potter’s cross caught the Leeds backline off‑guard and Schade, with his back to goal, turned the ball home expertly to silence Elland Road.As mentioned, perhaps the ­biggest gripe at that stage was that ­Brentford’s lead wasn’t greater. “I thought we could have done more in the first half,” Andrews said.“We could have tested Trafford more but we were outstanding. The storm was always going to come and they were forced into ­making changes they haven’t done for quite some time.”Those changes were pivotal. The back five was abandoned, with Leeds adding Tanaka as an extra man in midfield. It provided an instant impact, with the balance of play shifting the way of the hosts. James Justin forced a clever save from Caoimhín Kelleher before Dan James, on as a substitute, arguably could have done better after being set free on halfway.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn contrast, Brentford were struggling without as much space in the middle, with Igor Thiago cutting a slightly isolated and frustrated ­figure. The Leeds supporters, sensing the momentum was now with them, were beginning to come alive – as were their team. Just like in the first half, a goal was starting to feel more like an inevitability than a possibility.Farke tweaked things further, with ­Nmecha pro­viding direct support for Calvert‑Lewin, and the duo combined with 11 ­minutes ­remaining. Nmecha dragged a shot across goal to leave Kelleher flat‑footed, with Calvert‑Lewin ­poking into the empty net for his first of the season.A draw was the least Leeds deserved. Both sides showed their ambition by pushing for a winner, though they cancelled each other out in the final moments to underline further that these are two teams who should think positively about what lies ahead.Chelsea v Brighton, Leeds v Brentford, Sunderland v Fulham: Premier League – liveRead moreView image in fullscreenKevin Schade stretches to reach Keane Lewis-Potter’s cross and flicks the ball home with the outside of his boot.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLeeds UnitedBrentfordmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: European football: Bellingham sparks Real Madrid’s cruise to maintain perfect start | European club football | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid maintained their perfect start to the La Liga season by beating promoted Málaga 4-0, while in Italy Como won 2-1 at Napoli
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Real Madrid maintained their perfect start to the La Liga season by beating promoted Málaga 4-0, while in Italy Como won 2-1 at Napoli
Content: Jude Bellingham celebrates during Real Madrid’s win against Málaga in La Liga.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham celebrates during Real Madrid’s win against Málaga in La Liga.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersEuropean club footballEuropean football: Bellingham sparks Real Madrid’s cruise to maintain perfect startPromoted Málaga slump to 4-0 defeat at the BernabéuComo defeat Napoli; Jones makes Inter debut in winAgenciesSun 30 Aug 2026 17.19 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madridmaintained their perfect start to the season in La Liga with a comfortable 4-0 home ⁠win over promotedMálagaon Sunday, scoring three times inside 30 minutes before adding a late fourth.Jude Bellingham’s brilliant solo opener, an own ⁠goal by theMálagagoalkeeper, ⁠Alfonso Herrero, and ​a sharp Kylian Mbappé volley in effect settled the contest before half-time, with the substitute Arda Guler wrapping up the victory in added time at ⁠the Bernabéu.European football: Elversberg stun Leverkusen in dream Bundesliga debutRead moreThe win lifted Madrid to nine points from three matches, two clear of Atlético Madrid and Alavés. Barcelona, fourth on six points with a ⁠game in hand, host Rayo Vallecano on Monday.Bellingham opened the scoring in the 19th minute ‌with a superb burst through the middle, collecting a loose ball near the edge of the area, gliding past three defenders and firing low beneath Herrero. They ​doubled their lead seven minutes later after Herrero could only palm out Mbappé’s effort. Bellingham headed the rebound back towards goal and, as Herrero and a teammate collided while trying to clear, the ball ended up in the net.Mbappé then made it 3-0 in the 30th minute, meeting Trent Alexander-Arnold’s cross ⁠with a fine volley from the centre of the box. The second half drifted until Guler, shortly ​after coming on, started ‌and finished a ​slick move, feeding Vinícius Júnior before tapping in the Brazilian’s return pass to complete the rout.Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang scored for the third straight game asDeportivo La CoruñabeatValencia3-1. The former Arsenal and Chelsea forward, who joined Deportivo from Marseille in the off-season, scored his side’s second goal as the newly promoted side won for the first time this season.Napolisuffered a 2-1 defeat at home toComo⁠inSerie A, with all three goals coming in an entertaining opening half. Assane Diao looked the most threatening player in the opening stages ⁠and the winger was instrumental in the visitors’ 17th-minute opening goal. Diao went past ​Mathías Olivera on the right wing ‌and played a pass ‌across to Martin Baturina whose shot on the turn from close to the penalty ‌spot found the bottom corner of the net.View image in fullscreenTasos Douvikas scores Como’s second goal against Napoli.Photograph: Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNoa Lang missed an excellent chance to equalise, sending a header over from inside the six-yard box, beforeNapolidrew level on the half-hour mark. Rasmus Højlund collected a pass on the edge of the area and drilled the ball low into the far corner, but Como were back in front four minutes later when Napoli ​were caught napping at the back.André-Frank Zambo Anguissa underhit a pass back to Amir Rrahmani in his own box, allowing Baturina to nick the ball away. It fell to Tasos Douvikas and Como’s top scorer last season netted his second goal of this ⁠campaign.Hakan Calhanoglu’s early strike earnedIntera 1-0 win atCagliarias they continued a perfect start to their title defence. The Turkey midfielder guided home a first-time strike from the edge of the box after nine minutes to make it two goals in two games and set the tone for a first half dominated by the champions in Sardinia.Curtis Jonesmade his Inter debutfrom the bench in the second half, but Inter’s lack of composure in front of goal almost came back to bite them as Cagliari threatened a shock equaliser with a flurry of late chances.Paris Brunner netted a goal in each half asMonacobeat visiting ⁠Marseille2-0 to go top of Ligue 1 as the only team to win their first two games.Monaco ⁠took the lead in the 13th minute when the Marseille defence was caught ball-watching as Brunner leaped between two defenders ⁠to head home a cross from Aleksandr Golovin. Marseille controlled the ball for long ​spells but struggled to create ‌shots on target, with ‌their efforts often blocked by the home side’s resolute rearguard.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Timothy Weah came close ‌to equalising for the visitors in the 53rd minute with a powerful shot from a tight angle that hit the side netting. It was to prove a costly miss as Brunner latched on to a long ball a minute later, speeding away from the defence before nonchalantly cutting ‌inside and slotting the ball in at the far post to make it 2-0.Yuito Suzuki scored a hat-trick asFreiburgthumpedWerder Bremen4-1, whileSchalke’s first game back in ⁠the Bundesliga ended in a 3-0 defeat atAugsburgas they finished with 10 men.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballReal MadridMálagaDeportivo La CoruñaValenciaLa LigaNapolinewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve had a very hectic career’: Mario Balotelli on Italian football’s troubles and his future  | Mario Balotelli | The Guardian
description: Striker talks to Emanuele Giulianelli about life in the UAE, problems with the Azzurri and the ‘special feeling’ of playing for Manchester City
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Striker talks to Emanuele Giulianelli about life in the UAE, problems with the Azzurri and the ‘special feeling’ of playing for Manchester City
Content: Mario Balotelli plays alongside his brother Enock Barwuah at Al Ittifaqin the United Arab Emirates.Photograph: Marco Ravagli/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMario Balotelli plays alongside his brother Enock Barwuah at Al Ittifaqin the United Arab Emirates.Photograph: Marco Ravagli/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesMario BalotelliInterview‘I’ve had a very hectic career’: Mario Balotelli on Italian football’s troubles and his futureEmanuele GiulianelliStriker talks life in the UAE, problems with theAzzurriand ‘special feeling’ of playing for Manchester CitySun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 04.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenever the nameMario Balotelliis brought up, particularly in Italy, the conversation is almost inevitably laced with a sense of regret. There is that lingering “What if?”, a collective sigh over a player who possessed the raw, undeniable potential to be one of the best in the world, if only things had been different.Yet being in front of him, with a smile on his face, it becomes clear the 36-year-old striker has reached an unexpected level of wisdom and maturity, traits that shine through in his lucid analysis of Italian football’s current struggles and the vanishing street culture of the sport. As Balotelli reflects on what he would tell his adolescent self, there is also a distinct feeling that he has finally made peace with his own turbulent narrative, that he isn’t chasing the ghosts of unfulfilled expectations.Balotelli joined Al Ittifaq in the United Arab Emirates simply to enjoy the game, to find pure joy on the pitch, and to realise a long-held family dream of playing alongside his brother, Enock Barwuah. “To tell you the truth, it was an idea that came up more or less at the last minute,” he says. “The president wanted to meet me, and we talked. The project interested me. Everyone always says: ‘You go to Dubai for the money,’ but thank God, I’m not short of that. So, money wasn’t the only goal. The project was actually nice and competitive. I grew fond of the idea and decided to give it a try.”View image in fullscreenMario Balotelli signed for Al-Ittifaq in January 2026 on a two-and-a-half-year contract.Photograph: Al-IttifaqThe realities of playing in the Middle East present a stark contrast to Balotelli’s past experiences. “Infrastructure-wise, it’s very good. The stadiums are beautiful. The problem is the public: there’s no crowd, which is a bit sad,” he says. “The organisation is also lacking a bit, but I think they’ll improve on that with time. I’m talking about all the teams across the board.” On linking up with his sibling, he says: “It’s beautiful. Ever since we were little, we always said we’d play together one day. He’d always ask me: ‘If you play for Inter, Milan, or [Manchester] City, how can I play with you?’ I used to tell him that when I got older, I might play in a team of a slightly lower level and maybe they’d give us that opportunity. It’s always been a dream, and now it’s coming true.”Despite his new surroundings, Balotelli remains acutely aware of the deep-rooted problems plaguing football back home, particularly after Italy’s failure to qualify forthree successive World Cups. “The problems, in my opinion, are very simple,” he says. “I prefer to give practical explanations rather than technical ones, based on everyday life and what I see in Italy.“When we were little, we played hours and hours of football. I remember my mum getting mad at me because I’d stay out until it was too dark to see the ball. They’d threaten you that you couldn’t go out to play the next day. Now, when I walk around cities like Brescia, though I see it in other Italian cities too, the parks are empty. There’s no one around.”Balotelli continues: “Computers, phones, and PlayStations have ruined a lot. Above all, the parents’ mentality has changed. A seven‑year-old kid today might play football for two hours every three days. We had the same structured training sessions, plus three hours of playing at the park every day, which felt like fun but was actually extra training. I truly believe talents were born on the street and in the parks. You played a lot, learned a lot, and tested yourself against older kids. If you were good, they didn’t let you play with kids your age; they made you play with the older ones. Those were tests that served me well in the long run. Playing with people older than me has always been one of the most important things in my career.“Today, kids are on their phones. They feel like Ronaldinho because they watch his videos. I felt like Ronaldo because I could actually pull off the same tricks at the park. It’s very different.”Despite his pessimism over the state of Italian football, Balotelli, who earned 36 caps for theAzzurri, scoring 14 goals, remains confident of a bright future. “Yes, I think so for the upcoming generations,” he predicts. “Maybe not right away, but in the next two or three generations. It’s normal for a country to have downturns but then you bounce back. Spain, France, and Germany have all had them.”View image in fullscreenMario Balotelli has won 36 caps for the Italian national team – the last in September 2018 – scoring 14 goals.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APWhen it comes to the national team, it’s impossible to ignore Roberto Mancini,reappointed as head coachand someone who acted as a mentor for Balotelli, as well as a defining figure throughout his most successful years. “He texted me to wish me a happy birthday, and I joked with him, saying: ‘Look, I can still play!’” Balotelli reveals. “I’m very happy he’s back with the national team; I’m very fond of him and I wish him the best. In Italy, people tend to blame the coaches a lot but, honestly, the system should take more of the blame. It’s the truth that nobody wants to say.”As a curious footnote, the last time Balotelli played forItalywas on 7 September 2018, against Poland in Bologna. It also happened to be Mancini’s first competitive game in his first spell in charge of the national team. So, could Balotelli play for Italy under Mancini again? “If I keep scoring, yes,” he replies emphatically.Balotelli’s time in England remains a standout chapter in a career filled with highs and lows, especially the three years he had at Manchester City when he won the Premier League and FA Cup – under Mancini. “It remains one of the best memories of my career,” he says. “At that time, City wasn’t as renowned as it is today. We joined the team that took the first steps for City to become what it is today. That gives you a special feeling. It means a lot more, actually.”View image in fullscreenMario Balotelli had an eventful three years at Manchester City, where he won the Premier League and FA Cup.Photograph: Matthew Peters/Manchester United/Getty ImagesAs he navigates the twilight of his career, Balotelli’s focus is clear. “I’m feeling good,” he states. “I’m recovering from a slight leg issue but I’m training, and it’s going well. It’s hot, which makes it a bit difficult to give 100%, but if you pace yourself and use your head, you can manage to play quite well. The heat is definitely a drawback, however.“On the pitch I want to play as long as I feel good. Playing is what I love doing, so as long as my body doesn’t say: ‘Enough,’ I’ll keep going. Off the pitch, once I finish my career, I definitely want to manage my businesses and focus on my kids. I’d prefer tranquillity, though. I’ve had a very hectic career, so a sedentary lifestyle wouldn’t be a bad thing.”If Balotelli could offer one piece of advice to his 16-year-old self, what would it be? “I’d tell him not to make certain choices,” he says, “and to listen to certain people at specific times.”Explore more on these topicsMario BalotelliItalyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Carrick hails Manchester United’s grit after rout of Ipswich | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick praised his Manchester United players for bouncing back from their opening-day defeat at Hull to thrash Ipswich 5-2
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick praised his Manchester United players for bouncing back from their opening-day defeat at Hull to thrash Ipswich 5-2
Content: Bryan Mbeumo (right) celebrates with Harry Maguire (left) and other teammates after scoring Manchester United’s fifth goal.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBryan Mbeumo (right) celebrates with Harry Maguire (left) and other teammates after scoring Manchester United’s fifth goal.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedMichael Carrick hails Manchester United’s grit after rout of IpswichFernandes fires hat-trick as United enjoy home win‘The way they bounced back, that’s the biggest thing’Jamie Jacksonat Old TraffordSun 30 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA delighted Michael Carrick praised howManchester Unitedbounced back from the opening-weekend defeat at Hull with their 5-2 rout of Ipswich.Bruno Fernandes’s hat-trick, scored in the 40th, 61st and 68th minutes, ensured United’s comeback win after Leif Davis’s opener. A Jacob Greaves own goal after 56 minutes and Bryan Mbeumo’s 82nd-minute strike completed the home scoring, Chuka Akpom’s added-time finish giving Ipswich their second.Marcus Rashford’s Manchester United return feels like a marriage of convenience | Will UnwinRead moreThis was the first time United had scored five in the Premier League since the opening day of the 2021-22 season, a 5-1 home win over Leeds that also included a Fernandes hat-trick.Carrick was delighted by the manner of United’s reaction to last week’s disappointing 2-0 defeat at Hull. “It’s a week in football, isn’t it? The ups and downs,” said the manager. “The biggest pleasing thing was – we spoke about in the week, about dealing with setbacks if you want to be a successful team. Every team gets beat. You’ve got to deal with setbacks, whether that’s momentum in the game, whether that’s a goal, whether that’s losing a game or a run of games, whatever it may be. You’ve got to deal with the setback.“We spoke before about trying to overcome last week, and then we took a mini setback if you like, going a goal behind. But showing stubbornness, belief, confidence, and togetherness the boys showed at that stage – in a small part, because we’re so early in the season – I think that was really pleasing for me. The way they bounced back, that’s probably the biggest thing to take. There’s a lot of highlights, but that mentality was what we really relied on today.”Of Fernandes, who has led the side since January 2020, Carrick said: “He means a lot to us. He’s the captain, he’s been here for a good number of years now. He’s experienced a whole load of different emotions, different things. He’s got a lot of experience to pass on and show them the way a little bit, and lead by example, help in different moments.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Times like today – when you’re looking towards certain players to give us that little bit of something, and he did that particularly well.”Fernandes’s hat-trick came after he won the Professional Footballers’ Association Player of the Year on Tuesday, which followed him also winning the Football Writers’ Player of the Year. He said: “It was a massive result. We lost three points last week. First game at home, the fans have been waiting for this. It’s not to make up for last week, you can’t get six points from it.“Scoring before half-time is always important if it’s to get on top of the game or draw the game. We were in control of the game. In the second half, we were very good. Scoring goals is the best feeling in football. Doing a hat-trick at home with our fans is something I’m proud of. I hope I can do much more and help my teammate score goals too.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarcus Rashford started for United in the league for the first time since 1 December 2024 and impressed as United recorded 33 shots, their most since 38 against Burnley in 2016. The manager said: “Really pleased with Marcus. I am sure it was nice for him to be back and start games and be involved in a good performance. He will only get better.”View image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo (right) was ‘immense in the middle of the pitch for us’ according to Michael Carrick.Photograph: Ryan Crockett/Every Second Media/ShutterstockKobbie Mainoo also made a first start of the season. Carrick was asked how the midfielder could develop his game. “On today’s performance, not much really. I thought he was pretty much all-around very good for a first start back,” said Carrick. “I understand Bruno will get a lot of credit today, and he deserves that as well, but I thought Kobbie was immense in the middle of the pitch for us and underpinned the performance of the team.”Greaves’ own goal came after Harry Maguire had handled the ball then struck a shot that was going off-target, only for it to deflect in off the defender. The video assistant referee ruled the goal legal as Maguire did not score, which baffled Gary O’Neil. Ipswich’s manager said: “I was stood there and thought: ‘That is definitely getting disallowed,’ and then I thought: ‘What if Maguire’s shot is not going in?’”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickIpswich TownnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75 | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine succumbed to a heart attack on Sunday
Content: Indigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenIndigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPBoxingAustralian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75Father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine had a heart attack on SundayWarning:Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images and names of Indigenous Australians who have diedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSun 30 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, aged 75.The father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine had a heart attack on Sunday.Born in Baryulgil, near Grafton in northern New South Wales, Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions, challenging for the world middleweight title against Argentina’s Carlos Monzon in 1974, in a bout stopped in the seventh round.View image in fullscreenTony Mundine with former boxer and activist Rubin ‘Hurricane’ Carter in 2010.Photograph: Lee Besford/AAPMundine leaves a significant boxing legacy. Anthony was an IBO middleweight and WBA super-middleweight world champion, whose son Rahim won his fourth career fight from as many professional bouts on the Gold Coast only last week.Anthony Mundine posted a tribute to his father on social media, saying he was returning home for his funeral after travelling to Saudi Arabia.View image in fullscreenAnthony Mundine spars with Tony during a training session at his gymnasium in Redfern in 2013.Photograph: AAP“I don’t know what to say, I’m broken,” Anthony posted.“Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul.“I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.View image in fullscreenNBA star Clyde Drexler with Tony Mundine during a basketball clinic for the Aboriginal community at Mundine's gym in Redfern.Photograph: Tim Cole/AAP“Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength gonna miss you Tonza, there’s only one Tony Mundine.”Through a career in the middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight divisions, Tony Mundine recorded 80 wins – 64 from knockouts, 15 losses, and one draw.Explore more on these topicsBoxingIndigenous AustraliansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Durham finish off Gloucestershire on sixth ball of day; Surrey frustrate Essex: county cricket, day four – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Durham completed a 10-wicket win over Gloucestershire to cement their place at the top of Division Two
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Durham completed a 10-wicket win over Gloucestershire to cement their place at the top of Division Two
Content: 5h ago16.19 EDTRoundup: Durham sanguine over wait for winThe only result from this round of championship matches came 1min 45sec into the day when Matthew Potts cracked the four required to giveDurhama 10-wicket win againstGloucestershireat Chester‑le‑Street.Gloucestershire, who had refused to bowl spin on Saturday night amid bad light, therefore extending the game into yesterday, chose to open with Ollie Price’s fruity loops, with the winning runs coming off his sixth ball.Durham’s head of cricket, Ryan Campbell, was phlegmatic. “I guess it’s a bit ironic that they opened the bowling with a spinner this morning, but these things happen. We don’t worry about the opposition. We do things our way, and it was delayed, but same result.”Durham cement their place at the top of Division Two, 40 points clear with four rounds left. Things have more of a wooden-spoonish tinge for Gloucestershire, bottom with nine defeats in 10 games.Olly Stone continued his storming late-summer form, reducingWarwickshireto 43 for three in a swinging seven-over opening spell. He finished with five wickets, to go alongside the 10 he collected against Surrey last week. Earlier Joe Clarke had reached 150, to add to his achievement as the first batsman to pass 1,000 runs this season.Nottinghamshireremain top of Division One, by four points.At Chelmsford, Ben Foakes played one of his finest innings forSurrey, lifting them both away from defeat and the relegation zone.Essex, though, will be cursing the two early lives they gave him, a tricky missed stumping and a fluffed caught-and-bowled. Foakes batted from the start of the day till handshakes just before five o’clock, 120 not out from 226 balls.After a draw at Wantage Road, the Division Two promotion rivalsNorthamptonshireandKentare level, Kent staying second because of an extra win. Hundreds from Ricardo Vasconcelos and Nathan McSweeney ensured Northants pocketed maximum batting points.DespiteMiddlesexforfeiting an innings in an attempt to force victory, rain was the only winner at Derby. There was just time for young Naavya Sharma to grab four for 36 inDerbyshire’s sketchy 131 all out.Share

title: Joe Root urges England to celebrate Pakistan series win in ‘sensible, grown-up way’ | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Joe Root has called on his players to ‘celebrate in a sensible, grown‑up way’ after England clinched the series victory against Pakistan at Lord’s
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Joe Root has called on his players to ‘celebrate in a sensible, grown‑up way’ after England clinched the series victory against Pakistan at Lord’s
Content: Joe Root led England to their first multi-game Test series win since 2024.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJoe Root led England to their first multi-game Test series win since 2024.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEngland v Pakistan 2026Joe Root urges England to celebrate Pakistan series win in ‘sensible, grown-up way’Team have faced off-field scandals over the last yearRoot: ‘It’s hard to win Test series so enjoy it’Simon Burntonat Lord'sSun 30 Aug 2026 16.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Root has called on his players to “celebrate in a sensible, grown‑up way” after theysecured a first multi‑game serieswin since 2024 by beating Pakistan at Lord’s to take a 2-0 lead with one to play.England’s recent opportunities for celebration haveoften resulted in scandaland Root intends to end the scandals rather than the celebra­tions. “It’s important we’re not ­talking about [off-field matters], absolutely,” he said. “But it’s hard to win Test matches, it’s hard to win Test series, so enjoy it and celebrate it, but in a sensible, grown-up way. It’s been a really good start to, I don’t know what you want to call it, this new team.”Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue roll over Pakistan to give England series winRead moreIt has been a difficult summer so far for Root: in nine innings he is averaging 29.44 – compared with a career average of 50.38 – and has been dismissed lbw on seven occasions, including in both innings of this game. “I’ve always been quite good at understanding and ­eventually problem-solving,” he said.“I’ll continue to keep working hard. I might have been lbw a few times, but lots of those have been umpire’s call – if they go the other way it might not be as much of a talking point. We’ve also seen the ball move more than it ever has. So there has to be a sense of calm and realism around things. I know I’m a good player, and I’d like to think there’s a big score around the corner.”After another difficult match for the batters at Lord’s, Root deflected criticism of a pitch he described as “naughty” by spinning attention instead to the balls, which he says have been sapping the players’ spirits – and breaking their bats. “I think they’ve been very different this year,” he said. “I think there’s a different lacquer to them. I don’t know, I’ve not got evidence on that – you probably need to ask Dukes – but I think there’s lacquer on the seam. As a batter, when you practise, they’re cracking your bats more frequently. And they seem a lot firmer.“I think they’re affecting the wickets as well. I think they’re ­denting more. If they dent the wicket it’s going to seam off the dents as well, it’s going to move more. It’s been challenging. Sometimes you do come across summers where it’s the perfect storm: you get overcast conditions, you get a bit of rain to contend with, the balls are slightly different. But that’s part of the challenge of Test cricket, being able to adapt.”Pakistan’s Mohammad Abbas conceded that “everybody’s not happy with this performance” but insisted the team was improving. “We were much better in this match [than in the first Test]. You can see that as time passes we are getting used to the conditions and everything is ­getting better,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As a team, we aren’t doing well. But we are ­working on that. The next match will be in Birmingham, and hopefully victory will come.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamJoe RootCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women in UK arts feel they do not have equal opportunities for roles, says report | Discrimination at work | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexism
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Exclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexism
Content: Actor Maureen Beattie, who recently played Shakespeare’s Lear in a production in Pitlochry, said she was not surprised by the findings.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenActor Maureen Beattie, who recently played Shakespeare’s Lear in a production in Pitlochry, said she was not surprised by the findings.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Discrimination at workWomen in UK arts feel they do not have equal opportunities for roles, says reportExclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexismRachel HallSun 30 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen working in the arts believe they do not have equal opportunities for roles, especially as they get older, according to a report saying that the industry is fixated with “young and emerging” talent.Nearly all (95%) women working in the arts thought gender inequality persisted, while three-quarters (75%) reported experiencing unconscious bias or sexism, according to a survey of 76 arts professionals. More than two-thirds (69%) felt that age negatively affected their career success – a figure that rose to 100% among those working in artistic rather than managerial roles.The research said thatgender discriminationand ageism were being exacerbated by the use of AI in hiring, which can penalise women for taking career breaks for caring responsibilities, or reinforce historical biases.Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities ministerRead moreMany performers highlighted the additional pressure on women to look young relative to men. “Often younger actresses are cast to play opposite men who are older for parts that are supposed to be the same age,” said one actor.One participant said that casting opportunities “drop off at 39”, while another female actor said: “There are twice as many roles for my male colleagues as there are for me. There are even fewer roles for actresses over 50.”One respondent highlighted the obsession with words like “young and emerging” to describe talent. “There seems to be absolutely no celebration of experienced, seasoned, insightful, adult, et cetera. It’s always fresh. As if anything that isn’t fresh is mouldy,” she said.Another said that writers’ schemes tended to favour young people, while many emerging artist initiatives were aimed at young, graduating artists rather than developing later-life-stage artists.One person working in arts marketing said there was a prevalent idea that only young people truly understood the online world, while a writer felt that the stories of older women were seldom commissioned.View image in fullscreenMaureen Beattie cited the ‘waste of the great talent and life knowledge and technical skill older women bring to the table’.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe theatre and TV actorMaureen Beattie, who starred in Casualty and was a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said: “So, we have proof at last that age discrimination is one of the major issues women face in the entertainment industry. Are we surprised? I’m certainly not. I’m one of the lucky ones who have slipped through this particular net and at the ripe old age of 72 have just come back fromplaying Lear in Pitlochry.“We need far more of these great big meaty roles for women so that the current waste of the great talent and life knowledge and technical skill older women bring to the table doesn’t go on disappearing into the night.”Dr Jennifer Tuckett, the chief executive of the support group Women in the Arts, who authored the report, said: “The findings regarding age discrimination against older women in the arts, and the potential for AI to increase issues for older women in the arts, are particularly worrying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Researchers are just starting to look at thisarea of AIand it is urgent we investigate this issue more – research has shown older women stand to be disadvantaged during any recruitment processes which use AI.”The findings are from a survey undertaken as part of a five-year research project by Women in the Arts, run in partnership with the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, Equity, WOW, Sphinx Theatre, ERA 50:50 and the Women in Theatre Lab. It is funded byArts Council Englandand intended to feed into a taskforce addressing the needs of women in the cultural sector.An Arts Council England spokesperson said the group would “consider the challenges women face around issues such as glass ceilings, harassment and caring responsibilities”, with a view to identifying good practice and interventions that support women at work.The report called for more targeted work to address gender discrimination, including more funding to address the problem, representation targets – potentially mirroring those in Australia, where these are required in funding applications – and leadership programmes, as well as algorithmic audits to minimise bias.The research will also be handed to ministers on 12 October as part of a campaign to establish an all-party parliamentary group on women in the arts.Explore more on these topicsDiscrimination at workArts policyTheatreArts Council EnglandWomenGenderAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: The datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against big tech billionaires | Datacenters – US | The Guardian
description: The movement against datacenters is uniting Americans because they perfectly illustrate how a few individuals hold all the power to control decisions that affect our lives
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The movement against datacenters is uniting Americans because they perfectly illustrate how a few individuals hold all the power to control decisions that affect our lives
Content: The featured essayDatacenters – USThe datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against big tech billionairesThe movement against datacenters is uniting Americans because they perfectly illustrate how a few individuals hold all the power to control decisions that affect our livesAaron RegunbergSun 30 Aug 2026 12.08 EDTFirst published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTShareView image in fullscreenBryce Gustafson has been knocking on doors in Indiana for more than a decade. The lead organizer with Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), a consumer and environmental organization, he usually encounters a mix of reactions when he’s out canvassing; whatever issue he’s talking about, there’s always at least a few people on the other side. But at a recent festival in the rural town of Monrovia, Indiana, he was struck by an unusual spirit of unity.He was there about a proposeddatacenter, a 550-acre (222-hectare) Google project in this small town of 1,600 people. “I had 50 people I talked to,” Gustafson told me. “Nobody wanted that datacenter in their community. And at least a half a dozen people came up to me to say, ‘Hey, I voted for Trump. What the heck’s he doing, supporting these things?’”Gustafson said he’s had similar conversations all across the state. If there’s one thing he sees uniting Hoosiers of all stripes – from rural areas such asMorgan countyto suburbs such asFranklin Townshipto the historically African American neighborhood ofMartindale-Brightwoodin Indianapolis – it’s fury over these water-guzzling, air-polluting behemoths and the tech oligarchs imposing them.How the fight over US datacenters is scrambling this state’s politics: ‘We don’t want it’Read moreThese dynamics are playing out across the US. Over the last year, intensifying waves of local opposition to big tech’s datacenter buildout have surged into a nationwide tsunami of resistance. Elites on both coasts, from leaders of the AI industry in Silicon Valley to leaders of the political establishment in Washington DC, have struggled to make sense of the backlash. First they tried to write it off as business-as-usual nimbyism: just a few local bans passed here and there, maybe some unknown city councilorslosing re-electionafter signing datacenter deals – not such a big deal. Then senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez began calling for a national moratorium. Pretty soonUtah’s senate presidentgot tossed out of office for supporting hyperscale proposals. And the movement continues to grow.View image in fullscreenPeople protest during a news conference near the construction site of ‘The Barn’ datacenter, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on 30 July 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesToday,three-quartersof Americans oppose local datacenter development, a swing of more than 30 points in just a year. More than500 counties and municipalitieshave passed datacenter bans or moratoria, while dozens of proposed projects have been killed outright. And the issue has come to define some of the highest-profile political races in the country. In the battle for US Senate in Ohio, populist DemocratSherrod Brownhas made Republican senator Jon Husted’s support of datacenters the centerpiece of his campaign, promptingwarningsfrom the National Republican senatorial committee that “datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck”.Other Republicans are taking notice. The Texas governor, Greg Abbott once touted the state as the “epicenter of AI development”; last week he said datacenters had “dug their own grave”. In Michigan, days after The Lever news outletrevealedthat GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers held millions in AI-related investments, he announced his support for a one-year moratorium on their construction in the state.Big tech billionaires may finally bebeginningto realize that this backlash poses real complications for them. But they stilldon’t understandthe nature of the threat they’ve called down upon themselves, because the movement against datacenters represents more than just a series of local fights against a new kind of infrastructure project. It may, in fact, constitute the best opportunity we’ve had in generations to truly shake up American politics, by redirecting the partisan anger that oligarchic forces have long used to divide regular Americans and channeling that energy instead against the billionaires that are actually the cause of so many of our shared problems.double quotation markPeople are realizing that the left-to-right divide isn’t as important as the divide between the working class and big corporate interestsAnonymous organizerThe political science term for this strategy, coined byJennifer McCoy and Murat Somer, is “transformative repolarization”. McCoy and Somer argue that authoritarians and oligarchs often stoke what they call “pernicious polarization” – extreme toxic polarization that uses “us versus them” rhetoric, often on social and culture war issues, to divide the public in ways that harm democracy. In the face of such intense suspicion and distrust, depolarizing a society – trying to get people to stop viewing their fellow citizens as an existential danger – may not work on its own, in the absence of a unifying struggle to address underlying grievances. Instead, McCoy and Somer argue that opponents of authoritarianism need to redraw the lines of contestation that define their politics – to shift the “us versus them” struggle from, for example, a left-to-right polarization, to a different axis of conflict that can bring a large majority of the public together against real structural threats.When you speak to organizers and community leaders on the frontlines of local datacenter campaigns, it immediately becomes clear that they are seeing new configurations of people coming together in precisely this way. “On many issues, people come in with a baked-in partisan lens that influences their thinking,” said Ben Inskeep, program director at CAC. “On datacenters, we don’t have those firm camps formed. And so we’re seeing broad concern fromRepublicans, Democrats and everyone else on the political spectrum. We’re seeing folks saying, ‘Hey, I might be a Maga Republican and you might be a liberal yahoo from the big city, but if you’re coming to our community to help us fight this datacenter, you’re my best friend.’”View image in fullscreenWestfield, Massachusetts, residents applaud as their city council votes in favor of a temporary moratorium on the construction of a datacenter within the city on 6 July 2026.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesWilliam Lawrence has been seeing the same thing in Michigan. The Sunrise Movement co-founder and congressional candidate made opposition to datacenters a main focus of his successful campaign for the Democratic nomination to represent the Lansing area. He’s now hammering his Republican opponent on the issue – to great apparent effect, according to arecent pollfinding Lawrence leading in the district, which is now held by a Republican. “At a time when people are so polarized and isolated from each other, something that brings people together is rare,” he said. “We can all get together to watch the Spartans play at Spartan Stadium, but to get together in a context where you’re also talking about politics? That is a gift, and is not at all to be taken for granted.”An organizer I spoke with who’s been opposing datacenter construction in Texas (who asked to remain anonymous) noted a similar dynamic playing out in his state. “I’ve never seen anything that mobilizes this many rural Texans before,” he told me. “Folks are starting to get politicized through this work. They’re realizing when they reach out to their state reps, their state senators, that these people are not batting for them. They’re batting for the tech oligarchs. And so people are realizing that the left-to-right divide isn’t as important as the divide between the working class and big corporate interests.”The electoral implications of this process should be obvious. But for anyone too thick to draw their own conclusions, voters themselves are starting to get quite explicit. When MS Now asked a woman in Hood county, Texas, which is 80% Republican, “you’re willing to forgo every conservative issue and let the Senate fall into the hands of Democrats if that’s what it takes to kill datacenters?”, herresponsewas immediate: “Yep. My entire community’s going to break rank.”What remains to be seen is whetherDemocratswill seize this opportunity – or let Republicans regain the initiative.View image in fullscreenA manifestation of greed“I’ve been waiting a long time for people to wake up to how they’re being ripped off,” Gustafson said. So why are datacenters the issue that’s finally waking people up?For one, they’re essentially unique in the breadth of their odiousness, so everyone has a reason to be offended by them. Hyperscale datacenters are big industrial warehouses that can cover literally dozens of acres, generate debilitating noise pollution, and severely impactlocal watertables. They useobsceneamounts of energy,straininglocal infrastructure and in many cases causing utility rates to spike. This also has devastating climate and environmental impacts, as AI developers are overwhelmingly meeting their energy needs with dirty fossil fuel generators that spew outrageous amounts ofplanet-warming emissionsand severely impact local air quality.Then there are the process concerns: use ofeminent domain, the provision oftaxpayer subsidies, and big tech’s near-ubiquitous practice of pushing local officials to signnondisclosure agreements(NDAs) that shroud deals in suspicious opacity.View image in fullscreenA datacenter built by the Markley Group looms over a residential neighborhood in Lowell, Massachusetts, on 30 June 2026.Photograph: Matt O’Brien/APAnd all of this is for what? Though the development of datacenters creates temporary construction work, once developed, the facilities do not provide communities with significant long-term jobs. The only thing these sites produce (other than many shades of pollution) is added compute for a technology that we’ve all been told will soon put billions of people out of work. In the meantime, as we wait to see whether that dystopian future materializes or it was all an economy-wreckingbubble, AI is largely being experienced as the thing making the internet more annoying, our jobs more stressful, surveillance more terrifying, and big tech billionaires – already widely despised – more powerful than ever. It’s not hard to understand why this doesn’t constitute a very compelling case for datacenters.What it does provide is a perfect canvas on which to illustrate the broader problems with our political and economic system: how a few individuals have all the money and power to control the decisions that impact our lives. “Datacenters are the physical manifestation of the greed and the hubris and the power of the AI oligarchs,” Gustafson said. “That gets people thinking about why we are allowing these tech billionaires to just run roughshod over our state.”double quotation markPeople are seeing that they’re stronger together. It’s a beautiful thingBen InskeepWhat emerges from this process is a budding sense of solidarity that can extend far beyond the localized concerns that might have brought someone into a particular fight. Gustafson described how organizers from Evansville, a city in south-west Indiana, began supporting groups across the border in Kentucky when fights started ratcheting up there. Elsewhere, a farmer who became the leader of a datacenter fight in Henry county, Indiana, attended a meeting about a proposed project in a neighboring town. “Next thing you know, she’s helping that community, showing up for them, because it’s so much easier getting through this when you have somebody who’s been there and understands,” he said.As Inskeep put it: “When one campaign ends, people are saying, ‘Hey, we fought ours, now that it’s done, we’re going to go to the next county and help them.’” And that starts a snowball effect. “People are seeing that they’re stronger together. It’s a beautiful thing.”View image in fullscreenA singular opportunityClearly, these fights have created an opening for the left. But the politics around datacenters are still very much up for grabs. Democrats should have a strong inherent edge, given that – on this issue, like so many others – Donald Trump has forcefully aligned himself with his buddies in the billionaire class. The president’saggressive plansto accelerate big tech’s datacenter buildout include opening up federal lands for hyperscaler construction, axing public participation processes in permitting, and evenwaivingClean Air Act and Clean Water Act requirements on the radically absurd grounds that datacenter approvals need to be expedited fornational securityreasons.But other conservative forces have been ahead of the curve. Steve Bannon has long beenworkingto put Maga’s populist wing out front in opposing both datacenters and AI more broadly. The Texas organizer I spoke with told me he sees a significant number of people coming into datacenter fights casting blame not on big tech oligarchs, but on China or the United Arab Emirates, in ways that can feel decidedly xenophobic or Islamophobic. “This is an opportunity, but it’s a short-lived opportunity and we need to seize it,” said Inskeep. “Because this can also be used against us. If we are not effective at doing the political education and helping folks through that process, I do think you could have a far-right, nationalist, anti-immigrant person use this issue to come to power and then implement horrifying policies.”double quotation markFor the first time in generations, the billionaire class has overreached in a way that Americans of all stripes and ideologies are finding equally repulsiveNeedless to say, for Democrats to seize this opportunity, they first must actually take a unified stance against datacenters. And unfortunately, many Democratic leaders remain just as in-bed with big tech billionaires as their GOP counterparts. Maine’s Democratic governor, Janet Millsvetoedthe datacenter moratorium passed by her state legislature. Michigan’s Democratic governor, Gretchen Whitmer wasaccusedof dismissing her constituents’ concerns about the many datacenter projects she has supported. The Democratic minority leader, Hakeem Jeffriesopposesa datacenter moratorium andappointedthe aggressively corporatist Josh Gottheimer and big tech-backed Zoe Lofgren to help develop House Democrats’ AI platform.View image in fullscreenThe Texas agriculture commissioner, Sid Miller joins residents on the south steps of the Texas capitol to protest datacenter expansion before a Texas senate committee on finance hearing in Austin on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesAnd there are some races where Democrats are squarely on the losing side of the issue. In Wisconsin, the Democratic nominee for governor, David Crowley, is already beingblasted in adsby his Republican opponent for having said he wants Wisconsin to “become an AI and a data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe”. Crowley won his gubernatorial primary after the entire Democratic establishment united to oppose the left-leaning candidate in the race, Francesca Hong, on the grounds that old “woke” posts – including a call to “cancel Thanksgiving” – made herunelectable. But Crowley’s troubles demonstrate why Democrats need to update their assumptions regarding what kinds of past statements make for real electoral liabilities. After all, nobody is actually going to cancel Thanksgiving. But making Wisconsin into a hub of hated datacenters? That feels like a very real possibility to a lot of Wisconsin’s swing voters.The climate solution both the right and the left can get behind | Bill McKibbenRead moreWhen I asked Lawrence what he would want to say to party leadership on this point, his response was simple. “I would say, listen to the people. Nobody wants companies from Silicon Valley coming in, bullying us, making decisions that are going to impact the next century of our communities. Just listen to the people. You’ll be popular.”So will Democrats take the chance they’ve been given? For the first time in generations, the billionaire class has overreached in a way that Americans of all stripes and ideologies are finding equally repulsive. They’ve created a perfect opening to repolarize the public – not just against Trump, but against the oligarchic and authoritarian systems that produced him in the first place.The opportunity before us is singular. What a monstrous mistake it would be not to seize it.Aaron Regunberg is a former Rhode Island state representative and a contributing editor at the New Republic. He is the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, but is writing here in his personal capacitySpot illustrations by Ben Hickey

title: ProCook outdoor pizza oven review: a budget-friendly model that brings the pizzeria home | Pizza | The Guardian
description: This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people
Content: The flame game: the gas-powered ProCook is a ‘capable, compact and versatile pizza oven’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe flame game: the gas-powered ProCook is a ‘capable, compact and versatile pizza oven’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterPizzaReviewProCook outdoor pizza oven review: a budget-friendly model that brings the pizzeria homeThis no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most peopleThe best pizza ovens – testedOoni Koda 2 reviewRachel OgdenSun 30 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe market forpizza ovenstends to be dominated by a handful of specialist brands, so it can feel like a gamble to buy from a lesser-known manufacturer or a retailer that offers a wider range of goods.The ProCook outdoor pizza oven is no gamble, though. It’s every inch a capable, compact and versatile pizza oven, despite being just one product in an offering that includes pretty much everything from storage jars to squeegees.This outdoor pizza oven conforms to ProCook’s usual direct-from-manufacturer pricing. Coming in at a comparatively reasonable RRP of £249, the oven punches far above its weight in terms of functionality. As well as foldable legs for storage, it has room for 12in pizzas and a manual rotating stone for more even cooking. Turn the stone as the pizza bakes for an evenly blistered crust or simply adjust it as needed. At 12kg, it’s also light enough to take to a friend’s house or on a camping trip.View at ProCookHow I testedView image in fullscreenTest slice: one of the veggie pizzas cooked at 350C to caramelise the toppings.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianI tested the ProCook in the same way I test otherpizza ovensfor the Filter. As well as assessing the quality of the cook by making pizzas with different toppings – cheese and tomato at about 430C; a slow-cooked veggie pizza at 350C with onion, pepper and tomato to caramelise and soften the topping; and a salami pizza at about 400C – I rated the oven for ease of assembly, overall use, lighting, temperature control and storage. I also recorded heat-up times, although, as it was tested in cooler months, these may be longer than in the warmer months.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenRound here: the ProCook’s rotating stone sits on its own turntable.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView at ProCookThe ProCook outdoor pizza oven is cheaper than similarly sized models, but you’ll need to invest in aninfrared (IR) thermometerfor the best results. In tests, the oven heated from cold to 430C in about 25 minutes, which is about average for a compact gas-powered oven, and the rotating stone that sits on its own turntable doesn’t have much impact on heat-up times either way.The rotating stone has no raised edges, which means that you’ll need to be fairly accurate when launching pizza. Any other dishes you cook in the oven, such as chicken or fish, will also need to fit on the round stone.ProCook doesn’t offer much in the way of accessories. There’s no cover, but there is a great-valuepizza peelfor just £10.ProCook outdoor pizza oven specificationsDimensions:43.2 x 65.5 x 31.2cm (WDH) / mouth 35 x 10cm (WH)Maximum capacity:stone diameter 32cm (working capacity, 12in pizza)Features:manual rotating stone, control dial ignitionFuel:gasSpare parts:control knob, rotating knob and fixing nutWeight:12kgWhat we loveView image in fullscreenFire away: the salami-topped pizza was declared ‘best on test’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianFor what is effectively a budget-friendly model, the ProCook outdoor pizza oven gets all the basics right. It lit first time via the built-in ignition, but can also easily be lit with a match should this fail. I especially liked that there was no need for a turning peel – a utensil that helps you turn the pizza in the oven – and that the rotating stone is powered by hand, making the whole thing pleasingly low-tech, with no need for batteries or recharging.Some of the pizzas I made burned at the corners, but this is because the bought dough I tested with (for consistency) was shaped into rectangles, rather than circles. Overall, pizzas cooked well, although with less rise than I’ve achieved in pricier ovens. This was most noticeable on the cheese and tomato pizza. I also found thicker toppings needed a lower temperature and longer cook, with some of the vegetables remaining firm while others began to char. The salami-topped pizza was the best of all, with evenly melted cheese and just a slight singe on one edge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat we don’t loveView image in fullscreenControl freak: the rotating stone is turned using a dial on the side of the oven but for controlling gas … head to the rear.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThe dial for the rotating stone sits at the side of the pizza oven, relegating the control for the gas to the rear. This means you can’t see the flame as you light the oven and adjust the heat. You may need two people – one on the gas control, and one watching the oven’s flame size as it’s altered.Another drawback is the size of the oven’s mouth. It’s relatively narrow and short, with the space becoming even tighter around the stone. This makes launching and retrieving pizza trickier than with rival models such as my overall favourite, theGozney Arc Lite, and theOoni Koda 2. On the plus side, if you later invest in a bigger oven, the ProCook will at least mean you’ve honed some serious pizza-launching skills.Warranty, repairability and longevityThe ProCook outdoor pizza oven comes with a two-year guarantee, with spare parts also available via customer services once it’s out of warranty. Sadly, the rotating stone cannot be replaced if it becomes damaged or breaks. Despite being an outdoor oven, ProCook’s instructions advise storing it indoors, out of harsh weather conditions, such as heavy rain, strong winds and direct sunshine.ProCook outdoor pizza oven: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenMelting moment: ‘a smart buy for beginners’.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThe ProCook is my favourite budget pizza oven. The combination of good design and low price makes it a smart buy for beginners – and those who’d rather spend big on toppings for their next pizza party. It might not deliver the wow results of more expensive ovens, nor come with lots of fancy features, but unless you plan to cook pizza regularly, it’s unlikely you’ll miss them.Another point to bear in mind is that this is very much just a pizza oven. Unlike those models that double up as versatile outdoor ovens, this ProCook model offers limited space on the stone for roasting pans, slow cooking in ambient heat, and sizzling side dishes – so if you want to experiment with a wider range of dishes, this probably isn’t the oven for you.However, if pizza is what you want most of the time – and who doesn’t? – the ProCook outdoor pizza oven is an excellent choice for families, busy households and anyone keen to master homemade pizza.View at ProCookFor more:The best pizza ovens in the UKOoni Koda 2 reviewThe best BBQs and grills – testedRachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she is less successful at assembling and repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of appliances while her garden has seen a succession of pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters put through their paces. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failedExplore more on these topicsPizzaThe FilterFoodHomesGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works
Content: The OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI offices in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AIGene MarksSmall business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what worksSun 30 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTShareOne thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many casessquandered– by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.An AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene MarksRead moreWhat works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.Small businesses are watching. And now doing.A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.Big companies have also begun to discover theastronomical computingcosts that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companiesthrow away billonson large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.For months, onearnings callsand investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring,only to hirethose same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman,recently admittedthat their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)US small businesscommentShareReuse this content
