title: The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution
Content: A rare-earths mine in China. ‘Last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war … by the curbing of rare-earth exports.’Photograph: Imaginechina Limited/AlamyView image in fullscreenA rare-earths mine in China. ‘Last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war … by the curbing of rare-earth exports.’Photograph: Imaginechina Limited/AlamyOpinionCritical mineralsThe Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chainsEditorialOutsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solutionSun 30 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, Chinablocked exports of key rare earths to Japanin a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about70% of rare-earth miningglobally and 90% of separation and processing.Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, hasalready jumpedbecause of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.The 17 metals known as rare earthsare far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing arecostly, complexand often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedlyflowing to Asiabecause of the lack of domestic demand. While“Big shovel”is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worthless than $6bn globallylast year.Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it wouldspend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chainsas a “Manhattan Project”for rare earths. Othersquestionthe strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular,Brazil, raising grave concernabout the ecological impact. Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them frommining wasteor runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive.Earlier this year, the USlaunched a critical minerals coalitionwith 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland.Stockpilesof essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to thebiggest facilityoutside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals isunder discussion. But many fear that European countries are movingtoo slowly. That must change.Explore more on these topicsCritical mineralsOpinionMiningChinaEuropean UnionDonald TrumpEuropeeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Why is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Senatorial candidate James Talarico, a former vegan, eats barbecue during his election campaign in June 2026.Photograph: The Dallas Morning News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSenatorial candidate James Talarico, a former vegan, eats barbecue during his election campaign in June 2026.Photograph: The Dallas Morning News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesOpinionVeganismWhy is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur?Emma BeddingtonUS republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the waysSun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.23 EDTShareCool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble,tofu-eating wokeratito dangerous radicals unfit for public office.Politico reportsthat US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,”Trump warnedof Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is“neither man nor woman”.)Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretarydescribed him on Xas “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowadrew heatfor merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”.It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does Americaactually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official responseto “vegan accusations”(“accusations” – the word you’d use for say,corruptionorsexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’sfirst indictment” (despitemany years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime).Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”.Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office.Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle.And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome.Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of thelandmark 2018 studyon the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes,concludedthat excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”.Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsVeganismOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Italy may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?
Content: ‘Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionItalyItaly may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there?Dave SchillingThe move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 15.57 EDTShareImagine driving in Italy, with its narrow, cobblestone streets and scooter enthusiasts. I find it hard enough todrive in Los Angeles, a city designed specifically with the automobile in mind. I’d probably squash a pedestrian or two trying to navigate Italian roads.The modern world is just too hectic for the ancient streets of Europe, so Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can:outlawing texting in crosswalks. The Italian government’s updated draft of its highway code proposes fines of €75 or more for anyone caught sending a DM, updating their LinkedIn, finishing Wordle on the fifth guess, or anything else phone-related that might make them miss an oncoming metal projectile. I’m sure most people will risk the slap on wrist to get that message off, but it at least sends a signal to the Italian people that paying attention to traffic is actually kind of important.Distracted pedestrians aren’t just a problem inItaly, though. If I’m turning right on a red light, chances are there will be someone inching slowly toward the intersection with their thumbs furiously smashing against the glass of their iPhone, oblivious to the fact that I am planning to drive into the parcel of land they are currently occupying. It’s not just that this behavior is dangerous. It’s alsodeeply annoying. I’m forced to pay attention for both of us, like I’m a guardian angel or the arbiter of whether you, the clueless phone person, live or die. Sure, I might briefly get off on the power trip of having such authority over our mutual safety, but I’d much rather be thinking about where to have dinner instead of how long I should wait to honk at the drooling simpleton preventing me from turning.Distracted Italian pedestrians who cross road while on phone could be fined under new codeRead moreI applaud the Italian government for their forward thinking. Actually, I think it’s time we criminalize more small annoyances. Such as …Using a ringtoneSomeone please explain to me why anyone bothers with leaving their ringer on. We are decades past the era when, for a dollar, you could buy that Crazy Frog song and impress your friends every time you got a call. Now, it’s just pure sonic detritus, clogging up our ears with aural poison – bleeps, bloops, pings and plops. When AMC Theaters tells an auditorium full of grown adults to silence their phones before a movie, all I can think is: “Unless they’re an on-call heart surgeon, their phone should always be silent.”Fine amount: $200Interrupting me when I’m not done talkingI understand and accept that I have a lot to say. I make my meager living from writing, so pontificating just comes naturally to me. Sometimes, I wish it didn’t. But most of the time, what I’m saying is pretty important and you should be listening. Not waiting for your turn. I just listened to you try to captivate me with a treatise on gender roles in Christopher Nolan’s films. I respected you, even if I didn’t want to. Either let me finish or you’re fined!Fine amount: $200Not pushing in your chair when stepping away from a table at a restaurantWould you like to see the server at your favorite Olive Garden location break their tibia because you left your chair in the middle of a walkway? If that’s what you think of our restaurant industry workers, I’ve got a mind to go outside to my patio and bang on some pots and pans like it’s Covid lockdown to thank everyone carrying a plate of shrimp scampi who has to avoid rude customers. When you get up from your table, push in your chair. It takes two seconds and it could save a life … and a plate of delicious pasta.Fine amount: $250Riding an electric scooter on the sidewalkI would like to remind everyone that scooters from companies such as Lime and Lyft explicitly say to not ride these vehicles on the sidewalk. The sidewalk is called a sidewalk because it, much likeNancy Sinatra’s boots, was made for walking. A motorized conveyance doesn’t belong on the sidewalk, especially ones that actually can get some real speed behind them. Use the bike lane, for God’s sake. Or take the bus. Or anything else, really. It’s just beyond dangerous to be tooling around on a scooter while people are trying to go about their business.I mean, what if I’m looking at my phone and texting? Shame on you, scooter guy.Fine amount: $500Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsItalyOpinionEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina Toossi | The Guardian
description: As with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to play, says Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy
Author: Sina Toossi
Headline: As with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to play, says Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy
Content: Donald Trump boards Air Force One on 27 August.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump boards Air Force One on 27 August.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APOpinionUS-Israel war on IranTrump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higherSina ToossiAs with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to playSun 30 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTShareDonald Trump has found anew way to promise victoryover Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officialsacknowledge that oil exportsandaccess to foreign currencyhave been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has saidit should seek peacewhile it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, hascalled participation inWashington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran couldprevent Gulf oil exportsthrough routes designed to bypass Hormuz.These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It hasordered firms not to complywith US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has nowwarned it will take “all necessary measures”if Chinese interests are targeted.Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessentacknowledged the dangerwhen asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as“economic D-day”.With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issuesExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionDonald TrumpStrait of HormuzChinaUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: As a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriage | Nicholas Purcell  | The Guardian
description: Care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway
Content: Despite bitterness and distance, many marriages contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out, writes Nicholas Purcell.Photograph: Prostock-studio/AlamyView image in fullscreenDespite bitterness and distance, many marriages contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out, writes Nicholas Purcell.Photograph: Prostock-studio/AlamyThe modern mindMarriageAs a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriageNicholas PurcellCare and attention, the fundamentals to keep relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anywayThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 30 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 19.19 EDTShareI’ve killed every garden I’ve neglected, which is all of them: bring me a struggling houseplant and watch it die. But bring me a struggling marriage and I will sometimes encourage it back to life. Other times, when the conditions are right, by which I mean when something is wrong, I will kill it. Intentionally. Or, in more professional language, I will advise it to end. Not every plant gets to flower. Not every marriage should be saved.I have come to realise that care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway. I call them cactus marriages: alive, but I couldn’t tell you how.Jess* and Pete* came to see me: they had raised their kids and always turned up for their jobs – at least with work someone writes down what is required of you. Neglect, it turns out, takes longer to kill a marriage than it does a garden. When couples remember how to be loving, the cactus thrives, and sometimes it even flowers, which surprises everyone, including me.But not every struggling marriage I see is a neglected cactus. Sometimes the soil has gone sour. And sometimes the roots have been severed, intentionally, and no water reaches a severed root. From across the room, neglect and its harder cousins, soured and severed, look the same: quiet and unhappy. Up close, the difference is everything.Sour soil looks like Diane* and Thomas*, married more than 30 years, whose fighting had become a script neither could stop performing. She raised her voice. He corrected her grammar. She brought up his breath. A trade economy where no one wins. There was no innocent party in that room.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsUnderneath, this is mechanical failure. Contempt has become the default; the repair cycle – the small, ordinary apologies healthy couples make without noticing – has broken down and nothing is ever absorbed. But sour soil can be sweetened. Good gardeners do it all the time.This is the marriage I fight for because it so nearly wasn’t necessary; if only they had come in sooner, before the habit hardened into the marriage’s personality. Despite bitterness and distance, these marriages often contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out. And the honest news is that they are probably repairable if both are committed, and the equally honest news is that the window does not stay open for ever.I am burnt out from emotionally supporting my husband. Should I leave him? | Leading questionsRead moreThe severed root marriage is different. This marriage houses a person clinicians have names for: narcissist, abuser, controller, none of which quite closes over the thing itself: a way of being that depends on the other not fully having a self, let alone flourishing. These are the marriages you won’t see on TV shows like Couples Therapy: the erosion of a life that’s hard to capture on film. The soured marriage saddens me; this one disturbs me.The marriage with two people behaving badly worries me less than the marriage with one person doing real harm. Here the question is not how to love better. It is when to leave.An ordinary-looking couple came to me, Michael* and Liz*. It had begun small enough to mistake for love: his need to know where she was. He counted the seconds it took her to answer his texts. The tracking devices came next. Before long he was throwing her against walls, and worse. I challenged Michael privately: is your behaviour making your marriage more or less likely to last? His head turned to me, his breathing slowed and his eyes went black, the light stopped coming back out of them. I hesitate to use the word evil, but I’ve sat with it, there isn’t a better one. It is the look of someone who does not care whether you are alive, or whether they are the reason you stop being.This is not a relationship with a problem, the relationship is the problem. This marriage’s continuation requires one person’s diminishment, one person’s harm. To stay is a form of self-erasure. For anyone inside one, couples therapy is the wrong tool entirely. When only one person is being hurt, calling it “our relationship issues” launders the harm, and can keep a person in danger for years while they wait to become a better communicator.Almost everyone inside a marriage like this does the arithmetic and gets it wrong, not because they are foolish, but because the sums are rigged. The cost of leaving is concrete: money, housing, the children and even shame. The cost of staying is paid invisibly, in instalments of health and the self that keeps getting smaller. And the children, so often the reason given for staying, are there, absorbing what a husband is and what a wife is, and how one is allowed to treat the other.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo let me say it plainly, because this kind of marriage depends on it never being said plainly: some relationships must be left.But leaving is not the same as safe. The part people rush past, because it’s frightening to hear: the time around leaving is often when this kind of partner is most dangerous. Which is exactly when you need a safety plan, a domestic violence service, a friend or counsellor who knows the whole truth, not the version that’s easiest to say out loud.Liz left Michael. She survived. He repartnered.Sometimes I advise couples to end their marriage.*All clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. The Domestic Violence hotline is 1800 RESPECT.In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.orgNicholas Purcell is a relationship psychotherapist based in Adelaide. He is writing Raising Love, on why our theory of love is broken – and what an active one looks likeExplore more on these topicsMarriageThe modern mindRelationshipsFamilyDomestic violencePsychologycommentShareReuse this content

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live on | Ed Vulliamy | The Guardian
description: When I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia today, says Ed Vulliamy, an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian
Author: Ed Vulliamy
Headline: When I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia today, says Ed Vulliamy, an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian
Content: Supporters of the deceased Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladić display and light flares in Novi Sad, Serbia, 27 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of the deceased Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladić display and light flares in Novi Sad, Serbia, 27 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersOpinionRatko MladićRatko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live onEd VulliamyWhen I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia todaySun 30 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTShareMen age and die, but in the Balkans, time stands still and is stuck. General Ratko Mladić,who died in prisonin The Hague on Thursday aged 84, remains a hero in the Republika Srpskastatelet – the Serbian half of dismembered Bosnia that he carved out with ahurricane of violence between 1992 and 1995– and in Serbia itself.Too many Serbs in whose name Mladić carried out his mass murder of other ethnicities – mainly Muslim Bošniak and Roman Catholic Croats – adore him and mourn his passing.Since Bosnia’s war ended, Mladić’s portrait has adorned posters, gable ends, mantelpieces and football fans’ flags. Supporters of Red Star Belgrade marked his death at a match against Viktoria Plzeň on Thursday night with banners reading: “General: Eternal glory. Thank you.”Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik extended his condolences to the Mladić familyand paid tribute: “Republika Srpska will not forget his role, just as it has not forgotten it to this day. A man has died who was the commander in the struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people here, a commander who led the honourable army of Republika Srpska from the first day of its establishment. A man who demonstrated his human and military character.”Conversely, in the 30 years since the war ended, there has been scant apology from Serbian quarters to those people, most of them Muslims, who survived Mladić’s massacres, and no reckoning. Au contraire: across Republika Srpska, hatred of what remains of “the other” and for federal authority in the capital of Sarajevo is palpable and quotidian. A friend writes to me from Bosnia: “We’re still living with the legacy every day. Listening to Republika Srpska, to Dodik, to [Serbia’s president] Vučić, the same old lies, the same old denial.” There is mass collective amnesia, denial of or – nonsensically – justification for what was done.‘We know what is happening, we cannot walk away’: how the Guardian bore witness to horror in former YugoslaviaRead moreMourners who gather annually at the mass cemetery of victims of theSrebrenica massacreof some 8,000 men and boys in July 1995, and for commemorations at concentration camps, are routinely harassed by police and onlookers. It is made clear to Muslims and Croats who have dared to return to Republika Srpska in the north-west and east of the bitterly divided country that, if they could, the Serbs would do it all again.Mladić had a singular, and singularly nasty, squint. You can see it in the footage of him as he prepared the Srebrenica massacre, and in photo portraits that abound this weekend. For very many, it was a death sentence; for me, it was a stab across a courtroom at the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague as Itook the witness stand in 2012to testify against him. Having delivered that terrifying gaze, Mladić never met my eyes again during a half day of evidence from the ground of atrocities committed by those under his command. He sent a shiver of fear down the spine of anyone near him, and he knew it.Mladić was the military wing of an unholy trinity: at its apex, Serbia’s then president, Slobodan Milošević, resurrected the insane idea of a “Greater Serbia”, a form of nationalist fascism whereby wherever the Serbs lived, only Serbs would live – everyone else would leave or die, and every vestige of their culture and religion (Muslim or Catholic) would be erased. His political co-commander in Bosnia wasRadovan Karadžić,president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic.Milošević died while on trial at The Hague; like Mladić, Karadžić was convicted of genocide and other war crimes and remains jailed –surreally, on the Isle of Wight.If Milošević and Karadžić were dangerously deranged, Mladič was bloodthirstily effective. He was the killer,the “Butcher of Bosnia”. To invoke and invertHannah Arendt, if the others were the evil of banality, Mladić was the real thing: the banality of evil.Mladić was a military more than an ideological man, a career officer in the Yugoslav army. He knew what he was doing. Transcripts of the Bosnian Serb assembly submitted to The Hague by an historian at the University of Michigan, Robert Donia, show Mladić expressing concern in 1992 that the political leadership was setting goals that would be hard to achieve. “We cannot cleanse, or sift with a sieve, so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how … Mr Karadžić would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide.” And so it was – at Srebrenica at least, according to The Hague tribunal – and as a good military commander, Mladić obeyed his political masters and enforced his own orders.Mladić was convicted at The Hague in 2017. The media talked about “closure” for his victims. Wishful nonsense: there is no “closure”, nor can there be as long as the Serbs celebrate this creature.Most discussion of Mladić since his passing has inevitably invoked Srebrenica, the infamous massacre. There is the TV footage of him smirking, knowing what was to come. But it was not only Srebrenica. Srebrenica was the most egregious war crime, but it was a denouement: more than 55,000 Muslims and 7,000 Croats had already been killed in other places over those three years, and two million had fled their homes.Foca and Višegrad(sites of rape camps for the indulgence of Mladić’s soldiers); Rogatica, Vlasenica and Sokolac; Bjeljina and Brcko, Kozarac, Sanski Most, Ključ … the list goes on.The siege of Sarajevocounted 11,541 deaths, including 1,600 children.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMladić achieved most of what he set out to do. The “international community” granted the Bosnian Serbs a large part of what they killed, raped, tortured and burned for with theDayton peace agreement, signed in 1995. There was baffling agreement from the Muslim-led government, apparently more anxious to establish its own sectarian fiefdom than unite the republic in a war that the Bosnian army was – actually, finally – winning by that summer (in a counteroffensive that put Mladiċ’s soldiers to flight, liberating territory then returned at Dayton to Republika Srpska).Mladić succeeded in persecuting a very Bosnian, casually convivial interpretation of Islam into something more identitarian and polemical. In the absurd waltz of aspirant accession to the EU, Serbia leads the Balkan queue, ahead of truncated Bosnia, despite Belgrade’s open allegiance and subservience to Russia.Above all, Mladić has succeeded in death, as he did in life, because of the adoration he still commands. His mission to establish an ethnically “pure”, fascistic Greater Serbia remains a dream, anda plan. Through public celebrations, he continues to terrorisethe lives of those mostly Muslims and a few Croats brave enough to return to live under the insignia of those who mass murdered their families.Mladić’s funeral will probably tell us more than his death. Several Serbian government officials and ministers urge a “state and military funeral, and day of mourning”. The president, AleksandarVučić, says he will leave arrangements to the general’s son, Darko, who is of the faith. If Darko decides on full national honours, that is what will happen. Mladić is dead, but lives on.Ed Vulliamy is an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian and ObserverDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsRatko MladićOpinionSerbiaBosnia and HerzegovinaSrebrenica massacreSlobodan Milosevic trialWar crimesRadovan KaradziccommentShareReuse this content

title: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionDevolutionCities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?John HarrisLabour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get startedSun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareApart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons whyAndy Burnhamseems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with theEnglish Devolution and Community Empowerment Actpassed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift thatthe Whitehall PR machineis hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.One changebecame clearearlier this year, and now looks like it willbe turbocharged. By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts.These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne,Minehead, Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to aHouse of Commons library briefing, qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will includeWiltshire, Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took itsfirst stepsto joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades,finally agreedto become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer governmentpostponed mayoral electionsin Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring the State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news thatplans for new, larger police forces are being delayedbecause their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDevolutionOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourSomersetWiltshirecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was miserable for a lot of this century’: Stewart Lee on divorce, his adoption and the twisted children’s poem that explains his life | Stewart Lee | The Guardian
description: After a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: After a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?
Content: Stewart Lee in Abney Park cemetery, Stoke Newington, London. Portraits: Sophia Spring/The Guardian. Grooming: Celine Nonon at Arlington ArtistsView image in fullscreenStewart Lee in Abney Park cemetery, Stoke Newington, London. Portraits: Sophia Spring/The Guardian. Grooming: Celine Nonon at Arlington ArtistsStewart LeeInterview‘I was miserable for a lot of this century’: Stewart Lee on divorce, his adoption and the twisted children’s poem that explains his lifeZoe WilliamsAfter a rocky few decades, the standup is nearing 60 – and finding contentment at last. But what does his grotesque retelling of The Owl and the Pussy-cat tell us about his inability to connect with people?Sun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStewart Lee is somewhat fretfully tidying his kitchen. Nothing is exactly where he left it two months ago to go on tour. Plus, he says, “I’ve come back with a load of records that need to be alphabetised, and that’s really stressing me out.” His house is miles from minimalist – posters everywhere, for spaghetti westerns, avant-garde Welsh harpists, the Fall (who he said in aninterview in 2005 were the love of his life) – but if anything was an inch out of place, he’d notice. He puts things away with theatrical flourish, like a guy doing an impression of a guy who needs things just-so, for the comic effect of how absolutely impossible that guy would be, but at the same time, it’s funny because it’s true.In the show he’s been away for,Stewart Leevs the Man-Wulf, he – a 58-year-old lefty – enters into breakneck dialectic with toxic masculinity in werewolf form (age unknown). “Things have got worse in the 18 months I’ve been doing it,” he says. “I need to really amp the werewolf up. He would be much more explicitly racist and homophobic and transphobic now. But you don’t want people to be really upset in the room.” It feels quite a 2026 dilemma, being unable to even satirise the right without causing the distress it lives for.Then he went with his girlfriend to a treehouse in Scotland he found on Airbnb, but was surprised to find it was an “actual treehouse – to get out of it, you went down a slide”. He gestures vaguely at himself, as if to ask, “Can you imagine me going down a slide?”, although the answer – looking at his skater-boy aesthetic, record‑label T-shirt, shorts – is, in fact, yes. “It was quite good. You couldn’t really cook there. It had a bed.”double quotation markAfter my divorce I’m in the whole house rather than one bit of it. So I’m one of life’s winners. Look at all these posters I can put up. It’s greatView image in fullscreenLee at the grave of comedian and actor Herbert Campbell in Abney Park cemeteryHe was there to join his half-sisters, who “had instructions to put their father’s ashes – I didn’t know him, really – in a river in the west of Scotland where he used to go fishing”, he says, “and they invited me. The actual village was the location base of The Wicker Man. So I went and looked at its feet, which are still in the cliff.”What, the Wicker Man’s feet are still in the cliff? I ask, since it seems impossible. The film came out in 1973 – those feet are the same age as I am (53) and made of wicker.“Yeah. You’d have to know what you were looking for.”His other project is Pea Green Boat, a book based on theshow he devised in 2001, which became a pared‑downradio version of itself in 2004, and has come back to life a quarter of a century later thanks to some surreal and engrossing illustrations by David Waywell. It’s a retelling of The Owl and the Pussy‑cat by Edward Lear in which – spoiler alert – the mince that the owl eats at the end is actually the deceased cat, rotting in a bag. To introduce it, if such a simple thing were possible, Lee has written a candid essay about the state he was in when he first wrote it.One minute he was on the brink of screenwriting success, and the next his toilet had broken down and he was shitting in plastic bags that he left in bins in Finsbury Park, north London, the next morning. Can all that possibly be true? “In fact,” he says, gesticulating emphatically, “it was about 500 yards that way when I lived above a shop, where I had to shit in the bags. It’s funny – after my divorce, I’ve ended up living so close to where I lived in the 90s. But I’m in the whole house rather than one bit of it. So I’m one of life’s winners. Look at all these posters I can put up. It’s great.” He and the comedian Bridget Christie married in 2006, separated in 2021. They have two children, who are 15 and 19, and appear to be the platonic ideal of amicable divorcees. For a while he dated the comedian Rosie Holt, who heworked on a show with, but he is now seeing somebody else.The introductory essay concludes with a thought Lee absolutely must mean, because it’s poignant enough that it would choke him if he didn’t. “Never really having thought Pea Green Boat had meaning as such, it’s obvious to me as an older man what it’s about. We drift through life. We impose our hopes and desires on others, hopes and desires of which they are often unaware, or care not to reciprocate, or cannot reciprocate in the way we would wish. And then we die. Alone. But the journey to that ultimate destination can be beautiful, full of weird sights and strange creatures. And we should not wish it to be any other way.”But what slings and arrows of the past 25 years taught him that?He describes his “road to Damascus moment at 16”, when he saw a comedian supporting the Fall: “Before that, I thought you had to be a confident performer. I thought you had to run around like Ben Elton. Ted Chippington was silent and still to the point of having almost no presence whatsoever. A quarter of the audience would be in tears, and everyone else was really annoyed.” Lee was an immediate success in the 90s, on TV in adouble act with Richard Herring, out‑deadpanning each other; but the purer distillation of Stewart Lee-ness wasComedy Vehicle, which ran for four seasons on the BBC, from 2009 until 2016: half‑hour routines in front of a live audience, televised. Chris Morris script-edited and Armando Iannucci was an executive producer, and it was a high-water mark for the sheer art of comedy; incredible rigour and intellect and coherence, applied to the most ludic, surreal constructs. Later, he became the guy you read about politics (well, Brexit) if you wanted to keep yourself sane, and in his most recent tour, he is a guy nearing 60 whose intricate, absurdist satire has been out-absurded by the world around him, cracking open a new truthfulness that is both serious and incredibly funny.When Lee, less than a year out of university, in February 1990, won the Hackney Empire New Act of the Year, the judge (the comedy editor of City Limits, a huge tastemaker job back then) said, “That was great, mate. We need acts like you to get rid of all these Oxbridge wankers like David Baddiel,” Lee remembers now. “But I did go there” – he studied English literature at St Edmund Hall, Oxford – “and all the things I was supposed to get, Saturday Night Live, a paid gig at The Comedy Store, just disappeared.” In the 70s, if you were posh you might be the next Monty Python, “so you’d get a hearing. Whereas what we had was the misplaced arrogance and undeserved confidence that comes with having gone to a top university, but those doors were being gatekept. By people that wanted to be more fair, right?”View image in fullscreenLee in his show Stewart Lee vs the Man-Wulf.Photograph: Steve UllathorneBut what class is he, because he doesn’t read posh? He was adopted at the age of two, having spent his early life in foster care: “I know that I’m from the exact centre of society because the way that religious charities engineered adoption in those days was they were trying to place you in an entirely neutral environment.” His adoptive mum left school at 14, worked as a medical secretary, went to night school after she divorced his dad when he was four, worked her way up to being a GP practice manager. His dad was a rep for a cardboard company. He says of his birth father: “One of the few conversations I ever had with him was when he said an English degree was a colossal waste of time. I thought, ‘Well, actually, someone needs to know about Beowulf.’” Lee’s son is now studying English at uni; but he feels it’s becoming a luxury degree: “He’s relatively privileged. His parents have got two houses, and he can live in either one of them.” (Though this is not the typical take on being the child of divorced parents.)Lee’s route to Oxford came via a part-scholarship to Solihull, a private school, with the shortfall made up by “a masonic charity that provided educational help for orphans, waifs and strays. And I technically was an orphan, waif and stray, because I spent the first two years of my life in care.”double quotation markI’m not genetically connected to the world. It means you view it as otherHe didn’t give much thought to his origin story until he was about to become a dad himself, in 2006. “When Bridget was pregnant, I’m such a man, I thought, Oh, it’s quite hard work, isn’t it? I expect, if you had a baby, you would want to know what happened to it. Not even for me, but I thought I should find my mother just to tell her that I was all right. It opened a bit of a can of worms, really. But I’m in touch for 15 years or so now with my two half-sisters – my father’s children – and they’ve been great, I’m really glad I met them.”Not the half-sisters you’ve just been away with?“Yeah, they invited me to come.”So those were your birth father’s ashes?“Yeah. It’s interesting, when you’ve got nothing to go on, things seem hugely significant. Maybe that’s why I like The Wicker Man, because that’s where I’m from. My birth mother’s family can trace their roots back to leaving the village of Clonakilty in the west of Ireland during the famine. It’s famous for black puddings, which I really, really like.” The thinking around adoption has changed immeasurably since the 1968 Adoption Act. “Now, people view that as a very problematic start in life. Everyone in care for two years has post-traumatic stress disorder and we’re all drunk.” He’s still quite insistent that he was unscathed. When he was young, he read a “brilliant” book, Mister Fairweather and His Family, written as a tool to help adoptive children understand their origins. “It was about a bloke, and he was bored, so he got a cat. He was still bored, so he gets a dog, and he’s still bored, so he gets a wife. He’s still bored. And then they go, ‘Well, let’s get a baby’. That book is considered an absolute disaster now because it’s not child-centric. The baby isn’t supposed to be a pet for the parents. Anyway, I looked it up on Amazon, everyone was slagging it off, ‘This book ruined my life. I wanted to kill myself.’ And then there was one really good review of it. I thought, ‘That’s what I think. It’s a really nice little book with really nice pictures.’ And I’d written that review myself, 20 years ago, and forgotten.”Yet at the same time, what he describes is not an unscathed person. “Lots of comedians go, ‘We all do this, don’t we? Why do we all do this?’ Michael McIntyre, love him or hate him, is the king of that. Whereas what I do, I go, ‘Why doyoudo this? Why don’t you do what I do? Because I’m right.’ I think that’s partly through not being genetically connected to the world. It means you view it as other. I also think you view it as other if you’re a little bit on the spectrum, but that’s a hole that I’m not prepared to go down. Even though people have said I should.”View image in fullscreen‘We were ripped off in the way people in the music business are’ … Lee in 1998.Photograph: Julian Makey/ShutterstockLee’s 90s looked like living the dream – the successful double act with Herring, a TV series (Fist of Fun) – “but we were in a weird loop, the only way we could afford to do live work was if we were doing telly or radio. The last tour we did as a double act in 98 lost money, and the TV series didn’t get recommissioned, so it was just over, really.” He’d had mixed feelings about telly, anyway: “We were becoming much more like light entertainment, under pressure from the BBC, which wasn’t something I wanted to do.” But standup was his life, and his experience with a big comedy machine – where you’d always end up in debt no matter how big your crowds were, because comedy is always loss making – sounds as if it still stings. “We were only ripped off in the way that people in the music business are,” he says. But people in the music industry are ripped off royally.So by 2000, he was miserable. He’d stopped standup, about which he had a zealous perfectionism – “I’d gone to university, and I thought it was an incredible privilege. And I felt that I should ultimately try to do something with standup that was like a writer or someone creating a body of work” – and he was scratching a living reviewing music for Q magazine. Then he started working with Richard Thomas on Jerry Springer: The Opera.A few things have been lost about that musical and the controversy that followed: mainly how successful it was. It won a huge number of awards – Evening Standard, Critics’ Circle, Laurence Olivier, Theatregoers’ Choice – and musicals, when they fly, are career-defining. When the Christian right came after it, for blasphemy, it seemed almost like a curiosity – yes, there was a lot of profanity, it featured Jesus in a nappy, had zero respect for the crucifixion or any other sacred moments, but these were jokes-within-jokes, the butt of them never felt like Christianity at all. Legal actions brought against the BBC, for filming it, were given short shrift by the justice system. But, ultimately, the musical was brought down. Activists put pressure on local councils to pull it from theatres, a tour became impossible. For years, Lee was as likely to be approached in the street by someone wanting to know “Why didn’t you do it about Muslims?”, as by an obsessive fan. “Those people are still in play now,” Lee says. “Stephen Green, who was the self-styled reverend that led the campaign against it, was recently put up by thefake grassroots organisation Restore Trustto be on the board of the National Trust.”It was an inflection point in Lee’s career, just not in the way he’d have planned. “After that, I thought, right, things can get banned. You can be stopped from saying things. So it’s quite important that the things you say are worth saying. I didn’t becomeMark ThomasorLenny Bruceovernight. I did just start to think, there should be something important in this.”Even at his most political, Lee’s routines are never agitprop, being too surreal, resisting interpretation, not colouring within the lines; but for years, since Comedy Vehicle,when he takes an issue head‑on, it’s been magisterial. Hisimmigration monologue(“Bloody Indians, coming over here, inventing us a national cuisine … bloody French, coming over here, doubting transubstantiation …”) – “That’s become my parrot sketch.” He traces its origins to being in the car, listening to then-Ukip politician Paul Nuttall “say a really stupid thing about Bulgarians, so I went home, listened to the programme on catch-up, transcribed it, and the whole thing was done in half an hour. Whereas some things take years.” There’s a bit that’s resurfaced recently, sinceRod Liddle died: “It was basically 20 minutes of me, trying to talk about him, but I keep getting distracted by bits of food on his clothes. Loads of people didn’t know who he was, either, which made it even funnier – this long routine about a man nobody had heard of, with suet on himself. I remember one of those rightwing papers said the whole point of the routine was that the foods were working class. So I despised the working class. But, actually, I was thinking about things that were quite oleaginous: Angel Delight, pork pie jelly. It never would have occurred to me that it was a class warfare statement.”Brexit reradicalised him, and out of that came his Observer column, which was and remains a completely unparalleled display of what comic polemic can do (he now writes acolumn for The Nerve, an online magazine funded by Carole Cadwalladr and others. “What I learned from that was that you couldn’t afford to leave room for doubt about what you meant, because if you did, bad faith actors on the right would take legal action. You can’t be funny in the same way. You have to make sure that the sentence is bulletproof.”He now looks at the comics and personas his children “would call ‘edgelords’”, at Jeremy Clarkson, “suddenly going, ‘Oh, everything’s died in my farm. I spent a quarter of a century saying climate change was not worth worrying about, and only snowflakes cared about it.’ Dave Chappelle has started saying, ‘When I was taking the piss out of trans people, I didn’t mean for you to restrict their rights and kill them.’” Doing gigs in Colchester, he went to Wivenhoe, “the hippy town of Essex”, which now has a Reform council. “A councillor had said to a woman I know there, a lesbian, ‘Oh, withdrawing funding for Pride is coming from head office. We don’t feel like that. Don’t worry about it.’ But they’re still enacting the policies. And I expect, at the risk of committing the nuclear option, there were probably Nazi officials saying that to Jews in the 30s. ‘You’ve got to wear this badge, don’t worry about it, it’s coming from Berlin.’ All those people that played with that stuff – congratulations. The world’s on fire. Trump’s showing no sign of withdrawing from fossil fuels, there are councils where they’re literally enacting policies against LGBTQ+ people and removing references to climate change from council literature. So you’ve won, haven’t you? Is that what you wanted?”When Stewart Lee is out and about now, “pretty much everyone that stops you” – he always says “you” when he means “me” – “is really nice. They say it’s important to them, because they feel that no one talks about the things they’re interested in. They say they’ve watched me for a long time, or that they were going to kill themselves and they laughed their way out of it. Someone online said that I attracted an insular cadre of pseudo-intellectual, prematurely bald middle-aged men. I thought, ‘Yeah, that’ll do.’ I wish more women would come, though. I think it’s sort of perceived as something women wouldn’t like.”I think women think it’s going to be laced with references that they don’t get, I offer. Then there’s a bit of a pause.“I do joke about that,” he says eventually. “When I say, ‘You can’t come if you haven’t read this book’, that is supposed to be a joke.” Then he says, out of nowhere: “I think I was miserable for a lot of this century. It’s not really anyone’s fault.” He says it so matter-of-factly I have to double check.What, this century now?“Yes, the whole of the 21st century, until a few years ago. I like my kids, my kids are good fun.”double quotation markThe idea of leaving a legacy is entirely spurious because there’s obviously no future for humanityView image in fullscreenReturning to Pea Green Boat, he says: “The Owl and the Pussy-cat seems to be about a pair of characters of indeterminate gender, going to a place where normal laws are suspended, where a cat can marry an owl. I think it’s about the tragedy ofLear’s own life [he could never live openly as a gay man]. When I read it now, having lived a life, it’s also a little bit about me. I don’t really seem equipped to do certain sorts of things in life.”What kind of things?“That owl doesn’t know how to deal with another person and ends up eating their decomposing corpse out of a bag. There’s something in that about a failure to relate to people.”You don’t really think you can’t relate to a person?“Why do you end up choosing the life you’ve got? I spend most of my life on the move on motorways. I know a lot of people had a bad time in lockdown, but when I couldn’t do that any more, I found it really difficult.”So being on the road was an escape hatch from intimacy, and once you lost it, you found yourself unequal to the overall task?“Well, yeah. Not up to the job.”Mindful that he’ll be 60 soonish (in just over 18 months), he wants everything he’s done to be compiled into “some kind of physical media package, 13 DVDs with the same spine design, numbered”. It sounds kind of modest, but important. “Partly why I went round the bend in the mid part of this century, between about 2005 and 2015, was because I wrote about 15 hours of standup in eight years. No one’s ever done that. And now I think I’d like to at least show that I did that. Although the idea of leaving a legacy is entirely spurious because there’s obviously no future for humanity.”Hang on, I say, you say you went round the bend between 2005 and 2015, and you went round the bend in Covid?“Yeah, different. Worse.”So was there a period between 2015 and 2020 when you were the right side of the bend?“No.” He smiles. It’s funny because it’s true.Pea Green Boat by Stewart Lee, illustrated by David Waywell, is published by Ebury on 3 September (£16.99). To buy a copy for £15.29, go toguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsStewart LeeComedy (Stage)TV comedyComedy (Culture)TelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in Spain
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in Spain
Content: Willem Dafoe in Late Fame and Zendaya in Dune: Part ThreeComposite: Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreenWillem Dafoe in Late Fame and Zendaya in Dune: Part ThreeComposite: Guardian Design/AlamyAutumn arts preview 2026MoviesTom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in SpainSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?All release dates are UK and subject to changeLaurence Phelan,Andrew PulverandCatherine ShoardSun 30 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTShareLate FameView image in fullscreenPoetic postal worker … Willem Dafoe with  Greta Lee in Late Fame.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWillem Dafoe is typically grizzled and poetic for this study of a near-retirement postal worker who, it turns out, was a beatnik rhymester of cachet – but no lasting renown – back in the day, and who has now been rediscovered by a new generation of literary hipsters. Director Kent Jones, adapting a novella by Arthur “La Ronde” Schnitzler, was the longtime head of the New York film festival; he might be in for a spot of late fame himself.AP4 SeptemberEverybody Digs Bill EvansGrant Gee’s stylishly monochrome, coolly composed musical biopic finds the great jazz pianist at something of a crisis point in 1961, grieving for his bassist, facing down some demons, painfully thin and heroin addicted – and living with his parents while he tries to kick the habit. Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf are terrific as Mr and Mrs Evans, while Anders Danielsen Lie stars as the tortured artist on the cusp of making musical history and quitting.LP11 SeptemberPractical Magic 2If you wait long enough, everything will go into development for sequel, but they don’t always happen. This one, almost randomly, has:Sandra Bullockand Nicole Kidman’s nicely judged 90s witch tale, with equal helpings of empowerment and romance, is broomsticking into cinemas. Bullock and Kidman are back, a quarter century on, with the younger generation represented by Joey King and Maisie Williams.AP11 SeptemberQueen at SeaView image in fullscreenActing masterclass … Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Queen at SeaPhotograph: © Seafaring LLCAnother late-period acting masterclass fromTom Courtenayin a shattering drama from Lance Hammer. Courtenay plays Martin, whose wife (Anna Calder-Marshall) is in the grip of dementia. He tries to keep their connection alive with sex. But can she consent? Is it rape? Her daughter by an earlier marriage, played by Juliette Binoche, certainly thinks so, setting the stage for a heartbreakingly emotional confrontation.AP18 SeptemberDe Gaulle: LibertéNational heroes don’t come much more totemic than Charles de Gaulle, wartime resistance leader turned peacetime statesman. This is the second instalment of the two part film in which Simon Abkarian plays the legendary general as the momentum to liberate Paris builds up towards the end of the second world war.AP18 SeptemberShaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy BottomEveryone’s favourite flock is back for a Halloween instalment, 11 years afterShaun the Sheep Movie(masterpiece) andFarmageddon(superb). This plasticine mashup of Frankenstein and Weird Science sees Shaun brewing up a potion to supersize pumpkins ahead of the autumn fair, while the farmer turns to a hair-restoring lotion to pluck up the courage to ask the vet on a date. Hope the two bottles don’t get muddled …Catherine Shoard18 SeptemberSense and SensibilityView image in fullscreenAusten for the Insta age … Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesThirty-one years after Emma Thompson’s swift, witty take on Austen’s classic – still much loved today – Georgia Oakley (Blue Jean) gives us a version for the Instagram age, replete withHamnet-ish strings and many shots of women in fields with closeups on bugs. Daisy Edgar-Jones is Elinor, Esmé Creed-Miles is Marianne, George MacKay is Edward Ferrars and Frank Dillane is the dastardly Willoughby.CS25 SeptemberHer Private HellWe nearly lostNicolas Winding Refna couple of years back, when the Danish enfant terrible had a heart scare. Happily, everyone’s favourite sadomasochistic softie is back with a sci-fi set in a weirdly misty futuristic metropolis haunted by a “deadly and elusive entity”. Sophie Thatcher and Charles Melton star. There will be blood.CS25 SeptemberKnife: The Attempted Murder of Salman RushdieOscar-winning film-maker Alex Gibney tackles the shocking assassination attempt on the great writer in this unsparing and remarkably graphic documentary featuring the man himself, as well as his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths.CS2 OctoberDiggerView image in fullscreenOligarch oilman … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTaking a well-earned rest from running and jumping and saving the world, Tom Cruise teams with Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman,The Revenant) to do some acting, not action. He’s still trying to save the world but here he is the paunchy and balding oligarch oilman Digger Rockwell, who deigns to intervene to avert an environmental calamity of his own making. Filmed in VistaVision and billed as “a comedy of catastrophic proportions”, it looks like Dr Strangelove with shades of Les Grossman, Cruise’s hilarious cameo as a film studio head in Tropic Thunder.LP2 OctoberThe Social ReckoningView image in fullscreenGeek chic … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyJeremy Strong pulls on the geek-chic fleeces and takes over from Jesse Eisenberg in Aaron Sorkin’s what-Zuckerberg-did-next companion piece toThe Social Network. Oscar-winningAnorastar Mikey Madison plays whistleblower Frances Haugen, who went public about all of Facebook’s algorithmic wrongdoings in 2021.LP9 OctoberThe UprisingView image in fullscreenA riot … Andrew Garfield leads a peasants’ revolt.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyTaxes are too high, the boy-king Richard II is out of touch with his subjects and serfdom needs abolishing … say Wat?! Andrew Garfield plays the hunky farmer turned sword-wielding leader of a revolt against tyranny in a medieval action film from Paul Greengrass, the director of several docudrama classics and multiple Jason Bourne movies.LP9 OctoberKlara and the SunJenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered companion robot yearning and learning to become a real family member, in a colourful adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s soulful sci-fi novel byTaika Waititi. Waititi looks to have mined the story for every bit of comedy he can, and Ortega inhabits the uncanny valley with bright-eyed good cheer. Amy Adams and Natasha Lyonne also star.LP23 OctoberAli G: Who Iz I?View image in fullscreenCourting controversy? … Sacha Baron Cohen, who returns as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?, is seen in character at this year’s Wimbledon tennis tournament.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyIt’s the return of the West Staines Massiv, Mr Shell Suit himself, Alistair Graham – otherwise known as Ali G.Sacha Baron Cohen(for it is he) has unretired the character and has shot a new film in secret … though perhaps not so secret, as he was spotted in full costume at Cotswold Wildlife Park and at Wimbledon this summer. Baron Cohen is in the director’s seat for the first time; it’ll be interesting, as much as anything else, what sort of fist he makes of it.AP23 OctoberFatherlandPolish film-makerPaweł Pawlikowskimade his early strides in the UK, with a series of brilliant literary documentaries and then a shift into features including Last Resort and My Summer of Love.
