Since moving back to mainland Europe, Pawlikowski has gone from strength to strength; this latest, his third black-and-white film in a row, takes us into Germany of the immediate postwar era, using a trip by novelist-in-exile Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika (Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller) back to their homeland as a way of examining both sides of the east-west divide.AP23 OctoberGentle MonsterLéa Seydoux gives an awards-tipped performance as a musician and mother whose comfortable domestic life fractures the moment that police arrive at her door to arrest her husband and confiscate his hard drives. An impressive handling of tricky material by Austrian film-maker Marie Kreutzer, inspired in part by the arrest of an actor in her previous film,Corsage, forpossession of child sexual abuse imagery.LP30 OctoberAnimolAfter So Solid Crew, Top Boy and – yes – Grange Hill, Ashley Walters steps into the director’s chair for this jailhouse drama written by The Football Factory’s Nick Love. Tut Nyuot is a new arrival who pals up with Polish kid Vladyslav Baliuk; Sekou Diaby is the fearsome inmate who runs things, and Stephen Graham is on hand as a prison care worker. Tough stuff, not unlikeWastemanfrom earlier this year. AP30 OctoberI Love BoostersView image in fullscreenMellow yellow … Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige and Keke Palmer in I Love Boosters.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyKeke Palmer, LaKeith Stanfield and Demi Moore star in this wacky, maximalist, anticapitalist agitprop and fashion-biz satire weird-a-thon from rapper and Sorry to Bother You creatorBoots Riley. It’s a madcap, colour-saturated crime caper about a gang of shoplifters raiding fashion stores to redistribute style to the masses. There are also claymation sequences, cartoony slapstick and demons.LP30 OctoberWickerOlivia Colman continues her journey into the wilder reaches of the cinematic imagination, and you can’t say she hasn’t earned it. This is one of her weirdest films yet: a kind of satirical fairytale in which she plays a fisher whose pungency is such she is doomed to remain single, so she gets the local basket-maker to make her a husband out of, yes, wicker. (Cue wicker sex, for those interested.) It’s a film that has produced divided reactions, shall we say, but will definitely kick up a stink, to coin a phrase.AP30 OctoberGodzilla Minus ZeroView image in fullscreenA monster of a film … Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyThe 2023 period-set Japanese kaiju epicGodzilla Minus Onewas almost certainly the most real, most sincere, most impressive Godzilla film made to that point – and there have been about 40 so that’s no small boast. Writer-director Takashi Yamazaki brings back the surviving characters for the follow-up – and it’s filmed for Imax, to make all the enormo-destruction extra enormo.LP6 NovemberWild Horse NineAfter the comparatively sombre and reflective Banshees of Inisherin,Martin McDonaghrevisits larkier In Bruges territory with this bickering odd-couple black comedy. In place of Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson as hitmen in Belgium, we have John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents/hitmen on Easter Island, prior to the 1973 Chilean coup.LP6 NovemberI Play RockyView image in fullscreenEvery underdog has its day … Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyWhen Rocky took on all comers at the box office and Oscars in 1976, the legend of its production fed into its rousing tale of an underdog having his day. Sylvester Stallone was a penniless nobody when he reputedly wrote the script in three days – then turned down six-figure offers for it, as he insisted on playing the lead role himself. Now Green Book’s Peter Farrelly directs a biopic telling that story, and fires up the brassy theme music to rouse audiences all over again.LP6 NovemberLa Bola NegraThis won the best director award at Cannes, jointly with Fatherland, for its sweeping, time-crossing evocation of queer identity and experience in Spain. Starting in the early 1930s, it moves from Spain’s suffocating patriarchy through the turmoil of the civil war years, and on to the 21st century, showing how persecution and trauma descend through the decades. Penélope Cruz puts in a cameo as a nightclub singer.AP6 NovemberJosephineBeth de Araújo made a splash and won the top two prizes at Sundance with this raw and intense study of the after effects of a sexual assault on the family of an eight-year-old girl who witnesses it, has nightmares about it and is called on to testify against the perpetrator. Channing Tatum gives a nuanced turn as the traumatised girl’s father.LP20 NovemberFocker-in-LawView image in fullscreenNew blood … Ariana Grande with Robert De Niro in next gen Focker-in-Law.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyAriana Grande is the new blood added to the Focker family in this next-gen fourquel to Meet the Parents. Or she will be, if avuncular grandpaRobert De Niroadmits her to his circle of trust, and if overprotective prospective father-in-law Ben Stiller doesn’t do as was done unto him all the way back in 2000, and put her off marrying his son.LP25 NovemberThe Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff BoothThe cool-under-fire character Brad Pitt played in Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood gets to perform more laid-back (anti-)heroics in a spin-off episode – but now he has been promoted from a stuntman to a studio fixer. Twice upon a time, Tarantino has written the script butDavid Fincher– whom Pitt previously worked with on Seven and Fight Club – directs.LP25 NovemberI See Buildings Fall Like LightningThis is British director Clio Barnard’s first film since Ali & Ava in 2021, put together with what we now know is her customary empathy and intelligence, in a drama about life choices and the way things work out differently for different people. Five friends get together for a birthday; some have made good, others less so, and they each face up to their uncertain futures. The title refers to the demolition of tower blocks in Birmingham: a key symbolic event.AP4 DecemberAvengers: DoomsdayCan the Avengers (Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Paul Rudd, et al) unite with the X-Men (Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Channing Tatum), the Thunderbolts (Florence Pugh, David Harbour, Sebastian Stan) and the Wakandans (Letitia Wright, Winston Duke) to save the universe fromsuperhero fatigueDoctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr)? Marvel is betting a cast this star-studded must surely obliterate any and all resistance.LP18 DecemberDune: Part ThreeView image in fullscreenReturning … Jason Momoa as Hayt in Dune: Part Three.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesThe newDunefilm finally arrives, completing the projected trilogy conceived on a colossal scale from director Denis Villeneuve, featuring Timothée Chalamet’s floppy-haired Paul Atreides. This one is adapted from Dune Messiah, Frank Herbert’s follow-up to his original doorstep-size chunk of space fantasy, in which the emperor’s holy war is lurching out of control. Zendaya, Florence Pugh and Jason Momoa all return, with the ubiquitous Robert Pattinson brought in to play chief nasty Scytale, out to overthrow Paul. If this goes well, there are – count them – four more Dune novels on the shelf … be very afraid …AP18 December

title: The Bridge review – a funny, furious odyssey through occupation | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistance
Content: Witty … Writer and actor Alaa Shehada.View image in fullscreenWitty … Writer and actor Alaa Shehada.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Bridge review – a funny, furious odyssey through occupationAssembly George Square studios, EdinburghWriter and actor Alaa Shehada turns a simple bus trip from the West Bank into a vivid tale of bureaucracy, humiliation and resistanceMark FisherSun 30 Aug 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the simplicity of the task that gives this story heft. Recalling his formative years in the West Bank, actor and writer Alaa Shehada is asked by his mother to go on a bus journey that would take a couple of hours in any other part of the world.His mission is to deliver a plastic jerry can filled with the family’s home-pressed olive oil to his aunt in Jordan. His obstacle is the 180m crossing point known variously as the Dignity Bridge, the Allenby Bridge and the King Hussein Bridge, depending on your political standpoint.In this follow-up toThe Horse of Jenin, Shehada describes the journey with a cartoonist’s eye for human detail and a campaigner’s ear for injustice.With broad physicality, he takes on a cast of characters from the self-aggrandising taxi driver who picks him up to the smothering old lady who sits next to him on the bus and the cold-eyed Israeli teenagers who man the checkpoints. The heat is stifling, the air conditioning is ineffectual and the level of bureaucracy staggering, with each passenger laden with an all-or-nothing litany of passports, receipts and tickets.Shehada is a witty performer, brimming with life, but his tale is one of constant humiliation. This is the only way for West Bank Palestinians to reach the outside world, yet they must face arbitrary closures, endless queues, random arrests and disempowering regulations. After hours of indignity, they dream of their own international airport.Co-written and directed by Sam Beale for the Palestine Comedy Club, The Bridge is a tamer, more focused piece than The Horse of Jenin, but is no less urgent. For Shehada, the olive oil is not just a gift but a symbol of a violated land that isbeing bulldozed by settlersto this day. A story performed with fun is driven home with fury.AtAssembly George Square studios, Edinburgh, 30 August, thenBush theatre, London, 28 October–11 NovemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Hamza Yassin’s delightful  birding odyssey in Africa | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The wildlife presenter gets very excited about brilliant birds of prey in Kenya. Plus: Suranne Jones returns in cop drama Vigil. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The wildlife presenter gets very excited about brilliant birds of prey in Kenya. Plus: Suranne Jones returns in cop drama Vigil. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Like a kid at Christmas … Hamza: African Birds of Prey on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Silverback Films/Pauline KyaloView image in fullscreenLike a kid at Christmas … Hamza: African Birds of Prey on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Silverback Films/Pauline KyaloTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Hamza Yassin’s delightful  birding odyssey in AfricaThe wildlife presenter gets very excited about brilliant birds of prey in Kenya. Plus: Suranne Jones returns in cop drama Vigil. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil HarrisonandGraeme VirtueSun 30 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHamza: African Birds of Prey7pm, BBC One“I’m like a kid who’s just been shown their Christmas present!” It’s always a delight to see Hamza Yassin in the wild. He starts this new series about incredible but endangered birds in Kenya, where the martial eagle – huge yellow eyes, terrifying talons, thighs of steel – blows him away. Then, he makes a case for why we should love vultures more, and somehow pulls it off.Hollie RichardsonModern Classics at the Proms8pm, BBC FourCurated by Guardian columnist Tom Service, here is an exciting collection of new music at this year’s Proms to make note of. As well as three world premieres, expect a captivating bassoon concerto, and chats with the big names of tomorrow, plus composers Thomas Adès and Gabriela Ortiz.HRVigil9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenCold as ice … Longacre (Rose Leslie) and Silva (Suranne Jones) head north in Vigil on BBC One.Photograph: CREDIT LINE:BBC/World Productions/Mark MainzDCI Amy Silva (Suranne Jones) is off the hook for now, as this twisty cop drama returns. She’s now shacked up with DI Kirsten Longacre (Rose Leslie) and, to everyone’s slight surprise, it’s Longacre who has been selected to investigate a diplomatically sensitive murder in the Arctic. However, as events spiral, Silva might be forced to abandon her supervisory role and get involved.Phil HarrisonTrigger Point9pm, ITV1The magnificent Vicky McClure returns as flinty explosives officer Lana “Wash” Washington for a fourth series of this slick bomb disposal thriller. Judging by Wash’s fraught therapy sessions, her high-stress job is taking its toll. But when a C4-laden truck starts rolling toward central London, she dives into peril without hesitation.Graeme VirtueThe Terror: Devil in Silver9pm, Sky AtlanticView image in fullscreenTrue horror … Dan Stevens and Chinaza Uche in The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.The horror of this drama lies in the knowledge that, while the dysfunction of the mental institution is real, so is the distress and confusion of the inmates. The paranoia experienced by Pepper and Coffee is manifesting in ever more outlandish theories – another excuse for the fiendish Dr Walter to intervene again.PHLove Cheats10.15pm, Channel 4The fallout from Australian EDM DJ Olivia Nervo’s relationship with businessman Matthew Pringle travelled as far as the Houses of Parliament as it was seen as a possible example of reproductive coercion. title: Mere Mortals review – a dazzling, maddening ballet for the AI age | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: San Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s box
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: San Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s box
Content: Supple, sprightly, puckish … Wei Wang in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSupple, sprightly, puckish … Wei Wang in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMere Mortals review – a dazzling, maddening ballet for the AI ageEdinburgh PlayhouseSan Francisco Ballet brings a spectacular collision of dance, music and digital wizardry to the Edinburgh international festival in this bold reimagining of Pandora’s boxLyndsey WinshipSun 30 Aug 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is a spectacular show. Literally, it is full of spectacle: as much a visual extravaganza as it is a concert, as it is dance – and a gloriously maddening piece of dance at that. The dancers are as impressive as you’d expect fromSan Francisco Ballet, the US’s oldest professional ballet company, and the splashy concept is bold: artistic director Tamara Rojo commissioned choreographer Aszure Barton, composer Sam Shepherd (AKA electronic producer Floating Points) and multidisciplinary artists Hamill Industries, their starting point being the myth of Pandora’s box, transposed to the current world of AI technology and what unknowns we might be unleashing.Hamill Industries, who used some AI in their creation process, unleash something transfixing on a giant screen above the stage: morphing, pulsating pixels that look like lava or the surface of the sun. It’s intoxicating, easily dragging attention away from the dancers’ bodies (this may be the whole point – more on this later). Those dancers appear en masse in strict manoeuvres at driving tempo. Are they an army of mortals, gods, automatons or lines of code? Who knows. But they are moulded into large-scale moving images by Barton just as Pandora is moulded from clay in the best bit of integration between the digital and physical worlds, countless hands crafting this first woman out of dust.View image in fullscreenFuture shock … Wei Wang (left) and Jennifer Stahl in Mere Mortals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBarton is a magpie of a choreographer, always unpredictable, classical virtuosity sewn in among countless other ideas in unstoppable phrases. Jennifer Stahl as Pandora is an impressive creation, for sure, and Wei Wang is great: supple, sprightly, puckish. He represents Hope, although you wouldn’t know that without doing a bit of research. Choreographers are not duty-bound to enact a narrative; the Pandora tale is merely a creative trigger, they’d say, but in a story with such clear dramatic beats, and such a clever contemporary parallel, it does seem a waste to essentially throw that away.There are a few scenes where humans come to the fore, with black-clad dancers just about visible against a black backdrop: Prometheus (Joseph Walsh) and Epimetheus (Harrison James) being competitive brothers who hug and shove in one motion; a pas de deux for Pandora and her husband in which Barton’s unconventional choreography steers clear of romantic tropes and their bodies make uncommon shapes that fold in on each other.View image in fullscreenWild … Mere Mortals at the Edinburgh international festival.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianShepherd’s score is really impressive, a hybrid of electronics and orchestra (played live by the Royal Scottish National Orchestra). It’s full of drama and contrast, tension, propulsive urgency (hints of Stravinsky) and fascinating textures: slippery strings, woozily lurching or ricocheting arpeggios.At the moment that presumably represents the opening of the box (or the AI floodgates), the screens go into hyperdrive, vomiting up dazzling imagery. Then they go dark and we’re left with only bodies, a new world – black catsuits swapped for fabulous, shining gold. Precious bodies – is this the idea? Or mere robots? What the dancers do – how they relate, how they move – doesn’t really change between the two worlds. There’s no choreographic revelation. No judgment, it seems. Perhaps an exhortation to stop being distracted by the sparkly baubles of the AI gods and notice the real people in front of you. Or perhaps no moral at all, just a wild sensory experience, and the strangest non-ending, with the most human thing of all – feeling – frustratingly absent.AtEdinburgh Playhouseuntil 30 August, thenSadler’s Wells, London, 9-12 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceEdinburgh festivalFestivalsFloating PointsSan Francisco BalletreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s what saved me’: Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance on the prison drama workshop that brought them together | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performing
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: A masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performing
Content: Brothers in arms … Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanView image in fullscreenBrothers in arms … Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanTheatreInterview‘That’s what saved me’: Darren Raymond and Mark Rylance on the prison drama workshop that brought them togetherJN BenjaminA masterclass led by the actor helped set Raymond on a new path. Now the head of a theatre company, he has coaxed his friend back to the stage for a show to encourage young people to fall in love with performingSun 30 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDarren Raymond doesn’t remember having any significant interest in acting when he was growing up. And when he metMark Rylancefor the first time, on Christmas Eve 2004, he had never heard of the multi-award winning actor. These days, things are very different: Raymond is the artistic director of Intermission Youth, the London-based arts charity and theatre, and is directing his friend Rylance in the lead role of Tartuffe (Remixed), Raymond’s adaptation of the Molière play, which opens at London’s Marylebone theatre this week.It’s fair to say neither could have anticipated they’d still be in touch this long after their initial meeting. “Unlikely companions” is a tired cliche by this point, but that doesn’t make it any less true to say that on the surface, the two had very little in common. Raymond was a young twentysomething raised on an inner-city housing estate and serving a prison sentence at HMP Brixton. Meanwhile Rylance was twice his age, a successful professional actor, and artistic director of Shakespeare’s Globe. Nevertheless that meeting, at a Shakespeare workshop in the prison, turned into a professional connection, which soon evolved into a solid friendship.double quotation markIn terms of my debt to Shakespeare, my debt to all the great teachers I had, this is it – this will be it until the day I dieMark RylanceRylance has been a supporter of Intermission, the charity Raymond set up 20 years ago – which helps to transform the lives of young people aged 11-30+ through theatre – since the very early days. Its flagship programme takes 80 trainees a year for a regular schedule of masterclasses, pastoral support and professional performances. In a 2008 interview on Radio 4, Raymond mentioned the positive impact of his and Rylance’s Christmas Eve meeting and how it inspired his vision for Intermission. Rylance was listening, and was prompted to visit the theatre’s headquarters at St Saviour’s Church in Knightsbridge. “I was really knocked out by it, the production was everything I’d been looking for,” Rylance says of the performance he saw. We’re speaking today at Intermission’s temporary base at Omnibus theatre in Clapham – the organisation has struggled to secure a suitable permanent home since being asked to leave the church in 2019.Intermission’s output is why Rylance thinks it holds such a critical place in the context of the industry. It offers free-of-charge, rigorous, professional-standard training that produces high-quality results. For many, particularly those from working-class backgrounds, such an opportunity would be otherwise unaffordable. Rylance firmly believes in giving back, but in the current climate his preference is to invest in grassroots arts initiatives over major institutions. For him, that feels more impactful. “I don’t support my drama school, I don’t support the Globe any more, or the RSC,” he says. “In terms of my debt to Shakespeare, my debt to all the great teachers I had as a young person, this is it for me – this will be it until the day I die.”View image in fullscreenDarren Raymond in rehearsals for Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorRaymond’s own debt to Shakespeare started with that workshop he reluctantly attended while in prison. He was confused when his friend told him he’d signed them both up for drama classes, but saw it as an excuse to get more time out of their shared cell. On the day of the workshop about 20 prisoners were greeted by Dr  Bruce Wall, co-founder of the London Shakespeare Workout – a charity that uses work by major cinematic, musical and choreographic writers and thinkers, along with Shakespeare, to promote confidence and relationship-building among its participants.Casting his mind back to the first session with Wall, Raymond and his friend didn’t know what to expect. “This guy’s come in, like, ‘Drama!’, all flapping hands and flamboyant. I dunno how he got away with that because it’s just him and there’s 15 to 20 inmates in there. All serious inmates.” The group was initially hesitant, but Wall’s upbeat energy proved irresistible – the enthusiasm soon spread. Raymond remembers an exercise where participants were given a line of Shakespeare’s text and had to respond using their own words. The group reacted to Raymond’s contribution with a chorus of oohs and aahs. “When I look back, that was a really profound moment in my life because it was the first time I knew my words could have any kind of impact. When I left the session, Bruce said: ‘Well done, I thought you were excellent.’ I don’t know if he said it to everybody – probably did. But it meant something to me.”double quotation markI didn’t know what an audition was. But I went, met him, done the audition – and then they cast me as OthelloDarren RaymondBack in their cell, Raymond and his friend were energised by their first drama workshop experience. “Normally we’d be talking about how to get one back over the system, but that day we were talking about Shakespeare,” he remembers. Wanting to replicate that feeling, he returned every week, eventually becoming an advocate for the group – encouraging others to get involved, petitioning the prison to keep the initiative going when it was under threat of closure, and even declining relocation to a lower category prison with fewer restrictions as well as privileges such as home visits, knowing that the move would mean he’d no longer be able to attend. Nobody had ever turned down a move to a “D-Cat” prison before, the governor told him, adding: “You must be really into this drama thing!”Raymond’s commitment earned him the opportunity to represent the prison in a poetry convention, where he first met Rob Gillion, an actor turned reverend who maintained an active interest in the life-changing power of the arts. “For some reason there was a lot of clergy present, I don’t know why. I remember [Gillion] showing a real interest in my story, but I didn’t think anything of it,” he says. He didn’t know it at the time, but that was the beginning of his artistic journey.View image in fullscreenDarren Raymond and Mark Rylance.Photograph: Seamus RyanAt one of the final Shakespeare sessions Raymond attended, he met Rylance, who was guest-facilitating the session along with his late wifeClaire van Kampen. The group had been told Rylance was an acclaimed actor and the artistic director of Shakespeare’s Globe – “nobody knew what the Globe was!”, Raymond laughs. He describes his first impression as an anticlimax: “He’s come in with his shorts and sandals, looking like some dishevelled guy off the road. None of us really paid any mind to his stature. Nobody knew any Shakespeare, and that was a good thing – it made the playing field more even.”Rylance remembers that first meeting well. “It was a small workshop, with just four young men,” he says. “Each had learned a soliloquy and I listened to them. There was a definite marriage of what’s mortal and immortal, because of the interweaving of their own language right next to Shakespeare. The Shakespeare stuff will live as long as humanity lasts on the planet, but the mortal lives of these young people brought alongside the immortal, is very thrilling and delightful to me. That’s what was happening with those four guys that day”.The exercise was a revelation for the group. “We could talk to him very quickly” recalls Raymond, “and that was testament to how he came to us in the room. The way he spoke to us about Othello … it was riveting listening to these stories because he related it to us and the situation we were in and the lives we were living. At the end of it, he said: ‘Look, we don’t have to revere this work in the way people make you think you need to. Use whatever you want from it – take whatever you want and use it however you want.’ That’s what I do now. That’s what saved me.”Some time after his release from HMP Brixton, Raymond received an out-of-the-blue call from Wall – an invitation to audition for London Shakespeare Workshop’s national tour of Othello. “I really didn’t know what it meant. I didn’t know what an audition was really, I didn’t know what a UK tour was. But I went, met him, done the audition – and then they cast me as Othello.” Rehearsals took place at St Saviour’s Church, where Gillion was the resident vicar.View image in fullscreenMark Rylance and Blanche Williams in rehearsals for Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorThe relationship between Raymond and Gillion would be transformative – “I was really inspired by Rob, he was a role model to me,” Raymond says. They stayed in touch following the end of the tour, and when Gillion later took a sabbatical to do some international travelling, he asked Raymond to move into the vicarage and keep an eye on the place while he was away. With hindsight, he realises they both knew the vicarage probably didn’t need anybody to look after it but rather the “favour” was a calculated act of kindness in the knowledge that a young Raymond would have been too proud to accept the help he needed. In 2006 Gillion invited him to run Intermission theatre.Staging full productions has always been part of Intermission’s regular activity. Over the years Raymond has adapted 15 Shakespeare plays, each time weaving contemporary issues into the classical texts in order to demystify the language and make the pieces feel more relevant for a new generation of actors. The upcoming production of Tartuffe (Remixed), however, is the company’s biggest production to date, and a rare instance of a cast that brings together Intermission graduates and actors who have taken other, sometimes more traditional routes into the industry.double quotation markThis feels like a natural path forward for me as I try to figure out a new story to my lifeMark RylanceRylance wasn’t sure if he’d return to do any more theatre. “This is the first time I’ll be directed by Darren. First time back in the theatre since my wife has died, too.” Van Kampen passed away in early 2025 after being diagnosed with cancer. “When you lose your wife of 35 years – I keep thinking of wonderfulJoan Littlewoodwho, when she lost Jerry Raffles, stepped out of that theatre and never stepped in any theatre again. And that’s a temptation – but it’s like when you think you have a death wish but its not that you want to kill yourself – but you want to kill a certain way you’ve been living.”Returning to stage acting feels like part of a ritual of remembrance for his wife, who was also a passionate supporter of Intermission’s work: “It was something we gave money to, something we supported. And so this feels like a natural path forward for me as I try to figure out a new story to my life. What’s the story of my life without her?”For Rylance, Intermission is part of the journey of his life, and he’s not alone. When it comes to the organisation’s impact, there have been many success stories that have come from the training programme. The actor Tosin Cole graduated from the very first Intermission cohort in 2009, and has since worked consistently across TV, film and theatre. His CV includes series regular roles in Hollyoaks, Doctor Who, and most recently as the lead in Supacell on Netflix. “I never really had aspirations to become an actor,” he says. “It was just a cool thing to do on a Saturday.” It was going to Intermission that helped him not only realise his talent but also supported him to develop the tools he needed to take advantage of the opportunities that came his way.Asked what he thinks he would be doing if he wasn’t an actor, Cole laughs heartily as he says “Boy!”, elongating the short syllable as he diverts his gaze. That’s south London speak for let’s not even go there. Does he think there are still challenges facing young people who want to pursue a career in acting? “For a start, we need a lot more different types of stories from different types of cultures. [As Black people] our history is rich and full of those stories, and we are capable of telling them.”He’s also an advocate for more spaces like Intermission’s original venue to exist, lamenting the loss of the city’s youth clubs and adventure playgrounds. “That place was super special. It’s sad now when you’re in Knightsbridge and you walk past and see the place vacant.” The church has since been converted to a luxury home and was on the market for £35m last year. “Look at any artist or musician that’s come from an inner city and a lot of their skill and their success has come from resources being accessible. A lot of talent came out of the youth clubs where things were free.”“But every success is relative, right?” says Raymond. While he’s keen to note the commercial success of Cole and others, he also wants to spotlight the young person “who came to me from a youth offending team and was no question on the road to prison, or death. Now they have a job and a family. They’re not acting or working in the industry, but that’s also success to me.” For Raymond, the definition of success isn’t limiting, it’s expansive.Tartuffe (Remixed) is atMarylebone theatre, London,4 Septemberto 24 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreMark RylanceShakespeare's GlobeMolièrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tuscany’s treasured islands: five to explore | Tuscany holidays | The Guardian
description: Want to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free Giannutri
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Want to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free Giannutri
Content: Cannelle beach on Giglio.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCannelle beach on Giglio.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty ImagesTuscany holidaysTuscany’s treasured islands: five to exploreWant to avoid the crowds in Florence and Siena? Escape to these islands, from lively Elba to tiny, car-free GiannutriFrancesca LombardoSun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScattered between the Tuscan coast and Corsica, the seven islands of the Tuscan archipelago offer a striking contrast to mainland Tuscany. All are part of a protected national park, but each has its own character – some are lively, others tiny and sparsely inhabited. Montecristo and Gorgona are only accessible via strictly limited guided tours, but here’s a brief guide to the highlights of the other five.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Guardian GraphicsElba: theall-year-rounderAs Italy’s third-largest island, and with a year-round community, Elba is the archipelago’s main tourist hub, blending Napoleonic history with rugged landscapes, lively seaside towns and fine beaches. It is famous for Napoleon’s brief 1814 exile at thePalazzina dei Mulini, but its history runs much deeper, with 16th-century Medici fortifications to defend against pirate raids around the coast, and medieval hill towns, some standing on sites occupied since Roman times, inland.Beach lovers tend to divide between the white-pebble coves of Sansone and Capo Bianco near the largest town, Portoferraio, in the north, and the golden sands of Fetovaia and Cavoli in the south-west beneath Monte Capanne. Marina di Campo on the south coast is a favourite for watersports, and windsurfing and sailing schools are popular in many resorts, from Procchio in the north to Lacona in the south.View image in fullscreenThe Medici fortifications in Portoferraio on Elba.Photograph: Stevan ZZ/ShutterstockHikers can explore the 36-mile (58km)Grande Traversata Elbana,crossing the island from Cavo in the north-east to Pomonte or Patresi on the west coast, passing along mountain ridges and through traditional villages. Usually completed in three or four days, it’s best tackled in spring or autumn.Where to eat:In Portoferraio,Ristorante da Gianniis a favourite for handmade pasta, seafood and traditional cuisine. Try the house speciality, orecchiette with prawns and courgettes. In Marina di Campo,Da Pieroserves seafood-focused dishes right on the beach.Where to stay:Near Fetovaia,Hotel Montemerlo(doubles from about £88 B&B) offers a relaxed, eco-conscious stay among olive groves. In Marina di Campo,Hotel Punto Verde(doubles from about £90 B&B) is a charming family-run hotel near the beach. On the west coastHotel Gallo Nero(doubles from £79) is a family-run hotel overlooking Capo Sant’Andrea Bay. In an 18th-century building in Portoferraio’s historic centre,Indarsena(doubles from £86 B&B) is 10 minutes’ walk from several beaches.Getting there:Ferries from Piombino to Portoferraio take about an hour withToremar,MobyorBlu Navy.Giglio:the charmingisleView image in fullscreenThe village and harbour of Giglio Porto.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyAt just 21 sq km, Giglio is small but has three villages, secluded coves, an extensive coastline and a landscape of historic terraced vineyards. Access for private vehicles is heavily restricted during August, with exceptions for longer stays, which helps preserve its peaceful atmosphere, while buses and taxis link the harbour, villages and beaches, so a car-free holiday is easy.From Giglio Porto, trails lead to hidden coves and hilltop viewpoints, while the medieval lanes ofGiglio Castello, a fortified 12th-century hilltop village, are perfect for an aperitivo and an evening stroll.Beaches have distinct characters. Campese,on the north-west coast, is the largest, with reddish-gold sand and views of the 16th-century Torre del Campese. Cannelle, in the east, offers pale sand and crystalline water, while farther north, Arenella combines golden sand, granite boulders and clear water for snorkelling.Where to eat:In Giglio Porto,Ristorante Doriais a seafood favourite with a sea-view terrace (tryspaghetti alla chitarrawith sea urchin and toasted breadcrumbs). In Campese,Da Zio Meinoofferscucina povera(peasant cooking) such aspancotti di mareandspaghetti alle vongole e alla bottarga(with clams and cured mullet roe).Where to stay:On a hillside overlooking Giglio Porto,B&B La Vela(doubles from £87 B&B)is a small guesthouse with maritime-themed interiors. On a headland above Campese Bay,Le Poste di Simplicio(doubles from £100 B&B) is a family-run B&B with sweeping sea views.Getting there:ToremarorMaregiglioferries run from Porto Santo Stefano to Giglio Porto in about an hour.Capraia:a wild hikers’paradiseView image in fullscreenCapraia is best explored on foot.Photograph: Arkanto/AlamyLocated just over 20 miles (33km) north-west of Elba, Capraia is one of the archipelago’s most remote islands. Largely car-free, with few roads, it is best explored on foot along mule tracks winding between sea cliffs, hidden coves and 16th-century Genoese fortifications, although taxi boats and a bus provide limited transport.Highlights include the red rock formations ofCala Rossa, theGenoese fortress of San Giorgioand the 16th-centuryTorre dello Zenòbito.Beaches are few, but swimmers can cool off at Cala San Francesco, hike to Cala del Ceppo and Cala dello Zurletto, or take a taxi boat to Spiaggia della Mortola, one of the few sandy stretches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere to eat:In the main village, the fixed menu atIl Carabottinochanges according to what the local fishers happen to bring ashore, whileIl Pigghiolotakes a more contemporary approach, reworking island flavours in dishes such as squid parmigiana and cod croquette.Where to stay:Accommodation is limited, butLa Mandola Eco Hostel(doubles from £70 room-only) near the port is a restorative basecamp for walkers, beachgoers and divers, with a sheltered saltwater pool. In Capraia village,Il Saracino Boutique Suitesis a small, characterful retreat with sea views (doubles from £130 B&B).Getting there:The ferry from Livorno takes 1 hour 45 minutes withToremar.Pianosa:the protected isleView image in fullscreenThe harbour on Pianosa, where visitor numbers are strictly limited.Photograph: Fabiano Sodi/AlamyDaily visitor numbers to Pianosa are restricted, helping preserve the island’s fragile environment and tranquil atmosphere. You can either buy a ticket on the limited ferry service or join an authorised guided excursion.Roman remains (including early Christian catacombs) and abandoned prison buildings from when the island served as a penal colony offer glimpses of its history. And the restoredCasa dell’AgronomoandMuseo delle Scienze Geologiche e Archeologicheexplore its agricultural, geological and archaeological heritage.Guided walks, cycling and kayak excursions are among the best ways to explore. Swimming is restricted to Cala Giovanna, an easy walk from the small port and historic village, to help safeguard the marine ecosystem.Where to eat:Da Brunelloin the small harbour village is Pianosa’s only cafe/restaurant, with a focus on fresh fish and vegetables grown on the island.Where tostay:Close to the cafe and run by the same management, the island’s only accommodation,Albergo Milena(doubles from £95 half-board) offers simple rooms in a historic building.Getting there:There are authorised excursions from Elba withAcquavision(45 minutes), and limitedToremarferry services run from Piombino to Pianosa (about three hours).Giannutri:the roadless retreatView image in fullscreenA Roman column on the beach at Cala Maestra on Giannutri.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyWhile Elba hums with holidaymakers and Vespas, this tiny, car-free limestone crescent, where scent-heavymacchiaslopes into ink-blue waters, offers a radical detox from modern life.With only one restaurant-cafe, which also functions as a small grocery shop, day trippers are advised to bring their own water and lunch. Most people swim at Cala Spalmatoio and Cala Maestra, while much of the coastline forms part of a protected marine reserve renowned for its diving and snorkelling. A guided tour of aRoman villalinked to the Domitii Ahenobarbi family is a must.Where to eat:La Vela Giannutri, the island’s only dining option, focuses on seafood dishes, from tuna tartare tospaghetti alle vongole.Where to stay:Accommodation is limited to the family-runA Casa Diana(doubles from £123 B&B), with simple rooms and sea views, and a scattering of holiday rentals.Getting there:Maregiglioruns ferries from Porto Santo Stefano, or there are seasonal excursion boats (taking about an hour). In summer, Maregiglio also operates excursions andmini-cruisesbetween Giglio and Giannutri.Explore more on these topicsTuscany holidaysItaly holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make key lime pie – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: The indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy steps
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: The indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy steps
Content: Felicity Cloake's key lime pie.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's key lime pie.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make key lime pie – recipeThe indulgent, pleasantly mouth-puckering Floridian dessert in nine easy stepsFelicity CloakeSun 30 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeautiful as the Florida Keys are, with average August temperatures topping 30C and with hurricane season looming, I think I’d rather enjoy their most famous culinary export in the calm of our own more temperate isles (well, usually, at least). Cool and creamy, with a refreshingly sharp, citrus tang, this is the perfect make-ahead dessert for any bank holiday festivities.Prep20 minCook15 minChill3 hr+Serves6For the base75g butter, or coconut oil, plus extra for greasing200g digestive biscuits(about 13)1 pinch saltFor the filling4-5 limes4 egg yolks400g tin condensed milkFor the topping (optional – see steps 8 and 9)300ml whipping or double cream1 tbsp icing sugar1 A note on the biscuitsIn the States, this would involvegraham crackers, which are sweeter and more crisp than our digestive biscuits. The latter do make a decent substitute, but feel free to swap in any other biscuits you like the idea of with lime (I suspect ginger nuts would be rather good).View image in fullscreen2 Start on the pie crustHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and lightly grease a 20cm tart tin – not too shallow a one, ideally, and preferably loose-bottomed if you’re planning on taking the pie out of the tin to serve. Crush the biscuits to a fine crumb, either using a food processor or by wrapping them in a clean tea towel and whacking with a rolling pin.3 Pack the crust into the tinMelt the fat in a microwave or a small saucepan – butter is the classic choice, but I like the flavour of coconut oil here – then stir into the crumbs with a pinch of salt. Tip into the tin, use your hands to press down the mix into an even crust across the base and up the sides, then press down again with the base of a glass.4 Bake, then coolBake the crust for about 15 minutes, until it’s dry to the touch, then take out of the oven and leave to cool (though not mandatory, this step will give a crisper crust that holds together much better upon slicing, so it’s worth turning on the oven for).5 Wash and zest the limesView image in fullscreenKey limesare a distinct variety of thin-skinned, aromatic citrus that are hard to get outside the Americas. Happily, though not an exact match, this recipe works just as well with standard limes, especially if you use the zest as well as the juice. Scrub the fruit under hot water, then finely grate the zest into a large bowl.6 Juice the limesSqueeze the juice from the zested limes into a jug until you have about 120ml, straining out any pips as you go. Add the egg yolks to the zest bowl (the whites make a lovely meringue topping, if you’re looking for a way to use them up: see step 9 for a suggested recipe to replace the cream).View image in fullscreen7 Beat the egg yolks and zestBeat the yolks and zest for a couple of minutes with a whisk, electric beaters or a food mixer until the mixture thickens and turns pale green, then stir in the condensed milk. Beat in the lime juice – the mix should be shockingly tangy and sweet; chilling will mute the lime flavour, so add more juice, if you like – then pour the filling into the cooled biscuit shell.8 Chill, then top with creamChill for at least three hours, until set. If you’re planning on topping your pie with cream, whisk this and the sugar in a large bowl until the mix holds soft peaks, then dollop on top of the set filling. Garnish with extra slices of lime, if you have them, or some grated lime zest, and serve.View image in fullscreen9 … or top with meringueIf you prefer a meringue topping (and to use up some excess egg whites into the bargain) – for the sweet toothed only! – whisk two of the egg whites to soft peaks, then beat in 115g sugar a tablespoon at a time, until the mix is glossy and holds its shape. Beat in half a teaspoon of vinegar or lime/lemon juice, then spoon on top the pie. Brown briefly with a blowtorch or under a hot grill before serving.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassAmerican food and drinkDessertBakingFruitEggsCakefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for ages
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for ages
Content: Kismet, London SE1: ‘Soothing, filling and hearty.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKismet, London SE1: ‘Soothing, filling and hearty.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewKismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant reviewThe first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for agesGrace DentSun 30 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleATurkish-Cypriotmeyhane, which translates roughly as “wine house”, has slotted in upstairs atthe Globe Tavern in Borough Market, south London. Any cab driver worth his salt will bend your ear over the fact that this is “where Bridget Jones lives”, which might be a bit confusing if you’ve booked in to eatkuzu şiş(lamb neck kebabs) and to knock back a couple of rakis with a fermented turnip juice chaser.ThatBridget Jonestrivia, by the way, is completely true: the upstairs space at the Globe was used as the heroine’s gaff in that famous film franchise. Now, however, when you climb the staircase up toKismet, an old, slightly eerie and flickering TV by the restaurant entrance begins to tell a very different tale. This is chefKeiran Mustafa’s very personal tribute to his family’s homeland and the community they built in London. Mustafa was the opening head chef at BiBi,to my mind one of the best restaurants in London, and before that he worked at industry stalwartsChez Bruceandthe Harwood Arms.View image in fullscreen‘One of the best things being served anywhere at Borough Market right now’: Kismet’satom(strained yoghurt) with chilli butter.Mustafa’s partner in this new venture isDom Hamdy, the smart-cookie restaurateur behindCrispin,Bistro FreddieandCanal. The result is structured and very chic bedlam that’s lovable and edgy in equal measure. On a midweek lunchtime not long after opening, chaotic Turkish jazz gives way to Turkish techno on the speakers as the grill in the open kitchen roars and glasses of Karmen’s Diren white wine at £8 a pop slide down rather too easily for the lunchtime crowd. Mustafa tells us that our table is where the weekly live music sets up. I haven’t sat that close to a PA since I was on a cross-channel ferry eating chips beside the bingo caller, and I’m sure that Kismet in full swing will be just as choppy.The dining space is split into two rooms, all dark wood and white tablecloths, with lace over the windows and walls the colour of a 70-a-day Rothmans smoker’s lounge. Those walls are also festooned with Mustafa’s childhood photos, including one of his mum as a waitress in a long-gone restaurant.The menu, meanwhile, is soothing, filling and hearty, with all manner of Turkish favourites. There’sgirit ezme, or white cheese with walnut, dill and mint, andsigara boregi(feta rolled up inyufkapastry and deep-fried). There’s a grill, too, of course, blasting out the fragrant smells of beef and lambköfteandtavuk şiş(chicken thigh kebab). The cooking leans heavily, if not decadently, on lashings of strained yoghurt, chilli butter, good olive oil and tahini – six of the nine cold meze are built on one or other of them. But don’t expect a great deal of spicy heat because this is more about comfort and coddling. Kick back with a basket of warm, pillowy bread that’s begging to be pulled through someatom(strained yoghurt) in a red pool of chilli butter.View image in fullscreen‘Properly great’: Kismet’s grilled monkfish with yoghurt and chilli butter.In fact, that very humble-sounding atom with bread might well be one of the best things being served anywhere in Borough Market right now. I ate two whole baskets to myself, which finally killed off my ambition to be Victoria’s Secret’s most elderly thong model. Damn it, give me warm carbs. We ate monkfish straight off the mangal, which at £30 is the most expensive dish on the menu (the meze start at £6). To begin with, I was a little concerned that we’d never finish it and it would be a huge waste of fish, but no, it’s properly great: expertly grilled, succulent, and served with yet more yoghurt and chilli butter. The lamb neckkuzu şişwas likewise incredibly juicy, and we ate it with hand-cut fried potatoes that were unmistakably shallow-fried – proper staying-at-your-gran’s-house chips. Braised green beans were soft but fibrous, beautifully seasoned and the sort of beans that make you want to sell your house and move to the sun whenever you’re on holiday. A £14 plate of fried liver with onion salad lent some iron to proceedings, with a side of velvety and not-remotely bitter braised swiss chard.View image in fullscreenKismet’s baklava is ‘glossy and teeth-chatteringly sweet’, just as it should be.Over tiny glasses of tea and glossy, teeth-chatteringly sweet pistachio baklava, we picked at a pistachio ice-cream that was much, much less sweet than the pastries, and therefore balanced them beautifully. You must order both, and we asked for the bill without an ounce of regret for our overindulgence.Kismet will not make my confused definition of a meyhane any easier, nor will the Turkish-Cypriot community be in full agreement over whether it’s at all like one in Istanbul, either. What’s undeniable, however, is that Mustafa and Hamdy have come up with something that’s unique in its own right: the first genuinely cool, weird thing to have happened in Borough for ages. They’re only signed up to be here for a year, so go before that telly gets turned off.KismetUpstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London SE1 (no phone). Open lunch Weds-Sun noon-2.30pm (3pm Sun); dinner Tues-Sat 5-10pm (9.30pm Tues & Weds).
